# MitCad document API

The application and `mitcad-cli` drive a document only through JSON:
`Document::command`, `query`, `preview`, `run_script` and `report`
(`core/model-api/src/lib.rs`, exposed to C++ by `core/ffi/src/lib.rs`).
Geometry comes back as `Shape` handles (`body_shape`, `profile_shape`,
`preview_body_shape`, `preview_tool_shape`), so a new command needs no
change to the C++ bridge. A rejected command or query raises an error
(`rust::Error` in C++) with a message for the user and leaves the document
unchanged. The model's design (recompute, caches, file format, threads) is
in [docs/architecture.md](../../../docs/architecture.md).

## Identities and names

| What | Form | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| feature | `"F7"` | assigned when created and saved in the design file; its timeline position is separate |
| body | `"F7.b0"` | the creating feature and a number; its display name (`Body1`) is separate and can be renamed |
| component, occurrence | `"C2"`, `"O3"` | `C0` is the root component; names `Plate` and `Plate:2` are separate (see [Components and occurrences](#components-and-occurrences)) |
| sketch point, curve | `"p4"`, `"c3"` | one id space per sketch; `sketch.add_rectangle` makes lines `c<k>`..`c<k+3>` (line i from corner i to i + 1, corners counter-clockwise from the anchor) and then their corner points, a circle a curve and its centre |
| sketch constraint, dimension | `"k2"` | one id space per sketch |
| sketch text | `"t5"` | numbered with the points and curves |
| glyph contour of a text | `"t5.g2.c1"` | contour 1 of character 2 (spaces and line breaks counted) of text t5; usable wherever a curve id can stand in a name (`r{t5.g2.c0}`, `F3:side(t5.g2.c0)#1`, `#k` numbering the contour's pieces) |
| profile region | `"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"` | the sorted segments of its outer boundary; a circle alone is `"r{c5}"`; an end where several curves meet is `c2+c5`, a free end `-` |
| face | `"F3:side(c1[c4,c2])"`, `"F3:end(r{…})#1"` | named by the feature that made it; each feature type lists its face names below; `#k` numbers the pieces of a split face |
| edge | `"E{<face>\|<face>}"` | the two faces that meet there, sorted by text; `#k` when several edges lie between the same faces |
| vertex | `"V{<face>\|<face>\|…}"` | the faces that meet there, sorted |

The grammar is in `core/model-base/src/topo.rs`. A reference without `#k`
means every piece: `"E{F2:end(…)|F2:side(c1[c4,c2])}"` rounds both halves
of an edge a cut divided. A segment `c3[c2,c4]` is the piece of curve c3
between the curves c2 and c4, in the curve's own direction.

### Faces, edges and vertices a sketch change renamed

A side face is named by its segment, so a sketch edit that gives the
segment another neighbour renames the face although it is the same face:
deleting the arc `c72` at a corner and adding the circle `c103` there
turns `F31:side(c71[c104,c72])` into `F31:side(c71[c104,c103])`. Features
find such faces, edges and vertices again (mitcad#272,
`core/model/src/features/renamed.rs`), wherever they resolve a name on a
body: fillet and chamfer edges, faces and reference faces, the faces of
shell, draft, offset, delete, replace and split face, tools and targets
on faces, extents to faces, sketch planes and projections, hole
placements, threads, loft sections, sweep guide surfaces and paths of
edges, patterns of faces, construction geometry, alignments, joints and
assembly constraints:

1. A name that finds what it names is used as it is.
2. A face name that finds no face finds the faces of the same feature and
   role whose key has the most curves in common with it: a side face's
   segment must have the same own curve (then the most end curves, those
   at the same end first), a region key the most shared curves; names in
   keys (a fillet's edge, a shell's face) compare the same way. A
   reference takes the best match only when it is the only one (the
   pieces `#k` of one face count once); a tie fails with the candidates:
   `F31:side(c71[c104,c72]) is ambiguous after a sketch change:
   F31:side(c71[c103,c72]), F31:side(c71[c104,c103])`.
3. An edge name `E{A|B}` that finds no edge finds A and B each by rule 2
   and takes the edges between the faces found: one with `#k`, all
   without. Of tied faces only those that meet the other face count;
   several edges so found fail as a tie does.
4. A vertex finds each of its faces by rule 2.
5. A name with nothing like it fails as before (`the body has no face …`).

The feature keeps the name it was given (undo and the comparison of
versions see no change) and succeeds with a warning (`timeline` status
`warning`, the feature's `warnings`), shown in the timeline and the
browser as other warnings: `edge E{…c72…} found as E{…c103…} after a
change in Sketch10` (the sketch of the profiles of the feature that made
the face). Profile regions and face appearances follow the same rule
([Profile references after a sketch change](#profile-references-after-a-sketch-change),
[Appearances of faces](#appearances-of-faces)).

## Values

Every length or angle of a definition is a parameter. In commands a value
is a parameter name (`"d3"`), a number in millimetres or radians, or an
expression (`"d1 / 2 + 5 mm"`, `"30 deg"`; syntax and unit rules in
`core/expr/src/lib.rs`).

- A number or an expression creates a dimension parameter owned by the
  feature (the next free `d<n>`, with a comment like `Extrude1
  distance`). Editing a feature with a number or an expression in a slot
  whose parameter the feature owns changes that parameter instead.
- New dimension parameters show lengths in the document's length unit
  (`set_units`) and angles in degrees. A slot whose name ends in `angle`
  (`size.angle`, `extent.angle`, `dimensions[k3].angle`) is an angle,
  every other slot a length unless it is one of the unitless slots below.
  A slot refuses a parameter of another kind; a unitless parameter's
  number is used as it is.
- **Unitless slots** (counts, factors, fractions; mitcad#662): a number or
  an expression there makes a unitless parameter (`3`, never `3 mm`), in
  every document unit:
  - counts: a pattern's `quantity` (rectangular `direction1.quantity`
    and `direction2.quantity`, circular, path and scale patterns), a
    pattern's or mirror's `scale_groups` and `scale_copies` and
    `scales[i].groups` and `scales[i].copies`, a gear's `teeth` and
    `mate_teeth`, a pulley's `teeth` and `set_screws.count`, a printable
    bearing's `element_count`, a boss's `ribs`;
  - factors: a pattern's or mirror's `scale` and `scales[i].scale`, a
    scale's `scale.factor`, `scale.x`, `scale.y` and `scale.z`, a
    sweep's `end_scale`, a motion link's `coupling.ratio`, a gear's
    `profile_shift`, a sheet's `allowance.k`;
  - fractions, ratios and weights: a construction plane's or point's
    position along a path without `physical` (`definition.fraction`; with
    `physical` it is the length `definition.distance`), `extent.fraction`
    and every other slot whose name starts with `fraction`, a helix's
    `revolutions`, slots ending in `weight` (`tangency_weight`).

  An expression there that gives a length or an angle is refused with
  what to write instead: `d1 / 3` gives "the result is a length (5 mm);
  for a count write `d1 / 3 mm`". A count that is not a whole number is an
  error, never rounded, and says to use `floor(…)` or `round(…)`.
  Designs saved before keep these parameters in a length unit, whose value
  in millimetres the slot read as its number. On load, a slot's own
  parameter that only unitless slots of its feature use, that no other
  parameter refers to and that no configuration sets becomes unitless with
  that number (its expression stays when it gives the same number without
  a unit, else the number replaces it, with a load warning when the
  expression named parameters). Any other parameter there (a user
  parameter in a length unit) keeps its unit with a load warning; the slot
  reads its number as before and keeps it on edits until it is changed.
- Parameters a feature owns are deleted with it, unless another feature
  or parameter still uses them (they then become user parameters).
- Decimal point or comma: `"1,5 mm"` is `"1.5 mm"`. A comma directly
  between two digits is a decimal comma (also `,5` and `5,`); any other
  comma separates function arguments (`max(a, b)`, `max(1, 5)`), and `;`
  always does. `max(1,5)` is therefore `max(1.5)`, and its error says to
  write `max(1; 5)`. No thousands separators: `1,000` is 1 and `1 000` an
  error. Parameters keep their expressions with decimal points, in the
  design file and in the `parameters` query.
- `name = expression` in a slot (`"width = 40"`, `"width = d1 * 2"`)
  names the slot's parameter as it sets it, in the same command and undo
  step (mitcad#231): the parameter the feature owns there (or the one the
  slot uses, when it already has that name) is renamed and takes the
  expression; without one, a new dimension parameter of that name is
  made. A name another parameter has, or an invalid name, rejects the
  command. A single `=` after a word is this form; expressions compare
  with `==`. Renames by any command keep configurations in step.
- A driven sketch dimension has a read-only **reference parameter**
  (mitcad#231): the next free `d<n>`, commented `Sketch1 length (driven)`,
  kind `reference` in the `parameters` query, owned by the sketch. Its
  value is what the dimension measures, set each time the sketch solves;
  its expression is that value as a number. It can be renamed and used in
  expressions; `set_parameter` with a value, an expression or a unit is
  refused. `sketch.set_dimension` on the dimension makes it driving, and
  the reference becomes its model parameter under the same name;
  `sketch.set_driven` makes a driving dimension's own parameter its
  reference, keeping the name.
- A reference's value is known only after its sketch: only features after
  the sketch in the timeline may use it, directly or through other
  parameters' expressions. A use by the sketch itself, by a feature before
  it, or by a parameter such a feature uses rejects the command with an
  error naming the reference, its dimension and the sketch; so does a
  `reorder_feature` that would make one (`can_reorder` tells). A
  parameter no feature uses may use it.
- Deleting a driven dimension deletes its reference unless a parameter or
  a feature still uses it; deleting its sketch likewise. A reference still
  used becomes a user parameter with its last value as a fixed number.
- A driven dimension's `reference` in a sketch definition (`add_feature`,
  `edit_feature`: `{"type": "length", "line": "c1", "driven": true,
  "reference": "height"}`) names its reference parameter (mitcad#250): the
  sketch's own reference keeps it; a user parameter becomes the sketch's
  reference (its expression its value until the sketch measures it, the
  reference's comment when it had none), and the ordering rule above
  applies to its uses; anything else is left alone and the dimension gets
  the next free `d<n>`. The .f3d, .ipt and FreeCAD imports give a driven
  dimension the source file's parameter of it this way (a named FreeCAD
  reference constraint's, where the dimension measures the constraint's
  value), and add the sketch without these references when the model
  refuses one.
- **An angle of more than one turn where one turn is the most**
  (mitcad#714) warns: a move's or move face's rotation
  (`transform.angle`), a revolve's angles, a draft's, a chamfer's angle,
  an extrusion's tapers, a hole's taper, countersink and tip angles and a
  construction plane's angle. A JSON number there is radians, so
  `"angle": 90` meant as degrees turns by 5156.6°; the feature succeeds
  with the warning `Move1 angle: 90 is read as radians (5156.6°); write
  "90 deg" for degrees` (in its `warnings`, the timeline's `error`, and
  the `add_feature` or `edit_feature` result's `warnings`), or a failed
  feature's error ends with it. A value that is not a short number in
  radians (`"720 deg"`) says `Revolve1 angle: 720° is more than one turn`.
  Helices, coils, a sweep's twist and other slots that take several turns
  never warn (`parameters::one_turn_slot`, `recompute::turn_warnings`).
- Parameters are evaluated in dependency order. Cycles, unknown names,
  syntax errors and unit mismatches reject the command. Renaming a
  parameter rewrites the expressions that use it (features refer to
  parameters by id).
- A parameter change recomputes only the features whose inputs changed
  value; a parameter command that changes no value (a rename, a comment,
  an equivalent expression) recomputes nothing.

Defaults are metric ([docs/architecture.md](../../../docs/architecture.md#units)):
leaving out a unit means millimetres (degrees for angles). A new document
and a design file without `units` are in mm and degrees, and bare numbers
in expressions take the document's unit. `export` writes STEP and IGES in
mm (`unit`), `import_file` reads STL and OBJ in mm (`unit_mm` 1),
`sketch.import_dxf` reads a drawing that names no unit in mm; a file's own
units (STEP, IGES, a DXF's `$INSUNITS`, an .f3d design's) are kept. A
`thread` or tapped `hole` without a `standard` is ISO metric. Densities
are g/cm³ (steel, 7.85, without a material), masses kg, moments of inertia
kg mm². Tests: `api::metric_defaults_tests`, `tools/ui-units-test.sh`.

### Formulas in the style of spreadsheets

Expressions also take the syntax and functions of spreadsheet formulas
(mitcad#663), as a superset: every expression that parsed before parses
and evaluates the same. The full rules are in `core/expr/src/lib.rs`
(grammar, rules 13 to 22); tests `core/expr/src/tests.rs`.

- Function names and `PI` are case-insensitive (`FLOOR`, `Floor`,
  `floor`; `pi`); parameter names, units and `E` are not. A parameter
  name that is a function or `PI` in any case (`Max`, `pi`, `Sum`) is
  reserved: `add_parameter` and `rename_parameter` refuse it, and a design
  file or an import with such a parameter renames it (`Max_1`, a load
  warning or an import report row) and rewrites the expressions,
  configuration rows and features that use it.
- Inside parentheses a single `=` compares (`if(GridX = 6; a; b)`), the
  same as `==`. At the top level of a slot, `name = expression` still
  names the slot's parameter.
- Rounding: `round(x; [digits])`, `roundup`, `rounddown`, `trunc(x;
  [digits])`, `int(x)`; to a step `floor(x; [step])`, `ceiling(x; [step])`
  (and `ceil`), `mround(x; step)`: `floor(d1; 0.5 mm)`. Digits count in
  the default unit of the value's dimension; a step has the value's
  dimension and the result keeps it. `round`, `floor` and `ceil` with one
  argument are unchanged.
- Integers: `mod(a; b)` (sign of `b`; `%` stays the remainder with the
  sign of `a`), `quotient(a; b)`, `even(x)`, `odd(x)`. Aggregates: `sum`,
  `average`, `median` (one dimension), `product` (dimensions multiply).
  `clamp(x; low; high)`.
- Choice: `ifs(c1; v1; ...)`, `switch(x; k1; v1; ...; [default])`,
  `choose(i; v1; ...)`, `iferror(x; fallback)` (division by zero, a value
  out of range, no match; not unknown names or unit errors).
- `let(name1; value1; ...; result)`: names local to the formula, not
  parameter references (a parameter's `dependencies` do not list them);
  a name may not be a parameter's.
- `value(x; "mm")`: the number of `x` in the unit, unitless (15 for
  `d1` = 15 mm). Quoted text is accepted only there.
- `radians(x)`, `degrees(x)`: an angle from a plain number in degrees or
  radians, so `sin(radians(30))` is 0.5. `PI()` is `PI`.
- Texts in quotes, `&`, `concat`, `text`, `left`, `right` and `len`
  (mitcad#664): see [Text parameters](#text-parameters). A text is never
  a number: a slot that takes a number refuses one.

## References to geometry

Every feature or query that takes a plane, an axis, a point, a face, a
body or sketch curves takes it in one form (`GeomRef`,
`core/model/src/features/geom_ref.rs`):

| JSON | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"xy"`, `"xz"`, `"yz"` | origin planes; frames XY: x = +X, y = +Y; XZ: x = +X, y = -Z (normal +Y); YZ: x = -Z, y = +Y (normal +X) |
| `"x"`, `"y"`, `"z"`, `"origin"` | origin axes and point |
| `"F5"` | the datum (plane, axis or point) of construction feature F5 |
| `{"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(r{c5})"}` | a face; a plane when planar (outward normal), an axis when a cylinder, cone or torus |
| `{"body": "F2.b0", "edge": "E{…\|…}"}` | an edge; an axis (straight: along the edge's curve; circular: through the centre) or a point (a circle's centre, a line's middle) |
| `{"body": "F2.b0", "vertex": "V{…\|…\|…}"}` | a vertex; a point |
| `{"body": "F2.b0"}` | a body (a face feature's tool) |
| `{"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c4"}` | a sketch curve; a line is an axis from its start to its end, a circle or an arc (where an axis is wanted: pattern, align, move) the axis through its centre normal to the sketch. `"curves": ["c1", "c3"]` several, neither all (a face feature's tool) |
| `{"sketch": "F1", "point": "p3"}` | a sketch point |
| `{"origin": [x, y, z], "normal": [x, y, z], "x_axis": [x, y, z]}` | a fixed plane (`x_axis` optional) |
| `{"origin": [x, y, z], "direction": [x, y, z]}` | a fixed axis |
| `{"point": [x, y, z]}` | a fixed point |

- Frames: an origin plane has the frame above. A planar face and a fixed
  plane without `x_axis` have the model origin projected onto the plane
  as origin and the model X axis projected as x axis (Y when the plane
  faces ±X), with the face's outward normal; sketches on faces, mirror
  planes, primitives and extents to faces all use it.
- The axes of cylinders, cones, tori and circular edges point along their
  largest component (+Z for a hole along Z).
- A face name may name the pieces of a split face when they lie on one
  surface; an edge or vertex name must name one (`#k`).
- Older files' forms with a `"type"` (`{"type": "origin_plane", "plane":
  "yz", "offset": d}`, `{"type": "origin", …}`, `{"type": "plane" | "face"
  | "edge" | "vertex" | "construction" | "fixed" | "sketch_curve" | "line"
  | "body" | "sketch", …}`; a face without `body` means the feature's own
  body) are read and saved in the forms above.

### Paths

A path (of a sweep, a pipe or a path pattern, a sweep's guide rail, a
loft's centre line or rails, a rib's or web's curves, a construction
plane or point along a path) is a `PathRef`:

| JSON | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c4"]}` | curves of a sketch (any order), joined end to end |
| `{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"], "chain": true}` | also every curve joined to them end to end (construction curves only when listed) |
| `{"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c1"}` | one curve; a circle starts at its `start_angle` (the sketch x axis by default) and runs counter-clockwise |
| `{"body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{…}", …]}` | connected edges of a body, in order; each name must name one edge |
| `{"start": [x, y, z], "end": [x, y, z]}` | a fixed line |
| `{"helix": {"center": [x, y, z], "axis": [x, y, z], "x_axis": [x, y, z], "radius": r, "pitch": p, "start_angle": a, "end_angle": b}}` | a fixed helix (mitcad#385): the points `center + r (cos t x + sin t (axis × x)) + p t / 2π axis` (`x` is `x_axis` made square to the axis) for `t` from `start_angle` to `end_angle` (radians, either way round: the path runs from the first to the second); `p`, the rise per turn counter-clockwise about the axis, is negative for a left-handed helix |
| `{"fixed_curves": [{"type": "line", "start": [x, y, z], "end": [x, y, z]}, {"type": "conic", "center", "normal", "x_axis", "major", "minor", "start", "end", "closed"}, {"type": "spline", "degree": d, "poles": [[x, y, z], …], "weights": [w, …], "knots": [k, …]}]}` | fixed curves in model space, joined end to end (mitcad#548): lines, circle or ellipse arcs (`center + major cos t x_axis + minor sin t (normal × x_axis)` for `t` from `start` to `end`), B-splines (`weights` left out: not rational; the full knot vector, `poles + degree + 1` knots, never decreasing); the FreeCAD import's edges that lie in no plane, a conical helix as its file stores it. Not a construction plane's or point's path, nor a path pattern's |

A path runs from the free end of the first listed curve or edge when it
ends the chain, else along the first listed curve's own direction (a
closed chain from that curve's start). A path may not branch or have
gaps; a closed curve is a path by itself. A path pattern's path is a
sketch line, arc or circle, a chain of sketch lines and arcs (`{"sketch":
"F1", "curves": ["c1", "c2"]}`, mitcad#464), or a fixed line (not edges).

## Feature definitions

The `def` of `add_feature`, `edit_feature` and `preview`, and the `def`
the `feature` query returns. Design files store the same fields with
parameter names. Each type is a module `core/model/src/features/<type>.rs`.
Lengths in millimetres, angles in radians; every length, angle, quantity,
fraction and factor is a value ([Values](#values)).

Shared rules:

- `operation`: `new_body`, `join`, `cut`, `intersect`, or `new_component`
  (new bodies in a new component placed in the feature's component, see
  [Components and occurrences](#components-and-occurrences));
  `participants`: the bodies a join, cut or intersection works on (all
  bodies when empty or left out). Their results are described under
  [extrude](#extrude); "as for extrude" elsewhere means the same.
- A feature that asks for something the geometry kernel cannot do fails
  with a message starting `unsupported: ` (`mitcad_model::features::UNSUPPORTED`);
  the .f3d importer then falls back to the body the file stores.
- A face or edge that a later edit removed is explained (`face X no
  longer exists after Fillet2`, `... does not exist because Fillet1 is
  suppressed`).
- A feature an importer left a note on (a fallback, a partial item) is
  `warning` too, and a placeholder of an item the file had suppressed or
  failed is suppressed with that note ([The import's outcomes on the
  timeline](#the-imports-outcomes-on-the-timeline)).
- A feature that succeeds with a caveat has warnings (`timeline` status
  `warning`): a fillet or chamfer built 0.1 % smaller than asked (at the
  exact size it takes a face away, which OCCT cannot build) or built as
  rings about its circles ([fillet](#fillet)), a sketch
  text whose font is not installed. Evaluators call `EvalContext::warn`;
  `Kernel::notes` gives what the geometry gave up
  (`geometry::Shape::notes`).

### sketch

```json
{"type": "sketch", "plane": "xy",
 "entities": [
   {"id": "c1", "type": "line", "start": "p2", "end": "p3"},
   {"id": "p2", "type": "point", "at": [0, 0], "fixed": true},
   {"id": "p3", "type": "point", "at": [60, 0]},
   {"id": "c4", "type": "circle", "center": "p5", "radius": 5},
   {"id": "p5", "type": "point", "at": [45, 20]}],
 "constraints": [{"id": "k1", "type": "horizontal", "line": "c1"}],
 "dimensions": [{"id": "k2", "type": "length", "line": "c1", "value": 60},
                {"id": "k3", "type": "diameter", "curve": "c4", "driven": true}]}
```

Code in `core/sketch/`. Coordinates are sketch plane
millimetres, angles radians. Build sketches with the
[sketch commands](#sketch-commands), which pick the ids.

- `plane`: `"xy"` (default), `"xz"`, `"yz"` (the origin datums' frames), a
  construction plane feature before the sketch (`"F5"`), or a planar face
  `{"face": "<face name>", "body": "F2.b0"}` (`body` optional) of the
  bodies before the sketch (frame as in [References to
  geometry](#references-to-geometry)).
- `plane_link` (optional): `{"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}` when the
  plane is another component's ([Geometry of other
  components](#geometry-of-other-components)); `projections` may have a
  `link` of the same form.
- `frame` (optional): the sketch's own frame in the plane's frame,
  `{"origin": [x, y, z], "x_axis": [..], "y_axis": [..]}` in the plane
  frame's (x, y, normal) coordinates; imports keep a file's exact sketch
  transform this way, and Create Sketch stores an upright frame this way
  (`sketch.create` with `upright`, below).
- `placement` (optional): where the sketch lies on its plane after the own
  frame, `{"offset": .., "x": .., "y": .., "angle": .., "flip": true}`,
  each value optional (see [Redefine Sketch Plane](#redefine-sketch-plane)).
- `entities`: points `p<n>` and curves `c<n>` in one id space. Curves
  refer to points, and curves that share a point are joined there: `line`
  (`start`, `end`, `centerline`), `circle` (`center`, `radius`, and `start_angle`, in radians, where the circle starts: the seam of a cylinder made from it; default 0, the sketch x axis; an import sets it), `arc`
  (`center`, `start`, `end`, counter-clockwise), `ellipse` (`center`,
  `major`: the end point of the major axis, `minor_radius`),
  `elliptical_arc` (also `start`, `end`), `spline` (`degree`, `control`
  points, optional `weights` and `knots`; default clamped uniform on
  [0, 1]) and `fitted_spline` (`points`: a cubic through them; `closed`:
  it runs on from the last point back to the first, listed once, and is
  smooth (C2) through it: one closed curve without ends, at least three
  points; mitcad#783). Flags:
  `construction` (not in profiles), `fixed`, `reference` (projected),
  `axis` (`"x"` or `"y"`: the line that stands for a sketch axis and its
  far end, see [The sketch's axes and origin as
  entities](#the-sketchs-axes-and-origin-as-entities)).
  Positions and radii are the last solved ones and the start of the next
  solve; a new definition may give any reasonable positions.
- `constraints` (`k<n>`, shared with dimensions): `coincident` (`point`,
  `entity`: a point or a curve; `sketch.add_constraint` merges two curve
  ends instead, see [Points that become one](#points-that-become-one)),
  `horizontal`/`vertical` (`line`),
  `horizontal_points`/`vertical_points` (`a`, `b` points), `parallel`,
  `perpendicular`, `collinear`, `tangent`, `smooth` (G2), `equal` (lines; circles and arcs;
  ellipses by their minor radius); `tangent` and `smooth` take an optional
  `at` (a point, mitcad#783): the end of each curve at that point (joined
  to it, else the nearer end), so that a curve can be tangent at both ends,
  to different curves or to the same one; with `a` and `b` the same open
  spline whose ends are both `at`, the spline is smooth where it closes.
  Without `at` (older designs), at the point the curves share or their
  nearest ends,
  `concentric` (`a`, `b` curves), `midpoint` (`point`, `curve`),
  `symmetric` (`a`, `b`: points or curves, `axis`: a line; `radii`, two
  circles or arcs only, default true: their radii are made equal too,
  see [Symmetry of circles with fixed radii](#symmetry-of-circles-with-fixed-radii)),
  `equal_spacing` (`anchors`, `mode`, `direction`; see [Equal spacing in
  sketches](#equal-spacing-in-sketches)).
- `dimensions`: `distance`, `horizontal_distance`, `vertical_distance`
  (`a`, `b` points, and optional `signed`; see [Signed point
  dimensions](#signed-point-dimensions)), `point_line_distance` (`point`, `line`),
  `line_distance` (`a`, `b` parallel lines), `tangent_distance` (`circle`
  or arc, `line`: the gap between them, the centre's distance from the
  line minus the radius),
  `concentric_distance` (`a`, `b` circles or arcs about one centre: the gap
  between them, the difference of their radii; mitcad#445), `length` (`line`), `angle`
  (`a`, `b` lines, and optional `reverse_a`, `reverse_b`; see [Angle
  dimensions](#angle-dimensions)), `radius`,
  `diameter` (`curve`), `arc_length` (`arc`), `major_radius`,
  `minor_radius` (`ellipse`), `linear_diameter` (`axis`, `entity`),
  `spacing` (`constraint`: an equal spacing's common spacing). A
  driving dimension has a `value` (slot `dimensions[k3].<type>`, so
  `angle` is an angle and the others lengths); a driven one has `"driven":
  true` and only measures, with its reference parameter's
  name in `reference` (see [Values](#values)); a file without it gets one
  when it is read. `text`: where the value is shown.
- Constraints and dimensions alike may be inactive: `"active": false`,
  with an optional `inactive_reason` text; the solve leaves them out (see
  [Inactive constraints and
  dimensions](#inactive-constraints-and-dimensions)). Written only when
  false.
- `projections`: linked projections, `{"source": "<edge, face or
  vertex>", "body": "F2.b0", "entities": ["p7", "p8", "c9", …]}`; the entities
  follow the source when the model changes (`sketch.project`). The stored
  positions are those of the last edit of the sketch; the evaluation moves
  them (in steps, so that geometry constrained to them keeps its side), the
  `sketch` query shows them moved and the next edit stores them. The
  entities are listed as `sketch.project` makes them, each curve after
  its points (a line's start and end in the source's direction, an arc's
  centre, start and end); a circle keeps its `start_angle` (an import's
  seam) when it follows. Each entity follows the source's current curve
  of its kind most like it (its points and sizes; in the order the kernel
  lists them when that is as good), so a projection may hold only some of
  its source's curves (mitcad#232); an entity that finds none keeps its
  last geometry and the sketch has a warning (as does a projection whose
  source is gone). An entity the same as another of its projection follows
  the same curve. `"section": true` marks section curves: where the
  sketch's plane cuts the source face, or the points where it crosses
  the source edge (mitcad#736; [Section curves in
  sketches](#section-curves-in-sketches)). `"chain": ["E{…}", …]` (an
  import's, mitcad#389): the edges the source edge continues into, in
  order; the entities are one curve, the projection of the edges joined
  end to end into one B-spline (exactly, a line raised to the splines'
  degree; a curve the model splits into pieces, such as a thread's helix
  of an edge per turn). A piece gone, or pieces that no longer meet
  within 1e-4 mm, lose the source.
- `texts`: `{"id": "t9", "text": "…", "at": [x, y], "height": h,
  "angle": a, "font": "…", "bold": false, "italic": false}`, optional
  `align` (`left`, `center`, `right`), `valign` (`baseline`, `bottom`,
  `middle`, `top`), `spacing` (extra character spacing, % of the height),
  `frame` (three point ids: a corner and its neighbours along the text's
  x and y, the corners of a construction rectangle the text fills; `at`
  and `angle` follow it), `path` (`{"curve": "c4", "above": true, "fit":
  false}`: the text runs along the curve, fitted to its length when
  `fit`), `flip_x`, `flip_y`, `cap_height` (`height` is the capital letters' height, measured at the top of an A; a frame aligns the first line's capitals to its top and the last baseline to its bottom, a line aligns by its outlines, and lines are one ascender plus descender apart) and `wrap` (a text in a frame breaks its lines at spaces to the frame's width); the `.f3d` import sets both. `line_spacing` (mm from one baseline to the next; 0, the default, for the font's), `pen_align` (lines align by their pens, from the first pen to the end of the last advance, also with `cap_height`) and `ink_top` (the top of the lines, a frame's top or `valign` top or middle, is the first line's highest outline point instead of the capitals' top or the ascender); the `.ipt` import sets all three (mitcad#414). Multi-line text breaks at `\n`. Each glyph
  contour (`t9.g<k>.c<j>`, from the font's outlines through the kernel's
  `font_glyphs`; the bundled Droid Sans when the font is missing) bounds
  profile regions like a closed curve: a letter is a region with its
  counters as holes, a counter a region of its own.
  `glyphs` (mitcad#416): the outlines a file stores for the text's
  characters, `{"text": "…", "font": "…", "bold": false, "italic": false,
  "glyphs": [{"advance": a, "contours": [[piece, …], …]}, …]}`, one per
  character of `text` (newlines included), each piece the control points
  of a line or a quadratic or cubic Bézier curve (`[[x, y], …]`, two to
  four), each piece starting where the one before it ends; lengths in
  units of the text's `height`, from the character's pen on the baseline,
  y up; `advance` to the next character's pen. While the text's font is
  not installed and its `text`, `font`, `bold` and `italic` are still
  those of its `glyphs`, these outlines and advances take the place of
  the substitute font's: the text is laid out from them with all its
  options (height, frame, alignment, spacing, flips, path), so moving or
  resizing its frame, a new height or alignment keep the file's shapes,
  and the sketch has no font warning. The vertical metrics a file does
  not store (the ascender and descender, the font's line spacing) stay
  the substitute font's, relative to its capitals with `cap_height`. On a
  computer with the font the font is used. A new string, font or style
  (`sketch.edit_text`) drops `glyphs`: the text is laid out in its font,
  or in Droid Sans with the warning. The `.ipt` import sets it from the
  glyph contours the file keeps; `.f3d` files keep none.
  `glyphs` may also hold the font's vertical metrics in the same units,
  `ascender`, `descender` and `line_spacing`; then they are used instead
  of the substitute font's.
  `font_file` (mitcad#473, `sketch/fonts.rs`): `{"path": "…/Font.ttf",
  "index": 0, "licence": "…"}`, the font file the text's font comes from
  instead of an installed font (`.ttf`, `.otf`, a collection `.ttc` with
  the face `index`, `.woff` or `.woff2`), and what the file's name table
  says of its copyright and licence. `font` is then the file's family, and
  the text's `glyphs` (with the metrics) are the file's outlines of the
  text, stored when the file is chosen and whenever the string or the
  style changes: while they fit the text, the text is laid out from them
  and the file is not read, so the design is the same on every computer
  (`stored_outlines` is true). Outlines that do not fit are read from the
  file again only when the file was chosen in this session (`font_file`
  of `sketch.add_text` or `sketch.edit_text`); a file that is not there
  then fails the sketch with "choose the font file again". A path that
  came with a design file (opened, or a definition given as JSON) is never
  read (mitcad#929): without fitting outlines the sketch fails with "the
  text has no outlines stored for its font file …; choose the font file
  again", and a new string or style of `sketch.edit_text` without
  `font_file` is refused the same way, so a design cannot make the
  application read a file it names. The model reads the file itself (`skrifa`; `wuff`
  decodes WOFF and WOFF2), not through the kernel. A font file is one
  face: `bold` does not change it, `italic` slants an upright face by 0.2
  of the height.
  Shaping and both directions (mitcad#473): a text in a font file, and a
  text in an installed font with characters of right-to-left or joining
  scripts, combining marks or bidirectional controls (Hebrew, Arabic,
  Syriac, the Indic scripts, Thai, …; `sketch::fonts::needs_shaping`), is
  shaped by the model (`harfrust`: joined forms, ligatures, marks,
  kerning) from the font's file (an installed font's through the kernel's
  `font_source`), in runs of one direction by the Unicode bidirectional
  algorithm (`unicode-bidi`), each line on its own. Characters that shape
  together (a ligature, a letter and its marks) are one glyph `g<k>`, `k`
  the first character's index, with all their contours; the others of
  the cluster have none. Every line's characters are laid out in their
  visual order (`text::visual_lines`): a right-to-left run reads from
  right to left, numbers in it from left to right, and alignment,
  frames, paths and flips work on the visual line. Other installed-font
  text keeps the kernel's glyphs. Glyphs of joined letters overlap a
  little, as fonts draw them, so a letter's contour can cut its
  neighbour's region in two: extrude the whole word.
  `code` (mitcad#473, `sketch/code.rs`): `{"kind": "qr", "ecc": "M"}`, the
  text is a QR code of its `text` (the `qrcode` crate; error correction
  `L`, `M` the default, `Q` or `H`) instead of characters: `height` is a
  module's size (mm), `at` the lower left corner of the modules, turned
  by `angle`; fonts, alignment, frames and paths do not apply (a frame or
  a path is refused). The dark modules that share sides are one area,
  bounded by one contour along their outside and one round each light
  island in it, glyph contours `t9.g0.c<j>` numbered from the lowest
  leftmost one up; modules that touch only at a corner are apart there
  (their contours meet at that point). A region bounded by several such
  contours (a light island that meets another at a corner) still has
  the region's `text`, and `letter` true when a point inside it lies
  within an odd number of the text's contours (the material).
- `text_values` (mitcad#664): `[{"text": "t9", "value": "Label"}]`, texts
  whose text is a [text parameter](#text-parameters)'s value (slot
  `texts[t9].text`): a parameter's name, or in a command a text
  expression, which becomes the sketch's own text parameter of the text.
  The text is laid out with the parameter's text and follows it; its
  `text` keeps the string it had when it was last set.
- `patterns`: copy groups, `{"id": "k5", "type": "circular", "center":
  "p3", "count": 6, "angle": "d4", "entities": ["c2", "p7"], "copies":
  [{"index": [1, 0], "entities": {"c2": "c9", "p7": "p10"}}, …]}` or
  `{"type": "rectangular", "direction": [1, 0], "count": [3, 2], "symmetric":
  [true, false],
  "spacing": ["d5", "d6"], …}`. Each solve binds every copy to its
  original with the pattern's transform (solver constraints `Translated`,
  `Rotated`, `TurnedDirection`, `EqualSize`; not stored as constraints),
  so the copies follow the originals and add no degrees of freedom. Each
  copy is bound through its neighbour instance one step toward the
  originals (mitcad#677), so the solve's cost grows about linearly with
  the copies. Slots
  `patterns[k5].angle`, `.spacing1`, `.spacing2`. A new count regenerates
  the copies, keeping those that stay. A `symmetric` direction (an odd
  count) has the originals at its middle instance: the copies' indices
  count from the end against the direction, and the originals are the
  instance `[count / 2, 0]`. Copies cannot be patterned again or moved on
  their own.
- `offsets`: `{"id": "k8", "curves": ["c1", "c4"], "distance": "d6",
  "left": false, "results": ["c10", "c11"], "corners": [{"join": 0,
  "arc": "c12"}], "derived": true}`: the source chain, the distance (slot
  `offsets[k8].distance`, not negative; `left` is the side) and the curves
  made.
  - A chain of lines and arcs, or a circle, is offset exactly by
    constraints: the results are ordinary curves, and dragging one drags
    the source along (the distance dimension drives).
    The construction lines across the gap of its arcs and circles are
    listed as `helpers` (mitcad#358) and go with the results when
    `sketch.edit_offset` flips the side and makes them again. Each solve
    starts its results where the offset of the source is (mitcad#641), so
    that a source moved before the solve (a linked projection that
    followed its face farther than the distance) keeps them on their side;
    a shared corner starts where the two offset curves cross, an arc's
    free ends at the source's angles, and each helper across an arc's gap
    on its radius as it lay (mitcad#890).
  - Where the source curves touch at a corner by their definition (fixed
    curves, a linked projection's, that touch at their shared point;
    curves tangent by a constraint; results of an offset whose corner is
    held so), the solve also holds the results' shared corner where the
    result line touches the result arc, or where the two result arcs
    touch (mitcad#890, `offset::tangent_corners`). The corner was fixed
    only to the second order before: it slid along the line by the square
    root of the solve's rounding (2e-5 mm), the arc ended past the
    touching point and the profile turned there by about 1e-6 rad, so
    that a grid design's offset outlines lost the edges its chamfers name
    and a sweep along them cut its chute into rings after a width change.
    The sketch's `dof` and `fully_constrained` count such a corner as
    fixed. Free curves that only happen to touch are not held. A sketch
    that cannot be solved says what contradicts as it would without the
    corners held: the held tangencies restate what the offsets' own
    constraints imply, and counted in the failed solve's explanation they
    named every constraint of the offsets.
  - A chain with an ellipse, an elliptical arc or a spline is `derived`:
    its curves are computed from the solved source after every solve
    (lines and arcs exactly, an ellipse or spline as a C1 cubic B-spline
    within 1e-4 mm of the exact offset), with round arcs at outer corners
    and trimmed inner corners. Constraints cannot refer to them;
    `sketch.drag` or `sketch.move` of them moves the whole source chain
    by the same motion.
    A chain is closed by a shared point only, not by ends that lie at the
    same place (mitcad#360), when it is made and at every later solve; a
    curve of it is removed with the offset, not alone (mitcad#361).
  - The distance changes only in `sketch.edit_offset`. The source's
    constraints apply (a fixed source holds its offset). A copy
    (`sketch.move` with `copy`) is an ordinary curve that no longer
    follows the source. Each corner's kind is fixed when the offset is
    made: an edit that would change it is refused (as .f3d offsets fail
    likewise).

Evaluation solves the sketch (an over- or inconsistently constrained
sketch fails with the conflicting constraint ids; a solve that does not
converge is tried again at a tolerance of 1e-7 of the sketch's size, so
that fixed geometry that misses itself by rounding still solves) and cuts the
non-construction curves into profile regions: the faces of the planar
arrangement, with islands as holes; overlapping shapes split into
separate regions, and curves on each other (a circle drawn twice) bound
them once, the one with the lower id (a spline that follows a curve within a
micron, a projected edge, replaces it: they are one edge). A region reference whose key no longer exists means the
regions inside the outline its key traces on the changed curves (all
pieces of a region the change split), else the region with the most
curves in common, with a warning (see [Profile references after a sketch
change](#profile-references-after-a-sketch-change)). A region whose hole is a circle
that touches its outer boundary at a point (tangent circles) is one face
(the hole shares the boundary's vertex there); regions beside such a
region are united as faces before a feature extrudes, revolves or sweeps
them. Older files' `shapes` (rectangles and circles) are read as
entities, constraints and dimensions with the same curve ids and
parameters.

### extrude

```json
{"type": "extrude",
 "profiles": [{"sketch": "F1", "region": "r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}],
 "extent": {"type": "distance", "distance": 20},
 "flip": false,
 "operation": "join",
 "participants": ["F2.b0"]}
```

- `surface`, `curves`: a surface extrusion, walls without caps, of the
  profiles and of sketch curves ([Surface modelling](#surface-modelling),
  mitcad#455).
- `profiles`: regions of one sketch, a set (see [Profile
  selections](#profile-selections)); touching regions fuse into one body
  (and taper as one region).
- `start` (optional): `{"type": "profile_plane"}` (default), `{"type":
  "offset", "offset": s}` (the profile moved s along the sketch normal,
  whatever `flip` says) or `{"type": "object", "object": <object>,
  "offset": s}` (the profile projected along the sketch normal onto a
  plane or planar face, moved s along its normal; the distance is then
  measured from there, and a start plane not parallel to the sketch takes
  no taper).
- `extent`, each with an optional `"taper"` (radians; positive widens the
  profile away from the start: the outside grows and holes shrink):
  - `{"type": "distance", "distance": d}`: one side; negative goes the
    other way;
  - `{"type": "to_object", "object": <object>, "offset": o}`: one side up
    to an object; a positive offset makes the extrusion longer;
  - `{"type": "through_all", "both_sides": false}`: past every
    participant body (all bodies when there are none), one way or both;
  - `{"type": "symmetric", "distance": d, "full_length": false}`: d each
    way, or d in total (`isFullLength` in .f3d designs);
  - `{"type": "two_sides", "side1": <side>, "side2": <side>}`: side one
    along the direction, side two against it, each `{"type": "distance",
    "distance": d}`, `{"type": "to_object", "object": …, "offset": o}` or
    `{"type": "through_all"}` with its own `"taper"`. A side of distance 0
    leaves one side.
    - `"signed": true` (mitcad#765; what the Extrude panel sends): the
      distances are signed. Side one ends `d1` along the direction and
      side two `d2` against it, so a negative distance ends on the other
      side's side and the solid lies between the two ends only: 50 and
      -30 make a solid from 30 to 50 along the direction that does not
      touch the start, -30 and 50 the same on side two's side. The ends
      must not meet or cross (`d1 + d2 > 0` for two distances, else `the
      two sides overlap: side 1 ends at 50 and side 2 at 50 along the
      extrusion direction …`). A negative distance beside a side up to an
      object or through all cuts that side off where it ends. The side
      that holds the solid keeps its taper, measured from the start as
      without the other side's end (the solid is the part of that side's
      tapered solid past the other end); the short side's taper shapes
      nothing. The cap where the short side ends is named as that side's
      far cap (`start` for side one, `end` for side two), as without the
      sign. Join, Cut and Intersect take the solid as it is. A face
      profile's extrusion (`profile_face`) takes signed distances alike.
    - Without `signed` (designs saved before mitcad#765, the features the
      imports add) the sign of a side's distance does not turn the side:
      each goes its own way by its size (a negative second distance beside
      a side through all reaches that far the other way, as the stored
      designs measure it). `add_feature`, `edit_feature` and their
      previews refuse a negative side distance there, given as a number, a
      parameter or an expression (mitcad#693: `side 2's distance is -5:
      without "signed": true each side of a two-sided extrusion goes its
      own way …`). An edit that keeps a side's negative distance as the
      feature has it passes. Features the imports add keep their negative
      distances, which evaluation takes by their size.
  - A negative taper that leans the sides in until they meet before the
    end of a distance (the profile closes) ends the solid where they
    meet, as the stored designs do: a convex profile of lines closes into
    a pyramid or a ridge, a circle into a cone, and the far end has no cap
    (the volume is the pyramid's or the cone's, not the prism's). A
    profile with holes is its outline's taper less its holes' (each
    leaning the other way, mitcad#235): a ring whose walls a taper leans
    into each other ends where they meet in a ridge, and a round or convex
    hole that a widening taper closes ends in its cone's apex or its
    pyramid's. A profile without
    holes with arcs among its lines that a taper closes is an error (`the
    taper closes the profile`).
- `<object>`: `{"type": "plane", "plane": p}` (a plane reference: origin
  plane, construction plane, a planar face as an unbounded plane, or a
  fixed plane), `{"type": "face", "body": b, "face": f, "chained": false}`
  (the face's surface continued past its edges; with `chained` the face,
  the faces next to it and those joined to them tangentially) or `{"type": "body", "body": b, "through":
  false}` (to its first face reached, or through it). Up to a body's
  first face or a curved face, a profile may start inside the body or on
  its faces: each part of the profile then runs to the first face beyond
  it (a part inside the body to where it leaves it); through a body from
  such a profile, each part runs to the body's far side; a plane that
  crosses the profile is an error.
- `object_links` (mitcad#104): bodies of other components that the
  objects (the start's, the extents') are or are faces of, each with where
  it is seen, `{"F2.b0": {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}}` (an
  `OccurrenceLink`, as a combine's `tool_links`, [Geometry of other
  components](#geometry-of-other-components)): the body is read in its
  component and moved into the extrusion's coordinates by the
  occurrences' placements at its point of the timeline. Without a link
  another component's body fails the extrusion; a link for a body that is
  no object's is refused.
- `thin` (optional): `{"location": "side1" | "center" | "side2" | "both",
  "thickness": t, "thickness2": t2, "side2": {"location": …, "thickness": …,
  "thickness2": …}, "curves": <curves>}`: walls along the profile curves
  instead of the regions. Side 1 lies away from the region's material
  (outside the outer boundary, into a hole), side 2 towards it; `both`
  puts `thickness` on side 1 and `thickness2` (only there, and needed
  there) on side 2 (mitcad#463). `side2` is the wall of side two of a
  two-sided or symmetric extent when it differs.
  - `curves` (mitcad#463): walls along these sketch curves instead,
    `{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c4"], "chain": false}` (a
    [path](#paths)'s curves, any order; `chain` adds the curves joined to
    them end to end); the extrusion then has no `profiles` (refused with
    them). The curves make chains: runs joined end to end through points
    where exactly two of them meet, open or closed; walls that meet or
    cross (a T, a cross) make one solid. A closed chain walls like a
    region's boundary: side 1 outside the area it encloses, side 2 inside.
    An open chain runs so that it bends to its left (with its chord it
    encloses an area counter-clockwise about the sketch normal), a
    straight one the way its first listed curve was drawn; side 1 lies to
    its right, side 2 to its left (towards where it bends), and its ends
    are square to it; corners are mitred. A wall thicker than a curve's
    radius on its inside, or one that folds over itself, fails.
- `flip`: reverses the direction (the sketch normal by default).
- `operation`, `participants`: see the shared rules.
- `wrap` (optional, mitcad#473): `{"body": "F2.b0", "face":
  "F2:side(c1)"}`, a cylindrical or conical face the profiles are wrapped
  onto as an [emboss](#emboss) wraps them (`Kernel::wrapped_emboss`: by
  arc length on a cylinder, by the development on a cone), and grown
  along the face's normals by the distance: out of the material, or into
  it with `flip` or a negative distance (an engraving, with `cut`). It
  takes profiles and an extent `distance` without a taper, from the
  profile plane, without `thin` or `cut_scope`; the sketch plane is
  parallel to the axis. Faces as an emboss's.
- `profile_face` (optional, mitcad#535): `{"body": "F2.b0", "face":
  "F2:end(r{…})"}`, a planar face of a body as the profile instead of
  `profiles`: its bounded area, holes kept, swept along its outward
  normal (against it with `flip` or a negative distance) by
  `Kernel::extrude_face` (`geometry/src/face_extrude.cpp`). The face is a
  topological name found on its body at the feature's point of the
  timeline on every recompute (a face a sketch change renamed is found
  again, with the warning of [renamed faces](#faces-edges-and-vertices-a-sketch-change-renamed)),
  so an upstream edit moves or resizes the extrusion with the face; the
  body is read in the feature's component, and the feature depends on it
  and on the features the name refers to. It takes an extent `distance`,
  `symmetric` or `two_sides` of distances, each side with its `taper` as
  for profiles (mitcad#541: the outside grows away from the face and its
  holes shrink with a positive taper), from the face (`profile_plane`) or
  an `offset` along its outward normal, and a `direction` of its own
  (mitcad#541, not in the face's plane; the distances along it, a taper
  growing the face in its plane by `d tan(taper)` at distance `d`); no
  `profiles`, `thin`, `surface`, `curves`, `wrap`, `cut_scope` or start
  object (refused: `an extrusion of a body face …`). A face that is gone,
  not planar without a `direction` (`face F3:side0 is not planar: an
  extrusion takes a planar face …`; a curved face goes along a
  `direction` only, as its prism, without a taper or offset), a mesh
  body's, or names several faces fails the feature; no other profile is
  ever taken instead. Operations and participants as
  above (automatic operation too). Faces: `side(<edge>)` from each edge of
  the face, by the edge's name in the body (a surface body's free edge,
  which has none, by its index among the face's edges:
  `side(2)`), `start(<face>)` and `end(<face>)` keyed by the stored face
  reference, the caps as for profiles below:
  `F5:side(E{F2:end(r{…})|F2:side(c1[c4,c2])})`, `F5:end(F2:end(r{…}))`.

Faces: `side(<segment>)`; `outer(<segment>)` and `inner(<segment>)` for
thin walls (side 1 and side 2); `start(<region>)` and `end(<region>)`.
Walls along curves: `outer(<curve>)` and `inner(<curve>)` along each
curve, `tip0(<curve>)` and `tip1(<curve>)` at an open chain's start (on
its first curve) and end (its last), and the caps keyed by the chain's
curves (`start(r{c1,c4})`).
With one side the start is the cap at the start and the end the far cap;
with two sides (and symmetric) the start is the far cap of side one and
the end the far cap of side two (`startFaces` and `endFaces` in .f3d
designs). The faces of an object where the extrusion ends get the cap's
name. A side face that a two-sided taper bends at the start is two pieces
(`#0`, `#1`); `mid(<region>)` is what remains of the start between two
sides of different walls.

Operations: new body makes a body per solid (`<extrude>.b0`, `.b1`, …).
Join fuses the tool with every participant it touches; joined bodies
merge into the first of them, and a tool solid that touches nothing
becomes a new body. Cut and intersect work on each participant they
reach; a cut through all of a body removes it, and a cut that splits a
body keeps the body for the first piece in geometric order and makes the
others new bodies of the cut (after an upstream edit the pieces keep their
ids: [Body ids of a split's pieces](#body-ids-of-a-splits-pieces)); a piece with less than a millionth of the volume
of the largest piece (a needle left where the tool's wall lies almost on a wall
of the body) stays in that piece's body as a lump. A body of several lumps
(disjoint solids, as a combine of bodies apart makes it) is cut lump by lump
(mitcad#658): it keeps the first piece of each lump and the lumps the cut does
not reach (an intersection leaves nothing of those), and only the other
pieces of a lump the cut splits are new bodies; before, every piece of such a
body was a body of its own. A join, cut or intersection that reaches no
participant fails.

#### Assembly scope for Extrude Cut

An optional `cut_scope` enables a single cut across component definitions:

```json
{"context": {"component": "C1", "occurrence": "O1"},
 "targets": {"type": "automatic",
             "excluded": [{"component": "C2", "occurrence": "O2"}],
             "excluded_bodies": [{"component": "C1", "occurrence": "O1", "body": "F2.b0"}]}}
```

`context` names the sketch/feature's owning component and the exact absolute
occurrence path in which the tool is displayed. Root uses `C0` and `""`.
Target identities use the same absolute-path convention, including nested
paths such as `O3/O4`. Missing paths fail; there is no first-occurrence fallback.

`automatic` considers the bodies available before the cut across the assembly,
then cuts eligible actual intersections except the persistent component and
body exclusions. New intersections join the scope; changing an extent never
removes an exclusion. Alternatively, `{"type":"explicit","included":[...]}`
limits it to the listed component/path pairs; `included: []` means no targets.
Both modes accept `excluded_bodies` for finer selection. Missing stored targets
or excluded bodies fail the cut, instead of broadening its scope. Body references
and component creators must precede the feature. Automatic discovery reads only
the preceding timeline state, so later features cannot form a dependency cycle.
Deleting a component definition follows normal dependent-feature deletion,
including cuts that explicitly include or exclude it; Undo restores the cut and
its scope. Missing occurrence paths after other edits remain repairable failures.

Only Cut activates `cut_scope`, and an active scope cannot be combined with
nonempty legacy `participants`. Other solid operations may retain a dormant
scope so that changing back to Cut restores the chosen targets and exclusions.
For a modern non-Cut that has never chosen targets, the scope may contain
`"initialize_on_cut": true` (default false, omitted when false). The editor
then initializes automatic targets and samples current visibility when Cut
is chosen, removing this flag before submission. Cut rejects a scope whose
flag is still true. Automatic Join participants remain Join bookkeeping;
explicitly selected local participants keep local behavior without a scope.
A dormant scope affects no geometry, references, target discovery or feature
replay; it is checked when Cut activates it again. Surface, face-profile and
wrapped extrusions continue to reject scopes.
Omitting `cut_scope` preserves existing local-component behavior
and the meaning of an empty `participants` list. Through All uses all discovered
bodies, including excluded or disabled ones, to define the tool length; toggling
a target does not shorten the tool. Every Boolean uses the target's local frame.
The first surviving piece keeps its body ID; additional pieces receive IDs of
the cut and all pieces retain the target component's ownership (ids kept
after upstream edits as in [Body ids of a split's pieces](#body-ids-of-a-splits-pieces)). Results publish
atomically, so a target failure leaves all preceding bodies unchanged.

A definition with multiple available root-to-component paths is disabled,
including hidden occurrences and repetitions through shared parent assemblies.
Linked definitions and their descendants are also disabled. Automatic mode
skips these targets and reports why; explicitly including one fails. This
version does not create per-occurrence replacement geometry.

The extrusion's own component (`context.component`) is the exception
(mitcad#769): a cut made inside it changes its definition, as any of its
features does, so however many occurrences place it, its bodies are one
target, at the context occurrence, and every occurrence shows the result.
Its row is eligible and, with more than one occurrence, carries a `note`
(`Component being edited; the cut changes all 2 occurrences.`); its other
occurrences get no rows. Explicitly including it at another occurrence
fails; exclusions stored for its other occurrences are ignored. Other
components below it that are placed more than once stay disabled. Assembly-scoped
cuts cannot themselves be repeated by feature patterns/mirrors, whose replay
currently supports local-component tools only.

The normal feature preview adds `cut_targets`:

```json
{"mode":"automatic", "selected_components":2, "selected_bodies":3,
 "can_commit":true,
 "rows":[{"component":"C1", "occurrence":"O1", "name":"Bracket",
          "path_name":"Root / Bracket:1", "intersects":true,
          "eligible":true, "checked":true, "partial":false, "reason":null,
          "bodies":[{"body":"F2.b0", "name":"Body1", "checked":true}]}]}
```

Rows contain intersecting bodies, plus stored component/body exclusions or
explicit inclusions even when they no longer intersect. `partial` identifies a
component with only some intersecting bodies checked. Boolean intersection,
not bounding-box overlap alone, determines membership. The report is retained
for no-target and unsupported-target evaluation errors; the ordinary preview
status/error and `can_commit` control acceptance. A missing report means the
tool or context could not be evaluated and the previous list must not be used.

#### A direction of its own (mitcad#539)

`"direction": [x, y, z]` (any length but zero; left out by default)
extrudes the profiles along that fixed direction instead of the sketch
normal; `flip` and a negative one-sided distance reverse it, and it turns
with the profile in patterns and with Reorient Design. Distances are
measured along it (a prism of the profile slanted by the direction), a
start offset still along the sketch normal. A taper grows the profile in
its plane: every loop moves outwards from the material by `t tan(taper)`
at the distance `t` along the direction, each side face ruled from its
edge to that edge's offset moved along the direction (as the FreeCAD
import's pads along a custom direction are; along the normal it is the
usual taper). The geometry builds it as the taper along the normal to the
same height (the distance times the cosine c of the direction's angle to
the normal, the taper's tangent over c) sheared along the direction,
which keeps the planes parallel to the sketch, and gives the side faces
back their planes; a circle's side is the oblique cone through the grown
circles (`geometry/tests/test_extrude_feature.cpp`, `test_oblique`). A
direction in the sketch plane fails the extrusion (`the extrusion
direction lies in the sketch plane`); it is refused with a start object or
a wrap, and a tapered side up to an object along it is `unsupported`. A
body face as the profile (`profile_face`, mitcad#541) goes along it too,
tapered alike (`the extrusion direction lies in the plane of face …` for
one in the face's plane); a curved face goes only along a direction.

### Profile selections

The `profiles` of extrude, revolve, sweep and helix select an area of
their sketch (mitcad#199), the same in a preview and in the feature:

- A selectable area is one profile region: a face of the planar
  arrangement of the sketch's curves with its holes, as the application
  shows and highlights it. Nested and overlapping shapes are separate
  regions: squares A, B and C, each inside the one before, make the ring
  between A and B (B its hole), the ring between B and C and the square C;
  two overlapping shapes make each one's own part and their overlap.
- The selected area is the odd/even (XOR) composition of the selected
  regions: covered by an odd number of them, it is extruded. Regions of one
  sketch never overlap, so that is each selected region once: the outer
  ring alone is A minus B (its hole stays a hole, it is neither filled nor
  taken away twice), the outer ring and C are A minus B plus C (A xor B
  xor C), all three regions are A; the two own parts of overlapping shapes
  leave their overlap out (their xor). The order of the list does not
  matter for the area.
- The list is a set: a reference listed twice is read once (a definition
  keeps it once), and references that find the same region (a key that
  changed with the sketch and the current key) use it once. Neither is an
  error; an empty list is (`no profiles selected`).
- Toggling is the application's: a click on a selected region takes its
  entry out (every entry that finds that region; a click on one piece of
  a region a sketch edit split takes out that piece, the reference's
  other pieces staying listed under their own keys, mitcad#410), a click
  on another one adds it ([app/COMMANDS.md](../../../app/COMMANDS.md), "Selection
  inputs").
- The `profile` query (`sketch`, `region`) gives the region a reference
  means now: `sketch`, `region` (its current key: the same key, or the main
  region found when the sketch changed), `regions` (the current keys of
  every region it means, the main one first: more than one when a change
  split it), `exact` (the key is the region's own); null when no region
  shares a curve with it. `profile_shape` (the bridge) draws all of them.

### Profile references after a sketch change

A sketch edit can rename the regions later features use: their keys are
made of curve ids, and a curve that now crosses, touches or leaves a
region's boundary changes the key (mitcad#407). A reference whose key
is no longer a region's own is found again:

1. Each segment `c3[c2,c4]` of the key is traced on the current curves:
   the pieces of `c3` from where it meets `c2` to where it meets `c4`
   (both may meet it there with other curves now). When the traced
   segments close one loop, the regions inside it are what the reference
   selects: the region renamed, or all pieces of a region the edit split
   (a bar lengthened across another curve keeps both of its parts
   selected, so the area that was selected stays selected). Regions in a
   hole of those pieces (islands inside) stay out, as the old region's
   holes did; an area inside the outline that was a hole and is now
   joined to the boundary is taken as a piece.
2. When the key's segments trace no loop (a curve of it is gone, or no
   longer meets the curve at its end), the reference means the region
   with the most curves in common, then the most identical segments,
   then the fewest other curves, then the largest.
3. A key that shares no curve with any region fails the feature:
   `Sketch1 has no profile r{…}`.

The main region (the piece with the most curves in common, by rule 2's
order) carries the referenced key, so that the faces made from it keep
their names (`F2:end(r{…})`); the other pieces carry their own keys. The
feature keeps its definition and succeeds with a warning, shown in the
`timeline` (status `warning`) and the `feature` query's `warnings`, as
renamed faces do ([Faces, edges and vertices a sketch change
renamed](#faces-edges-and-vertices-a-sketch-change-renamed)): `region
r{c5[c11,c13],c11[c5,c12],…} found as r{c3[c11,c13],…} + r{c3[c11,c13],…}
after a change in Sketch1` (the current keys, the main one first). A loft
section, one region, lofts the main piece and warns that the section was
split. Reverting the edit restores the keys and removes the warning.

### revolve

```json
{"type": "revolve",
 "profiles": [{"sketch": "F1", "region": "r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}],
 "axis": "y",
 "extent": {"type": "angle", "angle": 1.5708},
 "operation": "new_body"}
```

- `surface`, `curves`: a surface revolution, walls without caps ([Surface
  modelling](#surface-modelling), mitcad#455).
- `axis`: a line reference: a sketch line `{"sketch": uid, "curve":
  "c4"}` (from its start to its end; any line, also a construction or
  centre line), an origin axis, a construction axis `"F7"`, a straight
  edge `{"body": b, "edge": e}` or a fixed axis. `project_axis: true`
  projects it into the sketch plane (`isProjectAxis` in .f3d designs).
- `extent` (positive by the right hand rule about the axis direction):
  `{"type": "angle", "angle": a}` (one side; negative turns the other
  way), `{"type": "full"}`, `{"type": "symmetric", "angle": a}` (a to each
  side, as .f3d designs measure it), `{"type": "two_sides", "angle1": a1,
  "angle2": a2}` (a1 not negative; a negative a2, mitcad#955, ends side
  two past the profile: the turn runs from -a2 to a1, so a1 + a2 must be
  more than zero; not for a body face) or `{"type": "to_object", "object": <object>}` (the
  positive way to the first face of the object reached; with a body's
  `"through": true`, mitcad#539, through the body to its last face, where
  the turn leaves it for the last time: the pieces of the turn are taken
  in the order of their angles about the axis up to the last one inside
  the body; `geometry/tests/test_revolve.cpp`, `test_to_object`).
- `object_links` (mitcad#762): the body of another component that the
  `to_object` object is or is a face of, with where it is seen, `{"F2.b0":
  {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}}`, as an extrusion's `object_links`: the
  body is read in its component and moved into the revolution's
  coordinates by the occurrences' placements at its point of the timeline.
  Without a link another component's body fails the revolution; a link for
  a body that is not the object's is refused.
- `operation`, `participants`: as for extrude.
- `profile_face` (optional, mitcad#539): `{"body": "F2.b0", "face":
  "F2:side(c1[c4,c2])"}`, a planar face of a body as the profile instead
  of `profiles`, as an extrusion's `profile_face`: its bounded area, holes
  kept, turned about the axis by `Kernel::revolve_face`
  (`geometry/src/face_revolve.cpp`). The face is found by its topological
  name on every recompute; the feature depends on its body and on the
  features the name refers to. Extents `angle`, `full`, `symmetric` and
  `two_sides` (as for profiles: a negative single angle turns the other
  way, a side of nothing leaves one side); no `profiles`, `surface`,
  `curves`, `project_axis` or `to_object` (refused: `a revolution of a
  body face …`). A face that is gone, not planar, a mesh body's, names
  several faces, crosses the axis or has the axis through it fails the
  feature; no other profile is taken instead. Faces: `side(<edge>)` from
  each edge of the face off the axis (by the edge's name in the body, an
  edge without one by its index among the face's edges), `start(<face>)`
  and `end(<face>)` keyed by the stored face reference, as for profiles
  below; a full turn has no caps.

The profile may touch the axis. Regions that touch are united into one
face before the turn (turned apart and fused, two parts of one surface
that their shared edge cut in two were merged back into a face built
wrong). A profile that straddles the axis line (an imported one: an edge
on the axis with a part beyond it) is parted at the line and each part
turns on its own side. An axis that passes through a profile is refused.
Faces are named as an extrusion's (a face across two regions carries both
their segments' names); a full turn has no caps.

### hole

```json
{"type": "hole",
 "placement": {"type": "face", "body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(r{…})", "points": [[30, 20, 20]]},
 "diameter": 10,
 "kind": {"type": "counterbore", "diameter": 16, "depth": 5},
 "tip_angle": 2.0595,
 "extent": {"type": "distance", "depth": 10},
 "thread": {"designation": "M10x1.5", "class": "6H", "modeled": false}}
```

- `placement`: `{"type": "face", "body": b, "face": f, "points": [[x, y,
  z], …]}` (points put onto a planar face's plane, one hole each; on a
  cylindrical face each point moved across its axis onto the cylinder,
  the hole along the radius into the material, mitcad#719),
  `{"type": "face_offsets", "body": b, "face": f, "edge1": e1, "offset1":
  o1, "edge2": e2, "offset2": o2}` (one hole at those distances from the
  lines of two edges, on the face's side of both) or `{"type":
  "sketch_points", "sketch": uid, "points": [[u, v], "c5", "p3", …]}`
  (sketch coordinates, the centres of the sketch's circles, arcs and
  ellipses, or its points; `setPositionBySketchPoints` in .f3d designs) or
  `{"type": "plane", "plane": g, "points": [[x, y, z], …]}` (points put
  onto an origin plane, a construction plane or a planar face's plane: the
  holes start on it, also inside a body, and cut the participants they
  reach; `setPositionByPoint` on a plane in .f3d designs) or `{"type":
  "cylinder_offset", "body": b, "face": f, "plane": g, "offset": o,
  "toward": [x, y, z]}` (one hole on a cylindrical face, at the point of
  its axis `o` from the plane `g` the axis crosses, measured along the
  plane's normal on the face's side of it (along the axis for a plane
  square to it), on the side of the axis where the point lies, along the
  radius into the material;
  `setPositionByPlaneAndOffsets` on a shaft's side in .f3d designs,
  mitcad#719). Holes go against the face, plane or sketch normal, into the
  material; `flip` turns them round (`isDefaultDirection` false). The Hole
  panel edits `face_offsets`, `plane` and `cylinder_offset` placements as
  they are (Placement From Two Edges, On a Plane, Along a Shaft), the
  distances as Edge Offset 1 and 2 or Offset (mitcad#733).
- `kind`: `{"type": "simple"}` (default), `{"type": "counterbore",
  "diameter": D, "depth": d}`, `{"type": "countersink", "diameter": D,
  "angle": a}` (the cone's full angle), `{"type": "counterdrill",
  "diameter": D, "depth": d, "angle": a}` (a counterbore whose floor is a
  cone of the full angle narrowing to the hole).
- `taper` (optional): the wall's angle to the axis, positive narrowing the
  hole from its diameter at the start as it goes deeper (a counterbore's
  floor and a countersink's or counterdrill's cone meet the leaning wall;
  the drill point starts from the wall's end). Not with a `thread`.
- `tip_angle`: the drill point's full angle, 118° when left out; `flat:
  true` for a flat bottom.
- `extent`: `{"type": "distance", "depth": d}` (to the shoulder, from the
  start; the point is extra), `{"type": "through_all"}` (past every
  participant, flat) or `{"type": "to_object", "object": <object>,
  "offset": o}` (the cylinder ends where each axis first meets the
  object, the point beyond).
- `thread` (a tapped hole): `standard` (`iso_metric` default, `unified`,
  `whitworth`, `npt`, `tyre_valve`, `forming_screw`, `trapezoidal`, `iso_taper`, `custom`), `designation`, `class`, `right_handed` (default
  true), `modeled` (ISO metric, Unified, tyre valve, forming screw, trapezoidal, custom and NPT only), and `length`, `offset`
  from the hole's start (the whole wall when left out), and for a
  modelled thread `radial_clearance` and `flank_clearance`; a custom
  thread's `custom` size and a modelled thread's `starts` ([Custom and
  multi-start threads](#custom-and-multi-start-threads-modelled-trapezoidal-threads));
  as for the [thread](#thread) feature.
  The bore is the size's basic minor diameter (a custom thread's D − 5H/4,
  a trapezoidal thread's D1 = d − P); `diameter` is then ignored.
  A taper pipe thread (`npt`, `iso_taper` `Rc …`; mitcad#733) with
  `"taper": true` keeps `diameter`, the tap drill (the `thread_sizes`
  query's `tap_drill`, the Hole panel's default), and tapers the bore from
  the hole's start: 1:16 on the diameter from its minor diameter at the
  opening, down to where it meets the drilled bore, cosmetic or modelled
  (see [thread](#thread)); `diameter` must then be greater than zero.
  Without `taper` (holes saved before) its bore is the size's minor
  diameter and nothing tapers, as it was, and NPT cannot be modelled.
  Patterns and mirrors of a tapering hole (or of one with a modelled
  thread) copy the hole feature, not only its tool.
- `clearance` (optional, mitcad#903): a clearance hole's screw size and
  fit, `{"size": "M6", "fit": "normal"}` (`fine`, `normal`, `coarse`;
  `normal` when left out), a size of the [hole_sizes](#clearance-holes-and-recesses-by-screw-size)
  query; not with a `thread`. It only names where the hole's values came
  from: the hole is cut at its own `diameter` and `kind`, plain values
  as any hole's. Holes saved before have none.
- `participants`: the bodies to cut, all when left out.

A simple hole (no taper, no thread) into one sheet-metal body, every axis
starting on the front or back surface of one planar panel, normal to it
and into the material, through all or at least as deep as the sheet,
cuts the sheet's material domain as `sheet_cut` does (mitcad#211): the
body stays a valid sheet for later sheet features, and the walls are named
as a cut's (`<sheet>:sheet_side…(<hole>:sheet_curve(<i>))`). The hole's
tool is the same, so patterns and mirrors of it repeat it. A hole the
domains cannot take (one reaching a bend) is an ordinary cut.

Faces: `hole<i>.wall`, `hole<i>.tip` (point or flat bottom),
`hole<i>.cbore_wall` (a counterbore's or counterdrill's),
`hole<i>.cbore_floor`, `hole<i>.csink`, `hole<i>.cdrill` (a
counterdrill's cone), `hole<i>.top` (at the start, gone after the cut); i
numbers the positions from 0.

### thread

```json
{"type": "thread", "faces": [{"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}],
 "thread": {"designation": "M10x1.5", "class": "6g"},
 "modeled": false, "length": 12, "offset": 2, "location": "high_end"}
```

- `faces`: cylindrical faces, all internal (hole walls) or all external.
- `thread`: `standard` (`iso_metric` default, `unified`, `whitworth`,
  `npt`, `tyre_valve`, `forming_screw`, `trapezoidal`, `iso_taper`,
  `custom`: a size of one's own, see [Custom and multi-start
  threads](#custom-and-multi-start-threads-modelled-trapezoidal-threads)), `designation` (`M10x1.5`, `M10` for the coarse
  pitch, `1/4-20 UNC`; Whitworth `1/4-20 BSW`, `1/4-26 BSF`, the parallel
  pipe threads `G 1/4`; NPT `1/4-18 NPT` (also `1/2 - 14 NPT`); the taper
  pipe threads of ISO 7-1 `R 1/2` on a shaft and `Rc 1/2` in a hole (the
  other side's fails: "Rc 1/2 is an internal thread; use R 1/2 for a
  shaft"), mitcad#733; the tyre valve threads of ISO
  4570 `5V1`, `8V1`, … on the 60-degree profile, mitcad#59; the forming
  screw threads of ISO 1478 `ST3.5x1.3`, the `ST` may be left out; the
  trapezoidal threads of ISO 2904 `Tr8x1.5`, a multi-start one by its lead
  and pitch `Tr10x4(P2)`, mitcad#449), `class` (`6g`
  external, `6H` internal; trapezoidal `7e`, `8e`, `8c`, `9c` external, `7H`,
  `8H`, `9H` internal; Whitworth `Close`, `Medium`, `Free`, `A`, `B`
  external, `Medium`, `Normal`, `A` internal (a pipe thread's `A` is on
  the internal threads of the stored designs); NPT, ISO 7-1 and tyre valve `Standard`;
  checked against the face: a class of the other side fails with the class
  to use, "class 6g is for external threads; use 6H for a hole"),
  `right_handed`. Sizes: `core/model/data/threads.json` (the
  `thread_sizes` query). An NPT size is listed at its pipe's outside
  diameter, an ISO 7-1 size at its gauge diameter.
- `modeled`: build the 60° profile on the faces (ISO metric, Unified,
  tyre valve, forming screw, custom, and NPT with `taper`), or the
  trapezoidal 30° one (trapezoidal, mitcad#893; the others, Whitworth and
  ISO 7-1, are cosmetic only); otherwise cosmetic: no
  geometry, listed by the `threads` query (a cosmetic thread's end
  chamfers, below, and a tapering taper pipe thread's cone are cut into
  the geometry). The profile is ISO 68-1's: flanks at
  30° to the radius, half a pitch wide at the pitch diameter, flat crests
  and roots on the major and minor diameters. Along the threaded part the
  material becomes the thread: removed beyond the profile, and added up
  to the crest where the face lies inside it (a shaft thinner than the
  major diameter, a bore wider than the minor one). The part ends in
  planes across the axis, and runs out through ends of the face with no
  material beyond them (a shaft's free end, a hole's mouth).
- `diameters` (modelled, or a tapering taper pipe thread): `{"major": D, "minor": D1, "pitch": D2}`,
  the profile's diameters, e.g. a tolerance class's (the middles of its
  tolerances, as `.f3d` designs store them: M10x1.5 6g is 9.85, 8.141,
  8.928); the size's basic diameters (D, D1 = D − 5H/4, D2 = D − 3H/4)
  when left out, a trapezoidal thread's with its crest clearance (below).
  A taper pipe thread's are those where it starts (below).
