- `taper` (`true`; taper pipe threads `npt` and `iso_taper` only,
  mitcad#733): the thread is tapered 1:16 on the diameter. Without it (a
  thread saved before) a taper pipe thread is straight, as it was:
  cosmetic only, its size's diameters, no cone, its end chamfers cut.
  The Thread panel sets it for new NPT and ISO 7-1 threads (*Tapered*).
  A tapering thread's diameters shrink by 1/16 of the length into an
  internal thread from where it starts and grows along an external one.
  It starts at the face's free end (nothing of the body beyond it: a
  hole's mouth, a shaft's end) where only one end is free, else at the
  end `location` names (`high_end` by default; a part measured from it
  starts there). Its diameters there are the size's unless given: NPT
  (ASME B1.20.1) the pitch diameter E1 = E0 + L1/16 at an internal
  thread's opening (the hand-tight plane) and E0 = D − (0.05 D + 1.1) P
  at an external thread's end, the major and minor diameters h = 0.8 P
  above and below it; ISO 7-1 the gauge diameter (the major diameter) at
  an `Rc` thread's opening and the gauge length before it at an `R`
  thread's end, h = 0.640327 P. Even cosmetic it changes the geometry:
  it cuts the cone of its minor diameter out of a bore (the tapered bore
  of a tapped pipe hole) or what lies outside the cone of its major
  diameter off a shaft, over its part, where the cone lies off the face;
  the cone's faces are named `<feature>:thread_taper(<face>)`. A modelled
  NPT thread sweeps its profile, flanks square to the axis, along the
  tapered helix (no teeth are added where the face lies inside the crest:
  they stay short, as a tap leaves them). It has no end chamfers:
  `chamfer` is left out with a warning (not refused); the `threads`
  query gives its `taper` (0.0625).
- `angle` (modelled only): the thread turned about its axis (right-hand
  rule), 0 when left out. At angle 0, with the axis pointing up (+Z; axes
  across Z towards +Y, the X axis towards +X), from the face's end at the
  low end of that axis and at the reference direction (the X axis
  projected across the axis; Y for axes within about 25° of X), an
  external thread's groove spans the first half pitch at the pitch
  diameter, an internal thread's tooth the same half pitch (a bolt and a
  nut threaded from the same plane mate).
- `length` and `offset`: part of each face, from the end its cylinder's
  axis points to (`location`: `high_end`, default) or from the other
  (`low_end`); the whole face when left out.
- `radial_clearance` and `flank_clearance` (modelled only, lengths of 0 or
  more, 0 when left out; mitcad#195): extra clearance for a looser fit,
  e.g. for 3D printing, on top of the profile's diameters (the size,
  class, pitch, hand and extent stay). `radial_clearance` moves the whole
  profile (crests, roots, flanks and the pitch diameter) along the radius
  away from the material, per side: an internal thread's diameters grow
  by twice it, an external thread's shrink (0.2 changes each diameter by
  0.4). Then `flank_clearance` moves each flank that far perpendicular to
  itself into the tooth (not along the axis, not a scale factor): an
  external thread's teeth get thinner, an internal thread's grooves
  wider; the flank angle, the pitch and the crest and root radii stay, so
  each flank moves `flank_clearance / cos 30°` along the axis and the
  crests narrow by twice that. Clearance on both mating parts adds up.
  A negative or non-finite value is refused; a flank clearance that
  leaves the crest narrower than P/50, or a radial clearance that leaves
  an external thread no core, fails the feature. The largest flank
  clearance a thread takes is (crest - P/50) cos 30° / 2, the crest
  without clearance being P/4 inside and P/8 outside for the basic
  profile: 0.0996 mm on an internal M6x1, 0.0455 mm on an external one.
  The failure names it, rounded down ("this thread takes a flank
  clearance of at most 0.0995 mm").
  - The printed-fit parameter `thread_flank_clearance` itself as the
    `flank_clearance` (the panels' default, [Printed fit
    parameters](#printed-fit-parameters); mitcad#691) is a printer's fit
    shared by threads of every size: on a pitch too fine for it, the
    thread uses the largest flank clearance it takes instead (a
    micrometre below the limit), so a new M6x1 in a 5 mm bore is made
    with the default 0.1 mm. The parameter keeps its value; a value that
    fits is used as it is. A number or any other expression is used as
    given and fails as above when it is too large.

- `chamfer` (mitcad#304): `"start"`, `"end"` or `"both"`, none when
  left out: a cone cut at those ends of each face, before the profile, so
  that the first turn starts on the cone and leaves no knife edge. The
  start is the end `location` names (`high_end` by default, also for a
  thread over the whole face), the end the other one. Only free ends get
  one: ends the thread reaches (a partial thread's end inside the face
  gets none) with nothing of the body beyond them (a shaft's free end, a
  hole's mouth; not the shoulder under a bolt's head). An external
  thread's cone widens from `chamfer_diameter` at the end into the
  material at `chamfer_angle` to the axis, cutting off what lies outside
  it; an internal thread's (a countersink) narrows from
  `chamfer_diameter`, cutting off what lies inside it. A cosmetic thread
  gets the same cones (its only geometry), and the `threads` query starts
  its rings where a cone meets the cylinder.
- `chamfer_angle`: the cone's angle to the axis, between 0 and 90°; 45°
  when left out (inside: a 90° countersink).
- `chamfer_diameter`: the cone's diameter at the end. When left out it
  follows the size (a size change changes it; the `thread_chamfer` query
  gives it): an external thread's minor diameter less P/10, an internal
  thread's major diameter plus P/10 (from the size table), and further in
  (out) when a modelled thread's root lies beyond that (a class's minor
  diameter, a radial clearance), so that no groove reaches the end's
  plane. A diameter that leaves the cone outside the thread (an external
  one not smaller than the face and the crest, an internal one not larger
  than the bore and the crest), or chamfers deeper than the thread is
  long, fail the feature. Only with `chamfer`.

A modelled thread's new faces (flanks, crests and roots) are
`thread(<face>)`, the chamfers' cones `thread_chamfer_low(<face>)` and
`thread_chamfer_high(<face>)` (the low and high end along the axis of
the face's cylinder). The thread's pieces, a crest, two flanks and a root
a turn, and the threaded face's pieces are numbered by their place along
the axis (their centres of mass along it, then from it, then their
areas), the same on every platform; the numbers start at the pieces'
count, `thread(<face>)#57` to `#113` for 57 pieces (mitcad#490). A piece
also keeps the number it had before that, where that number was the same
on every platform (pieces at the thread's ends); references saved to the
pieces of whole turns before then no longer find a face and are
reported, to be picked again. The work is local: only the body's faces near the
thread take part, so a large body does not slow it down. Imported
threads have no end chamfers: the thread properties the imports read
(`core/import/SCHEMA.md`, `ThreadFeature`) include none; a chamfer in
those designs is a feature of its own.

#### Custom and multi-start threads, modelled trapezoidal threads

(mitcad#893)

```json
{"type": "thread", "faces": [{"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}],
 "thread": {"standard": "custom", "right_handed": true},
 "custom": {"major": "12 mm", "pitch": "3 mm"}, "starts": 2, "modeled": true}
```

- A custom thread (`"standard": "custom"`) takes its size from `custom`:
  `major` (the major diameter D) and `pitch` (P), expressions, so it
  follows parameter changes. It has no `designation` and no `class` (one
  fails: "a custom thread has no tolerance class"), and is the 60-degree
  profile of ISO 68-1 at that size: D1 = D − 5H/4, D2 = D − 3H/4, H =
  0.866025 P. The pitch must leave a core (P < 0.9238 D; "too coarse"
  otherwise). Cosmetic or modelled like a size of the table, with the
  same `diameters`, clearances, `angle`, part and end chamfers (their
  default diameter from its minor or major diameter). Without `custom`
  the feature fails ("a custom thread needs its size"), and `custom` on a
  standard size fails. The `threads` query lists it with `standard`
  `custom` and `designation` `<D>x<P>` (`12x3`). A tapped hole takes the
  same `custom` in its `thread` (its bore D1).
- `starts` (an expression, a whole number from 1 to 64; 1 when left
  out): a modelled thread's number of starts. Its grooves are evenly
  spaced round the axis, a pitch apart along it, each on a helix of lead
  `starts` × P: the first is placed as `angle` says, rising a lead a turn,
  the others are it turned by 360°/`starts`. In every section through the
  axis its profile is a single-start thread's of the same pitch. A
  designation with a lead gives its own starts (`Tr10x4(P2)`: 2, lead 4);
  `starts` may only repeat it ("Tr10x4(P2) has 2 starts …"). Any size
  takes `starts`; the Thread and Hole panels offer it for Custom. The
  `threads` query gives a multi-start thread's `starts` and `lead`.
- A trapezoidal thread is modelled with the profile of ISO 2901: flanks
  at 15° to the radius (a 30° included angle), half a pitch wide at the
  pitch diameter d2 = d − P/2, flat crests and roots, and the standard's
  crest clearance `ac` (0.15 mm for P 1.5, 0.25 mm for P 2 to 5, 0.5 mm
  for P 6 to 12, 1 mm from P 14): an external thread's root d3 = d − 2
  (P/2 + ac), an internal thread's D4 = d + 2 ac, its crest D1 = d − P
  (Tr10x2: 10, 7.5, 9 outside; 10.5, 8, 9 inside). Extra flank clearance
  moves the 15° flanks: `flank_clearance / cos 15°` along the axis, at
  most (crest − P/50) cos 15° / 2 (0.3342 mm on an external Tr10x2, whose
  crest is 0.366 P).
- The kernel gets them as `ThreadSpec::starts` and
  `ThreadSpec::flank_angle` (`geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/thread.hpp`).

### fillet

```json
{"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{F2:side(c1[c4,c2])|F2:side(c2[c1,c3])}"], "radius": 2}
```

The short form is one set of edges with a constant radius. The general
form lists edge sets:

```json
{"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "sets": [
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 5}, "tangent_chain": false},
  {"faces": ["F2:end(r{…})"], "size": {"type": "chord_length", "length": 3}},
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "variable", "start": 2, "end": 4, "start_vertex": "V{…}",
   "mid": [{"position": 0.25, "radius": 3}]}, "continuity": "tangent"},
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 2}, "continuity": "curvature",
   "tangency_weight": 1.5},
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "asymmetric", "distance1": 2, "distance2": 4, "flip": false},
   "reference_face": "F2:side(c1[c4,c2])"}],
 "rolling_ball_corners": true}
```

- A set rounds its `edges` and every edge of its `faces`; an edge may be
  in one set only. Any number of fillets per body.
- `all_edges` (default false, mitcad#793): the set rounds every edge of
  the body as it is when the fillet is computed (the FreeCAD import's
  "use all edges"), so that the edges an edit upstream adds are rounded
  too and those it takes away are no error. Such a set lists no `edges`
  or `faces`, has no `start_vertex` and is the fillet's only set:
  `{"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "sets": [{"all_edges": true,
  "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 1}}]}`. Patterns that copy
  fillets onto their copies leave such a set out.
- `size`: `constant` (`radius`), `chord_length` (`length`, the width
  across the rounding; the faces must meet at a constant angle along the
  chain), `variable`, `asymmetric` or `spline`.
- `variable`: `start` at `start_vertex` (an end of the chain, or the
  kernel's start when left out) to `end` at the chain's other end,
  through the `mid` radii at their positions along the chain (0 to 1 from
  the start, increasing). The radius follows OCCT's smooth interpolation
  of all the radii, level at both ends, along the whole tangent chain
  (not confirmed to be the law of `.f3d` variable fillets). Mid radii
  around a closed chain are unsupported.
- `spline` (mitcad#464): `{"type": "spline", "knots": [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1,
  1, 1], "radii": [2, 6, 3, 4], "start_vertex": "V{…}"}`, the radius a
  clamped B-spline of the position along the chain (0 at `start_vertex`,
  an end of the chain or the kernel's start when left out, 1 at the other
  end; by arc length): `radii` its control radii (2 to 100, each greater
  than zero) and `knots` its full knot vector, as many as the radii and
  the degree and one more (degree 1 to 3), from 0 to 1, each end repeated
  degree + 1 times and an inner knot at most degree times. The radius
  keeps within its control radii, passes through the first and the last,
  and runs exactly as the spline does (the law goes to OCCT's fillet as
  it is, port patch 0920; `geometry/tests/test_dressup.cpp`,
  `test_fillet_spline_radius`). Slots `radii[k]`. Not around a closed
  chain and not with curvature continuity (unsupported); the kernel's
  chain, as for `variable`.
- `asymmetric`: `distance1` from the edge along the set's
  `reference_face` (or along the first face of each edge's name), and
  `distance2` along the other face; `flip` swaps the faces. The
  cross-section is a conic, the affine image of the circular arc, tangent
  to both faces (MitCad's own convention).
- `tangent_chain` (default true): the edges that continue an edge
  smoothly are rounded too: every edge that meets an edge of the set end
  to end in the same direction (within 0.01 rad) and lies between two
  faces at an angle, convex where the edge is convex and concave where it
  is concave (a rounding vanishes where a concave edge runs on into a
  convex one, mitcad#439), and so on from those (MitCad's own chain,
  mitcad#224; constant and chord length sets and chamfers; variable,
  asymmetric and G2 sets keep the kernel's chain), besides the edges the
  kernel follows itself where the faces at a vertex go on tangentially.
  The kernel stops where a third sharp edge meets the vertex (a ring
  that two chamfers split into two arcs); MitCad's chain does not. Where
  the kernel cannot build MitCad's chain, the set takes the kernel's
  chain alone, with a warning. The kernel chain of a fillet or a chamfer
  also stops where its edges turn (by 0.01 rad or more) although the faces
  go on tangentially across a shallow crease there (a wall drafted by a
  few degrees above a vertical one), unless the next edge is bevelled too
  (OCCT port patches 0180, mitcad#241, and 0531, mitcad#263): a rounding
  ends at that vertex, cut by the face beyond the crease, where the crease
  is concave (at a convex crease that end is not built and the fillet
  fails); a chamfer's analytic blend (a cone along an arc) runs on past
  the vertex, cut by the face beyond the crease, up to where its other
  contact reaches that face. Elsewhere the kernel follows its own chains,
  so a set without `tangent_chain` whose kernel chain reaches an
  unselected edge is unsupported, and edges the kernel chains beyond
  MitCad's chain stay bevelled.
- A rolling ball rounding of constant radius whose chain ends at a small
  notch in the rim it rounds (edges not rounded, each within the rounding's
  contact on the face the notch breaks and within the ball's diameter of
  the chain's end) carries on across the notch onto the next edge of the
  rim, when that edge lies on the same line or circle between faces of the
  same two surfaces, whether or not the set selects it or follows tangent
  chains (OCCT port patch 0260, mitcad#307): the rounding is one surface
  over both edges, cut by the notch's faces, as in the `.f3d` files'
  roundings. A wider notch ends the rounding.
- `continuity`: `tangent` (G1, default) or `curvature` (G2). A G2 set
  touches the faces where the G1 rounding of its radius would (the
  asymmetric one at its distances) and its quintic cross-section follows
  the faces' curvature there; `tangency_weight` (0.1 to 2, default 1)
  pulls it closer to the edge's corner (larger) or to the chord (smaller).
  MitCad's own shape; variable radius G2 sets are unsupported.
- Asymmetric and G2 sets are built from a chamfer at their contact
  distances whose bevels are replaced by blend surfaces (along circles
  between faces of revolution about their axis the cross-section turned
  about it, elsewhere Gordon surfaces through cross-sections and the
  chamfer's contact lines; the faces a chain ends on take the end
  cross-sections). Their chains must end on planar faces or close on
  themselves; a chain that meets another rounded edge at a vertex, or a
  non-planar end face, is unsupported. Rolling ball sets of the same
  fillet are built first.
- `rolling_ball_corners` (default true): false asks for setback corners
  where three or more rounded edges meet: the roundings stop 1.5 times
  the largest radius there from the vertex and an N-sided patch tangent
  to them and to the faces (OCCT's plate surface) closes the corner,
  named `corner(<vertex>)` (MitCad's own convention). An edge shorter
  than the setback is unsupported.
- Slots: `radius`, `chord_length`, `start_radius`, `end_radius`,
  `mid[k].radius`, `distance1`, `distance2`, `tangency_weight` (unitless),
  `radii[k]` for the first set, `sets[i].radius`, … for the others.
- New faces: `<fillet>:fillet(<edge>)` along every rounded edge (also the
  ones a tangent chain adds) and `<fillet>:corner(<vertex>)` where rounded
  edges meet.
- Rings: OCCT's roundings and bevels stop where they would run over the
  edge of a neighbouring face (the rim of a hole closer to a side than
  its radius). When OCCT fails and every selected edge is a whole circle
  between two faces of revolution about its axis with straight sections
  (planes square to the axis, cylinders, cones), the cross-section turned
  about the axis is cut from the body (convex edges) or joined to it
  (concave), running over what it meets; constant radius and chord
  length sets, and chamfers of every size (`geometry/src/ring_dressup.cpp`).
  The feature has a warning saying so.
- Second tries of OCCT's own rounding, before any of the above (mitcad#107):
  when it fails at the size asked, it is built again on the body with the
  pieces of its edges merged (a whole circle in two arcs, a line in
  pieces between the same two faces; the new faces carry the names of
  every piece), then with tighter tolerances of OCCT's fillet (knife
  edges, where the faces' normals are opposite), then with the faces of
  one surface that meet along an edge at the selected edges' vertices
  joined as well (a rounding's end cut by one face, not by the two halves
  of a pillar's full-rounded end, mitcad#343). A result OCCT's checker
  rejects only where the input body already was invalid, on faces the
  rounding neither changed nor touches, is taken as it is (stored bodies
  of imported designs are at times invalid in places); other invalid
  results are healed as before, never those of a second try.
- Edge overflow (mitcad#121, OCCT's fillet as patched in the port): a
  rounding wider than a face next to its edge along the whole edge runs
  onto the face beyond that face's far edge, or, where it cannot touch
  that face, rolls on the far edge; the narrow face vanishes (also all
  round a closed edge). It runs over several narrow faces in a row (a
  strip and a sliver beyond it) and over narrow faces on both sides of
  the edge, as long as the ball touching the faces it reaches clears
  those it passes; otherwise it rolls on the last edge before a face it
  cannot touch. Two roundings of the edges of a face narrower than both
  (their contacts on it cross) are one rounding over that face, from the
  face beyond one edge to the face beyond the other. Where a rounding is
  wider only along part of the edge, OCCT's rounding rolls on the far
  edge where its contact reaches it, and near an end of the edge it is
  cut by the face beyond, as before. Chamfers do not overflow.
- Overlapping roundings of opposite kinds (mitcad#235): where the
  roundings of a convex and a concave edge overlap on the face between
  them (a step narrower than the two are wide) and OCCT's fillet fails
  on that, the convex roundings are built first and the concave ones on
  that result (found by their edges' names): the concave ball rolls on
  the convex rounding, an S-shaped section without the step's face, as
  the `.ipt` files keep such steps rounded.

### chamfer

```json
{"type": "chamfer", "body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{…|…}"],
 "size": {"type": "equal_distance", "distance": 2}, "flip": false}
```

`size` is `{"type": "equal_distance", "distance": d}`, `{"type":
"two_distances", "distance1": d1, "distance2": d2}` or `{"type":
"distance_angle", "distance": d, "angle": a}` (0 < a < π/2). The first
distance and the angle (from that face) are measured on the first face of
the name (`E{<first>|<second>}`) of the first edge the set lists in a
tangent chain, or on its second face with `flip`; the chain's other edges
measure on the same side (the geometry kernel carries it along the chain),
whatever order their own names list their faces in.
The general form has edge sets with a reference face:

```json
{"type": "chamfer", "body": "F2.b0", "sets": [
  {"edges": ["E{…}"], "faces": ["F2:end(…)"],
   "size": {"type": "two_distances", "distance1": 5, "distance2": 3},
   "reference_face": "F2:side(c4[c3,c1])", "flip": false, "tangent_chain": true}],
 "corner": "chamfer"}
```

- `reference_face`: the face the first distance and the angle are
  measured on; every edge of the set must border it, and `flip` takes the
  edge's other face. Tangent chains as for fillets.
- `all_edges` (default false, mitcad#793): every edge of the body as it is
  when the chamfer is computed, as for fillets (no `edges` or `faces`,
  the only set).
- Slots: `size.distance`, `size.distance1`, … for the first set,
  `sets[i].size.distance`, … for the others.
- `corner` shapes the vertices where three or more bevelled edges meet:
  `chamfer` (default) is OCCT's corner face; `miter` runs the bevels on
  until they meet, with no face of its own (a corner of convex and
  concave edges is unsupported); `blend` stops the bevels 1.5 times their
  largest distance from the vertex and closes the corner with a patch
  tangent to them and through the faces' edges, named `corner(<vertex>)`.
  Where no three bevelled edges meet, `miter` and `blend` make the plain
  chamfer with the warning `the miter corner type shapes nothing here`
  (whether .f3d corner types change two-edge vertices is unknown).
- New faces: `<chamfer>:chamfer(<edge>)`, `<chamfer>:corner(<vertex>)`.
- Bevels of whole circles that run over a neighbouring face are built as
  rings, as for fillets.
- A failed bevel is built again on the body with merged edge pieces, and
  an input's own faults away from it are taken over, as for fillets.

### Face features: shell, draft, offset_face, delete_face, replace_face, split_body, split_face

These work on named faces of one body (`body`, `faces`). The plane, face,
body or sketch curves a feature works against (`plane`, `target`, `tool`)
is a [reference](#references-to-geometry): a plane (`"yz"`, `"F5"`, a
fixed plane), a face `{"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(…)"}`, a body
`{"body": "F4.b0"}` or sketch curves `{"sketch": "F6", "curves": ["c1",
"c3"]}`. Two fields go with it: `offset` (optional, a slot) moves a plane,
not a face, along its normal; `direction` (split body and split face,
optional) is the direction sketch curves are swept along, the sketch
normal by default.

```json
{"type": "shell", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"], "inside": 2, "outside": 0,
 "tangent_chain": true, "rounded": false}
```

Shell: the `faces` are removed (none: a closed void); the wall runs
`inside` into and `outside` out of the surface (at least one, not
negative). `tangent_chain` (default true) also removes faces tangent to a
removed one; `rounded` rounds the outer corners. The outside of the wall
keeps the face names; the inside is `<shell>:offset(<face>)` and the end
of the wall where a removed face was `<shell>:offset_cap(<face>)`. A face
whose surface is only C0 continuous (a B-spline with a crease in its
parametrisation, as imported bodies have them) is split at the creases
first, so its wall comes in pieces (`#k`) under the face's name. A face
that vanishes at the wall's thickness (a strip narrower, or a convex
rounding tighter, than the wall) has no inside face: the insides of the
faces beside it meet (mitcad#172, the OCCT port's patch 0100). One that
vanishes only in parts still makes the shell fail, and so does a wall
the kernel cannot close (an open face ending smoothly in a kept one,
without the tangent chain), which before came back as the body itself.

```json
{"type": "draft", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:side(c1[c4,c2])"],
 "plane": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:start(…)"}, "angle": 0.0873,
 "symmetric": false, "angle2": null, "flip": false, "tangent_chain": true}
```

Draft with a fixed plane (a plane or a planar face): the faces turn about
their intersection with it by `angle` (|a| < π/2, not zero). The pull
direction is the plane's normal, or from a face into its material; `flip`
reverses it. A positive angle removes material on the pull side, so a
side face drafted about the bottom face leans in towards the top.
`symmetric` drafts both sides of the plane by `angle`, `angle2` sets the
other side's angle: the faces are split at the plane (pieces `#k`) and
each side narrows away from it. Without `tangent_chain`, a face tangent
to a drafted one is unsupported. Parting line drafts are not modelled.

```json
{"type": "offset_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"], "distance": 5}
{"type": "delete_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F3:fillet(E{…})"]}
{"type": "replace_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"],
 "target": {"origin": [0, 0, 25], "normal": [0, 0, 1]}, "tangent_chain": true}
{"type": "replace_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"], "target": {"body": "F4.b0"}}
```

Offset face (also Press Pull on a face): the faces move along their
normals, positive out of the material; the neighbouring faces extend or
shorten along their own surfaces; the faces keep their names.

Delete face removes the faces and extends the neighbours until they close
the gap, failing when they cannot.

Replace face replaces faces of any surface type with a target: a plane, a
face of a body (any surface type; a face of the body itself works too) or
a body (all its faces, such as a surface body; not the body itself).

- The neighbours extend or shorten along their own surfaces to it; the
  new face is `<feature>:replace(<face>)` (pieces `#k`) and the
  neighbours keep their names.
- Planar faces onto a plane or a planar face move there. Otherwise the
  region between the faces and the target, closed by the neighbours
  continued along their surfaces and by the target (when it is one face)
  continued along its own, is added to or removed from the body;
  B-splines continue by extrapolation, so their results are close, not
  exact.
- MitCad's own rules: the target need not cover the faces' neighbourhood
  (it is continued); a face with the target on both sides goes to the
  nearer side (the smaller region); a region that would reach past the
  body's other faces does not count (`the target passes beyond the other
  faces of the body`).
- The tangent chain also replaces faces tangent to the replaced ones,
  such as the straight sides of a slot with its round end; replacing only
  the round end needs `"tangent_chain": false`.
- Other failures: `the target does not meet the body where the faces
  are`, `the target splits the body`, `face … could not be replaced` (the
  target does not reach all of it) and, for planar faces onto a plane,
  `the target is perpendicular to face …`.

```json
{"type": "split_body", "bodies": ["F2.b0"], "tool": "yz", "offset": 20, "extend": true}
{"type": "split_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:end(…)"], "tool": {"sketch": "F6"},
 "direction": [0, 0, 1], "extend": true}
```

Split body cuts each body with a plane, a face (with `extend`, the
default, grown along its surface: planes, cylinders, cones and spheres),
a body or sketch curves; a body the tool does not divide fails it. The
pieces come in order along a planar tool's normal (else in geometric
order): the first keeps the body (uid and name), the others are new
bodies of the split (`<split>.b0`, …, named `Body<n>`); later evaluations
keep the pieces' ids ([Body ids of a split's pieces](#body-ids-of-a-splits-pieces)). The cut faces are
`<split>:split` (`<split>:split(<tool face>)` for a face or body tool)
and faces cut in two get `#k`.

`more_tools` (a list of tools like `tool`) divides the bodies by further
tools as well, one after another: each divides the pieces it reaches and
leaves the others, and one that reaches none fails. The cells are those of
all the tools at once; `offset` and `direction` belong to `tool`.

A body tool, or the body of a face tool, may be a body of another
component when `tool_links` names where it is seen, as a combine's tools
do ([combine](#combine)); it is read there, moved into the split's
coordinates and left as it is:

```json
{"type": "split_body", "bodies": ["F7.b0"], "tool": {"body": "F2.b0"},
 "tool_links": {"F2.b0": {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}}}
```

Split face splits the faces along the tool (the same kinds; sketch curves
swept along `direction`); the shape does not change and the pieces keep
the face's name with `#k`. Every face must be split.

### remove_body

```json
{"type": "remove_body", "bodies": ["F4.b1"]}
```

Takes the bodies out of the design (`RemoveBody<n>`): the features before
it keep their results, and a later feature that refers to a removed body
fails. A body is listed once. A listed piece of a split that the split no
longer makes after an upstream edit is passed by with a warning
([Body ids of a split's pieces](#body-ids-of-a-splits-pieces)).

### sweep

```json
{"type": "sweep", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F2", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"], "chain": true},
 "orientation": "perpendicular", "twist_angle": 0, "taper_angle": 0,
 "guide_rail": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c9"]}, "profile_scaling": "scale",
 "extent": {"type": "partial", "fraction": 0.5, "fraction2": 1}, "flip": false,
 "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "sweep", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F2", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, "end_scale": 0.5, "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "sweep", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F2", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, "guide_rail": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c2"]},
 "guide_rail2": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c3"]}, "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "sweep", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F2", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, "guide_rail": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c2"]},
 "rail_point": "plane", "operation": "new_body"}
```

A surface sweep (`"surface": true`, with `curves`): [Surface
modelling](#surface-modelling) (mitcad#455).

Sweeps, lofts, pipes, coils, ribs and webs: kernel inputs in
`core/model-base/src/sweeps.rs`, geometry in
`geometry/src/{path_sweep,loft,rib,spine}.cpp`. Fractions of a path,
revolutions and loft weights are unitless values. Examples:
`tools/cli/tests/f3_*.json`.

- `profiles`: regions of one sketch (touching regions sweep together,
  holes stay holes). The sweep starts where the path crosses the
  profile's plane (the crossing nearest to the profile), or at the path's
  point nearest to the profile; a profile beside the path is swept as it
  is placed against it.
- `path`: a [path](#paths). Along a fixed helix (a spiral stair's rail,
  mitcad#385) a perpendicular profile keeps its angle to the helix's axis
  as it turns about it (`tools/cli/tests/f3_sweep.json`, Sweep6); the
  helix and coil features instead keep their section in a plane through
  the axis.
- Where a path turns at a corner, the sides of the swept profile run on
  until they meet (a mitre); a profile of one closed edge whose mitres do
  not build from its seam is swept as its two halves (mitcad#385: an
  ellipse whose seam lies along the normal of the path's plane), and a
  swept solid must enclose a positive volume (a mitre whose sides fold
  through each other can pass the shape check).
- `orientation`: `perpendicular` (default; the profile keeps its angle to
  the path, without twisting about it) or `parallel` (it keeps its
  direction and only moves; where the path turns back through the
  profile's plane, the copies passing over each other are fused into one
  body).
- `twist_angle`: the profile's turn about the path over the swept length
  (right hand about the path's direction). `taper_angle`: positive
  widens; every side of the profile leans out by the angle as an
  extrusion's taper does, the outline offset by `s tan(taper)` at
  distance `s` (a circle on the path becomes a cone, a square stays a
  square: 5 degrees over 50 mm turn a 10 mm square into one of 18.75 mm;
  checked against the stored body of a reference model, 10650.14 mm3).
- `guide_rail`: turns the profile towards the rail and with
  `profile_scaling` `scale` (default) sizes it by the rail's distance
  from the path, `stretch` only towards the rail, `none` not at all. The
  rail point is chosen by `rail_point`. Twist and taper are ignored with a
  rail.
- `rail_point` (mitcad#469, with `guide_rail`): where the rail's point is
  for each place along the path. `plane`: where the rail crosses the plane
  square to the path there. At the profile that is the crossing nearest to
  the path; from there the sweep follows the rail place by place, each
  time to the next crossing onwards along the rail in the way it runs
  with the path (back along it before the profile), so a rail that
  crosses a plane more than once is taken in order, and the rail's
  direction does not matter. An end of the rail within 1e-3 mm (or a
  millionth of the path's length) of a plane counts as crossing it; a
  rail that does not reach the plane of every place of the swept part
  fails the sweep (`the guide rail does not reach the plane square to the
  path …% of the way along the swept part`). `fraction` (left out, as
  designs saved before the option have it): the point at the same
  fraction of the rail's length as the place is of the path's, taken
  into the plane square to the path. The two agree for a rail that runs
  evenly beside the path (a straight rail beside a straight path) and
  differ where the rail's speed along the path varies: an arc that
  bulges away from a straight path (`geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp`,
  `test_rail_plane`; the `.solidcraft` test design `sweep-rail-plane`).
  The `.f3d` and `.solidcraft` imports and the Sweep command take
  `plane`.
- `guide_rail2` (mitcad#464, with `guide_rail`): a second rail. The profile
  moves with its point where the first rail starts (the first rail's point
  in the plane square to the path), turns with the line across to the
  second rail and is sized by that line's length against its length at
  the profile: `scale` evenly about the first rail's point, `stretch` only
  along the line, `none` not at all. Each rail's point is chosen by
  `rail_point` (each rail followed on its own), in the plane square to
  the path (`geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp`,
  `test_two_rails_and_end_scale`, `test_rail_plane`).
  Rails that meet are an error.
- `end_scale` (mitcad#464, unitless, 0.01 to 100): the profile's size at
  the ends of the swept part, from 1 at the profile in proportion to the
  length run along the path, about the path (a circle on a straight path
  becomes a cone frustum; with `extent` the scale is reached at each end
  of the swept part). With twist and taper; refused with a guide rail,
  guide surfaces or a fixed binormal (they decide the profile's size).
- `guide_surfaces` (mitcad#157): faces the path lies on, `[{"body":
  "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}, …]` (every piece of a split face),
  instead of a rail. The profile keeps its place in the frame of the
  path's tangent and the surface's normal where the path runs, so it turns
  with the surface (a thread's profile swept along a helical edge of the
  thread's flank keeps its angle to the flank). A path on the faces
  (within 1e-4 mm) takes their normal where it runs; a path beside them
  (mitcad#161: a thread's crest guided by its flank) takes their normal
  at their points nearest to it. The orientation must be perpendicular;
  twist and taper are ignored. The path is usually an edge of the faces,
  or sketch curves on them. A sweep that passes over itself (a profile
  taller than a helix's pitch) is swept in pieces that do not, each from
  the profile placed in the frame where it starts, and the pieces are
  fused.
- `body_links` (mitcad#161): bodies of other components the path's edges
  and the guide surfaces are on, each with where it is seen, `{"F2.b0":
  {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}}` (an `OccurrenceLink`, as a combine's
  `tool_links`, [Geometry of other
  components](#geometry-of-other-components)): the body is read in its
  component and moved into the sweep's coordinates by the occurrences'
  placements at the sweep's point of the timeline. A link for a body
  neither the path nor a guide surface is on is refused; another
  component's body without a link fails the sweep (`body F2.b0 (from
  Extrude1) belongs to A; …`).
- `extent`: `{"type": "full"}` (default: the whole path both ways from the
  profile, once round a closed path) or `{"type": "partial", "fraction":
  f1, "fraction2": f2}`: f1 of the path's part beyond the profile, f2 of
  the part before it (`distanceOne` and `distanceTwo` in .f3d designs;
  left out, the whole part before it, none on a closed path, where f1 + f2
  <= 1). The Sweep panel shows them as Distance 1 and Distance 2
  (mitcad#795, `app/COMMANDS.md`), and writes 1 / 1 as `full`.
- A sweep's preview adds `sweep_path` (mitcad#795): `{"closed": false,
  "profile_at": "start"}`: whether the path is closed and where the
  profile lies on it as it is swept (after `flip`): `start` or `end` when
  that end of an open path lies in the profile's plane (the end nearer
  to the middle of the profile's bounds when both do), else `inside`
  (always on a closed path). Reported also when the sweep then fails
  (an extent the path cannot take); not for a body face as the profile,
  fixed curves or a surface sweep of curves only. Test:
  `f3_tests::sweep_previews_tell_where_the_profile_lies_on_the_path`.
- `flip`: runs the path the other way (`isDirectionFlipped` in .f3d
  designs).

Twists, tapers, end scales and rails sweep copies of the profile placed
along the path through a smooth loft: the path must be smooth, the orientation
perpendicular and the sweep not round a whole closed path (otherwise
`unsupported: …`). Sharp corners of a plain sweep are mitred; a corner
whose mitre does not build (a slight kink between path curves) is
rounded, or else the profile turns through it. A profile within the
modelling tolerance (1e-7 mm) of an end of the path is at that end:
`fraction` 0 with the whole `fraction2` sweeps only backwards from it,
and an extent that covers none of the path is an error.

Faces: `side(<segment>)` from each profile segment, `#k` pieces where the
path has several curves; `start(<region>)` and `end(<region>)`: with the
profile at an end of the swept part `start` is at the profile, otherwise
`start` ends side one (beyond the profile) and `end` side two, as for
extrusions. A sweep round a whole closed path has no caps. With the
`parallel` orientation, where the path turns back through the profile's
plane the copy there is a face of its own, `turn(<region>)` (`#k` when it
turns back several times).

#### A fixed binormal (mitcad#397)

`"binormal": [x, y, z]` (any length but zero; left out by default) keeps
a perpendicular sweep's profile at its angles to that direction instead
of to the path: its frame along the path is the tangent, `binormal ×
tangent` and the binormal made square to the tangent. With the binormal
up, a profile whose x is level where the sweep starts stays level and
square to the path all along a sloped path (the `.rvt` import's sloped
elliptical rail pieces), where without it the profile keeps its angle to
a planar path's plane. It is refused with the `parallel` orientation, a
guide rail, guide surfaces, a twist or a taper, and fails where the path
runs along the binormal or turns at a corner (`unsupported: …`: the
frames either side of a corner do not meet in a mitre). The geometry
sweeps the profile with the path's curves on the surfaces they sweep
along the binormal, whose normals give the frames
(`geometry/src/path_sweep.cpp`; `test_fixed_binormal` in
`geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp`).

#### A Frenet or auxiliary frame (mitcad#539)

`"frame"` (left out by default) sets how a perpendicular sweep's profile
turns along the path instead of keeping its angle to it:

- `{"type": "frenet"}`: the path's Frenet frame (its tangent, its
  principal normal towards the centre of its curvature, their binormal);
  the profile turns with the path's curvature. Along a planar path it is
  the default frame, except where the path's bend changes side.
- `{"type": "auxiliary", "curve": <path>, "curvilinear": false}`: the
  frame's normal points from the path to a curve beside it (an auxiliary
  spine, a [path](#paths)), so the profile turns about the path as that
  direction does; the curve's point is where it crosses the plane square
  to the path there, or with `curvilinear` the point at the same fraction
  of its length as the path's (the frame's normal then the direction to
  it, its tangent square to that normal). The curve runs the way the path
  runs (`flip` reverses both) and must stay apart from the path. Unlike a
  guide rail it never sizes the profile.
- `{"type": "constant_binormal", "binormal": [x, y, z]}` (any length but
  zero): the frame keeps that binormal exactly, its normal `binormal ×
  tangent` and its tangent the path's made square to the binormal, so the
  profile turns only about the binormal. Unlike the fixed `binormal`
  above (which keeps the path's tangent and makes the binormal square to
  it), the profile leans with the path where the path leaves the plane
  square to the binormal; where the path runs at right angles to it the
  two agree.

The geometry sweeps them as OCCT's pipe shell's Frenet, auxiliary and
constant binormal modes, approximated within 1e-7 mm (`geometry/src/spine.cpp`,
`geometry/src/path_sweep.cpp`; `test_sweep_frames` in
`geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp`: along a straight path a curve crossing
from one side above it to the other turns a bar a quarter turn, by either
rule; the OCCT port's patch 1030 corrects the second derivative of the
curvilinear rule's frame, which bent the pipe between its sections). A
frame is refused with the `parallel` orientation, a guide rail, guide
surfaces, a fixed binormal, curves, a twist, a taper or an end scale. The
FreeCAD import's pipes in the Frenet, Auxiliary and Binormal modes are
sweeps with these frames (the Binormal mode's binormal turned by the
pipe's own placement, in which FreeCAD sweeps it).

#### A body face as the profile (mitcad#543)

`"profile_face": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(r{…})"}` instead of
`profiles` sweeps a planar face of a body (as an extrusion's and a
revolution's `profile_face`): its bounded area with its holes, found by
its topological name on every recompute, its plane the profile's
(`Kernel::face_sweep`); the body is left as it is. Faces: `side(<edge>)` by
the edges' names in the body (an edge without a name by its index among
the face's edges), the caps `start(<face>)` and `end(<face>)` keyed by
the stored reference. Perpendicular or parallel, with a frame or a fixed
binormal; refused with `profiles`, `curves`, `surface`, a twist, a taper,
an end scale, guide rails or guide surfaces. A face that is gone, not
planar or of a mesh body fails the sweep (`geometry/tests/test_sweeps.cpp`,
`test_face_sweep`). The Sweep command does not open such a sweep (its
profiles are a sketch's); the FreeCAD import's pipes of a face are these.

#### Fixed curves of a surface sweep (mitcad#548)

`"fixed_curves": [...]` (the curves of a path's
[`fixed_curves`](#paths)) with `"surface": true` sweeps curves that no
sketch can hold, lying in no plane, into walls without caps, as a surface
sweep's `curves`: their chains (open or closed) along the path, faces
`side(fixed<n>)` by the curves' places in the list. The sweep starts where
the path meets the plane through the first curve's start square to the
path at its start. Refused with `profiles`, `curves`, `profile_face`, a
solid sweep, a join or cut, a twist, a taper, guide rails, guide surfaces
or a frame. The FreeCAD import's Part sweeps of a section in no plane are
these.

### loft

```json
{"type": "loft", "sections": [
   {"type": "profile", "sketch": "F1", "region": "r{…}"},
   {"type": "face", "body": "F4.b0", "face": "F4:end(r{c1})"},
   {"type": "point", "point": "F7"},
   {"type": "point", "point": {"sketch": "F3", "point": "p5"}}],
 "start_condition": {"type": "free"}, "end_condition": {"type": "point_sharp"},
 "centerline": {"sketch": "F9", "curves": ["c1"]}, "rails": [],
 "closed": false, "ruled": false, "surface": false, "operation": "new_body"}
```

- `sections`: two or more, in order: sketch regions without holes, faces
  of bodies (their outer boundary), and points (a point reference) only
  first or last. Sections of different numbers of edges are matched by
  the kernel.
- `ruled`: straight between neighbouring sections; smooth otherwise (two
  sections are straight either way; three circles give the parabola
  through their radii). A smooth loft through three or more sections,
  without end conditions or rails, is a piecewise cubic Hermite surface
  (the form of the stored lofts, checked against the bodies of the
  reference models `diff_loft_closed_*`: 9503.318 mm3 open and 12880.53
  closed for four circles of 10 mm 30 mm from the axis at quarter
  turns): every point of a section follows the curve through its
  matching points of the sections, a cubic piece between two sections whose
  tangent at a section is the derivative of the parabola through its
  neighbours (by the chord lengths between the sections' centres), the
  curve continuous in its tangent but not its curvature; at an end the
  first piece is the parabola that arrives with the inner tangent. The
  sections' edges are matched corner for corner (each section turned and
  reversed to lie as near as possible to the one before it).
- `closed`: from the last section back to the first, without caps and
  without point sections; three or more sections. A smooth closed loft is
  tangent where it closes: the same curves, periodic, which needs sections
  of as many edges, starting at corresponding points.
- `surface`: the loft as a surface, a sheet body of the side faces only (no
  caps; `isSolid` false in .f3d designs). A new body or a new component,
  never joined or cut; a sheet has no volume.
  Sections of sketch curves (`{"type": "curves", "sketch": "F1", "curves":
  ["c1", "c2"]}`, one chain each) loft a surface only ([Surface
  modelling](#surface-modelling), mitcad#455).
- `centerline`: a [path](#paths); keeps the sections at right angles to
  it on the way (the part of it between the first and the last section).
- `frame` (mitcad#543, only with a `centerline`): how the sections turn
  along it instead, as a sweep's [frame](#a-frenet-or-auxiliary-frame-mitcad539):
  `{"type": "frenet"}`, `{"type": "auxiliary", "curve": <path>,
  "curvilinear": false}` or `{"type": "constant_binormal", "binormal": [x,
  y, z]}`; the pipe shell through the sections then follows that frame,
  approximated within 1e-7 mm (the FreeCAD import's pipes through several
  sections in the Frenet, Auxiliary and Binormal modes).
- `orientation` (mitcad#547, only with a `centerline` and without a
  `frame`): `perpendicular` (default, left out) keeps the sections' angle
  to the centre line; `parallel` keeps their direction, as a sweep's
  parallel orientation: they only move along it (a pipe shell of a fixed
  frame, approximated within 1e-7 mm; the FreeCAD import's pipes through
  several sections in the Fixed mode).
- `start_condition`, `end_condition`: how the loft leaves its first
  section and reaches its last one. `free` (default) and `point_sharp` (a
  point section's default) impose nothing. The others set the takeoff:
  the derivative of the surface across the section, from the section into
  the loft, its length given over the span to the next section (the
  derivative by the parameter from 0 at one section to 1 at the other;
  checked against the bodies stored in the reference models `loft_*`,
  kept outside the repository in `MITCAD_F3D_MODELS`):
  - `direction` (`angle`, `weight`; a sketch profile): at `angle` from
    the profile's normal (the side of the next section), -90° < angle <
    90°; `weight` times the distance between the sections' centres long.
    The angle is measured along the loft: a positive angle leaves the
    first section outward (tilted out of the profile) and arrives at the
    last one moving outward, so the takeoff into the loft from the last
    section tilts inward (the stored lofts with the condition at the end
    section arrive outward; with it at the start, 1.2 % and at the end
    1.6 % off their volumes, the takeoff fields of the stored surfaces
    carrying a fourfold ripple of their own that is not reproduced).
  - `tangent` (`weight`; a face of a body): each face next to the section
    continued across its edge (G1); `weight` times the mean distance
    between the section's vertices and the matching ones of the next
    section long. `smooth` also with that face's curvature across the
    edge (G2).
  - `point_tangent` (`weight`; a point): a rounded tip; the surface leaves
    the point at right angles to the line to the next section's centre,
    each point of that section by `weight` times its distance from the
    line (a circle to a point is a paraboloid).

  At a section's corners the neighbouring faces leave along the line
  where their takeoff planes meet. Weights are greater than 0 and at most
  10. Slots: `start_condition.angle`, `start_condition.weight`,
  `end_condition.weight`, …

  With two sections and a condition at one end only, the free end
  follows a rule too: every point reaches it with the derivative `2 c -
  (c·d) d` (`c` the chord from the conditioned point to the matching one,
  `d` the takeoff's direction), the end of the parabola that leaves along
  `d` by `c·d`, so a direction or tangent of weight 1 straight across is
  that parabola. Above weight `w` = 1 the part along `d` is `c·d - (w -
  1) max(0, c·d - r / w)`, `r` the mean distance between the sections'
  corresponding vertices (one value for the whole section). That is `r /
  2` at weight 2, and below 0 for large weights, the curves then rising
  beyond the far section and coming back to it. The stored bodies of the
  reference models of weights 1.5, 2 and 3 straight across
  (`loft_direction_w15`, `_w2`, `_w3`, `_squares_w2`) have exactly these
  curves; tilted takeoffs above weight 1 follow the same rule, not
  checked against stored bodies. The curves across are cubic; with
  `smooth` quintic, their second derivative at the section that of the
  cubic along `d` and the neighbouring face's curvature across, and at
  the far section the cubic's. With more sections the free end follows
  the interpolation.
- `rails`: [paths](#paths) the loft's surface passes through. Each must
  meet every section (within 1e-4 mm, or 1e-6 of the sections' size) and
  run through them in order; beyond them it is ignored. A rail splits the
  sections' edges where it meets them (pieces `#k` of their faces). Each
  face is bent towards the rails by their distance from the loft without
  them, in shares that fall from 1 at a rail to 0 at the neighbouring
  rails along the section, with no slope at the sections' vertices, so a
  closed section stays smooth along its rails. A single rail moves every
  section with it (circles through one bent rail give the cylinder
  shifted along it). With end conditions too, the rails decide where they
  run.
- With end conditions or rails the loft is MitCad's own surface
  interpolation (the sections matched edge for edge, each face's rows of
  poles interpolated with the ends' derivatives); without them the
  kernel's through-sections. The importer accepts these lofts within
  0.5 % of the file's history, with a warning beyond 0.1 %: the stored
  bodies build round sections from polynomial approximations of their
  circles, and the stored loft surfaces between them are not round (lofts
  of circles with a direction condition are stored 0.3 to 1.2 % smaller
  than the same rule on true circles); with a rail and an end condition
  together the stored surface is fitted otherwise.
- Errors: a condition that does not fit its section (`direction` at a
  sketch profile, `tangent` and `smooth` at a face, point conditions at a
  point); end conditions of a closed loft; end conditions or rails of a
  ruled one; a centre line and rails; a rail that misses a section or
  runs through them out of order. Unsupported (`unsupported: …`): end
  conditions with a centre line, rails with a point section, rails the
  matching of the sections' edges does not keep at corresponding points.

Faces: `side(<key>)` from the edges of the first section that is not a
point, keyed by segment for a region and by edge name for a face
(`F7:side(E{…})`), `#k` pieces between sections of a ruled loft;
`start(<key>)` and `end(<key>)` at the first and last sections, keyed by
the region or the face name (`F7:start(F4:end(r{c1}))`).

### pipe

```json
{"type": "pipe", "path": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"], "chain": true},
 "section": "circular", "size": 8, "thickness": 1,
 "extent": {"type": "partial", "fraction": 0.75}, "operation": "new_body"}
```

- `section`: `circular` (default), `square` or `triangular` (equilateral);
  `size` is the circle's diameter, the square's side or the triangle's
  height (the volumes of the .f3d variant models: mitcad#25). The section
  is at right angles to the path at its start; a square's sides follow
  the path's plane, a triangle's corner points along the plane's normal
  (along the normal of a straight path) and the path runs through the
  middle of the triangle's height.
- `thickness`: makes it hollow, the wall inside the section (`isHollow`
  and `sectionThickness` in .f3d designs); less than the radius of the
  circle inside the section (half the side, a third of the height).
- `extent`: as for a sweep from the path's start; `fraction2` only on a
  closed path (the part before the start).

Faces: `side<i>` for the section's edges (`side0` for a circle; the
square's and the triangle's sides in turn), `inner<i>` inside a hollow
pipe, `start` and `end` as for a sweep.

### coil

```json
{"type": "coil", "plane": "xy", "center": [0, 0], "diameter": 40,
 "helix": {"type": "revolutions_and_pitch", "revolutions": 3, "pitch": 10},
 "angle": 0, "clockwise": false, "section": "circular",
 "section_position": "on_center", "section_size": 4, "operation": "new_body"}
```

- `plane`: an origin plane, a construction plane or a planar face;
  `center` in its coordinates. The axis is the plane's normal; the coil
  starts on the plane on the side the plane's x axis points to and turns
  counter-clockwise about the normal (a right-handed helix) unless
  `clockwise` (`isClockwise` false in .f3d designs).
- `helix`: `revolutions_and_height`, `revolutions_and_pitch`,
  `height_and_pitch`, or `spiral` (`revolutions`, `pitch`: flat, growing
  `pitch` in radius per turn). Height and pitch are measured at the
  section's centre.
- `angle`: a cone, positive widening as it rises (not for a spiral).
- `section`: `circular`, `square`, `triangular_external` (a corner
  pointing out) or `triangular_internal`; `section_size` the diameter of
  the circle, the side of the square or the height of the triangle (its
  radial extent). `section_position`: `inside`, `on_center` (default) or
  `outside` the diameter: the section's radial extent touches the
  diameter from inside, is centred on it, or touches it from outside. The
  section lies in the plane through the axis and moves by a screw motion
  (the helix's; the volumes of the .f3d variant models, mitcad#25), so
  the volume is the section's area times the path of its centroid.

Coils whose turns would overlap, or whose section reaches the axis, fail.
Faces: `side<i>`, `start`, `end`.

### helix

```json
{"type": "helix", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F1", "region": "r{c1}"}],
 "axis": "z", "pitch": 5, "revolutions": 4, "left_handed": false, "flip": false,
 "operation": "new_body"}
```

The profiles turn about the axis (a line reference, as a revolve's) while
they move along its direction (against it with `flip`): `revolutions`
turns (need not be whole) rising `pitch` each, right-handed about the
direction of travel unless `left_handed`. Every section of the result in
a plane through the axis is the profile turned there (a screw motion; a
coil's sections are instead fixed shapes at right angles to its helix).
A height is given as a ratio: `"<height> / <pitch>"` for `revolutions` or
`"<height> / <revolutions>"` for `pitch` (as the FreeCAD import and the
application write it). `operation` and `participants` as for extrude.
A profile longer along the axis than the pitch overlaps its next turn:
the tool is the union of the turns (mitcad#60).

`growth` (a length, optional; mitcad#59) widens the helix: the profiles
move that far out from the axis per turn (negative: in); a cone's angle
is the growth `pitch * tan(angle)`. `construction` (mitcad#83) says how a
growth is built:

- `"mitcad"` (the default for commands): the screw motion, the profiles
  also moved out along the direction from the axis towards their centre
  (across their plane's normal when the centre is on the axis) in
  proportion to the turn. Every section in a plane through the axis is
  the profile turned there and moved out, the same for every profile
  position, growth sign and direction, so the volume of a profile in a
  plane through the axis is its area times `2 pi revolutions` times its
  centre's mean distance from the axis. A narrowing that would take the
  profiles to the axis fails.
- `"freecad"` (what the FreeCAD import writes): as FreeCAD builds its
  conical and growing helices, so that they import exactly. The profiles
  follow the Frenet frame of a spiral of the same pitch and growth a
  hundred times as far from the axis, which FreeCAD raises along the axis
  by ten thousand times the profiles' height above the axis' origin when
  the growth is not positive (otherwise by that much of the origin's
  height); the profiles stay nearly in planes through the axis, and a
  narrowing helix whose profiles sit at the axis' origin runs the other
  way, as in FreeCAD.

A growing helix always stores its construction. A command without one
gives MitCad's, or keeps the construction of the helix it edits; in files
written before the field (by the FreeCAD import, mitcad#59) a growing
helix without one is FreeCAD's, so it keeps its shape. Without a growth
both are the screw motion and the field is left out unless given.

`start` and `end` (optional; mitcad#235), each `{"transition_angle": a,
"flat_angle": b}`, make flat ends as a coil's: over the transition the pitch
changes linearly between zero at the outer end and `pitch`, and over the
flat part the profiles turn without rising. They come in addition to the
`revolutions`, which are the turns at the full pitch: the start's flat
part comes first, then its transition, the turns, the end's transition and
its flat part. With ends a growth follows the rise (the profiles move out
by `growth` for every `pitch` they rise, so a cone's growth stays
`pitch * tan(angle)` and the flat parts keep their distance from the
axis), and the helix is built by MitCad's construction (`freecad` with
ends is an error).

`piece_shift` (turns, optional, at least 0 and less than a third;
mitcad#235) shifts the seams of the pieces the helix is swept in (a third
of a turn each): the shape is the same, but a boolean that failed or left
part of the helix uncut where those seams meet the seams of the bodies'
faces about the axis can work with them moved. The `.ipt` import tries a
coil as decoded once more with `"piece_shift": 1/6` when it does not give
the file's state. Without it, a join, cut or intersection that fails, or
whose result the geometry kernel's checker finds invalid, is tried once
more with the seams shifted by a sixth of a turn, and the feature then has
a warning that says so; a helix whose boolean works is built once, as
before.

A helix of one profile (of corners, no closed curve) touching one of the
bodies' cylinders about the axis (a thread), whose turns do not overlap
and whose seams are not shifted, is built as a B-rep whose faces each run
all the turns, as the bodies stored in files keep threads: each edge of
the profile sweeps one face (a B-spline surface whose rows of poles are
the helices of the edge's poles, an exact cylinder for a straight side
along the axis), the profile at both ends closing it (mitcad#235: the
sweep in pieces left a thread running out past the end face of a body in
many small faces, some of them slivers, that a later union with that
body's surroundings could not take). The booleans on such faces work on
the parts of them they meet (OCCT port patches 0591 to 0593: the cut of a
25-turn thread and the union with its part take a few seconds each).

A side of such a profile on a cylinder as long as the pitch (at most one,
more than one turn) makes the turns meet in one edge there, as the bodies
stored in files have them: no strip of the cylinder is left between the
turns, and a rolling ball rounds that crest. The solid holds a core beyond that side
(out to a tenth of the pitch, at most a fifth of the room to the bodies'
next cylinder beyond it; twice that at the side's middle), so that its
turns join along faces instead of touching along an edge; along the
bodies' faces on that cylinder the core lies where the boolean changes
nothing. Beyond those faces the core is cut away over the whole helix,
and the turns meet in an edge there too (a thread running out past a
blind bore's bottom into the material). For the booleans the faces are
split every third of a turn into pieces that share their surface, and the
face merge after the boolean makes each face whole again. When the core
cannot be cut away, the helix fails.

Other helices with a side on a cylinder (more profiles, closed curves,
overlapping turns, shifted seams, more than one side as long as the
pitch) are swept in pieces, a side
as long as the pitch moved 0.1 µm off its cylinder along the bodies'
faces there (the shifted seams' retry), and their straight sides along the
axis made exact cylinders.

Faces: `side(<segment>)`, `start(<region>)` at the profile and
`end(<region>)` (`geometry/src/path_sweep.cpp`).

### rib, web

```json
{"type": "rib", "curves": {"sketch": "F6", "curves": ["c1"]}, "thickness": 4,
 "thickness_location": "symmetric", "extent": {"type": "to_next"}, "flip": false,
 "participants": []}
{"type": "web", "curves": {"sketch": "F9", "curves": ["c1", "c4"]}, "thickness": 2,
 "extent": {"type": "depth", "depth": 10}}
```

- A rib grows from one open chain of sketch curves in the sketch plane, at
  right angles to the chain's chord, to its left (the sketch normal up) or
  with `flip` to its right; its thickness is across the sketch plane,
  `symmetric`, `side1` (along the sketch normal) or `side2`.
- A web grows from each curve (lines and arcs) along the sketch normal
  (against it with `flip`); its thickness is in the sketch plane, side 1
  to the left of the curve.
- `extent`: `to_next` (up to the faces of the participant bodies it
  reaches first, which must close it off; otherwise it fails) or
  `{"type": "depth", "depth": d}`. The result joins the participants (all
  bodies when left out); one that reaches none becomes a new body.

Faces of a rib: `side(<curve>)` along the curves, `wall1` and `wall2` (its
sides along and against the sketch normal), `tip0` and `tip1` at the
chain's start and end, `end` at the depth. Of a web, per curve:
`wall1(<curve>)`, `wall2(<curve>)`, `tip0(<curve>)`, `tip1(<curve>)`,
`start(<curve>)` in the sketch plane and `end(<curve>)` at the depth.

### emboss

```json
{"type": "emboss", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F3", "region": "r{t1.g0.c0}"}],
 "face": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}, "depth": 1, "mode": "raise",
 "participants": []}
```

Profiles of one sketch (a set, as an extrusion's; the glyphs of its texts
bound regions too) raised from a face by `depth` (> 0) and joined, or
with `"mode": "sink"` sunk into it and cut (mitcad#458,
`core/model/src/features/emboss.rs`).

- `face` a planar face: the profiles are extruded along the sketch normal
  from the face's plane (projected onto it when the planes are not
  parallel), out of the material or into it.
- `face` a cylindrical face: the profiles are wrapped onto the cylinder
  (`Kernel::wrapped_emboss`, `geometry/src/emboss.cpp`). The sketch plane
  must be parallel to the axis. A sketch point at distance `s` across the
  axis (from the line where the axis lies under the sketch) and `z` along
  it goes to the angle `s / r` about the axis, at `z`, from the radial
  direction towards the sketch plane (the sketch normal for a plane
  through the axis): lengths around the face are the sketch's, not
  projected ones. The profiles grow radially by `depth`: outwards on an
  outer face when raised, inwards when sunk; on a bore's wall the other
  way. A sink that reaches the axis, profiles wider than the
  circumference and a sketch across the axis fail.
- `face` a conical face (mitcad#473, `Kernel::face_cone`): the profiles
  are laid onto the cone by its development, the sketch laid against the
  cone along the generator under the sketch's origin. With the sketch
  plane parallel to the axis, a sketch point at `s` across the axis and
  `t` along it (from the origin's height, towards where the cone widens)
  goes to the distance `hypot(s, t + ρ0)` from the apex along the
  generator turned `atan2(s, t + ρ0) / sin α` about the axis (α the half
  angle, ρ0 the slant distance of the origin's height): lengths, angles
  and areas on the cone are the sketch's. The profiles grow along the
  cone's normals by `depth` (the top a cone of the same angle), out of
  the material when raised; on a countersink's wall the other way. A
  sketch origin past the apex, profiles past the apex or around the
  cone, and a sink that reaches the axis fail.
- No `face`: from the sketch plane along its normal (raise) or against
  it (sink).
- `participants`: the bodies joined or cut; empty for the face's body,
  or all bodies without a face. A raise that touches none, or a sink that
  cuts into none, fails.

Faces are named as an extrusion's: `side(<segment>)` the walls,
`end(<region>)` the top of a raised profile or the floor of a sunk one,
`start(<region>)` its foot on the face (inside the body after a raise).
The `.solidcraft` import maps SolidCraft's emboss onto it (a deboss
sinks), and the `.f3d` import the file's embosses (a negative depth
sinks; `core/import/docs/f3d-components.md`).

### Patterns

```json
{"type": "rectangular_pattern",
 "objects": {"type": "features", "features": ["F4"]},
 "direction1": {"axis": "x", "quantity": 3, "distance": 20},
 "direction2": {"axis": "y", "quantity": 2, "distance": 20, "symmetric": false},
 "distance_type": "spacing", "compute": "adjust", "suppressed_elements": [4]}
{"type": "circular_pattern", "objects": {"type": "bodies", "bodies": ["F2.b0"]},
 "axis": "z", "quantity": 4, "angle": 6.283185307179586, "symmetric": false}
{"type": "path_pattern", "objects": {"type": "faces", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F4:side(c1)"]},
 "path": {"sketch": "F9", "curve": "c1"}, "quantity": 4, "distance": 15,
 "distance_type": "spacing", "start": 0, "flip": false, "along_path": false, "symmetric": false}
```

Patterns, mirrors, combine, moves and primitives: modules `pattern.rs`,
`mirror.rs`, `combine.rs`, `moves.rs`, `align.rs`, `scale.rs`,
`primitive.rs`. Examples: `tools/cli/tests/f4_*.json`.

- `objects`: `bodies` (each copy a new body), `features` (their tool
  bodies combined with the bodies again by the feature's operation; only
  features that leave a tool, see [Adding to the API](#adding-to-the-api),
  and fillets and chamfers, below)
  or `faces` of one body (with planar caps where they meet the body they
  bound a boss, joined, or a pocket, cut). A pattern or mirror of
  features among the `features` (a pattern of patterns) stands for its
  originals at each of its elements (the original's too, not the
  suppressed ones): the copies go to every product of the inner and the
  outer elements, the inner one applied first. A feature that the
  `features` reach at the same place more than once (a mirror of a
  feature and of a mirror or pattern whose original it is) is copied once
  there. A pattern or mirror of bodies among the `features` (mitcad#547)
  stands for its bodies as they were before it, at each of its elements:
  the copies of those bodies go to every product of the elements, new
  bodies `<pattern>.b<k>` (k counting them in order) or, with `combine`,
  joined to the body (as the patterns before left it) where they touch —
  FreeCAD's MultiTransform of the whole body, each copy of the body
  scaled and skipped on its own. Such patterns cannot be mixed with
  features. Patterns of faces cannot be patterned again.
- Quantities include the original. `distance_type`: `spacing` between
  neighbours or `extent` from the first element to the last. A negative
  distance or angle goes the other way. A full turn spaces a circular
  pattern by angle / quantity, a partial angle by angle / (quantity − 1).
  `symmetric`: the quantity's elements lie on both sides of the original
  (⌊quantity / 2⌋ before it, the rest after; the spacing as without; a
  full turn is not affected). Path distances are arc lengths along the path; `start` (0…1)
  is where the original sits on the path; `along_path` turns the copies
  with the path. `start_point` (optional, `[x, y, z]` mm; mitcad#673)
  gives that place as a point instead of `start`: the path's point
  nearest to it (the `.f3d` import passes the patterned objects' centre,
  which the file keeps).
- A path pattern along a chain of sketch lines and arcs (mitcad#464,
  `"path": {"sketch": "F9", "curves": ["c1", "c2"]}`): the curves joined
  end to end as for a sweep's path ([Paths](#paths): from the free end of
  the first listed curve), the distances arc lengths along the whole
  chain. Each copy moves from the original's place on the chain to its
  own; with `along_path` it also turns about the sketch's normal through
  the original's place by the angle the chain's tangent turns between the
  two (at a vertex between two curves the first curve's tangent). Before
  the start and past the end the first and the last curve go on
  (straight, or around their circle); a closed chain (its last curve ends
  where the first starts, from the first listed curve's start) goes round
  again instead (mitcad#673). Ellipses and splines in the chain are
  refused.
- A path pattern's `combine` (mitcad#673) also takes `features`: the
  bodies its copies make (copies of a feature that made a new body, with
  the fillets and chamfers patterned with it) join, in one operation, the
  one body the patterned features made or changed, where they touch it;
  other patterns refuse `combine` with features.
- Signed distances (mitcad#447): a rectangular pattern's direction keeps
  one signed `distance` (spacing or extent); a negative one puts the
  copies against its axis, and a symmetric direction then has the copies
  of the positive distance (an even quantity's extra element on the other
  side). Zero is refused when there are copies. The panel's Flip of a
  direction negates the distance it builds (`-(expression)` for an
  expression); an edited pattern shows its stored signed distance with
  Flip off. The arrows in the view follow the sign. A direction the panel
  makes Symmetric hides its Flip (mitcad#545, app/COMMANDS.md *Pattern
  options*).
- `scale` (optional, a factor; mitcad#59): the copies grow (or shrink)
  element by element up to that factor: element e of n is scaled by
  1 + (scale − 1) · e / (n − 1) about the centre of mass of the first
  object (a feature's tool, the first body; not for faces) carried to the
  copy (FreeCAD's Scaled transformation after a pattern). In a pattern of
  patterns each copy of an inner pattern's copy is scaled about its own
  centre: the first original's centre carried through the inner elements
  too (mitcad#539). Not with fillets, chamfers or sheet features among the
  features.
- `scale_groups` (optional, with `scale`; mitcad#539): the copies of the
  originals, numbered j = p + P · e (p the copy's number among the P
  copies the patterns among the features make, the innermost pattern's
  element turning fastest; e the element), fall into this many runs of
  equal length: run g = ⌊j · groups / (P · n)⌋ is scaled by
  1 + (scale − 1) · g / (groups − 1) (FreeCAD's Scaled transformation of
  fewer occurrences than the copies before it). From 2 to n; the runs
  must divide the P · n copies. Default n: each element a run.
- `combine` (bodies, and patterns of bodies among the features,
  mitcad#547; mitcad#539): each copy that touches its
  original is joined to it, one after another (a copy that touches the
  original joined with the copies before), as a [mirror](#mirror)'s
  `combine`; the body keeps its id, a copy that touches nothing stays a
  body of its own. A pattern of that body then copies it with the copies
  joined to it (FreeCAD's MultiTransform of the whole body).
- `scale_copies` (optional, with `scale`; mitcad#542): the N copies the
  runs are counted over, run g = ⌊j · groups / N⌋ (default P · n, the
  pattern's own copies; at least those): a pattern inside a pattern of
  patterns whose runs an outer pattern's scale continues, so that runs
  may split the copies of the patterns among the features (groups up to
  N). Each copy of an inner copy is scaled relative to that copy: to the
  factor of its run over the factor of the inner copy's run, so that it
  ends up at its own run's factor whatever the inner pattern scaled it
  by (with the default N and at most n groups the inner copies are the
  first run, factor 1, and nothing changes).
- `scales` (optional; mitcad#542): more scales, `[{"scale": f,
  "groups": m, "copies": N}]` (groups and copies optional, as
  `scale_groups` and `scale_copies`); the factors of all scales multiply
  (FreeCAD's MultiTransform with several Scaled transformations).
- `scale_center` (optional, a point reference; mitcad#542): the copies
  are scaled about this point carried to each copy instead of the first
  object's centre of mass (FreeCAD scales a whole body's copies about the
  Body's origin).
- `skipped_copies` (features and bodies, not faces; mitcad#542, bodies
  mitcad#547: the body of a skipped element is not made, the others keep
  their ids): copies the pattern does
  not make, by their numbers j = p + P · e (as for `scale_groups`; never
  0, the original). Unlike `suppressed_elements` a pattern of the pattern
  still places the originals there: the inner pattern's copy left out at
  its own element and copied at the outer ones (FreeCAD 1.0 and 1.1 leave
  out the copies a Scaled transformation does not change).
- Elements: element 0 is the original. Along a direction the positions
  are 0, 1, …, q − 1; when symmetric 0, 1, …, q − 1 − ⌊q / 2⌋, then −1,
  …, −⌊q / 2⌋ (q elements again); a rectangular pattern numbers
  direction 1 first, element = k1 + n1 · k2.
  `suppressed_elements` leaves elements out (not 0).
- `compute` (features and faces): `adjust` (default) applies the elements
  one after another, rebuilding a feature's tool in place where the
  feature can (a primitive; an extrusion up to an object or through all
  bodies: its profile moved, its end found again; a face the feature
  itself took away, as a join up to a face of the body it joins does, is
  found in the body as it was before the feature), and skips elements that reach no body (a cut or join
  applies them in one boolean when that gives the same bodies: nothing
  split apart); `identical` and `optimized` move the feature's tool to
  every element and combine all at once; `optimized` with fillets or
  chamfers among the features copies the faces the features made instead
  ([Optimized: copying the faces](#optimized-copying-the-faces)). The
  pattern fails if no copy reaches a body. Consecutive features whose
  copies all join, or all cut, the same one body, with the copies of
  different features more than 0.1 mm apart (their boxes), are applied
  in one boolean (mitcad#855) when that gives the bodies and face names
  the features give one after another: no body split apart or new, each
  feature's copies in the result, and a face split into pieces near the
  copies of one feature only; otherwise one after another.
  `MITCAD_NO_PATTERN_RUNS=1` turns it off, for comparisons.
- `original_bodies` (features; default false, mitcad#74): the copies of a
  feature without participants of its own act only on the bodies that
  feature changed (still there), as in `.f3d` designs, where a pattern of
  a hole leaves another body its copies reach alone; by default they act
  on the feature's participants, every body without them. The `.f3d`
  import sets it for patterns and mirrors of features.
- Participants the feature itself consumed (mitcad#406): the copies act on
  the bodies there are at the pattern. A join that touched several of its
  participants merged them into the first of them it touched (the others
  are removed), and its copies join that body instead of the removed ones
  (a post joined to two rings of one revolve, `participants: ["F2.b0",
  "F2.b1"]`, leaves `F2.b0`, and a circular pattern of the post joins its
  copies to `F2.b0`). When the join made several merged bodies, a removed
  participant went into the one (of the participants before it) whose box
  after the join holds its box before it, the smallest such. A
  participant the feature removed otherwise (a cut that left nothing of
  it) fails the pattern with `participant F4.b0 of Extrude3 was consumed by
  Extrude3 itself`; one that a later feature removed with `body … does not
  exist at this point of the timeline`.
- Names: copied faces are `<pattern>:inst<element>(<original face>)`,
  e.g. `F5:inst4(F4:side(c1))`; their edges follow. A pattern of a
  pattern names its copies of the inner copies around the inner names
  (`F6:inst1(F5:inst2(F4:side(c1)))`). Copies of bodies are
  bodies `<pattern>.b<k>`, k = (element − 1) · (number of bodies) +
  (position of the body), so suppressing an element keeps the other ids.
- The `preview` of a pattern lists `elements` (see [Preview](#preview)).

#### Fillets and chamfers among the features

A `fillet` or `chamfer` may be among the `features` of a pattern or mirror,
