`features` (the carried features). The query does not recompute: a move
the plan allows can still be refused by the command's recompute (above).
Tests: `core/model-tests/assembly/src/reparent_tests.rs`, `cli.reparent_occurrence` and
`cli.reparent_occurrence_reopened` (real geometry, undo/redo, save/reopen,
a joint that goes to the root with its occurrence), `app.unit` (the
picker), `tools/ui-move-test.sh`.

## Autoselect profile groups

`{"query": "autoselect_profiles"}` returns the current profile groups for
Solid mode's Autoselect box (mitcad#193):

```json
{"eligible": true, "sketch": "F3", "component": "C0",
 "projected": [], "drawn": ["r{c9}", "r{c11}", "r{c13}"],
 "hybrid": ["r{c1[c7,c3],c3[c1,c5],c5[c3,c7],c7[c5,c1]}"],
 "all": ["r{c1[c7,c3],c3[c1,c5],c5[c3,c7],c7[c5,c1]}", "r{c9}", "r{c11}", "r{c13}"]}
```

Only the final item of the whole history can qualify: an evaluated,
unsuppressed sketch with closed regions, no feature using the sketch and
the timeline marker at the end. A consumer of any of its profiles,
curves or points makes the whole sketch used; suppressed consumers and
consumers beyond the marker count too. The query never searches older
sketches. Otherwise it returns `eligible: false`, null `sketch` and
`component`, and empty group lists. The application controls Solid-mode
visibility and maps the component to its displayed occurrence.

The three origin groups are disjoint, and `all` is their union, with each
current region key once. Every segment of a region's outer boundary and
holes contributes its original curve's provenance. `reference` entities
(including unlinked projections) and entities in linked `projections`
are projected; other sketch curves and text contours are drawn. `fixed`
alone does not make a drawing projected. A region with both origins is
hybrid. Intersection segments retain their source curve's origin.

For a projected rectangle containing three drawn circles, the three
circle interiors are drawn and the surrounding rectangle region is
hybrid: its holes have drawn boundaries. Nested loops likewise produce
individual regions with their immediate holes, not one selection per
closed curve. Open curves and construction geometry add no candidates
on their own; an open curve may help bound a closed region where it
intersects other geometry.

This query neither changes selection nor creates features. The
application toggles each candidate against the actual current selection,
preserving unrelated items; hover only previews. Query again after edits,
undo/redo and timeline changes. Keys are current exact identities, not
cached or best-matched references; `profiles` lists the current identities
of all evaluated sketches when pruning stale application selection.

## Adding to the API

- A feature type: a module in `core/model/src/features/` with its
  definition struct (generic over the value form `P`), `map_params`,
  `FeatureInfo` and `Evaluate`, and one line in `feature_types!`
  (`features/mod.rs`). Its serde form is then its command and file form;
  the dispatch, the cache, undo, preview and the design file need no
  change. Add its section under [Feature definitions](#feature-definitions).
  When every value maps under its field's name, `map_params!`
  (`features/mapping.rs`, mitcad#586) writes `map_params` from the list of
  all fields, each `clone`, `copy`, `param`, `option`, `map` (a type with
  its own `map_params`), `with(helper)` or `phantom`, in the order the
  values are visited (parameter numbering depends on it); a mapping with
  other slot names or prefixes is written by hand.
- Patterns and mirrors of features: `FeatureInfo::tool_use()` returns the
  operation and participants of the tool body the feature leaves in
  `FeatureOutput::tool`; without it a feature cannot be patterned
  (extrude, revolve, hole, sweep, loft, pipe, coil, helix, rib, web and
  the primitives have it). `Evaluate::placed_tool(ctx, feature,
  placement)` optionally rebuilds the tool with the feature's own
  placement moved by a rigid transform, faces named after `feature`, for
  `adjust` (the primitives and the extrusions whose end depends on bodies); without it the stored tool is moved. Reading
  another feature's tool goes through `EvalContext::feature_tool`, which
  the recompute cache tracks by the version of that feature's result.
- A kernel operation: a `Kernel` method with a default
  `Err(KernelError::Unsupported(…))` (`kernel.rs`), a family bridge in
  `core/ffi/src/kernel/` with its C++ half in `core/cpp/bridge/`, and the
  geometry in `geometry/src/<family>.cpp`.
- A command or query: a variant of `Command` or `Query` in `mod.rs` (or
  of a family's command enum), a line in the tables above, and its class
  in `classes.rs` (see [Classes of commands and
  queries](#classes-of-commands-and-queries); a test fails without one).
  The enums are declared with `named_enum!` (`api/dispatch.rs`), each
  variant with its name on the wire before it (`"add_feature" =>
  AddFeature { … }`), which gives the variant its serde name and the
  enum its list of names, `NAMES` (mitcad#585). A family of commands
  with an enum of its own (components, joints, sketches, …) is one row of
  `Document::command_families` (its names and the method that runs it);
  every other name goes to `Command`, whose error for an unknown name
  lists its commands. A test checks that every name reaches its own
  family and that no name is in two lists.

## Sheet rules and base Face

`sheet_rules` owns fabrication parameters. A `sheet_face` refers to an earlier
rules feature and closed regions of one sketch in its owning component. Rule
features may be shared across components. Rules use ordinary numeric or named
parameter inputs; `allowance.k` is dimensionless, all other rule values below
are lengths. Editing a shared rule changes all of its consumers.

```json
{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"sheet_rules","thickness":1,
 "bend_radius":2,"allowance":{"type":"k_factor","k":0.4},
 "reference_side":"front","bend_relief":{"type":"round","width":1,"depth":3},
 "corner_relief":{"type":"rectangular","width":1,"depth":3}}}
```

```json
{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"sheet_face","rules":"F2",
 "profiles":[{"sketch":"F1","region":"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}]}}
```

Lengths must be finite and exceed the modelling tolerance, `1e-7 mm`; K must be
finite in `[0,1]`. Relief types are `rectangular`, `round` or `tear`. These are
stored defaults for subsequent sheet operations; base Face does not create a
bend or relief. With `front`, material runs from sketch offset 0 to `+thickness`;
with `back`, it runs from `-thickness` to 0 along the sketch normal. Face creates
new bodies; it does not join existing solids.

Face retains exact line, arc, ellipse and spline boundaries, holes and separate
islands. Adjacent selected regions form one solid while keeping their semantic
panel identities, also after later folded features, whatever curve they meet
along (an arc or a spline as well as a line; mitcad#242). Missing exact region references fail; Face does not bind to
the nearest profile. Initial panel slots follow canonical profile-key order.
Settled `panel_slots` in saved definitions retain removed references as
tombstones, so editing selection order does not reassign a panel. A solid's
body index is its smallest contributing panel slot. Semantic face names include
`F3:sheet_front(0)` and `F3:sheet_back(0)`; source curve aliases remain on walls.

A Face with `"body": "F3.b0"` is joined to that sheet in a panel's plane
(mitcad#242): its sketch lies on the front or back surface of a planar panel
of the body, it uses the body's rules, and its regions are added to that
panel's material through the thickness (one union, so the regions must
touch or overlap the panel; touching several coplanar panels is refused).
The added material has no panel identity of its own: its sketch curves are
the panel's boundaries (lineage), as a coplanar join leaves no seam.

```json
{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"sheet_face","rules":"F2","body":"F3.b0",
 "profiles":[{"sketch":"F4","region":"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}]}}
```

```json
{"query":"sheet_state","body":"F3.b0"}
```

The body query returns `body`, `owner`, `status`, hex `version` and
`shape_generation`, `rules`, `rules_version`, exact `panels`, `invalidated`,
`blockers` and textual `diagnostics`. Each panel has `id:{feature,slot}`, a
component-local sketch `frame`, and `region.loops`, each with named exact curve
segments. Omitting `body` returns an array of current sheet entries. A missing
or unavailable body returns `{body,status:"unavailable"}`. `status` is `valid`,
`invalid` after an operation without a sheet adapter, or `blocked` when a
failed operation retained geometry but prevents using it as valid material.
Invalidity takes precedence when both causes exist; `blockers` still reports
every responsible failed feature. `invalidated` names the first operation that
took the sheet meaning away; later operations on the invalid body do not
replace it.

`{"query":"sheet_rules","feature":"F2"}` returns
`{feature,status,version,rules}` with resolved numeric rules. An unavailable
rule returns `{feature,status:"unavailable"}`. Omitting `feature` returns all
available rule outputs. Both queries are available through MCP's read-only
query interface. Feature previews additionally report `sheet_states` from the
preview result; querying the committed document does not publish the preview.

Shape and sheet domains are one evaluated result, including cache restoration.
Ordinary Booleans, scales and face operations invalidate affected sheet meaning;
they retain the solid. An ordinary feature (or a base feature) that replaces a
valid sheet's body goes through the sheet-domain adapter first (mitcad#242):
where its result is still the sheet's material changed through the thickness of
planar charts (a cut, a hole, a mirror or pattern of them, a rounded or bevelled
contour corner), each planar chart's new outline is read from the result's
faces on its front surface, the material it lost is removed from the domains as
`sheet_cut` removes regions (new curves are generated curves of the feature,
`F<feature>/g<k>`), and the rebuilt sheet must have the result's volume, area
and centre of mass; the body then stays a valid sheet. Otherwise (material
added, a bend changed, walls not normal to the material, faces on the surfaces
broken by a dressup) the sheet is invalidated with that reason (`ordinary
modelling replaced this body and the sheet-domain adapter could not re-derive
its material: …`). An ordinary fillet or chamfer the domains cannot hold (a
countersink at a hole's edge, a rounded surface edge) is instead kept as a
`change` overlay of the sheet (`sheet_state.overlays`: `{"feature", "type":
"change", "placement", "removed"}`): every later sheet feature rebuilds the
solid from the domains and makes the material it changed again (its body
before it against its result, moved with the body), and the developed form
(Unfold, Refold, Fold, Bend, Flat Pattern) is refused, as for straight cuts.
`sheet_reference` names an edge such an ordinary feature named (a thickness
edge at a panel corner) by where it runs: the corner whose vertex it joins on
the front and back surfaces.

A pattern or mirror of features may repeat sheet features (a joined
`sheet_face`, `sheet_flange`, `sheet_cut`, corner rounds, chamfers and reliefs)
together with ordinary ones on one valid sheet body (mitcad#242). The copies are
made one after another in timeline order and keep the body a sheet: a flange
is built again on the copy of its boundary (the panel boundary of the current
sheet that the element's transform carries the original's boundary onto), its
bend turning to the side the transform carries the original's side to, its
offsets and width turned with the boundary; every other feature repeats the
material it changed (what it added joined, what it removed cut, both moved by
the transform), after which the sheet's domains are re-derived as above. A
straight `sheet_cut` is cut again from the copy of its sketch's plane along
the copy of its direction (re-derived, or an overlay where it crosses a bend),
and the copy of a feature the sheet keeps as a `change` overlay (an ordinary
fillet or chamfer, also on its own in the pattern) is kept as one too, the
original's change moved by the transform. Each
copy's domains and curves carry the pattern's identity, numbered per copy
(slots offset by 100000 for each). Copies of features on several bodies, or on
a body that is not a valid sheet, are made as for ordinary features (the
material they changed, without re-deriving the sheet). A rigid Move or Align transforms the domains, and
Component from Bodies changes their owner atomically. Occurrence placements do
not change component-local domains. Generic body copies and split pieces without
a sheet adapter report invalid sheet semantics. A failed operation blocks only
its intended sheet targets; suppression, rollback and Undo remove that failure
when it no longer applies. An automatic participant set is a dependency even
when empty. Assembly-scoped cuts track target BodyUid ownership and exclusions.

Paste New copies the sheet rules and their parameter-expression dependency
closure, including rules outside the component subtree. The copied rules are
independent by default and precede their consumers. Feature, sketch, body and
panel provenance references are remapped. Save/reopen recomputes definitions or
restores matching geometry and sheet deltas together; old designs without sheet
features retain ordinary-solid behaviour. Rules, Face and the folded operations
below are native model features. Production Unfold/Refold, Flat Pattern, sheet
Cut and DXF follow [the sheet-metal contract](../../../docs/sheet-metal.md).

## Folded sheet features

The five operations below use `add_feature` and `edit_feature`, ordinary
parameters, preview, Undo and persistence. They consume a valid native sheet;
an invalid or blocked upstream sheet is an error. Body references edit their
component definition, including all occurrences of that definition. Geometry,
semantic domains, ownership and body consumption publish atomically.

A boundary is `{panel:{feature,slot},curve:SheetCurveId}`. Sketch curves use
`{type:"sketch",sketch:"F2",segment:"c2[c1,c3]"}`; generated curves use
`{type:"generated",feature:"F4",slot:13}`. Optional `piece` and directed
`range:{first,last}` disambiguate a split reference. A missing or ambiguous
reference fails instead of choosing the first or nearest boundary. The graph
records full-side coplanar adjacency even when the kernel merges physical caps.

```json
{"type":"sheet_flange","body":"F3.b0",
 "boundary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
             "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"length":{"mode":"tangent","value":15},
 "position":"inside","offsets":{"start":3,"end":4},
 "relief":{"type":"tear","width":2,"depth":3}}
```

Flange requires a straight free material boundary. Length modes are `tangent`,
`inner` and `outer`. The straight length is respectively entered length,
length minus `r*tan(abs(angle)/2)`, or length minus
`(r+t)*tan(abs(angle)/2)`; it must remain positive. Positions `inside`,
`outside` and default `bend_line` place the stationary tangent at minus the
outer setback, minus the inner setback, or minus half the allowance. The
signed angle is nonzero and at most pi either way: a 180-degree flange is a
hem (mitcad#242), whose inner and outer virtual sharps do not exist, so
`inner`, `outer`, `inside` and `outside` refuse it. Two more references
(mitcad#242, the `.f3d` flanges) use the bend's outer extent
`X = (r+t)*sin(min(abs(angle), pi/2))`, how far its outer surface reaches
past the stationary tangent: position `side_tangent` places the
stationary tangent at minus `X`, so the outer surface touches the side
plane through the selected boundary (normal to the panel) and does not
pass it, and length mode `outer_tangent` measures from the plane touching
the outer surface normal to the wall, a straight length of the entered
length minus `X`. At 90 degrees they equal `inside` and `outer`. Where the
flange's trim of its panel reaches the seam between that panel and a bend
(a flange on an edge next to an earlier flange, or on the side edge of a
flange's wall), the trim goes on through that bend, developed, so the bend
ends where the panel now ends: a rectangular relief of the trim's depth at
the corner (mitcad#211). Position `edge`
(mitcad#211, the imports' flanges whose bend starts at the edge) places the
stationary tangent on the selected boundary, so the panel keeps all its
material. Positive bends move
towards the material front-to-back normal; signs do not change the rule's
reference side. Optional `radius` overrides the inside-radius rule. Thickness
and K always come from the referenced rules.

Omitted offsets are zero. Start/end are nonnegative distances along the
canonical axial direction `e`, chosen with `e cross outward = material normal`.
They leave positive axial width. Instead of offsets a flange may take
`"width": {"type": "middle", "before": b, "after": a}` (mitcad#242): it
covers `b` from the boundary's midpoint towards the start of `e` and `a`
towards its end. Such a width may pass an end of the boundary: the bend
covers the boundary only, and the wall continues past it beside the bend,
cut back at its root by the relief depth so that the bend's side stays
free (the `sheet_reference` answer for a straight boundary gives its
`axial` start and end, where these are measured from). An optional
`"root"` in the width sets that cut-back instead; `0` starts the
overhangs at the bend's moving tangent line, beside the bend's side (the
`.ipt` flanges' overhangs, mitcad#242); it must not be negative. Endpoints inside
material receive reliefs
outside the selected axial interval, opening through the moving side to its
free boundary. Explicit `relief` overrides the complete `bend_relief` rule.
Width is the actual positive clearance. Depth is penetration behind the
stationary tangent and must be positive (mitcad#242; it was at least one
thickness before, a convention rules of half a thickness do not follow). Rectangular relief has
a flat termination; round relief has a semicircular end and its depth includes
that tip, so depth must also exceed half the width. Tear uses the explicitly
entered positive-width, square-ended slit. Its contour is rectangular; the
policy does not invent an unreported gap or claim a zero-width solid cut.

```json
{"type":"sheet_bend","body":"F3.b0","moving_body":"F5.b0",
 "stationary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
               "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "moving":{"panel":{"feature":"F5","slot":0},
           "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F4","segment":"c4[c3,c1]"}},
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"port_mode":"tangent_ports"}
```

Omitted `moving_body` means `body`. On one body, `virtual_sharp` inserts the
finite allowance strip at a full shared coplanar seam and moves the unique
detachable branch. Separate bodies use `tangent_ports`: their already placed
full-span ports must agree with the requested radius, angle and material sides.
Both bodies must have the same owner and the same rule reference. Success keeps
the stationary BodyUid and consumes the moving body once; failure retains both.
An omitted port mode is resolved and persisted from this body relationship.
Radius and relief overrides use the Flange forms. Graph cycles, another path
to the stationary domain, incompatible ports or insufficient material fail.

```json
{"type":"sheet_bend","body":"F3.b0","moving_body":"F5.b0",
 "stationary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
               "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "moving":{"panel":{"feature":"F5","slot":0},
           "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F4","segment":"c4[c3,c1]"}},
 "angle":0.7853981633974483,"port_mode":"double","fixed":"stationary"}
```

Port mode `double` (mitcad#280) joins two parallel panels of separate bodies
by a jog: two opposite bends of `|angle|` each (more than 0, at most 90
degrees, inside radius `radius` or the rule's) and a straight panel between
them. The two straight boundaries face each other (their panels' material
on either side, outward directions opposite), cover the same axial interval
and their panels lie in parallel planes `h` apart. The first bend starts on
the `fixed` boundary (`stationary`, the default, or `moving`), whose panel
keeps all its material, and turns towards the other panel's plane; with the
middle radius `rm = r + t/2` the straight between the bends is
`(h - 2 rm (1 - cos angle)) / sin angle` long and the second bend ends
`2 rm sin angle + straight cos angle` from the fixed boundary, where the
other panel is cut back to (through the bends seamed to it along the cut,
developed, as a flange's trim does). A straight that would be zero or
negative (the panels too close for the bends), a second bend ending short
of the other panel, boundaries of different extent and panels in one plane
are refused. A moving body whose front surface lies on the other side of
the stationary body's takes the stationary body's front and back (its
charts keep their material coordinates; a moving body with bends of its own
is then refused). The jog's panel is `{feature, slot 0}`, its bends slots 0
and 1 of the feature. Between panels of one body the jog would close a loop
of material, which the sheet model does not develop: refused. Unfold, Refold
and the Flat Pattern develop the jog like any other bends.

A mirror or pattern of a face that made new sheet bodies (a `sheet_face`
without `body`, alone in its objects) copies each of those bodies as a new
sheet body of the pattern (`F<pattern>.b<k>`), its panels moved by the
element's transform (a mirror turns the material's side with the planes)
and renamed as the pattern's, slots offset by 100000 per copy, rebuilt from
the moved panels (mitcad#280). A pattern whose copies are all of one
straight `sheet_cut` cuts the copies clear of the bends' seams in one
operation and the others one by one after them (mitcad#288): the same
result as one copy after another.

```json
{"type":"sheet_fold","body":"F3.b0","panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "line":{"sketch":"F4","curve":"c1"},"stationary_side":"left",
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"position":"bend_line",
 "relief":{"type":"round","width":2,"depth":3}}
```

Fold requires a directed straight sketch line on the selected panel's front or
back surface (the back surface since mitcad#280: the line lies across the
thickness at the same place). `stationary_side` is explicitly `left` or `right` relative to that line.
The selected finite interval divides the panel into stationary material, a
finite allowance strip and moving material. Interior endpoints use the same
explicit relief policy. Existing connected bends move rigidly with their
branch; their original sign, radius and material parity remain unchanged.
The line may cross holes and cut windows of the panel (mitcad#288): the
bend's two lines then run through material in stretches, each stretch its
own piece of the generated curve (numbered along the bend's axis) with a
seam of its own, and the bend's strip keeps the openings.

```json
{"type":"sheet_corner_chamfer","body":"F3.b0",
 "corners":[{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
   "incoming":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c1[c4,c2]"},
   "outgoing":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}}],
 "distances":{"first":2,"second":3}}
```

`sheet_corner_round` uses the same corners and `radius` instead of `distances`.
Incoming/outgoing follow the directed material contour and meet at one vertex;
the first chamfer distance measures away from the vertex along incoming, the
second along outgoing. Optional `incoming_piece`/`outgoing_piece` disambiguate
source pieces. These operations currently require straight adjacent boundaries
and reject tangent-port corners. A corner may take a whole adjacent boundary,
to its far vertex (mitcad#242); a longer one is refused, unless the contour continues
on an arc beyond it: then a round takes that side whole and is tangent to the
arc (mitcad#280). All corners of one feature are found on its input sheet. Convex corners remove material; concave hole
corners add the bounded wedge and reduce the void. Oversized, degenerate or
ambiguous corners fail. Saved `corner_slots` retain removed selections as
tombstones, so reordering or readding a corner does not change its provenance.

`sheet_state` keeps its reference-frame `panels` projection and additionally
reports authoritative `charts`, `bends`, `joins`, `opened` and curve `lineage`.
Charts have a tagged panel/bend domain ID, exact bounded material curves and a
plane or cylinder embedding. Plane `front_to_back_sign` is `positive` or
`negative`; this is independent of chart winding and remains explicit when a
bend is opened by the geometry primitives. A failed or disconnected folded
result publishes no partial pieces and blocks only the intended input sheets.

## Sheet Unfold, Refold and Flat Pattern

`sheet_unfold` and `sheet_refold` are timeline features of a valid native sheet
(mitcad#208). They change the actual evaluated body between folded and
developed configurations and keep every panel, bend and curve identity, so later
features, cuts and a Refold work on the same named material.

```json
{"type":"sheet_unfold","body":"F3.b0","stationary":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "bends":[{"feature":"F4","slot":0}]}
```

`stationary` is a planar panel that stays fixed; `bends` is an explicit nonempty
set of distinct bends. Unselected bends keep their folded shape and move rigidly
with their panels. The labelled panel/bend graph is traversed from the fixed
panel across the registered tangent ports. A developed bend becomes the neutral
strip `[0, BA] x axial` in the tangent plane of the side it is reached from: the
front surface continues the neighbouring front surface, developed lengths are
neutral-surface lengths `|angle| * (r + K*t)`, and the panel beyond follows it
rigidly. A bend already open, a missing or stale bend record (its allowance no
longer matches the current rules), a stationary domain that is not a planar
panel, material not connected to the fixed panel through registered seams, or a
second graph path whose placement does not close (a non-developable cycle) fail
explicitly. Coplanar developed material of distinct panels and strips must not
overlap (shared seams are not overlaps); a self-overlap names both domains.
Folded configurations are checked for collisions by the constructed solid.

```json
{"type":"sheet_refold","body":"F3.b0","unfold":"F5",
 "bends":[{"feature":"F4","slot":0}]}
```

`unfold` is an earlier `sheet_unfold` of the same body. `bends` is the subset to
close and defaults to every bend still open by that Unfold. A bend opened by
another Unfold, or one already folded, is refused. Refold holds the panel that
the Unfold held, so it restores the folded placement exactly. It rebuilds the
cylinder from the bend's own radius, angle, K and material-side parity at the
current material; it never restores an old shape, so material edited while the
bend was open is folded with it. `sheet_state.opened` lists each open bend with
the Unfold that opened it (`by`) and its fixed panel (`stationary`). Nested and
partial Unfold/Refold operations are ordinary timeline features: suppression,
rollback, Undo and reopening give the configuration of the features before the
marker.

### Cut across bends

```json
{"type":"sheet_cut","body":"F3.b0","stationary":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "open_bends":[{"feature":"F4","slot":0}],
 "profiles":[{"sketch":"F8","region":"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}]}
```

`sheet_cut` removes material through the thickness inside closed regions
(mitcad#208, production form mitcad#209). `profiles` may come from several
sketches; each sketch must lie on the front or back surface of the developed
`stationary` panel, and a region whose key no longer exists after a sketch edit
resolves as for extrusions, all pieces of a region the edit split, with a
warning ([Profile references after a sketch change](#profile-references-after-a-sketch-change)).
Regions may have holes, and several contours may overlap. The listed
`open_bends` are developed while `stationary` stays fixed (bends already open
stay open). Every chart developed into that plane is trimmed in one operation
whose seams are the registered ports, so a contour crossing a tangent line
splits both sides of the seam at the same axial position, and a strip can keep
several material pieces under one bend identity. A contour ending exactly on a
tangent line removes material on one side only: that interval stops being a
seam and becomes a free edge of the other side, also at the seam of a bend
that is not developed, when the panel's boundary keeps one stretch of it
(mitcad#280). The input configuration is
then restored: charts keep their coordinates, so the cut is folded with the
material and survives a later Unfold/Refold, rule edits and sketch edits that
change which seams it crosses. Fragments of one boundary curve get distinct
`piece` numbers ordered by their midpoints.

A domain the profiles cover completely is removed with its ports; a removed
bend also loses its record and its open state, so a later Unfold or Refold of
it fails ("not a bend of this sheet"). When the cut disconnects the material,
every connected piece becomes a body with its own sheet state (its charts,
ports, bends, open bends and lineage): the first piece in geometric order
(centre of mass, then the lower corner of the bounding box) keeps the body's
id, the others become the Cut's bodies `F<cut>.b0`, `F<cut>.b1`, ... in the
same component. A Flat Pattern item stays with the original body id. A cut
that reaches a seam to material that is not developed ("open that bend for
it"), a sketch off the fixed panel's surfaces, or profiles removing all
material fail; profiles that touch no material give a warning.

With `"mode": "straight"` (mitcad#242) the cut is an extrusion's: the profiles
of one sketch, anywhere, swept along the sketch's normal (`"flip": true`
against it) from the sketch's plane as far as `"extent"`
(`{"type": "distance", "distance": d}` or `{"type": "through_all"}`), are cut
from the folded sheet; it has no `stationary` or `open_bends`. Where the result
is still the sheet's material changed through its thickness, the domains are
re-derived from it as for an ordinary feature (below). Where the cut crosses a
bend or an inclined panel its walls follow the sweep, which the domains cannot
hold: the cut is kept in `sheet_state.overlays` (its profiles, frame,
direction, extent and the volume it removed) and is cut again from the solid
every later sheet feature rebuilds. A rebuild in which it would remove more
material than it did (material added later in its way) is refused, and so are
Unfold, Refold, Fold, Bend and the Flat Pattern of a sheet with overlays (its
developed form does not exist).

```json
{"type":"sheet_cut","body":"F3.b0","mode":"straight","extent":{"type":"through_all"},
 "flip":true,"profiles":[{"sketch":"F7","region":"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}]}
```

The developed chart of an opened bend keeps its chart coordinates: `u` along
the neutral strip from its stationary-side tangent line (`u = 0`) to the moving
side (`u = BA`), `v` along the axis. A bend's `folded_embedding` in
`sheet_state` is its cylinder while folded, and the cylinder refolding would
build while holding its `u = 0` side while it is open.

### Corner relief

```json
{"type":"sheet_corner_relief","body":"F3.b0",
 "bends":[{"feature":"F4","slot":0},{"feature":"F5","slot":0}],
 "relief":{"type":"round","width":6,"depth":2}}
```

`sheet_corner_relief` (mitcad#209) relieves the junction of two bends. The
junction is found with a panel held and the bends developed into its plane:
the panel both bends leave (`panel` selects it when they share several). Bends
that leave no common panel (mitcad#125: their panels meet through planar seams,
other panels or bends) are developed together with every bend on the seam path
between them, holding the panel next to the first bend on the shortest such
path, or `panel`, which must then join one of the two bends ("joins neither"
otherwise). `s` measures distance from the tangent line through which the
development reaches a bend (the one on the common panel) into its strip; the
`s = 0` lines meet at the junction `J0` and the centrelines (`s = BA/2`) at `C`,
which does not depend on that choice. The relief is cut from all material in
the panel's developed plane exactly as `sheet_cut` does, then the input
configuration returns. `relief` overrides the rules' `corner_relief`:

| `type` | Removed region |
|---|---|
| `round` | disc of diameter `width` centred at `C` |
| `rectangular` | the crossing of two bands of width `width` centred on the two centrelines: for perpendicular bends the square of side `width` centred at `C` with sides along both bends' developed directions, otherwise the parallelogram with sides parallel to both bend lines and `width` across each strip (area `width^2 / sin(angle)`; mitcad#125) |
| `tear` | exactly the crossing zone `0 <= s1 <= BA1`, `0 <= s2 <= BA2`, the minimum separation of the two bend zones; no size |

`depth` is used by bend reliefs only. Relief curves are generated curves of the
feature (`F<relief>/g<k>`) and keep that provenance through later cuts,
Unfold and Refold. Parallel bends (no junction), bends not connected through
registered seams, a relief that removes a whole panel or strip (the flange is
too short for it) or disconnects the sheet, and one reaching a seam of a
third, folded bend fail. A relief that removes nothing gives a warning.

### Flat Pattern

A Flat Pattern is a derived document item, one per sheet-metal body, saved in
the design file (`flat_patterns`). It is not a timeline feature and never a
body: body lists, occurrences and physical properties do not see it, and all
occurrences of a component share it. It is evaluated on demand at the timeline
marker from the body's current sheet state, so edits made after it was set are
included.

```json
{"cmd":"set_flat_pattern","body":"F3.b0","stationary":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "x_axis":{"type":"panel_x"},"reference_side":"front"}
{"cmd":"remove_flat_pattern","body":"F3.b0"}
```

`set_flat_pattern` creates or changes the item; omitted fields keep their
previous values, and a new item fixes the body's first panel, the panel's own x
axis and the front side. It fails for a body that has no sheet state at the
marker or a panel the sheet does not have. Setting the same values again is no
undo step; each change and `remove_flat_pattern` is one undo step that
recomputes nothing.

Paste New and inserting a copy of a design (mitcad#125) copy the items of the
copied bodies, split pieces `F<cut>.b<k>` included, with their settings and the
fixed panel's feature mapped to its copy; each copy has its own item. A
component copied as bodies (made from bodies, or linked) has no sheet state
and no item.

```json
{"query":"flat_pattern","body":"F3.b0"}
```

Every bend is developed while the fixed panel stays where it is. The drawing
is in the fixed panel's material coordinates (its chart), so it does not move
with the body and does not depend on which bends the timeline has opened.
`reference_side: "back"` views the back surface: the drawing is mirrored
(`x -> -x`). A valid answer has `status: "valid"`, the source `sheet_version`,
`stationary`, `x_axis`, `reference_side`, `thickness`, the 3D `frame` of the
drawing on the viewed surface in the body's coordinates (`origin`, `x_axis`,
`y_axis`, `normal`), `regions` (the union of all developed charts: one closed
material region, exterior loop first, then holes, as exact bounded curves),
the developed `area`, the developed solid's `volume`, 2D `bounds`, `domains`
(`domain` and `to_flat`, each chart's isometry into the drawing) and `bends`.
Each bend has `bend`, signed `angle`, `radius`, `k_factor`, `allowance`,
`direction` (`up` when its inside is on the viewed side, otherwise `down`),
`centerlines` at `u = BA/2` and `tangents` at `u = 0` and `u = BA`, each line
clipped to the bend's remaining material. A sheet without a body or sheet state
at the marker gives `status: "unavailable"`; an invalid sheet, a stale or
inconsistent development, a self-overlap or a developed solid that does not
build gives `invalid`; a later failure that blocks the sheet gives `blocked`.
They return `diagnostics` and no `regions`, so nothing can be exported from
them. Omitting `body` lists every item. Repeated queries reuse the evaluation
while the sheet state, rules, settings and algorithm are unchanged.

```json
{"query":"flat_point","body":"F3.b0","flat":[2.8,10]}
{"query":"flat_point","body":"F3.b0","model":[3.5,10,-0.5]}
```

`flat_point` maps a drawing position to the body (`model`, on the front
surface), or a point of the body (inside its material) to the drawing (`flat`),
both with the `domain`, its `chart` coordinates and the material `depth` from
the front surface. A point outside the material fails. Both queries are
available through MCP's read-only query interface. The DXF export and what
the command UI asks follow (mitcad#210).

## Sheet-metal command UI and Flat Pattern DXF

What the Sheet Metal commands, the browser and the export use (mitcad#210;
the application's side in [app/COMMANDS.md](../../../app/COMMANDS.md#sheet-metal)).

### A Face with rules of its own

```json
{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"sheet_face",
 "profiles":[{"sketch":"F1","region":"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}],
 "rules":{"thickness":"2 mm","bend_radius":"1 mm","allowance":{"type":"k_factor","k":0.44},
          "reference_side":"front","bend_relief":{"type":"round","width":1,"depth":2},
          "corner_relief":{"type":"round","width":1,"depth":2}}}}
```

In `add_feature` and its `preview`, a `sheet_face` whose `rules` is a rules
definition (`type` `sheet_rules` may be left out) adds a `sheet_rules`
feature just before the Face and the Face using it: one undo step named after
the Face (`Add SheetFace1`), one recompute, the Face's `uid` and `name` and
the new `rules` uid in the answer. The preview evaluates both on a copy and
reports the Face. A saved Face always refers to its rules by uid; `edit_feature`
takes no inline rules (editing the rules is editing their feature, which every
Face using them follows).

### Picks as semantic references

```json
{"query":"sheet_reference","body":"F3.b0","face":"F3:sheet_side0(F2:sheet_curve(c2[c1,c3]))"}
{"query":"sheet_reference","body":"F3.b0","edge":"E{F3:sheet_front(0)|F3:sheet_side0(F2:sheet_curve(c2[c1,c3]))}","at":[5,10,0]}
{"query":"sheet_seam","body":"F3.b0","stationary":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},"moving":{"feature":"F3","slot":1}}
```

`sheet_reference` names what a face or edge of a sheet body picked in the view
stands for. Sheet faces are named by their domains: `sheet_front(<slot>)` and
`sheet_back` for a panel, `sheet_bend_front`/`sheet_bend_back` for a bend, and
`sheet_side<slot>(<curve>)` (`sheet_bend_side` on a bend) for the wall along a
boundary curve, whose key is `<S>:sheet_curve(<segment>)` for a sketch curve or
`<G>:sheet_curve(<slot>)` for a generated one. The answer has `body` and
`domain` (`{kind, id}`); a wall, or the edge between a wall and its own
panel's surface, adds `boundary` (the Flange/Bend form `{panel, curve,
piece?}`), `pieces` (how many pieces of the curve the panel has) and
`straight`; the edge between two walls of one panel adds `corner` (the
Corner Round/Chamfer form, incoming and outgoing in the contour's direction,
with pieces when the curves have several) and `straight`. When a curve has
several pieces, `at` (a point of the pick in the body's coordinates) chooses
the nearest; without it `piece` is left out and the feature reports the
ambiguity. The kernel joins the coplanar caps of panels that meet at a seam
into one face named after one of them: on a panel's surface, an `at` outside
the named panel's material that lies on another panel's surface picks that
panel. A face of another kind, a domain the sheet does not have or a body
that is no sheet at the marker fail. `sheet_seam` gives the two boundaries of
the registered seam two panels share (a coplanar seam a Bend can fold),
stationary first; none or several fail.

### Sheet bodies for the browser

`{"query":"sheet_bodies"}` lists every sheet-metal body at the marker: `body`,
`name`, `status`, `rules` and `rules_name`, the resolved `thickness`,
`bend_radius` and `k_factor`, the numbers of `panels`, `bends` and `open`
bends, and `flat_pattern`: null without an item, else its `status` (with
`area` and `bends` when valid, `diagnostics` otherwise), `shown`, `stationary`
and `reference_side`.

### Showing the Flat Pattern

`set_flat_pattern` takes `shown` (default: as before, false for a new item):
the application then shows the developed solid in place of the folded body. It
is a display choice saved with the item (`flat_patterns[].shown`): an undo step
labelled `Show Flat Pattern` or `Show Folded Body` that evaluates nothing
again (it is not part of the evaluation's fingerprint). The solid comes from
`analysis_shape` `{"shape":"flat_pattern","body":"F3.b0"}`, in the body's
coordinates (the fixed panel where it is folded); null for a pattern that is
not valid.

### DXF export

```json
{"cmd":"export_flat_pattern_dxf","body":"F3.b0","path":"flat.dxf",
 "unit":"mm","version":"r2000","tangents":false,"reference_side":"front"}
```

Writes the body's (uid or name) Flat Pattern to a `.dxf` file: the item's
settings, or those a new item would get when the body has none (its lowest
panel, the panel's x axis, the front); `reference_side` views the other side
for this file only. Only a valid pattern is written; an invalid, blocked or
unavailable one fails with its reasons and writes nothing. The drawing is made
from the evaluated outline and bend lines, never from the solid: each cut
contour once (no front/back duplicates), with consecutive pieces of one line or
circle that chart seams split joined again (a straight edge across a bend is
one `LINE`, a hole one `CIRCLE`); exact arcs, ellipses and splines are kept.

| Layer | Entities | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| `CUT_OUTER` | the exterior contour | 7 |
| `CUT_INNER` | holes and other inner contours | 6 |
| `BEND_UP` | centre lines (`u = BA/2`) of bends whose inside is on the viewed side | 3 |
| `BEND_DOWN` | centre lines of the other bends | 1 |
| `BEND_TANGENT` | with `tangents`: lines at `u = 0` and `u = BA` | 8 |

All four (five) layers are declared even when empty. Coordinates are the
pattern's frame (the fixed panel's material axes on the viewed side; `back`
mirrors `x`), so the drawing stays put when the body is edited, and are
written in `unit` (`mm` default, `cm`, `m`, `in`, `ft`) with `$INSUNITS` set.
`version` is `r2000` (default) or `r12`. The answer has `path`, `body`, `unit`,
`stationary`, `reference_side`, `entities`, `layers` (`name`, `entities`),
`bends` (`up`, `down`) and `bounds` (in the unit). `mitcad-cli export-flat`
runs it; MCP's `model_export` takes `format: "dxf"` with `flat_pattern` (the
body) instead of `sketch`. The `sheet_reference`, `sheet_seam` and
`sheet_bodies` queries are MCP read-only queries, and the sheet feature types
and `set_flat_pattern`/`remove_flat_pattern` are MCP model commands.

## Design policy

Every owner, the root and each component, has a policy of nine settings
of its own (mitcad#220, `core/model/src/policy.rs`,
`core/model/src/document/policy.rs`); nothing is inherited through the
hierarchy. A policy governs new actions only: changing it never deletes,
moves, detaches or recomputes anything, and what breaks it is reported as
a violation.

The general defaults allow everything (mitcad#421): every setting is
true, so a design is a hybrid of parts and assemblies, and the `part`
and `assembly` presets are the stricter choices.

| Setting | Allows | General default |
|---|---|---|
| `sketches` | creating or moving sketches directly into the owner | true |
| `features` | creating or moving modelling features directly into it | true |
| `components` | creating, inserting, pasting or moving components directly under it | true |
| `attach_to_others` | its sketches on another owner's face or plane | true |
| `attachments_from_others` | other owners' sketches on its faces and planes | true |
| `first_sketch_attaches` | its first sketch on another owner's face or plane, also when `attach_to_others` is false (mitcad#293) | true |
| `first_sketch_attachments_from_others` | other owners' first sketches on its faces and planes, also when `attachments_from_others` is false (mitcad#293) | true |
| `reference_others` | its sketches and features referencing other owners' geometry | true |
| `references_from_others` | other owners referencing its geometry | true |

- **Containment.** A sketch counts under `sketches` only; a child
  occurrence (also one a feature makes: Component from Bodies, a new
  component operation, a pattern of occurrences) under `components`.
  Assembly features that arrange occurrences (joints, as-built joints,
  joint origins, rigid groups, assembly constraints, occurrence moves,
  captured positions, patterns at points) are not modelling features.
- **Sketch attachment** is a sketch's `plane_link` to another owner: both
  the sketch's owner's `attach_to_others` and the other owner's
  `attachments_from_others` must allow it. It is not also checked by the
  reference settings. An owner's **first sketch** (a sketch of the owner
  that no other sketch or modelling feature of the same owner precedes in
  the timeline) may also attach when the sketch's owner has
  `first_sketch_attaches` and the other owner
  `first_sketch_attachments_from_others` (mitcad#293): on each side either
  of its two settings allows it. So under the `part` preset a new
  component can start with a sketch on another component's face. Later
  sketches follow the first pair only. When both settings of a side are
  off for a first sketch, the violation and the refusal name the first-sketch setting
  (`… does not allow its first sketch to attach to other components`,
  `… does not allow first sketches of other components to attach to it`).
  Reordering or deleting follows the usual rules: a sketch that stops
  being the first, and so breaks the policy, is a violation (refused by a
  command, listed and counted, never detached).
- **References** are every other link to another owner's geometry: linked
  projections, an extrusion's or revolution's `object_links`, a combine's tools in
  occurrences, a combine's or split's `tool_links`, a sweep's `body_links`
  and a construction plane's `links`.
  The consumer's `reference_others` and the source's
  `references_from_others` must allow them. An unlinked projection
  (`"linked": false`) keeps no link and is never refused. Joints and
  assembly constraints are not governed by the reference settings.
- Same-owner attachments and references are never governed.

**Presets.** `hybrid` (Hybrid in the application): the general defaults,
everything allowed; `defaults`, its name before mitcad#421, is accepted
as an alias. `part`: sketches and features, no components; `assembly`: no
sketches or features, components allowed. `part` and `assembly` refuse
sketch attachment in both directions, except first sketches (`part`: both first-sketch settings on;
`assembly`: `first_sketch_attaches` off, as it has no sketches, and
`first_sketch_attachments_from_others` on), and allow references in both
directions. A preset is only a set of values; a policy without sketches is
recognised as `assembly` whatever its `first_sketch_attaches`.

**New designs** (`Document::new_design`, the bridge's
`new_design_document`, File > New, MCP's `document_create`, a project's
`new_design`) start with the root and an empty component `Component1`,
active, both with the general defaults (mitcad#421): the first sketch or
feature goes into Component1, Component1 takes components, and a
component's sketches may lie on Component1's faces. Component1 is named
as any new component is (`Component1`, `Component2`, …; mitcad#711):
designs made before keep their `Part1`, as the name is stored in the
file. Neither policy is stored, as they are the defaults. `Document::new`
(and so the importers and `mitcad-cli`) has the
general defaults everywhere. Components get the general defaults when
made (`create_component` takes `policy`, a preset name or settings; the
application's New Component, the command and the browser's, gives none);
copies (Paste New, Make Unique, an unlinked insert) keep their source's
policy and an inserted design brings its root's; a new component that Move Features
into a Component makes keeps the link settings of the owner the features
came from, with containment allowed.

**Existing designs** (mitcad#421). The file format did not change. A
stored policy (`root_policy`, a component's `policy`: written whenever it
differed from the general defaults of its time, so every `part` and
`assembly` and every changed setting) keeps its values. An owner without
a stored policy reads the general defaults of now, everything allowed:
the root and Part1 of a design made before mitcad#421 kept the presets
they were saved with, and an attachment that broke the old defaults
(`attach_to_others` and `attachments_from_others` false) is no longer a
violation. Nothing is recomputed, moved or detached when a design is
opened; the policy governs new actions only.

**Enforcement.** Every JSON command and preview (`Document::command`,
`run_script`, `preview`, the bridge's `add_base_feature`) is checked:
the change is computed on a copy of the definition and refused, with the
reason, when it adds a violation, before anything is evaluated or
committed. Violations are counted per owner, setting, object and owner on
the other side, so editing an existing sketch or feature that breaks a
setting is allowed, a new link of it that breaks one is not, and removing
violations always is. Moves (`move_to_component`, also into an existing
component), pastes, inserts and new components are covered by the same
check: a move that would put a sketch where sketches are refused, or
change which owner an existing link reaches into one that refuses it, is
refused atomically. Importers that call the model directly replay a file
as it is and are not checked (`Document::without_policy_checks` around
commands they run). Activating an owner is always allowed; nothing is
redirected into another component, except a new component (below).

**A new component beside a part** (mitcad#292). A new component that would
go under an owner whose policy has `components` false, from
`create_component` (New Component, also the browser's on a part) or from a
feature's new-component operation (`add_feature`, and `edit_feature` when
the edit makes the component), is placed instead in the nearest owner
above it that takes components: along the owner's first occurrence path
from the root, its parent, then that one's parent, up to the root. The
new occurrence's transform composes the owner's placement in that owner
(at the marker) with the one asked for, so nothing moves; a feature
itself stays in its own component, with the same geometry, and only its
component's parent changes. The reply names where it went: `placed_in`
(that owner), `instead_of` (the refusing owner) and `placement_warning`,
the text the application shows as a hint (`Bracket does not take
components (its policy): New Component made in Assembly instead`, or
`…: Extrude3's new component made in …`). It is one undo step, and the
active component follows the usual rule (the new component when
`create_component` activates it). When no owner above takes components,
the command is refused as before, with that reason. Commands run without
policy checks (importers) place it where asked. Under the general
defaults every owner takes components, so this happens only below an
owner set to `part` or with `components` turned off (mitcad#421).

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `set_policy` | `component` (uid or name; the active one when left out), `preset` (optional, applied first), `policy` (optional: settings to change, the others stay) | `component`, `policy` |

`set_policy` is one undo step named `Policy of <name>` that recomputes
nothing.

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `policy` | `component` (default: the active one), `preset` and `policy` (optional: report as if set) | `component`, `name`, `active`, `policy` (the nine settings and `preset`: `hybrid`, `part`, `assembly` or null), `settings`: per setting in the order above `setting`, `allowed`, `count`, `items` (each `type`: `sketch`, `feature` or `occurrence`, `uid`, `name`, `component`, `component_name`, `others`: `uid`, `name` of the owners on the other side); `refusals`: for each blocked containment setting the reason a new object is refused |
| `policies` | | every owner: `component`, `name`, `policy`, `violations` (count) |
| `sketch_supports` | `component` (default: the active one) | `component`; `denied`: owners whose faces and planes its next sketch (made at the marker; while the component has no sketch or modelling feature before the marker, its first, and the first-sketch settings apply) cannot be attached to, `component`, `name`, `reason`; `denied_paths`: the occurrence paths (`O1/O4`, `""` for the root) that show them, with the reason; `sketches`: the reason the component refuses sketches, or null |

Violations list each object once per setting: for containment the
objects directly in the owner (not the whole subtree), for attachments and
references the consumer sketch or feature (not each projected edge), with
the owners on the other side. The `components` query includes each
component's `policy`, and the design file stores `root_policy` and a
component's `policy` when they are not the general defaults (missing
settings are their general default, true; a stored policy has every
setting except, when stored before mitcad#293, the two first-sketch
settings, which then read as on). The application leaves denied geometry
out of sketch-plane picking and its hover highlight
([app/COMMANDS.md](../../../app/COMMANDS.md), "Design policy").
`set_policy` is an MCP model command and the three queries are MCP
read-only queries. Tests: `core/model-tests/assembly/src/policy_tests.rs`.

## Equal spacing in sketches

An equal spacing (mitcad#221) keeps the successive intervals between
independent sketch objects equal: one constraint, without copies,
construction lines or chains of dimensions, and without binding the
objects' sizes or shapes. Code in `core/sketch/src/spacing.rs`; the
solver's `EqualSpacing` and `Spacing` equations (`core/solver/README.md`).

```json
{"id": "k4", "type": "equal_spacing", "anchors": ["p1", "c2", "c5", "c9"],
 "mode": "along", "direction": "c12"}
{"id": "k5", "type": "spacing", "constraint": "k4", "value": "d3"}
```

- `anchors` (at least three, in order): a point `p<n>`, a circle or an arc
  `c<n>` (its centre), a line `c<n>` (its midpoint). Nothing else is an
  anchor (no centres of ellipses, splines or boxes); two anchors for the
  same point (a circle and its centre) are refused. As with any
  constraint on an arc's centre, a moved centre leaves the arc's ends
  where the solve can keep them: a radius dimension keeps its size.
- `mode`: what equal intervals mean between A-B, B-C, C-D (successive
  anchors only, never every pair):

  | Mode | Equal quantity |
  |---|---|
  | `horizontal` | successive x offsets |
  | `vertical` | successive y offsets |
  | `along` | successive offsets projected on the direction of the line `direction` (kept as a reference, so the spacing follows the line when it turns) |
  | `point_to_point` | the distances between successive anchors (a chain; it may bend) |

  The directional modes compare signed offsets, so the stored order holds;
  nothing across their direction is constrained, and a point-to-point
  chain is not made straight. Alignment is a separate constraint.
- The common spacing is free unless one `spacing` dimension
  (`dimensions[k5].spacing`, positive, a value or an expression like any
  dimension) drives it: every interval is that value; no interval is a
  master and no other interval has a dimension. A driven `spacing`
  dimension measures it. At most one per constraint; removing it leaves the
  intervals equal with a free size; removing the constraint removes it too.
- Order: stored, and never sorted again by later geometry edits (a drag
  stretches the row as it is). A new or edited `horizontal`, `vertical` or
  `along` spacing is sorted along its direction unless `keep_order`; two
  anchors at the same place along it (within a millionth of the row) are
  refused, naming them, so the caller gives their order. A
  `point_to_point` chain takes the order given.
- Deleting an anchor's entity takes it out of the chain (the others keep
  their order and its neighbours become successive); a chain left with
  fewer than three anchors, or without its direction line, is removed with
  its dimension. No anchor reference is left dangling.
- Refused, with nothing changed: anchors that are all instances
  (originals or copies) of one sketch pattern (its spacing governs them:
  `sketch.edit_pattern`), and, like other constraints and driving
  dimensions, a spacing the other constraints already imply (redundant) or
  contradict (conflicting).
- A copy (`sketch.move` with `copy`) of all the anchors copies the
  constraint among the copies (a turned copy drops a horizontal or
  vertical one).

| Command | Fields | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `sketch.add_equal_spacing` | `anchors`, `mode`, `direction` (a line, for `along`), `keep_order` (default false), `dimension` (default false), `spacing` (a value), `driven` (default false), `text` [x, y] | the constraint and, with `dimension`, `spacing` or `driven`, its common spacing dimension (driving with `spacing`, else with the mean of the current intervals; driven with `driven`), in one undo step `Equal Spacing in Sketch1`; result as other edits, `made` [the constraint's id] |
| `sketch.edit_equal_spacing` | `constraint` (`k4`), and any of `anchors`, `mode`, `direction`, `keep_order` | the members, their order, the mode or the direction; what is not given stays, a directional spacing is sorted again unless `keep_order`; its dimension stays and keeps driving; undo step `Edit Equal Spacing in Sketch1` |

`sketch.add_dimension` with `{"type": "spacing", "constraint": "k4"}` adds
the common spacing to an existing equal spacing (measured: its first
interval), `sketch.set_dimension` changes it and `sketch.remove` removes it,
as for any dimension.

## Classes of commands and queries

Every command, query and feature type of this API has a class (mitcad#265,
`classes.rs`): what it works on besides the document's data. External
clients allow and refuse by the class, not by lists of names of their
own: the MCP server (`docs/mcp.md`, headless and live) runs the **model**
class and refuses the others.

| Class | What | Commands and queries |
|---|---|---|
| model | the document's own data | every feature type (`add_feature`, `edit_feature`), the sketch commands but `sketch.import_dxf`, parameters, bodies' attributes, components, joints, configurations, views, analyses, groups, policy, `undo`, `redo`, `merge_undo`, `recompute`; every query but those below |
| file IO | reads or writes files | `import_file`, `export`, `export_sketch`, `export_flat_pattern_dxf`, `export_drawing`, `sketch.import_dxf`, `insert_component`, `update_links`, `mark_saved` (the design file's saved state); the queries `dxf_info` and `compare_step` |
| remote | the library resolver's repositories | `update_library_parts` |
| internal | the application's own workflows | `begin_command`, `restore_command`, `discard_command` (a command panel's checkpoints), `clear_cache` |

Three commands are classified per call (`classes::command_class_with`,
mitcad#383): `create_appearance`, `edit_appearance` and
`set_render_settings` are file IO by name, because a texture or an
environment image may be read from its path, but a call that names no
file is the model's own and MCP runs it. A texture reads a file when its
base colour image or one of its maps has neither `data` nor
`"embedded": true`; a texture that is null or left out reads none;
`set_render_settings` reads a file when `environment.image` is a path
(null clears it). `classes::file_path_read(request)` gives the path, which
the MCP server names in its refusal.

`api::classes::command_class(name)`, `query_class(name)` and
`feature_class(type)` give the class (none for a name the API lacks);
`external_command_allowed` and `external_query_allowed` are the model
class. A `cache` query with `disk` also reads the result store's files: the
MCP server refuses that form. The module's tests read the command and query
names from the API's own enums and fail for one without a class, and for a
classified name the API no longer has.

## Body geometry in a sketch's plane

`{"query": "plane_geometry", "sketch": "F3"}` (mitcad#256,
`document/plane_geometry.rs`) lists the edges and vertices of the visible
bodies before the sketch that lie in its plane, in sketch coordinates:
what the sketch Dimension tool picks and the Point tool snaps to
(mitcad#258), each projected (`sketch.project`, linked) only when a
dimension or a point is made from it. The answer is an array:

```json
[{"source": "E{F2:end(r{…})|F2:side(c1[c4,c2])}", "body": "F2.b0", "kind": "line",
  "geometry": {"start": [-30, -20], "end": [30, -20]}},
 {"source": "V{F2:end(r{…})|F2:side(c1[c4,c2])|F2:side(c2[c1,c3])}", "body": "F2.b0",
  "kind": "vertex", "geometry": {"at": [30, -20]}}]
```

- `source`, `body` and `occurrence` are what `sketch.project` takes to
  project the item; `occurrence` (the occurrence path from the root, as in
  [Geometry of other components](#geometry-of-other-components)) only for
  a body of another component, which counts at each occurrence that shows
  it, moved into the sketch's coordinates, and only when the design policy
  lets the sketch reference that component's geometry. The sketch's own
  component's bodies come once, without `occurrence`.
- `kind`: `vertex` (`geometry.at`), or the sketch entity type the edge
  projects to, `line`, `circle`, `arc`, `ellipse`, `elliptical_arc` or
  `spline`, with `geometry` as the `sketch` query gives a curve's (a
  circle's or an arc's `center` is where a centre pick lies).
- An edge counts when every point of it is in the plane within the model's
  linear tolerance (1e-6 times the body's size, at least 1e-6 mm): a line's
  ends, a conic as a whole (an arc of a circle that leaves the plane meets
  it in two points only), a B-spline's poles. Edges the kernel names none
  for are left out. A vertex counts when its point is in the plane.
- The kernel lists a body's named edges (`Kernel::edges`), their curves
  (`Kernel::curves_of`) and its vertices with their names and points
  (`Kernel::indexed_element`); the coplanarity test is the model's. A body
  whose bounding box does not reach the plane is skipped.
- Visibility is the model's (the body and every occurrence on its path
  shown, as the `instances` query's `visible`); Hide Above Sketch only cuts
  what the view draws, so the edges in the plane stay in the answer.

### Out of the plane

With `"out_of_plane": true` (mitcad#866, the sketch Dimension tool) the
answer also lists every other named edge and vertex of the same bodies,
after the items in the plane (which come first, as without it). Each is
what `sketch.project` makes of it: projected onto the plane along its
normal, `kind` and `geometry` as above (a line as its line, a circle in a
parallel plane as its circle, a tilted one as an ellipse or a line, a
vertex as its point), and an edge along the normal (seen end on: a line
whose projection has no length) as `kind` `point` with `geometry.at`. Each
also has:

```json
{"source": "E{…}", "body": "F2.b0", "kind": "line",
 "geometry": {"start": [30, -20], "end": [30, 20]},
 "in_plane": false, "height": -10,
 "path": [[30, -20, -10], [30, 20, -10]]}
```

- `in_plane`: false (the items in the plane have no such field);
- `path`: where it is, for a client that picks it where the view shows it:
  its points in sketch coordinates with their height above the plane
  along its normal (negative below), from its start to its end: a line's
  two ends, 25 points of a conic, a helix or a B-spline (its poles when
  its knots do not fit), a vertex's one point;
- `height`: a vertex's height, a conic's centre's, else that of the middle
  of `path` (where a client shows a circle's centre).

The bounding box test that skips a body is not made in this form.

Tests: `core/model-tests/analysis/src/plane_geometry_tests.rs`.

## Angle dimensions

An `angle` dimension between the lines `a` and `b` (mitcad#296) measures
one of the four sectors the two lines' extensions make where they meet,
from 0 to 180 degrees. `reverse_a` and `reverse_b` say which: the sector
between the rays `a.end - a.start` and `b.end - b.start`, each reversed
where its field is true. The sector's angle is what the dimension
measures and the solver holds: a new value keeps the side, also one
closer to the other angle. Reversing both rays gives the opposite sector
(the same angle); reversing one, a neighbouring sector (the supplement).

- Sketch Dimension sends both fields, from the sector the value is placed
  in: `cursor - corner = s (a.end - a.start) + t (b.end - b.start)`,
  `reverse_a` = `s < 0`, `reverse_b` = `t < 0`.
- Without either field (sketches stored before, `sketch.chamfer`'s angle,
  commands that give neither), the dimension measures the angle between
  the directions when driven, and a driving one the angle between the
  directions or its supplement, whichever is closer to its value where the
  lines are when the sketch is solved, as before. One field alone counts
  as the other false. The `sketch` query and saved files give the fields
  only when the dimension has them.
- Clean Up Projections keeps the side when a line is replaced by one
  running the other way (the replaced line's field is flipped).
- The `.f3d` and `.ipt` imports set both from the file: the sector its
  value is shown in (`textPosition`) when that sector's angle is the
  file's value (within 0.001 rad), else the neighbouring sector nearer to
  the text when the supplement is (without a text position, the sector
  between the directions or a neighbour of it); without a value, or with
  neither angle being it, none (as before).

Tests: `core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_tests.rs` (`an_angle_dimension_*`),
`core/sketch/src/tests.rs`, `core/model-tests/sketch-refs/src/projection_tests.rs`,
`core/import/src/tests/constraint_tests.rs`, `tools/ui-sketch-angle-test.sh`.

## Tangent chains

`{"query": "tangent_chains", "body": "F2.b0"}` (mitcad#290) gives the
tangent chains of a body at the timeline marker: what a pick takes with
Tangent Chain on, so that the application's hover can show it before the
click (`Kernel::tangent_chains`, `geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/tangent_chain.hpp`).

| Fields | Result |
|---|---|
| `body` | `kind` `edges`, `chains`: the groups of two or more edges (names) that a fillet or chamfer with a tangent chain rounds together when one of them is selected |
| `body`, `faces: true` | `kind` `faces`, `chains`: the groups of two or more faces (each by its first name) that a shell, draft or replace face with a tangent chain takes together |
| `body`, `edge` (or `face`) | `chain`: the chain that holds the edge (face), or the edge (face) alone; `count`: its length. An edge or face the body lacks is an error |

- Every edge and face is in at most one chain; one in none stands alone.
- An edge chain is the dressups' own (`fillet`, `chamfer`): an edge
  continues into every edge that meets it end to end in the same direction
  (within 0.01 rad) and lies between faces at an angle, and on from those,
  until the chain closes or stops. It stops where the edges turn, as the
  fillet's contour does (mitcad#241), and where a concave edge meets a
  convex one (mitcad#439). A rounding with a variable radius,
  an asymmetric one or one of curvature continuous (G2) cross-sections
  follows the geometry kernel's own chain instead, which can be shorter
  (it also stops at a vertex where a third sharp edge meets). An edge
  between tangent faces (no dressup rounds it) is in no chain.
- A face chain is the faces connected through smooth edges (the faces
  meet at less than 0.001 rad along the whole edge), as the face tools grow
  their selections.
- The chains are worked out for the whole body at once, so a client asks
  once per body and looks each hovered item up; the application does so
  per command run (app/COMMANDS.md, `withHoverChain`).

## Join tolerance of imported designs

A design the `.f3d` import made (`import_f3d`) has a join tolerance: the
import's geometric tolerance (`geometric_tolerance`, default 0.01 mm,
mitcad#224, mitcad#298). The bodies it keeps match the file's within that
tolerance (mitcad#285), so a tool the file joins to a body can miss the
replay's body by a few micrometres, touch it only along an edge, or meet
it on a face so nearly coincident that the exact join's result is invalid.
With a join tolerance, the joins of the features that apply a tool
(extrusions, revolutions, sweeps, lofts, base features, primitives and
patterns; `Kernel::join_within`) are widened only where the exact join
fails:

- a tool that touches no target joins the targets within the tolerance;
- a tool solid the exact join leaves on its own beside a target within
  the tolerance is merged with it;
- a join whose result is invalid is tried again;
- a join that builds no solid of the targets, or leaves faces unused or
  loose beside its solids (OCCT cannot orient them: a tool against a
  stored body's rounded wall, mitcad#235), is tried again, and a fuzzy
  value is taken only where it builds solids of the targets with every
  face;
- a join that leaves more edges shorter than 1e-5 mm than its operands
  had (two vertices a micrometre apart kept apart, as where a sketch's
  tangent point is found a micrometre along a wall, mitcad#326) is tried
  again until it leaves no more.

Each takes the smallest fuzzy value that works (1e-5 mm, then 3 and 10
times each power of ten up to the tolerance). A join that works exactly
is the exact one, and tools farther away stay apart. The design file
keeps it as `"join_tolerance"` (mm; left out without one), so a saved
import recomputes the same; a design made in MitCad has none and its joins
are exact. Rust: `Document::join_tolerance`, `Document::set_join_tolerance`
(one undo step, part of the import's own). Tests: `core.model`
(`document::import_notes`), `core/import` (`tests.rs`), `geometry`
(`test_boolean.cpp`).

## Cuts within the join tolerance of imported designs

The cuts of the features that apply a tool in an imported design with a
join tolerance (above) are widened alike where the exact cut fails
(`Kernel::cut_within`, mitcad#235): a cut of a body that gives an error,
an invalid result, a result whose solids could not be built with all
their faces, or one with pieces of the tool left inside it (where the
section edges of neighbouring faces of a body kept within the tolerance
end micrometres apart and the tool lies on a face of the body, OCCT's
boolean leaves faces out or puts the tool's pieces inside) is tried again
with the smallest fuzzy value, as above, that gives a valid result of all
its faces. A cut that works exactly is the exact one. Tests: `core/import`
(`tests.rs`), and the named parts of mitcad#235.

## Joins that lose volume (mitcad#964)

A union never holds less than the bodies it joins, so a join of a
feature's tool whose result holds less volume than a target it merged
(by more than a millionth of the target's box, measured on the faces the
two do not share) is wrong, with or without a join tolerance: it is
tried again with the smallest fuzzy value from 1e-5 mm (up to the join
tolerance where the design has one) whose result merges every target and
loses none. Where none does, the exact result stands. Found on a reported
FreeCAD model: OCCT's exact join of a pad flush with two tangent walls of
the body (its faces merged by the earlier joins and cuts) took the pad's
overlap with the body away; a fuzzy value of 1e-5 mm gives the union. A
join that holds its targets is the exact one. Test: `geometry`
(`test_boolean.cpp`, `test_join_that_loses_volume_is_retried`, on that
model's two bodies from `MITCAD_GEOMETRY_CASES`; no synthetic layout
reproduced OCCT's failure).

## Combine's joins within the join tolerance; the .rvt import's tolerance

A design the `.rvt` import made (`import_rvt`, mitcad#397) has a join
tolerance too, the default geometric tolerance (0.01 mm): its rebuilt
elements meet in the faces the file keeps of them, which can lie on each
other only within a micrometre (a rail's sloped elliptical piece and the
level arc after it, their joint faces 1.2 µm apart). In a design with a
join tolerance a Combine's join (`Kernel::unite_within`) is widened alike:
a union whose result is invalid is tried again with the smallest fuzzy
value, as above, that gives a valid one; a union that works exactly is the
exact one. Tests: `core.model` (`document::import_notes`), `core/import-rvt`
(`tests/corpus/rvt_rails.rs`).

Two more repairs of the geometry kernel's results apply to every design
(mitcad#235):

- A cut that removes nothing from a body with a cylindrical or conical
  face whose seam steps (a face merged from two whose seams lay apart,
  joined along an arc of the circle between them) is tried again on the
  body with that face rebuilt with one straight seam, the boundary edge
  the seam crosses split in the neighbouring face too; the faces keep
  their names. OCCT's cut of a thread's helix removed nothing from such a
  bore. Test: `geometry` (`test_boolean.cpp`).
- A rounding's or chamfer's result whose vertex tolerances OCCT inflated
  far beyond what the vertices' edges need (above 1 mm and ten times it)
  has them cut down to that; where the result is not valid without them
  (a corner left open behind a tolerance of hundreds of millimetres) the
  rounding fails instead of handing the later booleans a body they build
  nothing from. Test: `geometry` (`test_fillet_results.cpp`).

## Extrude's automatic operation

Extrude previews can suggest an operation from where the tool lies
(mitcad#289, mitcad#575; the app: `app/COMMANDS.md`, *Extrude*). The
`preview` of an `add_feature` or `edit_feature` asks for it with
`"auto_operation": true` (optional, false by default). The application
asks it only for a new extrusion: an edited one keeps its stored
operation (mitcad#868), so it sends no `auto_operation` with an
`edit_feature`; the model still answers one that does:

```json
{"cmd": "add_feature", "auto_operation": true,
 "def": {"type": "extrude", "profiles": [...], "extent": {"type": "distance", "distance": -5},
         "operation": "new_body"}}
```

An edit uses the same response field:

```json
{"cmd": "edit_feature", "uid": "F4", "auto_operation": true,
 "def": {"type": "extrude", "profiles": [...], "extent": {"type": "distance", "distance": -5},
         "operation": "join"}}
```

The model evaluates the extrusion as a new body first (its tool does not
depend on the operation, and a Cut that reaches nothing makes none), tries
the tool against the visible bodies of the feature's owning component,
and then evaluates `def` as it is; the report is `def`'s, with

```json
"auto_operation": {"operation": "cut", "objects": ["F2.b0"]}
```

- `cut` with the bodies the tool goes into: the inside of a solid of the
  tool is inside the body (a profile on a body's face extruded into it);
- else `join` with the bodies it touches or overlaps (extruded away from
  the face);
- else `new_body` with no objects (nothing near, an empty design, hidden
  bodies, other components' bodies).

An addition considers bodies at the current marker. An edit considers the
bodies strictly before the edited feature's timeline position, regardless
of the current marker: its own result and later features' geometry and
bodies never count. Visibility is the document's current body visibility;
the active component does not change the edited feature's ownership.
The returned geometry and retained preview are the ordinary `def` preview,
including its stored participants or assembly Cut scope, even when the
suggestion differs. Computing that suggestion changes no stored definition,
marker, body result, revision or undo/redo step. A cancelled computation
clears the preview and leaves the document unchanged.

The test is cheap enough to follow a dragged distance: bodies whose
bounding boxes the tool's does not reach are apart without more
(`Kernel::enclosing_box`); the others get `Kernel::tool_contacts`, the
contact test Join uses (`geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/contact.hpp`)
and a point inside each solid of the tool classified against the body.
Only extrusion previews answer it; other feature types return their normal
preview without `auto_operation`. The suggestion is optional report data:
the application decides whether to follow it, and the stored definition is
always the one explicitly committed.

## BUILD: profile assemblies

The BUILD tab (mitcad#375; the app: `app/COMMANDS.md`, *BUILD*) places
library parts with a `build` block ([docs/libraries.md](../../../docs/libraries.md#build-parts)):
slot profiles, connectors and their nuts and screws, panels and linear
parts. Everything it makes is ordinary design content: components,
occurrences, features, joints and parameters on the one timeline,
editable with every other command. What is new is a part's **source**,
kept once in the design; the **derived part** a placed part's body is
made from; the **bound length**; and the commands and queries below.
Code: `core/model-build/src/` (placement rules, junctions, cut list),
`core/model/src/build/` (what the design file keeps),
`features/derived_part.rs`, `features/bound_length.rs`, `api/build.rs`;
tests `core/model-tests/build-frames/`, `core/model-tests/build-timber/`, `tools/cli/tests/build_*.json`,
`tools/ui-build-test.sh`, and on the generated parts library the ctest
`build.profiles` (`tools/cli/build-profiles-test.cmake`, with
`MITCAD_PROFILES_LIBRARY`).

### Sources

```json
"library_sources": [
  {"id": "S1",
   "library": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "<commit>", "label": "v1.0.0",
               "component": "p30x30-b8", "path": "profiles/p30x30-b8.mitcad",
               "license": "MIT", "authors": ["Mitcad contributors"]},
   "design": {"sha256": "..."},
   "build": {"role": "profile"},
   "supplier": "Motedis", "part_number": "P30_N8_B", "supplier_url": "https://..."}]
```

A design's top-level `library_sources` (left out when empty) holds each
library part that BUILD placed, once, whatever its configuration row or
length. Each source has:

- its `id` (`S1`);
- the library record (as a component's `library`, [Library parts](#library-parts));
  its `designation` is the library's pattern (`{L}` and the source's other
  parameters in braces are replaced by each part's values in mm), its
  `config` is left out (each derived part has its own row);
- `name` and `standard`, the component's in the library;
