- the part's design text (in a project, a reference into the project's
  store, like a base feature's B-rep, `{"sha256"}`; inline `{"sha256",
  "text"}` in a single-file design). A hand-written file may give the
  design itself as an object in `text` and leave out `sha256`; a design
  whose B-rep data was in the library's store is written as a single file
  with its data inside;
- the manifest's `build`, `supplier`, `part_number` and `supplier_url` as
  they were at that version.

A part without `build` can be a source too: the nuts, screws and clamps a
connector or a panel brings are derived parts of their own sources.

A source is read from the library when it is first used (class `remote`,
as `insert_component` with `library`). After that the design needs no
library to open or recompute. A source that no derived part uses any more
is removed with the last one, in the same edit; a source no derived part
has used yet (one a file brings along) stays until one uses it and that
one goes.

`update_library_parts` takes `{"source": "S1", "rev": "..."}` in its
`changes`. The source takes the other version's design and `build`, and
every derived part made from it recomputes, in one undo step (`Update
Profile 30x30 B8 to v1.1.0`). A change names a source or a component, not
both; one command changes sources or components, not both; a source's
rows are its parts' own (`build_edit`'s `config`). The `library_parts`
query lists each source as an entry of `parts` with `source`, `component`
(null), `name`, `library` (the record: `library`, `url`, `rev`,
`component`, `label`, ...), `url`, `rev`, `label`, `designation` (the
pattern), `build`, `supplier`, `part_number`, `supplier_url`, `config`
(null), `version` and `uses` (the derived parts).

The parts list (`parts_list`) has `supplier`, `part_number` and
`supplier_url` in every row: a BUILD part's from its source (the row's
own `part_number` first) and its designation with its values; an
inserted library part's as the library gave them when it was inserted
(a component's `library` record keeps them). A configuration row may
have its own `part_number` and `supplier_url`.

### derived_part

```json
{"type": "derived_part", "source": "S1", "config": "M6",
 "parameters": {"L": "d12"},
 "ends": {"a": {"angle": "45 deg", "tilt": "x"}, "b": {"angle": 0}},
 "operation": "new_body"}
```

The first body of a placed part's component (named `Part<n>`). To make
it, the model:

1. evaluates the source's design with the configuration row `config`
   (the source's default when left out) and `parameters` set ({the
   source's user parameter: a [value](#values)}; a cut-to-length part
   always lists its length parameter);
2. copies its visible bodies in;
3. cuts its ends.

- **Ends** (cut-to-length parts only):
  - `angle` is the cut's angle from square, from 0 up to (not including)
    90°.
  - `tilt` is the section axis the cut turns about: `x` or `y` of the
    source's section, the cut leaning towards +y or +x; `-x` and `-y`
    lean the other way.
  - The length is the part's outer length, its long point (mitcad#443).
    End A is cut at z = 0 and end B at z = L, each by the plane through
    the section's outermost edge on the long side (the side the cut leans
    away from, measured from the section's bounds, so an asymmetric
    section works too). The body never reaches past 0 and L; the short
    point is the section's width across the tilt × tan(angle) shorter (a
    20 mm profile of 500 mm cut at 45°: 500 on the long side, 480 on the
    short one). The cuts only take material away; the frames stay those
    of the length itself.
  - The cut is made inside the feature, not as a cut feature of its own,
    so the cut list reads it from the definition.
- **Names.**
  - The bodies are `<feature>.b<i>`, in the source's order.
  - A face of the source is `<feature>:part(<the source's face name>)`.
  - The end faces are always `<feature>:end_a` and `<feature>:end_b`,
    cut or not, so a sketch or hole on an end stays on it when its mitre
    changes.
  - The source's names do not change with its parameters (a profile's
    side faces are named after its section's curves). So sketches, holes
    and cuts on the part keep their place when the length or a mitre
    changes.
  - The face in `part(...)` is named in the source's own ids: they are no
    features of the design (references to `F7:part(F2:side(c1))` depend
    on F7 only, and copies leave the inner name as it is).
  - A square end's faces are the source's planar faces at z = 0 facing −z
    (z = L facing +z); the faces of the kernel's other names are kept.
- **Frames.**
  - Every `mount:<name>` joint origin of the source becomes a frame of
    the feature, `<feature>:mount(<name>)`, moved with the part's
    parameters (`end_b` follows the length).
  - A joint origin's `geometry` may name one: `{"mount":
    "F7:mount(slot_x+_1)"}` ([Kinds and frames](#kinds-and-frames)). Its
    origin and axes are then the frame's, not a face's middle.
- **Editing.**
  - The component can be activated and given features like any other
    component: a sketch on `F7:part(...)` and a hole, a cut.
  - Paste New copies the derived part with its own `parameters`. Move to
    Component, of its bodies and of its occurrence (another parent), keeps
    it.
  - Results are cached by the source's digest, the row, the parameters'
    values and the ends; they are not kept in the result store (the
    source is evaluated again when the design opens).
  - `parameters` take lengths (a number is millimetres). A length outside
    the `build` block's limits is a warning of the feature (the commands
    refuse it).

### bound_length

```json
{"type": "bound_length", "parameter": "d12",
 "from": {"occurrence": "O3", "geometry": {"mount": "F5:mount(slot_y+_1)"},
          "shift": {"x": "d9", "y": 0, "z": 0}},
 "direction": "z",
 "to": {"occurrence": "O4", "geometry": {"body": "F8.b0", "face": "F8:part(...)"}},
 "mode": "face", "add": 0}
```

`BoundLength<n>` is a feature of the component that places both parts:
the BUILD commands make it in the parent of the two occurrences. It owns
`parameter`, a **reference parameter** (kind `reference`, like a driven
dimension's, [Values](#values)). Its value is a length measured at the
feature's point of the timeline:

- The ray starts at `from`'s frame, an origin as for a joint, taken in
  the feature's component through the occurrences' placements there.
- The start is shifted along that frame's axes by `shift`, a set of
  values. BUILD writes there the parameters of the joint that slides the
  new part along a slot, so the ray follows the part when it is moved
  along the slot.
- The ray runs along the frame's `direction` (`z`, the default, `-z`,
  `x`, ...), or a vector `[x, y, z]` in the frame's coordinates (a part
  turned at an end).
- It ends on `to`, a planar face or a frame (the plane through its origin
  across its z axis). `mode` decides where:
  - `face`: the distance to the face;
  - `centre`: to the middle of the profile the face belongs to, half its
    section further;
  - `through`: to its far side.

  (The part is the body of the face, or of the derived part the frame is
  of; its far side is the farthest corner of its box along the ray.)
- `add` is added to the result: an overlap or a gap, and may be negative.

**Timeline order.** BUILD always puts the three features in this order:

1. the `bound_length`;
2. the derived part whose length the parameter sets;
3. the joint that places that part.

The ray never depends on the part it sizes. So moving the target
(dragging its joint), or moving the part along its slot, recomputes the
length.

**Failures and detaching.**

- A ray that meets nothing (its target behind the start or along the
  ray), a length of zero or less, or a target that is gone, fails the
  feature with the reason, and the reference keeps its last value.
- Two lengths bound to each other (each part's ray ends on the other)
  make a cycle, and the second one is refused when it is made. A length
  is bound only to a part placed before it in the timeline (its joint
  before the part's derived part): one placed later is refused too.
- **Detaching** (`build_edit` with a length value) replaces the reference
  with a dimension parameter of the same name, keeps its last value, and
  deletes the feature; the value given is then the length.
- A new bound length's `parameter` is given as a number, its first value:
  it becomes the feature's own reference parameter.

### Placement

**Where parts go (mitcad#394).** BUILD needs no component to be
activated first. Its commands place parts in the **BUILD host**: the
active component when its policy takes components, else the nearest
component up from it (along its first path from the root) that takes
components and can be edited, as the design policy puts a new component
beside a part (*Design policy*, mitcad#292). In a new design Component1
takes components (the general defaults, mitcad#421), so the host is
Component1, the active component, and nothing is redirected; a component
set to `part` still sends its parts up. When no component up takes
components, the active one (and the policy's refusal).
The `build_host` query names it. Every path (`at.occurrence`,
`length.bind.occurrence`) is from the host and every point and direction
(`at.point`, `at.direction`) in its coordinates; the joints and bound
lengths go into it. Bound lengths are assembly features, as joints are:
a component with the Assembly policy takes them. So no policy refusal
comes from where BUILD puts things.

A placed part is one component with one occurrence in the BUILD host.
With it come:

- its `derived_part`;
- the joint that places it;
- its `bound_length` features, when its length or size is bound.

The component records what BUILD made, in the design file too:

```json
"build": {"role": "profile", "source": "S1", "part": "F7", "joint": "F9",
          "bound": ["F6"], "added_by": null, "adds": [], "from": "b"}
```

- `added_by` is the connector component that added this one (a nut, a
  screw).
- `adds` lists the components and features a connector added (`"C5"`,
  `"F12"`): its fasteners, and the holes it machined into the profiles; a
  panel's clamps; a part's own end machining (`build_edit`'s
  `machining`).
- `junction` (a connector's only) is the `build_junctions` id it was
  placed at.
- `bound` lists the part's bound lengths (a panel has one per size).
- `from` (a part on a side or a rail, mitcad#417) is the reference its
  joint's slide is bound to: `a`, `b` or `middle` (*Side placements*).
- `tilt` (a part on a side tilted along its target, mitcad#444) is its
  tilt in radians, positive towards the target's end B (*Tilt*).
- BUILD reads these records. Other commands treat the component as any
  other, and a component without `build` is not a BUILD part.

**Joints BUILD makes.** Two frames that mate face each other: their z
axes are opposite, so every joint BUILD makes between two frames is
flipped (`flip: true`, `docs/libraries.md`, *Which way a frame's z
points*).

- **A profile on another profile's side** gets a `slider` joint along the
  slot (`slide_axis` `x`, the slot's direction). The joint is between the
  new profile's `end_a` frame (`end_b` with `flip`) and the slot frame,
  flipped:
  - its `position.tx` is the distance of the new part's frame (its
    centre line, for a profile standing on the slot) from the target's
    end A along the slot, bound to the placement's reference `from`
    (mitcad#417; kept in the component's record, *Side placements*
    below), so that the part keeps its place from it when the target's
    length changes:
    - from end A the offset is to the new part's **near face**
      (mitcad#394): `tx` is the offset plus the part's reach behind its
      frame (half the section for a profile: offset 0 is flush with end
      A), a number (or the typed expression, shifted);
    - from end B the offset is to its far face (far from end A: its face
      nearer end B): `tx` is `L - offset - reach`, an expression of the
      target's length
      parameter (`d12 - 65` for offset 50 of a 30 profile);
    - from the middle the offset is of the new part's middle from the
      target's, positive towards end B: `tx` is `L / 2 + offset - middle`
      (`d12 / 2 + 15` for offset 30 of a 30 profile, `middle` the part's
      middle from its frame);
  - without an offset the click places it, and its reference and offset
    are stored as if typed (see *Side placements* below);
  - its `angle` is the rotation about the axis: 0, 90, 180 or 270°;
  - the part can be dragged along the slot, as on a T-nut.
  - A part that is not a profile (a rail, a plate) mounts with its first
    frame of kind `slot`, `face` or `hole` the same way.
- **A profile on an end** gets a `rigid` joint between its `end_a` (or
  `end_b`) and the target's end frame, flipped. Its `angle` is the
  rotation. Straight, the new profile continues the target on its axis.
  Turned (a corner, *End placements* below), the target's frame has a
  `frame_override` whose z is the new direction (in the target's
  coordinates), whose x is the end frame's first axis not along it, and
  whose `shift` (along the turned frame's axes) aligns the corner; the
  shift moves with the end frame, so the corner follows the target's
  length. A bound length's ray starts at the shifted frame (its `shift`
  in the end frame's axes).
- **The first part,** on a plane, a point or a face, gets a `rigid` joint
  to that geometry, flipped, with a `frame_override` origin at `point`;
  without `at.geometry` it has no joint and is grounded at `at.point`
  (the origin when left out; the app's Enter without a pick), along the
  host's +Z. `at.direction` (mitcad#394; the app's X, Y and Z buttons)
  turns it: grounded, its axis runs along it; on a plane or face the
  joint's `frame_override` turns the frame's z to it (its first axis that
  is not along it keeps the roll), so the part lies on an XY pick along
  X or Y from the click. The picked geometry may be the host's own (its
  origin planes, construction planes and faces) or any occurrence's
  under it, resolved through the occurrence path as joints resolve it.
- **A part that moves on another** (`linear.mate`: a carriage on its
  rail) gets the `mate`'s joint (`joint`, `axis`; slider by default)
  between its `mate.frame` and the target's first frame of kind
  `mate.on`, flipped, its slide at `at.offset` along x from `at.from`
  (end A, end B or the middle, as on a side but to the part's frame).
  One whose `mate.on` is `slot` (a slider) placed on a profile's side (a
  side face or a slot frame as `at.geometry`) goes on that side as a
  profile does (mitcad#448): `place` is `side`, the slot is the one of
  the face picked nearest `at.point`, its `mate.frame` slides on it at the
  click's snaps or `at.offset` from `at.from`. A cap gets a `rigid` joint between its first `end` (or `face`)
  frame and the picked end, flipped.
- **A connector** gets a `slider` joint between its first mate's frame and
  profile a's frame of the mate's kind (`to`) that faces the inner corner
  (the one turned most towards b), at the distance from a's meeting end
  that the second mate's frame lies from the first one's plane, turned
  about z so that its second arm lies towards b. Its fasteners (`nut`,
  `screw`, `washer`) get `rigid` joints, flipped, between their first
  `slot`, `hole` or `face` frame (their design's XY when they have none)
  and the connector's fastener frame.
- **A panel** gets a `rigid` joint (not flipped) between its design's XY
  frame and the picked profile's slot frame with a `frame_override` that
  puts the middle of the design's box at the panel's middle: its x along
  that profile, its z across the frame's plane. A panel design has its
  width along X, its height along Y and its thickness along Z (centred on
  its XY origin, or drawn from its corner and extruded from XY: its box
  says where it is).

### Commands

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `build_place` | `part` (`{"library", "url", "rev", "component", "config"}`, or `{"source": "S1", "config"}` to reuse a source), `at` (below), `rotate` (an angle: 0, 90, 180 or 270 deg; a number is radians), `flip` (true: the other end first), `length` (a value, or `{"bind": {"occurrence", "geometry"}, "mode": "face"/"centre"/"through", "add"}`; left out: the source's default), `mitre` (`{"angle", "cut": "new"/"existing"/"shared"/"none"}`; left out: none, also on a square corner; `shared` on a corner at another angle at offset 0, mitcad#427; every cut keeps the lengths as long points and a shared one makes the outer corners meet, mitcad#443), `tilt` (on a side, mitcad#444: an angle from -80 to 80 deg, positive towards the target's end B; *Tilt*), `parameters` (other source parameters), `name` | `component`, `occurrence`, `name`, `features` (everything it added), `joint`, `bound`, `adds`, `warnings`, `place` (`side`, `end`, `frame`, `geometry` or `grounded`); undo step `Place <designation>` |
| `build_edit` | `component`, and any of `at.offset`, `at.from` (on a side or a rail, mitcad#417: `a`, `b` or `middle`; an offset alone is from the part's reference, a `from` alone keeps the part where it is and recomputes its offset), `rotate`, `flip` (true or false: which end meets), `length` (a value detaches, a `bind` binds), `ends` (`{"a": {"angle", "tilt"}, "b": ...}`; null squares an end; the length stays the long point, mitcad#443), `tilt` (a part on a side, mitcad#444: its tilt again, its ends recut; 0 squares it), `config`, `parameters`, `machining` (`[{"end": "a"/"b", "hole": {"diameter", "depth", "thread"}}]`: the part's own end machining, not a connector's; it replaces the whole list, an empty list takes it away) | `changed` (`offset`, `from`, `rotate`, `flip`, `detached`, `length`, `bound`, `tilt`, `ends`, `config`, `parameters`, `machining`); undo step `Edit <name>` |
| `build_connect` | `junction` (an id from `build_junctions`), `part` (as `build_place`'s), `fasteners` (default true), `machining` (default true), `name` | `component`, `occurrence`, `adds`, `warnings` (a fastener that cannot be read is left out with a warning); undo step `Connect <designation>` |
| `build_panel` | `at` (`{"occurrence", "geometry", "point"}`: a face or a slot frame of one of the frame's profiles), `part`, `thickness` (for a part whose thickness is a parameter), `parameters`, `name` | `component`, `occurrence`, `bound`, `fits` (false, with `reason`, when a fixed-width sheet is too narrow or too wide), `adds` (the clamps of a surface panel); undo step `Place <designation>` |
| `build_remove` | `component` | `removed`: `components` (it and what it `adds`), `features` (its bound lengths, its holes in other parts, and what depends on them) and `detached` (the bound lengths of other parts that end on it or start from it, detached first, so those parts keep their lengths); the parts placed on it keep where they are; undo step `Remove <name>` |

`at` says where the part goes: `{"occurrence", "geometry", "point",
"place", "offset", "from", "direction", "snap"}`.

- `occurrence` is a path from the BUILD host (uids or names).
- `geometry` is what was picked: a face or a frame of a placed part, or,
  for the first part, a plane, a point or a face. Without it the part is
  grounded at `point`.
- `point` is where it was picked, in the host's coordinates.
- `place` is `auto` (the default), `side` or `end`. With `auto`, the
  click decides:
  - a pick on a profile's end face (`<F>:end_a`, `<F>:end_b`) or end
    frame is `end`;
  - a pick on a side face is `side`: at the slot of that side nearest to
    `point` (of the slots on the face's plane when the kernel tells the
    face's plane; none there is a closed side), where `point` is along
    the profile (*Side placements*);
  - a slot frame is `side` at that slot; another frame (a rail's) is a
    mate.
- `from` (mitcad#417) is what `offset` is measured from on a side or a
  rail: `a` (the default), `b` or `middle`. It is accepted on an end and
  not used there.
- `offset` (a length: a number in mm or an expression) replaces the
  click on a side:
  - from `a`: the new part's near face from end A (0: flush with A);
  - from `b`: its far face (its face nearer end B) from end B (0: flush
    with B), positive towards A;
  - from `middle`: the new part's middle from the target's, positive
    towards end B (0: centred).

  On a turned end (a corner) it is the new part's end from the target's
  outer side (*End placements*); on a straight end it is not used.
- `direction`: on an end, the new part's axis in the host's coordinates
  (along the target: straight; or one of the four square to it, or any
  other); left out, a click on the end face decides (*End placements*).
  For the first part, the axis it runs along (+Z when left out).
- `snap` (mm, optional, mitcad#417): the app's least snap distance, about
  12 pixels at the click's depth. The model uses the larger of it and its
  own for the side snaps and the end face's zones, so that snapping works
  when the view is zoomed out and is never a one-pixel target.

**Side placements (mitcad#394, mitcad#417).** On a side the new part
never overhangs the target, a click snaps, and the placement is bound to
the reference the click resolved to:

- The part's reach along the slot is that of its box, turned as the joint
  turns it: a profile standing on the slot reaches half its section to
  either side of its centre line; its *width* along the slot is the
  whole section.
- A click centres the part on `point`'s distance along the profile, then
  (each distance at least `at.snap`):
  - within one section width of end A (its near face less than a width
    from the end, or past it) it goes flush with end A: from `a`,
    offset 0;
  - likewise flush with end B: from `b`, offset 0;
  - within a quarter width of the middle it is centred on the middle:
    from `middle`, offset 0;
  - within a quarter width (at most a quarter of the grid, at most half
    of it with `at.snap`) of a grid point of the target's system
    (`system.grid`: its near face a whole number of grids from end A) it
    goes there;
  - at a grid point or between the snaps it is from the nearer end, its
    offset the distance of the new part's face from that end (to a
    thousandth of a millimetre).

  With `at.from` and no `at.offset`, the click's place is measured from
  that reference instead.
- The click's reference and offset are stored as a typed one would be:
  the joint's `position.tx` follows the target's length from end B and
  from the middle, and the component's record keeps `from`. So a part
  flush with end B stays flush with it, and one on the middle stays on
  it, when the target gets longer or shorter.
- Every placement on a side, a click's or a typed offset's, is kept
  within the target's length; one that would overhang goes flush with
  that end (from it, offset 0), a typed offset with a warning (`... flush
  with end B instead`). A part longer than the target stays flush with
  end A.
- `build_edit`'s `at.offset` and `at.from` are measured the same way: an
  offset alone is from the part's reference; a `from` alone keeps the part
  where it is and recomputes the offset from the new reference (its
  `changed` has `offset` and `from`).
- `build_preview`'s `side` gives `from` and `offset` as `at.from` and
  `at.offset` take them.

**Tilt (mitcad#444).** A profile on a side can lean along its host: a
brace. `tilt` (an angle, `build_place`, `build_preview`, `build_edit`;
0 or left out: square) leans it in the plane of the host's axis and the
side's normal, positive towards the host's end B, negative towards end A,
never across the slot. It is from -80° up to 80°; more is refused (`the
tilt is 85 degrees; it is from -80 up to 80`). Only a part on a side
tilts (a profile standing on the slot with an end); on an end its
direction turns it, and a tilted part takes no `mitre`.

- The foot (the end on the slot) is cut by the tilt's angle about the
  section axis across the slot, so it lies flat on the side; the cut
  keeps the length as its long point (*Ends* of the derived part), and
  the foot's long point stands on the slot's centre line.
- `at.offset` and `at.from` refer to the foot's long point on the slot:
  from `a` its distance from end A, from `b` from end B, from `middle`
  from the host's middle. A click and the snaps place the foot (its
  reach along the slot is the foot's, the section's width / cos(tilt)),
  and the foot stays within the host's length.
- The far end: with a bound length (`face`, `centre`, `through`) it is
  cut flush with the plane the length ends on (parallel to the face it
  meets), and the length is measured along the axis to that end's long
  point; with a typed length it stays square.
- The cuts are ordinary end cuts (`ends`): the cut list shows them and
  `build_edit`'s `ends` changes them. `build_edit`'s `tilt` sets the tilt
  again and cuts both ends anew (0: square, square ends); a turn, a flip
  or a new length of a tilted part keeps its tilt and recuts its ends.
- How it is made: the joint's side a (the part's end frame) has a
  `frame_override` that turns it and moves it to the foot's long point;
  the slot's frame and the slide (`position.tx`, the long point's place)
  stay as they are. A bound length's ray starts at the far end's long
  side in the foot's plane (`from.shift.x` the slide plus that shift)
  and runs along the part's axis (`direction`). The component's record
  keeps `tilt` (radians).

**End placements (mitcad#417).** On a profile's end the new part
continues it straight or turns 90° at a corner:

- Without `at.direction`, a click on the end face (`at.point`) decides,
  in the target's own axes (those of its end frame, so a tilted profile
  turns as well):
  - in the inner half of the face both ways (at least `at.snap` across,
    as far as the face allows) the part continues straight;
  - in the band along an edge it turns 90° towards that edge (in a
    corner of the face, towards the nearer edge).

  A pick of an end frame, or without a point, continues straight.
- A corner is aligned: the new part lies in the target's plane (the plane
  of the two axes), centred on the target's section across the turn, and:
  - without a shared mitre it lies on the target's end face, its end
    flush with the target's outer side (the side away from the turn);
  - with a shared mitre the outer corners meet (mitcad#443): the two
    overlap fully, the new part's outer side (away from the corner's
    inside) through the target's outer edge at its end and its end on
    that edge, and both are cut on the bisector of their axes through
    that shared outer corner, each at its long point. Both lengths are
    outer lengths: two 500 mm parts make a corner 500 × 500 mm outside,
    at 90° or any other angle;
  - `at.offset` moves the new part's end from the target's outer side
    along its axis, positive towards the turn (0: flush; negative: past
    the outer side).
- A corner's mitre left out (mitcad#427): a square corner (90°, as the
  four `turns` are) has none, lying on the target's end face flush with
  its outer side; a corner at another angle is `shared` at offset 0 (by
  half the angle the corner has), none at another offset. `cut: "none"`
  places it without one, `cut: "shared"` mitres a square corner at 45°. A
  shared mitre at another offset is refused (`a shared mitre needs
  offset 0`).
- A direction back along the target is refused.

**Mitres.**

- On an `end` placement, `cut` decides which ends are cut:
  - `existing` cuts the target's end by `angle` and leaves the new part
    square;
  - `shared` cuts both on the bisector, each by half the angle between
    their axes (45° each for two profiles at 90°; `angle` is not needed);
  - `new` cuts only the new part (the default `cut`);
  - `none` cuts nothing (a corner's default is `shared`, *End
    placements*).
- On a `side` placement only `new` is accepted.
- The cut's `tilt` comes from the two axes at the moment of placing and
  is stored in each part's `ends`: the target's end leans towards the new
  part's axis, the new part's end towards the target's. On a side the new
  part's end leans along the slot. Later rotations do not change it;
  `build_edit` does.
- Only cut-to-length parts have mitres.
- Every cut (`new`, `existing`, `shared`, the Ends command's and
  `build_edit`'s `ends`) keeps the part's length as its long point
  (*Ends* of the derived part): a mitred part never reaches past its
  length, and `build_cut_list`'s `length` is the length the body has on
  its long side. Designs made before simply rebuild with this rule.

**Refusals.** The command changes nothing when:

- the part has no `build`;
- the role cannot go there (a panel, a connector or a fastener through
  `build_place`: they have `build_panel`, `build_connect` and their
  connector);
- the side has no slot frame (a closed side);
- the systems do not fit (a B-type slot 8 connector on an I-type slot 5
  profile), or the frame does not take the role (its `accepts`);
- the placement does not allow the mitre's `cut` (a shared mitre on a
  corner with an offset);
- an offset from end B or the middle on a part without a length;
- a direction on an end runs back along the target;
- a bound length would make a cycle, or ends on a part placed later;
- the length is outside the part's limits;
- the rotation is not a quarter turn.

### Queries

Frames in answers are `{"origin", "x_axis", "y_axis", "z_axis"}` in the
design's coordinates; lengths are numbers in mm and angles numbers in
radians, as joints have them.

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `build_preview` | `build_place`'s, `build_panel`'s or `build_connect`'s fields | what the command would do, without changing anything. A placing: `frame` (the new part's own axes at its end A, z running from A to B), `place` (`side`, `end`, `frame`, `geometry` or `grounded`, as `auto` decided), `length` (`value`: the length given, else what the part's ray gives in `mode`, else the source's default; `default`; `target`: what the ray meets first, `{occurrence, geometry}` with a frame of another BUILD part facing it, or the `bind` given, null when nothing; and `mode`), `ends` (`a`, `b`: `{angle, tilt}` or null; `target`: the target's end cut), `tilt` (radians, mitcad#444), `snaps` (on a side, mitcad#394: `{kind, offset, point}` for each place a click snaps to: `kind` `end_a`, `end_b`, `middle` or `grid`, `offset` the new part's near face from end A, `point` where its middle then stands on the slot, in the design), `side` (on a side: `{kind, from, offset, point, width}`: the snap the click took (`end_a`, `end_b`, `middle`, `grid`), null between snaps, or `clamped` when the placement was kept within the target; the reference and the offset from it the click resolved to, or the typed ones, as `at.from` and `at.offset` take them (mitcad#417); where the part stands; its width along the slot; `foot`, where the part's frame meets the slot, a tilted part's foot long point, in the design; null elsewhere), `end` (on an end, mitcad#417: `{zone, direction, turns, offset, mitre}`: `zone` `straight` or `edge` (what the click chose) or `given` (`at.direction`); `direction` the new part's axis in the host's coordinates; `turns` the four unit vectors square to the target in the host's coordinates, +x, +y, -x, -y of its end frame; `offset` a corner's offset, null when straight; `mitre` `{cut, angle}` the placement will use, the default resolved (`cut` `none`, `new`, `existing` or `shared`, `angle` in radians or null); null elsewhere), `host` (as `build_host` answers), `designation`, `warnings`. A panel: `frame`, `fits`, `reason`, `width`, `height`, `bound`. A connector: `frame`, `junction`, `fasteners` (`{frame, at}`), `fastener_parts`, `machining` (`{component, at, point, diameter, depth, thread}`). All: `body` (`"see analysis_shape"`) and `problems` (the refusal the command would give, then nothing else) |
| `build_parts` | | `parts`: for each BUILD component, `component`, `name`, `role`, `source`, `part`, `joint`, `designation`, `supplier`, `part_number`, `config`, `length`, `ends`, `bound` (`{feature, parameter, to: {occurrence, geometry}, mode}`, or null), `flip`, `rotate`, `tilt` (radians, 0 square, mitcad#444), `machining` (its own, as `build_edit` takes it), `added_by`, `adds`, `junction`, `from` (a part on a side or a rail: `a`, `b` or `middle`, else null) |
| `build_junctions` | `components` (optional: only the junctions of these) | `junctions`: `id` (`<a's component>:<a's at>\|<b's component>:<b's at>`, stable while the two parts and their meeting stay), `kind` (`L`, `T`, `cross`, `inline`), `a` and `b` (`component`, `occurrence`, `at` (`end_a`, `end_b`, the slot frame, or `side` on a closed side), `frame` (the part's own axes at its end A), `at_frame` (the `at` frame)), `angle` (between the axes), `systems` (`B8/30`), `space` (the free room in the inner corner: `{"x", "y", "z"}`: along a, along b to its farther end, across), `connectors` (components already there) |
| `build_cut_list` | `kerf` (optional, default 3 mm) | `rows`, one per group of identical results (source, row, length, ends, machining and own features the same): `source`, `designation`, `supplier`, `part_number`, `config`, `length` (the part's length, its long point: the body's length on the long side of its angled ends, mitcad#443), `ends` (`a`, `b`: `{angle, tilt}` or null), `machining` (`{at, diameter, depth, thread, connector}`: holes from connectors, and the part's own, `connector` null), `features` (how many own features the part has: holes, cuts), `quantity`, `mass` (each, kg), `components`. `stock`: per source, cut from its longest stock length, `{"source", "designation", "stock_length", "pieces": [lengths in cutting order], "bars" (where each stock piece's cuts end in `pieces`), "needed", "offcut", "too_long"}`, longest pieces first into the first stock piece they fit (a kerf after each). `kerf`. `other`: the parts list's rows for everything else |
| `build_host` | | the BUILD host (mitcad#394, *Where parts go*): `component` (its uid), `name`, `path` (its first occurrence path from the root, uids joined by `/`, `""` for the root) and `active` (the active component); the app gives paths from it and points in its coordinates |

`analysis_shape` with `{"shape": "build_preview", ...}` and the same
fields gives the new part's bodies (a connector's, a panel's) in the
design's coordinates, as other analysis shapes, for the view to show
while a command is open. A profile's bodies are at the length the query
says (`length.value`): a bound length or none given is what the ray
meets, not the source's default. With `spacing` (a set, *Spacing sets*)
it gives every member's bodies, the last one ripped when the set rips it
(mitcad#487).

**How junctions are found.** From the derived parts' frames and boxes at
the marker: two profiles meet when their boxes touch or overlap within
the model's tolerance (0.001 mm). Then:

- an end on a side face (on a slot frame's plane, facing it, or on a
  closed side of the box) is `T`, or `L` when it is within the section's
  size of that side's end;
- two ends at one point are `L` (axes at an angle) or `inline` (on one
  axis);
- two sides crossing are `cross`.

`a` is the part whose end meets; of two ends, and of two sides, the
newer part.

**Cut ends** (mitcad#521). A part whose metadata gives its section (a
timber member) has its material as its box on the inner side of its end
cuts, the planes its derived part cuts them by: an end on a side is in the
other part's material, not only its box; a cut end whose frame (on its
axis at the end, beyond the cut) is on no side meets a side with its cut
face's middle, the junction's frame there with z out of the cut (a
rafter's plumb cut on a ridge board: a `T`, `L` near the board's end);
two cut ends are a shared mitre only when their cut planes are one plane;
and two sides cross only where their materials meet: touching or
overlapping square to both axes and with an area in common across that
direction. So the two rafters of a pair, whose plumb cut ends stand on
the two sides of a ridge board and whose boxes overlap above it, are no
junction. A part of no such section is found by its box, as before.

A connector fits a junction when its `junctions`, `systems` and `space`
match the junction. The list of fitting library parts comes from the
library side (`library_build_candidates` in [Library
commands](#library-commands), given the junction), since the model knows
no library. `build_connect` refuses a connector whose `junctions` or
`systems` do not fit, or whose `envelope` is larger than the junction's
`space`.

**Panels.** A panel in slots is placed from a picked inner face (or slot
frame) of a frame's profile: the slot there, the profile across the
frame whose slot faces it in the same plane, and those beside to the left
and right along the picked profile. Its height is the room across plus
twice the slot's depth less the clearance, its width the room between
the profiles beside likewise; bound lengths keep both so (from the
picked slot to the one across, from the left slot to the right). A size
that is no parameter of the panel (a sheet sold in widths) keeps its
value: it fits when it reaches into both slots and is no wider than
their depth less the clearance. A face with no profile across is refused
(`not inside a frame`). A surface panel (`mount: "surface"`) lies on the
picked outer face, its back on it. Where its width and height are
parameters it covers the frame around the face: across from the outer
side of the picked profile to that of the profile whose slot faces the
picked one's inner side, along between the outer sides of the profiles
beside (without them, the picked profile's length, with a warning);
bound lengths in `through` mode keep both so. Without a profile across it
keeps its size (a warning). Its clamps slide in the picked slot at the
panel's two ends, kept on the profile and inset by their own reach along
the slot (one in the middle when there is no room for two); they are its
`adds`, and `build_remove` takes them with it.

### Classes

- `build_place`, `build_connect` and `build_panel` read a new source from
  a library, so they are class `remote` (as `update_library_parts`).
  With `part.source` (a source already in the design) they need no
  library, and the MCP server allows them (`classes::command_class_with`,
  which looks at the fields).
- `build_edit`, `build_remove` and the queries are class `model`.

## BUILD: timber construction

Timber members, wood fasteners, brackets and hangers, joinery and sheets
(mitcad#478) use the commands of *BUILD: profile assemblies* above,
extended here. Everything said there holds; the slot path (profiles with
`slot` frames, their connectors, nuts and panels) is unchanged: no field
below is needed for it and none changes what it does. The app's Timber
tool (`app/COMMANDS.md`, *Timber*) and its Profile tool drive the same
commands; the Profile picker lists no timber. Code: `core/model/src/build/meta.rs`,
`core/model-build/src/` (`place.rs`, `timber.rs`, `spacing.rs`, `wood.rs`,
`joinery.rs`, `cut_list.rs`); tests `core/model-tests/build-timber/src/timber_tests.rs`.

### Library metadata the model reads

The library's format is in [docs/libraries.md](../../../docs/libraries.md#build-parts)
(*Timber*). The model reads these fields of a source's `build` block,
leniently (unknown fields are ignored, a value is a number in mm, kg,
kg/m³ or % or a text with its unit):

- **Rows.** `build.rows` is `{"<configuration row>": {a partial build
  block}}`. For a part made in a row, the row's block is deep-merged over
  the component's: objects merge key by key, other values (numbers, texts,
  arrays) replace. The component's own fields are the default row's. Every
  read below is of the merged block of the part's row (`config`, or the
  source's default row when left out).
- **A timber member**: `role: "profile"`, `kind: "timber"`. `section`
  `{width, height}` is the actual size: the section lies on XY centred at
  the origin, `width` (W) along X and `height` (T, the thickness) along Y;
  `L` runs along +Z. `nominal` `{width, height}` is the nominal size (at
  20 % moisture). `material` `{species, finish, grade, density, moisture,
  product}`: `species` `spruce`, `pine`, ...; `finish` `sawn`, `planed` or
  `dimensioned`; `grade` (`""` or `C24`, ...) the default grade;
  `density` kg/m³; `moisture` %. `availability` `standard` or
  `less common`. `tolerance` is carried, not used. `length` as a
  profile's (`parameter` `L`, `min`, `max`, `stock` the stock lengths,
  `default`). `frames`: `end_a`, `end_b` (kind `end`) and four `face`
  frames `face_xp`, `face_xn`, `face_yp`, `face_yn` at z = 0 on the side's
  centre line, z out of the side, x along +Z (as slot frames). No
  `system`, no slot frames, no `mass_per_metre`: the mass is the density
  times the volume (W × T × the length).
- **A wood fastener**: `role: "fastener"`, `wood` `{kind: "screw" |
  "nail", diameter, length, head}` (the row's sizes, through `rows`), and
  an `axis` frame (kind `shaft`): on the axis at the head's bearing
  surface, z along the shank towards the tip (the tip at z = length).
- **A bracket, joist hanger or post base**: `role: "connector"`,
  `connector.placement: "outer"`, `connector.fit` `{kind: "angle" |
  "hanger" | "post_base", section: [a, b], width: [min, max]}`,
  `connector.mates` whose first frame (`{"frame": "mount", "to": "face"}`)
  places it (*Brackets, hangers and post bases* below), and
  `connector.fasteners`: `[{"frames": [hole frames], "count": n, "on": "a"
  | "b", "screw" | "nail": {library reference, with its row}}]`. A hole
  frame (kind `hole`) lies on the connector's surface the head bears on,
  z out of it towards the head (facing the screw's `axis` frame). `on` is
  the member the fasteners are driven into (`a` the one whose end meets).
- **A sheet**: `role: "panel"`, `panel.mount: "face"`, `panel.thickness`
  (a value or its parameter), `panel.width` and `panel.height` (the
  parameters that size it), `panel.stock` (`[[w, h], ...]`, the sheet
  sizes sold, mm), `material` `{product, density}`; thicknesses as rows.
  The design's width runs along X, its height along Y and its thickness
  along +Z, as other panels.

A part is **timber** when its merged block's `kind` is `timber`; a design
**has timber** when one of its BUILD parts is. A placed part whose block
names a `material` (timber, sheets, their brackets and screws) takes its
source's body appearance and material, when the source's bodies that set
one set the same (a document appearance of the source is copied in); slot
profiles keep their look. A cut-to-length part whose source gives the caps
of its extrusion (`<F>:start(...)`, `<F>:end(...)`, its faces at z = 0 and
L) one face appearance (`set_face_appearance`; the timber's end grain,
mitcad#484) shows it on its end faces, `<F>:end_a` and `<F>:end_b`, square
or cut at an angle.

### Face sides

A `face` frame of a member (`role: "profile"`) is a side as a slot frame
is: `build_place` (and `build_preview`, `build_edit`, `build_junctions`,
bound lengths) treat it as one, with these differences:

- `at.geometry` may be a face frame (`{"mount": "F7:mount(face_yp)"}`) or
  a side face of the member with `at.point`: the face frame of that side
  (the one on the face's plane when the kernel tells it, else the nearest
  to `at.point`). A side with a slot frame takes the slot as before; a
  face frame is taken only where a side has no slot frame.
- The new part sits anywhere along the side: no grid snaps (a member has
  no system); the end and middle snaps, `at.offset` and `at.from` (`a`,
  `b`, `middle`), keeping within the length, `rotate`, `flip`, `tilt`,
  `mitre` (`new`), bound lengths (`face`, `centre`, `through`), corners
  and shared mitres on an end work as for profiles.
- Across the side the new part stands centred on the side's centre line.
- No systems are checked between members (a part without `systems` fits
  any); a slot connector or nut is refused on a member (`a member has no
  slots`).
- A bound length's ray meets a member's face frames as it meets a
  profile's slot frames.

### Members by two points

`build_place` takes `to` and `lie`:

```json
{"cmd": "build_place", "part": {"source": "S1", "config": "48x148"},
 "at": {"occurrence": "", "geometry": "xy", "point": [0, 0, 0]},
 "to": {"point": [3000, 0, 0]}, "lie": "edge"}
```

- `at.point` is the start and `to.point` the end, both in the BUILD
  host's coordinates. The member runs from start to end (end A at the
  start, unless `flip`). Without `length` its length is the distance; a
  `length` (a value or a `bind`) replaces it.
- `at.geometry` (optional) is what the member lies on: a plane (`"xy"`),
  a planar face, or a face frame or side face of a member (with `at.occurrence`).
  The member lies on that plane: its axis is lifted off it by half the
  section across it, and it is held to it by a `rigid` joint whose
  `frame_override` gives the start and the axes (so it follows a member
  it lies on). Without `at.geometry` it is grounded, its axis through the
  two points.
- `lie` turns it about its axis: `flat` (the default), the section's
  smaller dimension across the plane it lies on (without a plane: along
  the host's +Z, its "up"); `edge`, the larger one. On a plane the side
  that faces it lies on it. A member standing square to the plane (a
  post) stands centred on the start, its X along the host's X. `rotate`
  (quarter turns) turns it further.
- **A point and a direction** (the app's Timber tool: a click, then a
  typed or auto length, mitcad#478): with `length`, `to.point` gives only
  the direction. A value runs the member that long from the start; a
  `bind` (`mode` `face`, `centre`, `through`, `add`) binds it to what the
  ray from its start along the direction meets, as on a side: its
  `bound_length` starts at the plane it lies on (the host's origin when
  grounded), shifted to the start, so the length follows the target.
- The answer's `place` is `points`. `build_preview` answers as for any
  placing (`frame`, `length`, `box`). Without `length` its `length.value`
  is the points' distance (as placed), and `length.target` names what the
  ray from the start towards `to.point` meets first, the target an auto
  length binds to (null when nothing is in the way).
- `build_edit` of a member by two points takes `to` (`{"point"}`), `at`
  (`{"point"}`) and `lie` again: it is placed anew from them (the same
  component, derived part and junctions).
- **Between members** (mitcad#509): without `length` (and without
  `spacing`), an end whose point is inside another member cut to length
  (a timber member or a profile; its box), while the other point is not
  on that member, is cut back to where the member's axis meets that
  member's face: a square butt there, so that a member clicked between two
  studs (on their centre lines, as the app's snaps give them) fits between
  them, not into them. A free member (no `at.geometry`: its axis through
  the points) is cut so too where its point is on a member's face and its
  axis runs through that member (a click on its far side); on the near
  face it ends there already. A member lying on a plane has its axis off
  the points: only a point inside a member counts (members lapped on a
  plane stay so). The far end so cut that meets a member end to end closes
  the corner (*Frames of members*: a square butt, `closing`). Ends that
  would meet leave nothing between them: refused (`nothing is left between
  them`). The member keeps the points given (`build_edit` places it anew
  from them, cut again). `build_preview` answers `points`: `{"start":
  {"on", "name", "cut"}, "end": {...}, "lies": "plane" | "free"}`, the
  member each point is on or in (its component and name, or null), whether
  that end was cut back, and whether the member lies on `at.geometry` or
  is free; its `length.value` is the length after the cuts.

### Spacing sets

`build_place` with `spacing` places a member and repeats it: studs,
joists, rafters (a centre distance), deck boards, fence boards and
cladding (a board row: a gap).

```json
{"cmd": "build_place", "part": {"source": "S1", "config": "48x198"},
 "at": {"occurrence": "O3", "geometry": {"mount": "F9:mount(face_yn)"}},
 "length": {"bind": {"occurrence": "O4", "geometry": {"mount": "F12:mount(face_yp)"}}},
 "spacing": {"mode": "centre", "distance": 400}}
```

`spacing` is `{"mode", "distance", "count", "from", "to", "along",
"length", "fit"}`:

- `mode`: `centre` (the default: `distance` is the centre distance) or
  `gap` (a board row: `distance` is the gap between boards).
- **On a side** (`at` on a member's side or slot, the base placement a
  side placement): the members stand along the host member, the first
  flush with `from` (an offset of its near face from end A, default 0)
  and the last flush with `to` (its far face's offset from end A; default
  end B, and then the last is bound from end B, so it stays flush when the
  host's length changes). A set between two members is this with
  `length` bound to the second member (as above): the members stand on
  the first and reach the second, each with its own bound length.
- **Otherwise** (members by two points, or one at a point): `along`
  (a direction in the host's coordinates, required) and `length` (the
  span along it, required): the first member is the one `at` and `to`
  give, the others moved along `along`.
- The span is from the first member's near face to the last one's far
  face. With `w` the member's width along the set (its box along it):
  - `centre`: the members at 0, d, 2d, ... and the last at `span - w`;
    the count is `ceil((span - w) / d) + 1` (the last space is at most
    `d`);
  - `gap`: the step is `w + gap`; with `fit` `cut` (the default) the count
    is `ceil(span / (w + gap))` and the last board is ripped to
    what is left (a `rip` cut, *Joinery*, when less than `w`); with `fit`
    `spread` the count is `floor((span + gap) / (w + gap))` and the gaps
    are widened so that the last board ends at the span. Profiled boards
    that join are laid edge to edge instead (*Profiled boards* below).
  - `count` (optional) fixes the count instead: `centre` spreads the
    members evenly over the span, `gap` spreads the gaps; `0` (in
    `build_edit`) goes back to the count from the span.
- `build_preview` with `spacing` answers the first member as a placing does
  and adds `spacing`: `{count, frames, rip}` (each member's own axes at its
  end A, and whether the last is ripped); `analysis_shape` with the same
  fields gives every member's bodies (mitcad#487).
- One member is placed when the span holds only one. A refusal of any
  member refuses the whole set.
- The answer's `component` is the first member (the set's **lead**),
  `set` lists every member's component, `count` their number; undo step
  `Place <designation> x<count>`.
- The lead's record keeps the set (`spacing`: the definition and the base
  placement, the part as `{"source", "config"}`); every member's record
  has `set`, the lead's component. `build_parts` gives both.
- **Editing the set**: `build_edit` with `spacing` (any of its fields; `{}`
  lays the set out again from the members' places now, after the host or
  the span changed) and optionally `config` acts on the whole set, through
  any of its members: the members are laid out anew in one undo step. The
  first `min(old, new)` members keep their components (their joints,
  bound lengths and lengths are made anew; connectors and junctions on
  them stay), new ones are added after them, extra ones removed as by
  `build_remove`. `changed` has `spacing` (and `config`); the answer adds
  `set` and `count`.
- `build_remove` with `"set": true` removes every member of the set;
  without it one member goes and the set keeps the others (laying it out
  again counts what is left as its members).

### Wood fasteners

`build_connect` at a junction of two members with a wood fastener as
`part` drives screws or nails through one member into the other:

```json
{"cmd": "build_connect", "junction": "C5:end_a|C3:face_xp",
 "part": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "...", "component": "wood-screw"},
 "count": 2}
```

- **Which way.** An end on a side (`T`, and an `L` whose end meets the
  other's side or end face): through the member whose side it is (`b`)
  into the end of `a`, along `a`'s axis, from `b`'s far face; at a cut
  end met by its cut face (mitcad#521) square to the cut face, the contact
  the cut face within `b` (a rafter nailed through the ridge board into
  its plumb cut end, horizontally). Two members
  crossing or lying on each other (`cross`): through the newer (`a`) into
  `b`, square to both axes, from `a`'s far side. Ends meeting on one axis
  (`inline`) are refused (`an inline joint takes a plate`).
- **Where.** `count` (default 2) fasteners in a row along the longer side
  of the contact (the end's section on the side face, or the members'
  overlap), centred across it, at `(i + 0.5) / count` of its length.
- **The size.** `part.config` names the row. Left out, for a source with
  rows: the diameter is the largest row's `wood.diameter` not over the
  thinner member's smaller section dimension / 7 (else the smallest
  diameter); the length the shortest of that diameter at least the
  thickness gone through + 8 × the diameter (else the longest).
  `build_junctions` gives the numbers for a picker (`wood` below).
- **Seating** (mitcad#512). A wood screw or nail is driven until its head
  top lies on the unchanged entry face. `build.wood.seat` can name a mount
  frame or use `head_top` / `head_underside`. A named frame has z along the
  shaft. Without one, `head_top` is the least body coordinate along the
  source's axis-aligned shaft; oblique library parts must supply a frame.
  Pan, hex, washer, button and socket heads default to `head_underside`
  (the existing axis bearing frame); other wood screws and nails default
  to `head_top`. A non-wood bolt keeps its existing bearing placement.
  Nominal `wood.length` and row selection are unchanged: a head K mm
  behind the axis is driven K mm deeper, with tip and embedment increased
  by K. A countersunk source already starting at its axis needs no shift,
  and keeps its tip at L. No head holes are cut; intentional head/shank
  overlap with wood is not an error of the frame's fastening checks.
  Fasteners on a metal connector keep their hole's bearing placement.
  Swap Fastener recomputes seating from the new source and selected row
  while keeping the member's entry frame, component and joint.
  `build_parts.parts[].seating` gives the measured `head_top_distance`
  from the entry face (negative stands proud, positive is sunk) and
  `tip_distance`, in millimetres; both come from the placed body's bounds
  for an axis-aligned source (otherwise `seating` is null), whatever way
  the fastener is driven (a sloped roof's too). With them `members` and
  `of` (mitcad#521): how many of its junction's members its shaft passes
  through (its points from the entry face to the tip, every half
  millimetre, in a member's material) and how many the junction has.
- **Warnings, not refusals** (in `warnings`, `d` the diameter):
  - the embedment (the length less the thickness gone through) under
    6 × `d`: `screw 1 embeds 22 mm in Beam1: at least 30 mm` (the
    members by their component names);
  - a fastener nearer than 3 × `d` to an edge of the contact:
    `screw 2 is 10 mm from an edge: at least 15 mm`;
  - nearer than 10 × `d` to an end of the member it goes through, along
    that member's axis: `screw 1 is 37 mm from the end of C3: at least
    50 mm`;
  - longer than both members together: `screw 1 goes through C5`.
- **What is made.** One component per fastener (role `fastener`, its
  source the wood fastener's), each with a `rigid` joint, flipped, between
  its `axis` frame and the member it is driven from, at its entry point
  (that member's `end_a` frame with a `frame_override`: the entry point,
  z out of the member towards the head). The first is the answer's
  `component`; its record's `adds` lists the others, and `build_remove` of
  it takes them all. Every one's record has `junction`. No holes are cut.
- `build_preview` with the same fields answers `fasteners` (`{frame, at}`
  per fastener, `at` the joint's frame in the design), `fastener_parts`,
  `size` (`{config, diameter, length}`) and `warnings`.

### Brackets, hangers and post bases

`build_connect` with a connector whose `placement` is `outer` fits it by
the members' sections and places it on their outer faces:

- `fit.kind` `hanger` and `angle` go on a junction with an end on a side
  (`T`, `L`); `post_base` on a member's free end, named instead of a
  junction: `"end": {"component": "C3", "end": "a"}`.
- `fit.section` `[a, b]`: the member that is carried (`a`; the post) has
  that section, either way round, within 1 mm; `fit.width` `[min, max]`:
  its smaller section dimension is within it. Otherwise refused (`the
  hanger fits 48 x 148, C5 is 48 x 123`). A slot connector at a junction
  of members, or an outer one at a junction of slot profiles, is refused.
- The connector's first mate's frame (`mount`; its `to`, `face` or `end`,
  is not read) is placed by a `rigid` joint, flipped, on `b`'s (the
  post's) `end_a` frame with a `frame_override` whose z points out of `b`
  towards the connector; so in the connector's design the `mount` frame's
  z points into the carrier or the post. Where the `mount` frame goes, its
  axes in the connector's design:
  - `hanger`: at the middle of `a`'s end on `b`'s face, z into `b`, x the
    direction of `a`'s section most up (the host's +Z; of a vertical `a`,
    its +X);
  - `angle`: on `b`'s face at the middle of the edge where `a`'s chosen
    side meets it, z into `b`, x that side's outward normal; `side`
    (`x+`, `x-`, `y+`, `y-` of `a`'s section; default the larger side,
    `y+` when W ≥ T, else `x+`) chooses it;
  - `post_base`: at the middle of the end, z into the member along its
    axis, x its +X.
- Its fasteners: one per hole frame of each `fasteners` entry, a `rigid`
  joint, flipped, between the fastener's `axis` frame and the hole frame;
  the warnings above (embedment into `on`, edges) apply to each.
- The answer and the record as a slot connector's (`adds`, `junction`).

### Joinery

`build_connect` with `joint` instead of `part` cuts the members:

```json
{"cmd": "build_connect", "junction": "C7:end_b|C6:side", "joint": {"kind": "half_lap"}}
```

`joint` is `{"kind", "depth", "on"}`:

- `housing` (an end on a side): a pocket in `b` the size of `a`'s
  section where it meets, `depth` deep (default a third of `b`'s
  thickness there, at most 15 mm);
- `notch` (members crossing or lying on each other): a cut in `on`
  (default `a`) the size of the other's section across it, `depth` deep
  (default their overlap, or a third of `on`'s thickness when they only
  touch);
- `half_lap` (members crossing in one plane, overlapping): both are cut
  over their overlap, `a` from below and `b` from above (along `a`'s axis
  × `b`'s, turned towards the host's +Z), `a` by `depth` (default half
  the overlap's thickness) and `b` by the rest. Members that do not
  overlap are refused (`a half-lap needs the members overlapping`).

The cuts are kept in the members' derived parts, in `cuts` (beside
`ends`):

```json
{"type": "derived_part", "source": "S1", "config": "48x148", "parameters": {"L": "d12"},
 "cuts": [{"kind": "half_lap", "with": "C7", "junction": "C7:end_b|C6:side",
           "origin": [-74, 0, "d12 - 148"], "x": [1, 0, 0], "y": [0, 1, 0],
           "size": [148, 24, 148], "depth": 24}]}
```

- Each is a box in the part's coordinates: from `origin` along `x`, `y`
  and their cross product by `size`; `origin` and `size` are values;
  `depth` (a number) is the depth the joint was asked for, kept to cut it
  anew.
  `kind` is `housing`, `notch`, `half_lap` or `rip` (a board ripped to the
  width left, *Spacing sets*), or `birdsmouth` (a rafter notched over a
  wall's top plate, *BUILD: timber frames*). `with` and `junction` name the other
  member and the junction.
- **Bound to the members.** The coordinate along the member is an
  expression: of the other member's slide when it slides on this one
  (`d20 + 24`), else of this member's length when the cut is nearer end B
  (`d12 - 148`), else a number. So a cut follows a joist moved along its
  beam and a member's end when its length changes. `build_edit` with
  `"cuts": "refit"` cuts the member's joinery anew from where the members
  are now.
- The cuts are made inside the derived part after the end cuts; the cut
  list reads them from the definition. `build_remove` of a member takes the
  cuts `with` it out of the others.
- The answer: `component` null, `features` (the derived parts cut),
  `cuts` (`{component, kind, size}`), `warnings`; undo step `Connect
  half_lap`. `build_preview` with `joint` answers `cuts` likewise.

### Sheets on a face

`build_panel` with a sheet (`panel.mount: "face"`) picks a member's face
(a face frame, or a side face with `at.point`) and lays the sheet on it:

- `faces` (optional): more picks (`[{"occurrence", "geometry"}]`). The
  sheet covers the rectangle of the picked faces in the picked face's
  plane (x along the first member, y across); without `faces`, of every
  member face on that plane facing the same way.
- Its width and height, where they are parameters, are that rectangle's
  (numbers, not bound: placing it again sizes it again); a fixed size
  keeps its value and `fits` is false with `reason` when it does not cover
  the rectangle. `thickness` and `part.config` as for other panels.
- It is held by a `rigid` joint (not flipped) on the first member's face
  frame with a `frame_override`. The middle of the design's box at its
  sizes goes to the middle of the rectangle and the box's back (its least
  z) lies on the face, so the design may be drawn from a corner (a box
  from (0, 0, 0) to (W, H, T)) or centred; no frame of the sheet is read.
  The answer as for panels (`fits`, `bound` empty).

### Lists

`build_cut_list` (a design without timber answers exactly as before):

- With timber the answer adds `timber: true` and `totals`
  (`{running_metres, volume, mass}` over the timber rows), and every row
  adds `kind` (`timber` or null), `material` (`{species, finish, grade,
  density}`, the grade the part's own), `nominal` and `section`
  (`{width, height}`, mm), `availability`, `running_metres` (length ×
  quantity / 1000) and `volume` (m³, the section's area × length ×
  quantity; the area W × T, a profiled board's `board.area`). A timber
  row's `mass` (each) is the density × the area × length.
- With profiled boards (*Profiled boards* below) the answer adds
  `profiled: true` and `totals.area`, and every row `profile`, `cover`
  and `area` (null for other rows).
- Rows are grouped by the grade too, and `machining` lists the joinery
  cuts after the holes: `{at: null, kind, size, with, diameter: null}`.
- `stock` is per source and configuration row (`config` in the entry when
  the source has rows). A timber entry adds `stock_lengths`: each stock
  piece's length, the shortest of the source's stock lengths that holds
  its cuts (first fit of the longest pieces into the longest stock, then
  each piece shortened).
- `build_parts` adds to each part `kind` (`timber` or null), `grade`,
  `set` (the lead's component or null), `spacing` (the lead's: the
  definition and `count`), `cuts` (`{kind, with, junction, size}`), and
  `board` (a profiled board's `{profile, cover, joined}`, else null).
- `build_junctions` adds `wood` to a junction whose members are both
  timber: `{through, into, thickness, max_diameter, sections}` (the member a
  fastener goes through and the one it goes into, the thickness gone
  through, the largest diameter by the sizing rule, and `sections`
  `{"a": [W, T], "b": [W, T]}` for the pickers).
- `build_place`, `build_edit` take `grade` (text; null clears): the
  part's own grade, else its row's `material.grade`.

### Profiled boards

Tongue and groove boards, shiplap and feather-edge cladding and deck boards
(mitcad#477; `build/profiled.rs`, tests `build/profiled_tests.rs`) are
timber members with a `board` block (docs/libraries.md, *Timber parts*):

```json
"board": {"profile": "tongue_and_groove", "cover": "112 mm", "area": 3123.5,
          "tongue": {"length": "8 mm", "thickness": "8 mm"}}
```

- `profile`: `tongue_and_groove`, `shiplap`, `feather_edge` or `deck`;
  `cover` the width a board covers in a row (a deck board's: its width,
  when left out); `area` the section's area in mm²; `tongue`, `overlap`,
  `edge_radius` and `grooves` the sizes of its joint or edges (a row's own
  through `build.rows`). The section's box lies as any member's (centred,
  `section.width` its full width along X, the thickness along Y), its
  visible face towards +Y.
- **Boards that join** (tongue and groove, shiplap, feather-edge) have
  two more frames: `groove` (kind `groove`) on the box's −X side, z −X,
  and `tongue` (kind `tongue`) the cover width on from it, z +X, both at
  y = 0 and z = 0, x along +Z. The tongue's edge goes under the next
  board (a shiplap's lip, a feather-edge board's thin edge).
- **Against another board.** `build_place` with `at.geometry` a board's
  `tongue` frame mates the new board's `groove` there (its `tongue` in a
  `groove` frame): a `rigid` joint, flipped, so the new board lies beside
  it the cover width on, tongue into groove, its ends level (its length as
  `length` gives). The profiles must match: both boards of one `profile`
  and thickness, with the same tongue (length and thickness) or overlap
  within 0.01 mm; otherwise refused (`the profiles do not match: the
  tongues of <new> and <target> differ`). The answer's `place` is `frame`.
- **Rows.** A spacing set in `gap` mode (*Spacing sets*) of boards that
  join, laid across their width (the set's direction along the board's X),
  is laid edge to edge: the step is the cover width `c`, no gap (a gap
  asked for is not kept, and `warnings` says so: `<part> joins edge to
  edge: laid without the gap of 5 mm`), the count `ceil((span - (w - c)) /
  c)` with `w` the full width, and the last board ripped to what is left
  (`span - (n - 1) × c`) when that is less than `w`. `fit` `spread` lays
  them as `cut`; a `count` lays that many edge to edge (refused when they
  do not fit the span). Deck boards, and boards laid another way, keep the
  gap and the rules above.
- **Lists.** A profiled board's `mass` and `volume` come from its
  `board.area`. With profiled boards the cut list adds `profiled: true`,
  each row `profile`, `cover` (mm) and `area` (m², the area covered: the
  cover width × length × quantity; a ripped board covers what is left of
  it up to its cover width), and `totals.area`. `build_parts` gives each
  part's `board`.

### Pickers

`library_search` and `library_build_candidates` (*Library commands*):

- `role: "profile"` with `kind: "timber"` lists timber only; `role:
  "profile"` without `kind` lists no timber (the Profile picker).
- `role: "panel"` with `mount: "face"` lists sheets; without `mount`, no
  sheets.
- A junction with `wood` (from `build_junctions`) is offered wood
  fasteners and outer connectors whose `fit` fits its members, and no
  slot connectors; a junction without `wood`, as before.

### Frames of members (mitcad#485)

Three rules for frames of members (code `build/place.rs`; tests
`build/close_tests.rs`):

- **A member on the ground lies flat or on edge.** `build_place`'s `lie`
  (*Members by two points*) also turns a member placed on the ground
  along `at.direction`: on a plane or a face (the plane's normal is "up")
  or grounded (the host's +Z): `flat` puts the section's smaller dimension
  across the plane, `edge` the larger one. A member standing square to the
  plane keeps its X along the host's X. Without `lie` (Profile) the
  placement is as before.
- **A member on a member's end lies as that member does.** A timber
  member placed on a timber member's end, straight on or turned at a
  corner, has its thickness axis (its section's smaller side) parallel to
  the target's where the direction allows it: the end frame's x is turned
  a quarter about the new axis when only that does (straight on, a
  `frame_override` with `x_axis` only). Two boards of one size meet with
  ends of the same width and flush faces. `rotate` and `flip` turn it
  further; a square section, or a slot profile, is placed as before.
- **Closing a frame.** A part placed on an end (`place` `end`) whose length
  is bound (`length.bind`) to a member its far end meets end to end, as a
  corner, gets that end made as its start: the ray from its start along
  its axis meets the member, not along the member's axis, within the
  member's section size of one of its ends (as `build_junctions` finds an
  `L`), and the member is not the one the start is on. Then:
  - with the start mitred (a cut at the end that meets, a corner's shared
    mitre), both ends at the corner get a shared mitre, each by half the
    angle between the axes (45° in a square frame), leaning towards the
    other's axis away from the corner, and the bound length's `mode` is
    `through`: the length runs to the member's outer side, the long point,
    so the outer corners meet;
  - with the start square, the bound length's `mode` is `face`: a square
    butt on the member's face, never into it.

  The bound length stays: moving either member (a length changed, a joint
  dragged) keeps the corner. `build_preview` answers it as `closing`:
  `{component, end ("a" or "b": the member's end at the corner), mitre
  ("shared" or "none"), angle}`, null when the placing closes no corner;
  its `length.mode` is the mode the length gets.

### Resting, lying as the host, typed corners (mitcad#492)

Four more rules (code `build/place.rs`, `build/spacing.rs`; tests
`build/close_tests.rs`, `build/timber_tests.rs`):

- **A member lying on a plane rests on it.** A part placed on the ground
  (`place` `grounded`: on the host's XY plane; `geometry`: on a picked
  plane or planar face) with `at.direction` along the plane is lifted
  along the plane's normal until its box's lowest point is on the plane:
  it lies on the normal's side (+Z on XY, +Y on XZ, +X on YZ, a face's
  outward side), not centred on the plane, timber and slot profiles
  alike, as `lie`, `rotate` and `flip` turn it. On a picked plane or face
  the lift is in the joint's `frame_override.origin` (and a bound
  length's ray starts from the lifted axis); `build_edit`'s `rotate` and
  `flip` lift it anew, so it keeps resting. A part standing along the
  normal (or without `at.direction`) stands on its end as before.
- **A member on a member's side lies as that member does.** A timber
  member placed standing on a timber member's side (`place` `side`, not
  tilted) is turned a quarter about its axis when only that puts its
  section's thickness axis parallel to the target's or, where its axis
  takes the target's thickness axis (on the target's wide face), its
  width axis parallel to the target's width axis: same-size members have
  flush sides. The turn is the joint's own frame override (`a.frame_override`
  with `x_axis`), so the slide along the side and its offsets are as
  before; `rotate` turns it further, and a `flip` edit sets the turn anew
  for the end that then meets. A square section, or a slot profile, is
  placed as before.
- **A typed length closes a corner too.** A part placed on an end whose
  typed length (`length` a value) ends on the face or the outer side of a
  member it meets as a corner (as *Closing a frame* finds it, the far
  end within 0.05 mm of that face or side) closes the corner as a bound
  length does: ending on the outer side after a mitred start, both ends
  get the shared mitre; on the face, a square butt. A typed length that
  ends inside the member gets a warning naming the two lengths that would
  meet it. `build_preview` answers it as `closing`. Its axis must run
  through the member, not along one of its faces. A member by two points
  (`place` `points`, whose start is square) with the points' distance or
  a typed length gets the same: a square butt where it ends on the
  member's face, else the warning; a bound length keeps the mode given.
  With the points' distance, an end in the member (or, free, on its outer
  side) is cut back to its face first (mitcad#509, *Members by two
  points*): the square butt, no warning.
- **A set on a side starts at the typed offset.** In a spacing set on a
  side whose base placement has `at.offset` (the app's Offset and From)
  and no `spacing.from` or `spacing.to`: from end A (or the middle) the
  first member's near face is where that offset puts it; from end B the
  last member's far face.

### Classes

`build_connect` with `joint` (no `part`) is class `model`; with a part,
as before.

## Section curves in sketches

`sketch.project` with `"section": true` (mitcad#389) adds the curves where
the sketch's plane cuts a face (`source`, a face name; every face of a
name without `#k`) instead of the face's projected boundary:

```json
{"cmd": "sketch.project", "sketch": "F5", "source": "F2:side(c3)", "body": "F2.b0",
 "linked": true, "section": true}
```

- The fields are `sketch.project`'s: `body`, `linked`, and `occurrence`
  and `context` for a face of another component ([Geometry of other
  components](#geometry-of-other-components)); the sketch's plane is moved
  into that component's coordinates, cut there, and the curves moved back.
- The kernel cuts each face by itself (`Kernel::section_curves`,
  `geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/sketch_ref.hpp`): a line, circle or
  ellipse per piece; B-spline pieces that meet end to end where no other
  piece ends (a thread's faces cut along its axis) become one B-spline,
  exactly. The curves come in as `sketch.project` makes entities: fixed
  reference geometry, ends that meet sharing a point.
- A linked section is recorded as a projection with `"section": true` in
  the sketch's `projections`; it is recomputed from the body at every
  evaluation and its entities follow it as a linked projection's do (each
  the fresh curve of its kind most like it; one that finds none keeps its
  last geometry and the sketch warns). A face the plane no longer cuts is
  a lost source.
- An edge (Intersect, mitcad#736): `source` an edge name; the entities
  are points where the plane crosses the edge (every edge of a name
  without `#k`; `Kernel::section_points`, OCCT's section of the edge by
  the plane): a point where it passes through or touches the plane, the
  ends of an edge or a piece of it lying in the plane. Linked, the record
  is a projection with `"section": true` whose source is the edge, and
  its points follow the fresh crossings.
- A whole body (Intersect, mitcad#736): no `source`, `body` given. The
  kernel cuts all of the body's faces (`section_curves` without a face)
  and the pieces come in grouped by the face they lie on: each face's
  pieces are a section of that face of their own (linked: one projection
  record per face, as a face's section would be), a B-spline joined
  across faces one of its first face with the others as its `chain`, and
  pieces on faces without names unlinked. One edit, one undo step
  (`Section Curves to Sketch1`). Each record follows its face; a face the
  body gains later in the plane adds nothing.
- Refused: a vertex (`a section's source is a face, an edge or a body`);
  a face or edge that is not before the sketch or that the plane does not
  cut (`the sketch's plane does not cut it (or nothing named so is before
  the sketch)`); a body the plane does not cut (`the sketch's plane does
  not cut the body`); `sketch.project` without `source` and without
  `section` (`needs a source`).

Tests: `core/model-tests/sketch-refs/src/section_curve_tests.rs` (mock kernel: the section
of a face is where the plane cuts the body's bounds; a whole body's
section puts side k of it on the body's face k; an edge's crossing is
where the plane crosses its line in `named_curves`);
`geometry/tests/test_section_curves.cpp` (an edge through the plane and
one lying in it).

## Projecting another sketch's curves and points

`sketch.project` takes a curve or a point of an earlier sketch as its
`source` (mitcad#904), in the form the [references to
geometry](#references-to-geometry) give sketch entities:

```json
{"cmd": "sketch.project", "sketch": "F4", "source": {"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c3"}, "linked": true}
{"cmd": "sketch.project", "sketch": "F4", "source": {"sketch": "F1", "point": "p7"}}
{"cmd": "sketch.project", "sketch": "F4", "source": {"sketch": "F1"}, "linked": true}
```

- Any entity of the source sketch: lines, arcs, circles, ellipses and
  elliptical arcs, splines (by control points and through fit points) and
  points, construction and projected ones too. `{"sketch": "F1"}` without
  `curve` or `point` (a whole sketch picked in the browser) takes every
  curve of it, each as a projection of its own; its loose points are not
  curves and are left out.
- The geometry is where the source sketch's last evaluation solved it,
  in model space, projected along the sketch's normal onto its plane as
  body edges are: on the same plane an exact copy, on a parallel plane the
  same shapes, on an oblique plane lines shorter, circles and arcs
  ellipses and elliptical arcs, splines with their poles projected; a curve
  seen edge on is a line, a point stays a point. The entities are fixed
  reference geometry, joined to the projected geometry already there as
  [projections of model geometry](#projected-outlines-and-their-offsets)
  are, but only to that of the same source sketch.
- Linked (`"linked": true`), each entity's projection is recorded in the
  sketch's `projections` with the entity as its `source`:
  `{"source": {"sketch": "F1", "curve": "c3"}, "entities": [...],
  "by_geometry": true}`. Entity ids stay with a sketch's entities across
  its edits, so the record follows the same curve when the source sketch
  is edited, solved again or its parameters change: at every evaluation
  its entities take the fresh geometry, each the fresh curve of its kind
  most like it. A source entity removed from its sketch makes the
  projection lost, as a body edge that is gone: its entities keep their
  last geometry, the `sketch` query marks the record `"lost": true`, and
  the sketch warns `the projection of F1/c3 does not follow it: it is
  gone, ...` (messages name the entity `F1/c3`). Unlinked, the entities
  are fixed copies with no record.
- Order: only a sketch before the edited one in the timeline. A later
  sketch is refused (`Sketch3 (F3) comes after Sketch2 (F2) in the
  timeline; only the curves and points of a sketch before it can be
  projected`), so no sketch follows one that follows it; a linked
  projection whose source the timeline later puts after it fails the
  sketch's check, as a reference to a later feature does. The sketch's
  own geometry is refused (`a sketch does not project its own geometry`),
  as is an entity the sketch does not have (`Sketch1 has no c99`), a
  `body` with a sketch's geometry, and `"section": true` with it.
- Another component's sketch, and a sketch of a component placed more
  than once, come through `occurrence` and `context` as its bodies' edges
  do ([Geometry of other components](#geometry-of-other-components)): the
