| `angle` | turns the pulley about its axis: tooth 1 is centred on the plane's x axis without it; the keyway and the first set screw lie in this direction. Not with `belt_with` (refused: `belt_with.angle` places the pulley, its teeth then start on that plane's x axis) |
| `teeth` | the toothed kinds' number of teeth: whole, from the profile's minimum (12 for HTD 5M, 10 for the others) to 1000 |
| `diameter` | an `idler`'s running diameter (instead of `teeth`) |
| `belt_width`, `clearance` | mm; the toothed (running) width is `belt_width + clearance`, the clearance 1 mm without it |
| `pitch_correction` | mm added to the outside diameter (a pitch-diameter correction, e.g. for backlash), at most a quarter of the pitch either way; 0 without it. The belt's values keep the nominal pitch diameter |
| `flanges` | `sides` (`none`, `one`, `both`; `both` without it), `diameter` (more than the outside diameter; optional, mitcad#656: without it the outside diameter plus, all round, the profile's groove depth and 1 mm, MitCad's default; the outside diameter plus 2 mm without a profile), `thickness`. One flange lies on the plane's side, away from the hub |
| `hub` | `diameter` (optional, mitcad#656: without it the bore (a seated pulley's too) plus a wall all round of 2 mm, or of a set screw's tap drill when that is more; half the root diameter without a bore, at least two walls), `length`: after the toothed part and the second flange, away from the plane |
| `bore` | `{"type": "plain", "diameter": d}` or `{"type": "thread", "thread": {"designation": "M8x1.25"}}` (the size's minor diameter, its tap drill), through the whole pulley; it stays 0.5 mm inside the groove bottoms (an idler's running face) with its keyway |
| `keyway` | a DIN 6885-1 (form A) keyway in a plain bore of 6 to 230 mm, at the pulley's `angle` |
| `set_screws` | `count` (1 to 4, 90 degrees apart from `angle`), `thread` (a tap drill of that size, radial from the axis through the hub; listed as cosmetic threads by `threads`), `position` (mm from the hub's outer end along the axis; the hub's middle without it). Needs a hub |
| `belt_with` | `{"pulley": "F3", "center_distance": 80, "angle": <angle>}`: in the plane of an earlier pulley feature of the same component, at `center_distance` from its centre in the direction `angle` (from its plane's x axis; 0 without it), for one belt round both. The two share the belt profile (an idler without one takes the other's); their pitch circles must not overlap |
| `seat` | on a shaft instead of `plane` and `center` ([Seats on shafts](#seats-on-shafts), mitcad#578): the pulley's plane (where its first flange starts) at the seat's offset along the shaft, running along the shaft from it; not with `belt_with` (a pulley running with a seated one lies in its plane). Without `bore` the bore is plain, the shaft's diameter plus `bore_clearance`, and follows the shaft (a `keyway` in it too); a `thread` bore stays the thread's; a plain `bore` of its own is refused |
| `bore_clearance` | mm added to the shaft's diameter for a seated pulley's plain bore (0 without it; a printed fit 0.2, say); only with `seat` and without `bore` |
| `operation`, `participants` | as an extrusion's |

Values are parameters: numbers in mm (radians for angles; `teeth` and
`set_screws.count` unitless) or names and expressions, as for gears.

- **Diameters:** the pitch diameter is z p / pi (the belt's pitch line);
  the outside diameter is the pitch diameter less twice the profile's
  pitch line offset (PLD), plus `pitch_correction`; the root diameter is
  the outside diameter less twice the groove's depth.

  | Profile | Pitch | PLD | Groove |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `gt2_2mm` | 2 mm | 0.254 | round: 0.764 deep, 1.494 wide, bottom radius 0.555, tip radius 0.15 |
  | `gt2_3mm` | 3 mm | 0.381 | round: 1.169 deep, 2.31 wide, bottom radius 0.85, tip radius 0.25 |
  | `htd_3m` | 3 mm | 0.381 | round: 1.289 deep, 2.27 wide, bottom radius 0.86, tip radius 0.3 |
  | `htd_5m` | 5 mm | 0.5715 | round: 2.199 deep, 3.781 wide, bottom radius 1.49, tip radius 0.43 |
  | `t5` | 5 mm | 0.425 | straight-sided: 1.75 at the bottom, 1.25 deep, 50 degrees, bottom radius 0.4, tip radius 0.6 |
  | `xl` | 5.08 mm | 0.254 | straight-sided: 1.32 at the bottom, 1.65 deep, 50 degrees, bottom radius 0.41, tip radius 0.64 |

- **Grooves:** our own construction around the published belt
  dimensions (the sources per profile are in `pulley_profile.rs`); one
  fixed groove per profile, not generated by the belt's motion. A round
  groove has a bottom arc centred on its axis and straight flanks tangent
  to it through the corners its width and depth give; a straight-sided
  groove a flat bottom with fillets and flanks at half its included
  angle; both have tip fillets tangent to the flanks and the outside
  circle. Too few teeth for a groove's width leave no land and are
  refused.
- **Faces:** tooth k (from 1, counter-clockwise about the axis) has
  `tip(k)` (its land on the outside circle), `tip_fillet_a(k)`,
  `flank_a(k)` and `root_fillet_a(k)` (straight-sided grooves) on its
  clockwise side, `tip_fillet_b(k)`, `flank_b(k)`, `root_fillet_b(k)` on
  the other, `root(k)` the groove bottom after it; an idler's `running`;
  the caps `start`, `end`; `flange_a`, `flange_a_end`, `flange_a_inner`,
  `flange_b`, `flange_b_inner`, `flange_b_end`; `hub`, `hub_start`,
  `hub_end`; `bore`, `keyway_a`, `keyway_top`, `keyway_b`; `set_screw(k)`.
- **Mount frame:** the result keeps its frame as the mount `bore` (x, y
  and the axis as columns, the origin on the axis on its plane), as a
  library pulley's: joints and joint origins take it as
  `{"mount": "F3:mount(bore)"}` (a plane, the axis or its origin); a
  joint origin there with a `mount` (kind `hole`) is a mount frame of the
  design for Place Part ([Mount frames](#mount-frames)).
- **Belts:** the open belt round two pulleys of pitch radii R and r (an
  idler's running radius), C apart: L = 2 C cos(t) + pi (R + r) +
  2 t (R - r), sin(t) = (R - r) / C. It wraps pi - 2 t of the smaller
  pulley and pi + 2 t of the larger. A belt body is not made.

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `pulley_values` | `uid` (a pulley feature) or `def` (a definition as `add_feature` takes it, without `type`); `belt_lengths` (optional: catalogue belt lengths in mm) | `kind`, `tooth_width` (the toothed width), `length` (along the axis); `bore_diameter` (given, or a seated pulley's from its shaft at the timeline marker, with `shaft_diameter` and the `seat` as `seat_frame` gives it); `flange_diameter` and `hub_diameter` (given or worked out, with flanges and a hub) and `computed` (those worked out, so that a panel shows them as computed until one is typed); with a profile `profile`, `pitch`, `pitch_line_offset`, `min_teeth`; the toothed kinds' `teeth`, `pitch_diameter`, `outside_diameter`, `root_diameter`; an idler's `diameter` (and `outside_diameter`); `section_area` (the toothed or running section's, without bore and flanges); with `belt_with` `center_distance`, `mate` (the other pulley's uid), `belt_length` (the belt's pitch length), `wrap_angles` (on the smaller and the larger pulley), `belt_teeth` (belt_length / pitch, with a profile), `teeth_in_mesh` (whole teeth on the smaller toothed pulley), `catalogue_length` (the nearest of `belt_lengths`, only when given); `error` when the values make no pulley or no belt |

## BUILD: timber frames

A wall, floor or roof frame of timber members made from a few values
(mitcad#479), edited afterwards as one. Its members are ordinary BUILD
parts (*BUILD: timber construction*): grounded members by two points of
the library's timber, in the cut list, junctions and lists like any
other. The app's Wall and Floor / Roof (mitcad#520) make them and Timber
Frame lays them out again (`app/COMMANDS.md`, *Timber*). Code:
`core/model-build/src/frames.rs`; tests `core/model-tests/build-frames/src/frame_tests.rs`.

```json
{"cmd": "build_frame", "kind": "wall", "part": {"source": "S1", "config": "48x98"},
 "start": [0, 0, 0], "end": [3600, 0, 0], "height": "2400 mm", "spacing": 600,
 "openings": [{"offset": 600, "width": 900, "height": 1200, "sill": 900}],
 "fastener": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "...", "component": "wood-screw"}}
```

`build_frame` (class `remote`) takes `kind` (`wall`, `floor` or `roof`),
`part` (the members' timber: studs, joists, rafters; `role: profile`,
`kind: timber`, cut to length, with its `section`) and, by kind, the fields
below. Points are in the BUILD host's coordinates, lengths values (mm or
an expression), openings numbers in mm. `name` (optional) names the frame
(`Wall 1`, `Floor 1`, `Roof 1` by default; unique among the frames); the
members' components are named after it and their role (`Wall 1 stud
(3)`). `fastener` (optional) is a wood fastener: two of them, sized from
the members (*Wood fasteners*' default), are driven at every junction of
two of the frame's members that has no connector; a junction they are
refused at is left as it is.

- **A wall** (`kind: wall`): `start` and `end`, its centre line at its
  base (made level with the start); `height` (default 2400 mm, the
  underside of the bottom plate to the top of the top plate); `spacing`
  (the studs' centre distance, default 600); `plates` `{bottom, top}`
  (1 or 2 each, default 1); `plate` and `header` (parts, default `part`);
  `openings` `[{offset, width, height, sill}]` (`offset` from the start
  along the wall to the rough opening's near side, `sill` its underside's
  height above the base; 0 or left out: a door); `joins` `{start, end,
  start_on}`: the wall frames (any member of each) its ends butt against,
  `start_on: end` (mitcad#510) when instead that wall's end face butts
  against this wall's side at its start (left out: `side`); `corner`
  (mitcad#510): how they meet those walls, `butt`, `lapped` or `straight`
  (mitcad#524: a start on an end face continues in line, its ends
  otherwise butting) (left out:
  `lapped`, as walls saved before it keep their corners), kept in the
  definition and changed with `build_edit`.
  - The plates lie flat, the studs stand with the larger section size
    across the wall: the wall's depth is the stud's larger size. The end
    studs stand flush with its ends; the others at `k × spacing` from its
    start (centres), one that would touch the end stud left out.
  - **Spliced plates** (mitcad#536): a bottom or top plate longer than the
    plate's timber's longest (its `length.max`, else its longest stock
    length) is made of pieces butted end to end, from end A each as long as
    the longest stock length allows (at most its longest), the last one the
    remainder; each piece at least the timber's least length (and two stud
    thicknesses). Each joint lies over the centre of a stud that bears on
    the plate (one reaching the top plates for a top plate, one standing
    on the bottom plates for a bottom plate: studs, king studs, junction
    studs, trimmer and cripple studs), the farthest that keeps the piece
    within the stock length; where no stud is in reach a **backing stud**
    goes in (full height, `stud.splice.<n>`, as far along as the piece may
    run, beside the openings' framing and the other studs). The joints of
    a second plate (`plates.top: 2` or `plates.bottom: 2`) are at least a
    stud spacing from the first's (else a warning, `Wall 1: the joints of
    its top plates are less than a stud spacing apart`). A bottom plate is
    cut at its doors first, each run spliced alone. A plate's first piece
    keeps its place (`plate.top.0`, so a top plate still leads the frame),
    the others `plate.top.0.1`, `plate.top.0.2`, ...; a bottom plate's
    pieces are `plate.bottom.0.0`, `plate.bottom.0.1`, ... as at its doors.
    The pieces are ordinary members: the cut list lists each, cut from the
    stock. A frame's `fastener` goes at the junction of each piece with
    the stud under the joint (each piece's end over half the stud); the
    pieces' own butt joint is an `inline` junction, which takes no wood
    fastener (`an inline joint takes a plate`), so it gets none. The wall is
    refused only when a piece cannot be made at all (no stud and no room
    for a backing stud within reach: `Wall 1: its top plate from 0 to
    7819 mm is longer than its timber's longest, 6000 mm, and no stud can
    take a joint between ...`) or another member is longer than its
    timber (a stud taller than the stock: `Wall 1: the stud stud.start:
    the length 6904 mm is longer than the part's longest, 6000 mm`).
    Plates no longer than the timber's longest stay one piece, as before.
    Tests: `core/model-tests/build-timber/src/wall_splice_tests.rs`.
  - An opening: king studs (full height) and trimmer studs (the bottom
    plate to the header) on each side; a header on edge between the king
    studs on the trimmers, of as many plies as the wall's depth takes
    (`floor(depth / thickness)`, two 48 mm plies in a 98 wall); a window's
    sill flat between the trimmers; cripple studs at the stud places in
    the opening, above the header and below the sill. A door cuts the
    bottom plates. The studs at the opening's place give way. Refused:
    an opening that does not fit between the end studs, openings whose
    studs overlap, a header above the top plate, a sill below the bottom
    plate.
  - **Load-bearing or not** (`load_bearing`, mitcad#519; kept in the
    definition and changed with `build_edit`): `true` or left out (as
    walls saved before keep) frames the openings as above; `false` (a
    partition, the app's default for a new wall) leaves the trimmer studs
    out: the king studs stand at the opening's sides (`opening.<n>.king.a`
    from `offset - thickness`, `.king.b` from `offset + width`), and one
    header lies flat between them, its wide face down as a plate
    (`opening.<n>.header`, role `flat header`, the `header` part, from
    `offset` to `offset + width`); the cripple studs above start at its
    top, the sill and the cripple studs below are as above. The opening's
    framing is a stud narrower on each side, so an opening fits nearer the
    end studs. The preview's `roles` and the cut list follow it.
  - **Butting** (`corner: butt`, mitcad#510): a wall's end in `joins`
    stops at the face of the wall it names (on the side the wall is on),
    its end stud and plates square against it, neither lapped nor notched.
    That wall is neither run on, lapped nor notched; it gets a backing
    stud on each side of the joining wall (its keys as at a T,
    `junction.<wall>.<end>.a` and `.b`), one that would take its end
    stud's place left out, so the sheathing of both walls has a stud
    behind its edges at the junction. With `joins.start_on: end` that
    wall's end face butts against this wall's side: that wall is not
    changed at all, this one runs from its own start and gets the backing
    studs on each side of that wall's centre line where they fit
    (`junction.<that wall>.0.a`, `.b`). Either way the walls stay joined:
    editing one lays the other out again.
  - **Corners and T-junctions** (`corner: lapped`, left out): a wall's end
    in `joins` stops at the face of the wall it names (on the side the
    wall is on); that wall gets a stud for each wall that joins it: where
    the joining wall's centre line
    meets it within that wall's depth of its end, a corner (it runs on to
    the joining wall's outer face, the stud just inside the corner), else
    a T (a stud on each side of the joining wall). A wall that joins
    another one lays that one out again with it. At a corner the plates
    lap (mitcad#493): where each wall has one plate (at the top, and at
    the bottom), both run to the corner's outer faces and are half-lapped
    over the other wall's depth (a `half_lap` cut each, no `junction`,
    `with` the other wall's lead), the joining wall's half outside (the
    upper half of a top plate, the lower half of a bottom plate); with two,
    the joining wall's outer plate (the upper top plate, the lower bottom
    plate) runs over the corner to the other wall's outer face and the other
    wall's stops at the joining wall's inner face, the inner plates as at a
    butt. At a T the plates butt.
  - **A wall started on another wall's side** (mitcad#493): with `square:
    true` and `joins.start`, `start` is a point on that wall's side (a
    click; within its depth of its ends) and the wall starts square to it,
    at its base, towards the side the point is on (the end's side when the
    point is on its centre line, else its left). With `corner: butt`
    (mitcad#510):
    - **from the side** (`side`): its centre line starts at the point's
      place along the wall (snapped, or From and Offset, below), but at
      least half its own depth from the wall's end faces (it never hangs
      past an end: its outer face at most flush with the end face); it
      butts against that wall's side, which gets the backing studs;
    - **from an end** (`end`): a point on one of the wall's end faces
      (within 0.5 mm of the face and inside its depth, or beyond the end;
      the faces where its plates end now) starts it beyond that end, its
      side against the end face: its centre line half its own depth past
      the face, its start flush with the wall's side away from the side it
      runs to (the end's side first here, then the point's). It stays
      joined to the wall (`joins.start_on: end`): that wall is not changed,
      the new wall gets the backing studs where it meets it.

    With `corner: lapped` (or left out):
    - an **L corner** when the point is near one of its ends (within half
      its stud spacing, at least its depth, at most half its length): the
      new wall's centre line starts at that end of the wall's centre line;
    - a **T** elsewhere: its centre line starts at the point's place along
      the wall.

    **From and Offset** (mitcad#514): on the side its place along the wall
    is measured as a side placement's (mitcad#417), between the wall's end
    faces (where its plates end now): `from` `a` (end A to the new wall's
    near face), `b` (end B to its far face) or `middle` (the middle to its
    centre line, positive towards end B), `offset` that distance (a value;
    0 is flush with that end, or centred). Without either, the point
    decides, snapped: flush with an end when the new wall's face would be
    within its depth of that end (butting; lapped: within the L corner's
    reach above), centred within a quarter of its depth of the middle,
    else the point's place from the nearer end; `snap` (mm, optional) is
    the app's least snap distance, as `at.snap`. With either given (end A
    and 0 when one is left out) they place it, the point only choosing the
    side (never an end face). It never hangs past an end: a typed offset
    that would is made flush with that end, with the warning `<name>: flush
    with Wall 1's end A instead`. Butting, flush with an end is a clean
    corner: its outer face in the plane of that end face, its end stud and
    plates against the side, the wall's end stud outside it and a backing
    stud inside it; lapped, flush with an end is the L corner there, any
    other place a T.

    Its length runs from there: as far as `end` is along it (a second
    click, anywhere); else, unless `auto_end` is false (mitcad#515), to the
    first wall frame its run meets: one it crosses (not one parallel to
    it), its centre line between that wall's end faces (not one it merely
    touches at a corner), beyond the side it starts from, their heights
    overlapping; the nearest along the run. It ends there butting against
    that wall's side as a start on a side does (`joins.end` that wall: its
    end stud and plates square against the side, a backing stud each side
    of it in that wall; with `corner: lapped` that wall's corner or T), its
    length to that wall's face. Else (nothing met, or `auto_end: false`)
    `length`. Refused without `end` or `length` when nothing is met, and
    when it would not reach beyond the wall's side (from an end, beyond its
    other side). The definition keeps the `start`, `end` and `joins`
    worked out (not `square`, `from`, `offset`, `snap`, `auto_end`). The
    answer, and `build_preview`'s with `frame`, add `junction`: `{kind
    ("side", "end", "L" or "T"), corner ("butt" or "lapped"), wall (its
    name), frame (its lead), end ("a" or "b" for an end or an L, else
    null), at (mm along the wall from its start to the new centre line),
    length (mm), from ("a", "b" or "middle"; null at an end), offset (mm;
    null at an end), to ({wall, frame, auto}: the wall its end butts
    against, `auto` true when its run met it, false for an end clicked on
    it; else null), run (mm: the new wall between the faces it butts
    against, from the wall's side, at an end from its far side)}`; null
    without `square`.

    **Straight** (`corner: straight`, mitcad#524): a start on one of that
    wall's end faces continues it in line (`kind: "straight"`, `end` the
    end clicked): its centre line that wall's, its start on the end face,
    running away from it; the two walls are not joined (neither changes
    the other). On the side it starts as `butt` does.

  - **A wall started on another body's face** (case B, mitcad#524): with
    `square: true`, no `joins.start` and `face` `{body, face, occurrence}`
    (the body's uid, the face's name and the occurrence that places it, its
    path from the root; left out: the body's first placement), `start` the
    click on the face. A Timber wall frame's member is case A above,
    recognised first (the app sends `joins.start` for it), so its
    behaviour does not change. The clicked body (an imported wall, a
    modelled solid, a loose Timber member, a floor frame's member) is not
    changed and not linked; everything comes from the geometry:
    - **side**: the face's outward side (its normal out of the body's
      material, `Kernel::face_plane`), never into or behind it;
      **direction**: square from it, along its normal; a face that is not
      vertical (its normal more than 0.001 off the horizontal) is refused
      (`<name> starts from a vertical face: the face of <body> clicked is
      not vertical`);
    - **base**: the floor under the click: the first body a line down from
      a millimetre in front of the click enters (`Kernel::segment_crossings`,
      a slab's top), else the face's bottom edge (its box,
      `Kernel::face_boxes`, else the body's), its bottom plate's underside
      there, `height` from it;
    - **along the face**: at the click, or `offset` from `from` (`a`, the
      face's end A: its left end seen from in front of it, `b` or
      `middle`), snapped as on a wall frame's side with `corner: butt`
      (flush with an end within the new wall's depth, centred within a
      quarter of it, else from the nearer end), never past an end;
    - **an end face** (narrower than the body is deep behind it: a solid
      wall's thin end) makes a corner: with `butt` (or `lapped`, which has
      nothing to lap here) its side against the end face, running to the
      side of the face's middle the end (else the click) is on, its start
      flush with the body's far side, longer than the face is wide
      (`kind: "face_end"`); with `straight` in line beyond it, its centre
      line the face's middle (`kind: "face_straight"`); a side face
      (`kind: "face"`) is the same with any corner.
    - Its length as a start on a wall frame's: `end`, else (unless
      `auto_end` is false) what its run meets first, else `length`. **The
      auto end** (mitcad#515, both cases) stops the run at a wall frame
      (as above) or at **any other body's face** it meets nearer (the
      bodies shown other than timber frames' members), butting it (no
      link: `to.frame` null, `to.face` true). The nearest face along the
      run is taken (mitcad#536): it looks along lines a quarter, half and
      three quarters of the wall's height up and 10 mm under its top (the
      wall over a door in the wall ahead), each at its centre line and a
      millimetre inside each of its sides (a post or a wall's end only its
      side meets); the body it starts on counts too, beyond its own face
      (a millimetre on), so a room modelled as one body ends it at its far
      wall.
    - The definition keeps the `start` and `end` worked out (the start at
      the base's height), not `face`. The junction's `kind` is `face`,
      `face_end` or `face_straight`, `wall` the body's name, `frame` null,
      `at` along the face from its end A, and `base` `{z, on ("floor",
      "face" or "origin"), body}` names what it stands on. Tests:
      `core/model-tests/build-frames/src/face_start_tests.rs`.
- **A floor or ceiling** (`kind: floor`): `outline` (a closed outline,
  three points at least, at its first point's height: the joists'
  underside), `spacing` (default 400), `direction` (the joists'; default
  square to the outline's first side, into it), `rim` (default `part`),
  `blocking` (rows of blocking, default 0), `openings` `[{offset: [a, b],
  size: [w, l]}]` (from the outline's least corner across the joists and
  along them), `trimmers` (default 2).
  - Rim joists on edge along every side, inside the outline; at a corner
    the side across the joists runs through (exact at square corners).
    Joists on edge at `k × spacing` from the outline's least point across
    them, from rim to rim (each place cut where the outline is open, as an
    L or a U), one that would touch a rim along the joists left out.
  - A row of blocking runs across the joists halfway (rows evenly along
    them), a block between each two neighbouring joists or rims.
  - An opening (a stair's): `trimmers` trimmer joists each side, full span;
    as many header joists each side between the inner trimmers; tail
    joists from the rims to the headers at the joist places inside it.
    Refused when it does not fit inside the rims with its trimmers.
- **A roof** (`kind: roof`): `walls` (two parallel wall frames, any member
  of each), `roof` (`gable`, the default, or `mono`), `pitch` (an angle,
  5 to 75 degrees; a gable's default 30; a mono-pitch roof's default from
  the walls' heights), `spacing` (the rafters', default 600), `overhang`
  (the rafters' horizontal run beyond the walls' outer faces, default
  300), `ridge` (default `part`).
  - The rafters stand on edge at the centre distance along the walls
    where both run (the first and last flush with those ends), each plumb
    cut at both ends (`ends` at the pitch: end A leaning up, its long
    point the bottom edge at the eave; end B leaning down, its long point
    the top edge) and notched by a **birdsmouth** over each wall's top
    plate: a `birdsmouth` cut (*Joinery*) in its derived part, the box
    under the top of the plate over its width, `with` the wall's lead. The
    seat is the plate's width, or less so that the notch is at most a
    third of the rafter's depth; a gable roof's rafters bear on the outer
    edge of each wall.
  - Gable: the rafters of each side run from the eave to a ridge board on
    edge halfway between the walls' outer faces, its top at the rafters'
    tops; the walls must be of one height. Mono-pitch: from the lower wall
    over the higher one, notched over both.
  - Warnings: a ridge board shallower than the rafters' plumb cut, a
    birdsmouth deeper than a third of the rafter, rafters that do not bear
    on a wall.
  - Its `fastener` goes at the junctions of its own members (mitcad#521):
    through the ridge board into each rafter's plumb cut end, square to
    the cut, from the board's far side (*Cut ends* after *How junctions
    are found*); the two rafters of a pair are no junction, and a
    mono-pitch roof's rafters have none among them. The rafters are not
    fastened to the walls' plates (junctions of two frames).

The answer: `component` and `frame` (the lead), `frame_component` (the
frame's own component, below), `name`, `kind`, `members`
(`[{component, member}]`), `count`, `fasteners` (the junctions given
fasteners), `relaid` (other frames laid out again with it), `warnings`
(the frame's, the layout's, and the first ten fasteners' warnings),
`splices` (a wall's plates made of pieces, mitcad#536: `[{plate, role,
at, pieces, longest}]`, `plate` the first piece's place, `at` the joints
in mm along the wall from its start, `longest` the longest piece); undo
step `Place wall frame Wall 1`, one step with the fasteners.

**A frame is a component of its own** (mitcad#522). `build_frame` makes
a component named after the frame (`Wall 1`, `Floor 1`, `Roof 1`; `Wall 1
(1)` when a component has that name) in the BUILD host, placed at the
host's origin, and makes the frame's members, their fasteners and the
fasteners' joints inside it: the host gets one component per frame, not
its members, and a frame's Joints are only its own. Joints between frames
(a fastener connected by hand at a junction of two frames' members) stay
in the host, the common parent. Everything that works on a frame takes
its component as well as any member: `build_edit` with `frame` (laid out
again inside the same component, renamed with the frame), `build_preview`
with `frame` and `component`, `build_remove` with `set` (the members,
their fasteners and the component when nothing else is left in it; the
answer's `components` lists the parts as before, not the component),
`joins` and a roof's `walls`. The definition's points (`start`, `end`,
`outline`, `direction`) are in the component's coordinates, the host's
until the component is moved: a frame moved as one (its occurrence
moved) is laid out again where it is, and the frames around it read it
there; a frame edit's points are in the component's coordinates too.
`build_parts` gives each member `frame_component`; the lead's record keeps
it with the definition (`framing.component`). **Frames saved before**
keep their members flat in their host and load and edit unchanged: laid
out again (MODIFY Timber Frame, or as a frame another one depends on)
they stay in the host, their fasteners there too; nothing is re-parented,
so paths other parts' joints and bound lengths name stay valid. Only a
new frame is made as a component. **The cut list** goes by frame: a
frame's members are grouped only with members of the same frame, each row
names its frame (`frame`, null for parts in no frame), the rows of parts
in no frame first, then each frame's by name; the stock is worked out
over all of them as before. Tests: `core/model-tests/build-frames/src/frame_component_tests.rs`.

**What is kept.** The lead (a wall's top plate, a floor's first rim, a
gable roof's ridge board, a mono-pitch roof's first rafter) keeps the
frame's definition in its record (`framing`: `{frame, count}`, its parts
as `{source, config}`, `joins` and `walls` as the frames' leads); every
member's record has `frame` (the lead) and `member`, its place in the
frame: `plate.top.0`, `plate.bottom.0` (`.0`, `.1`, ... when a door cuts
it or it is spliced; a spliced top plate's further pieces `plate.top.0.1`,
..., mitcad#536), `stud.start`, `stud.end`, `stud.<k>`, `stud.splice.<n>`
(a backing stud under a plate's joint), `junction.<wall>.<end>`,
`opening.<n>.king.a`, `.trimmer.b`, `.header.<ply>`, `.sill`,
`.cripple.top.<k>`, `.cripple.bottom.<k>`; `rim.<side>`, `joist.<k>`,
`joist.<k>.tail.a`, `opening.<n>.trimmer.a.<i>`, `.header.b.<i>`,
`block.<row>.<k>`; `ridge`, `rafter.a.<k>`, `rafter.b.<k>`,
`rafter.<k>`. `build_parts` adds `frame`, `member` and the lead's
`framing` (`{definition, count}`).

**Editing a frame.** `build_edit` with `frame` (any of the fields above;
`{}` lays it out again as it is) and optionally `config` (the members'
row) through any member: the frame laid out again with these fields over
its definition, in one undo step `Edit Wall 1`. A wall's `length` moves
its end along it. The members whose place stays keep their components
(placed anew, their length, row and cuts; connectors on them stay), new
places are made, the others removed as by `build_remove`; the frame's
fasteners are taken away and driven anew. The frames that depend on it
are laid out again too: the walls it joins and those that join it
(before and after the edit), and the roofs on any of these walls; one
that can no longer be laid out stays as it was, with a warning. The
answer as `build_frame`'s, with `changed` (`frame`, `config`).
Members of a frame are otherwise ordinary parts: a member edited alone
(its length, ends) keeps its change until the frame is laid out again.

**Preview.** `build_preview` with `frame` (`build_frame`'s fields, or a
frame edit's with `component`) answers `place: "frame"`, `kind`, `name`,
`count`, `roles` (`{role: count}`), `members` (`[{member, role, start,
end, length, x, section}]` in the design: the axis, the section's X and
its `[W, T]`), `warnings`, `problems`, and for a wall `length` (as worked
out: the auto end's, mm) and `splices` (as `build_frame`'s, mitcad#536).
**A refused preview** (mitcad#536) still answers which frame it is and
what its start and auto end worked out: `name` (the default name given
first, `Wall 1`), `kind`, `junction`, `length`, `count: 0`, no members,
and the reason in `problems` (the same as `build_frame`'s refusal, which
names the frame too).

**Removing.** `build_remove` with `"set": true` on a member removes the
whole frame with its fasteners. A lead removed alone hands the frame to
the next member. Walls that join a removed wall keep their layout until
they are laid out again (their join is then left out, with a warning).

`build_edit` with `frame` is class `remote` (the fasteners are read from
a library).

## BUILD: choosing and swapping fasteners

The wood fastener of a timber frame and of a spacing set, its size and
count, and fasteners of a design made from another fastener where they
are (mitcad#497). The app's Timber tool chooses them in its Frame and
Spacing modes, Swap Fastener swaps them (`app/COMMANDS.md`, *Timber* and
*Swap Fastener*). Code: `core/model-build/src/frames.rs`, `spacing.rs`,
`swap.rs`; tests `core/model-tests/build-timber/src/fastener_tests.rs`.

**A frame's fastener.** `build_frame` (and a frame's `build_edit`) takes
`fastener` (a wood screw or nail, *Wood fasteners*) and `fastener_count`
(how many at each junction, default 2). With a row in `fastener.config`
every junction gets that size (a nail `3.1x90`); without one each
junction's are sized from its members, as `build_connect` sizes them. The
definition keeps both: a frame laid out again drives the same fastener,
size and count. The warnings are `build_connect`'s (the first ten).

**The default fastener** (mitcad#516). The model takes the fastener it is
given; without `fastener` a frame has none. The app's Timber tool sends,
until the user chooses another, the library's default wood fastener:
the one marked `wood.default` (`docs/libraries.md`, *Timber parts*;
`library_build_candidates` with `kind: wood` lists it first). MitCad's
library marks **Wood screw, countersunk**, seated by its head's top
(flush with the wood, *Seating* below), not the pan-head **Connector
screw** (`head_underside`, for a metal connector's plate), which by name
came first and stood proud of every default frame. Without a mark the
app takes the first screw seated by its head's top. Tests:
`core/vcs/src/tests/library_build.rs` (the mark, the picker's order, the
shipped group file's one default) and `tools/cli/build-timber-test.cmake`
(the generated library's first wood fastener, a frame with it seated
flush).

**A spacing set's fasteners.** `build_place` with `spacing` takes
`spacing.fastener` and `spacing.fastener_count` (as a frame's; none: no
fasteners, the default). Each member is then fastened to its hosts: at
every junction of a member with a part outside the set that has no
connector (a joist on the beams it stands on and reaches, a deck board on
each joist it crosses), `fastener_count` of them as `build_connect` drives
them, in the same undo step as the set. The answer adds `fasteners`, the
junctions fastened, and its `warnings` the fasteners'. The set keeps them
in its definition: `build_edit` with `spacing` (which may change
`fastener` and `fastener_count`) takes the set's fasteners away and
drives them anew with the members, in its one undo step, and answers
`fasteners` too; `build_remove` with `"set": true` removes them with the
set. A set's fasteners are the wood fasteners at junctions of exactly one
of its members with another part; one connected there by hand is taken
away with them when the set is laid out again. `build_edit` with
`spacing.fastener` is class `remote`.

```json
{"cmd": "build_swap_fasteners", "fasteners": ["C41", "C42"],
 "part": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "...", "component": "ring-nail",
          "config": "3.1x90"}}
```

**Swapping fasteners.** `build_swap_fasteners` (class `remote`; `model`
with `part.source`) makes each fastener of `fasteners` (components of
role `fastener`) from `part`, in place: the component, its occurrence,
its derived part (another source and row), its joint (holding it by the
new part's frame of the same kind) and its junction stay, so it stays
where it is and what removes or lists it finds it as before; its name
becomes the new designation. One undo step, `Swap 2 fastener(s) for Ring
nail 3.1x90`.

- **Which can replace which.** A wood screw or nail (a `wood` block)
  only another wood fastener (`... is no wood screw or nail: C41 is
  driven into timber`); a connector's nut, screw or washer only another
  fastener without `wood`, and when both name slot `systems`, one that
  fits (`the systems do not fit: ...`). Another part is refused (`... is
  no fastener`).
- **The size.** `part.config` names the row. Left out, a wood fastener at
  a junction is sized from the junction's members as `build_connect`
  sizes it (once per junction); one without a junction (a hanger's
  screws) and a connector's fastener take the source's default row.
- **The warnings** of each wood fastener at its junction for the new
  size, as `build_connect` gives them (embedment, edges, the member's
  end, through), numbered by the fastener's place at its junction.
- The answer: `swapped` (the components), `count`, `designation`,
  `sizes` (`[{component, config, diameter, length}]`, the diameter and
  length a wood fastener's) and `warnings`.

## Properties

Typed property sets (mitcad#496; `core/model-base/src/properties.rs` the types,
values and the store, `document/properties.rs` the commands, what the
document works out and the answers, `api/properties.rs` the JSON). A
property is a key in a named set with a typed value and its source:
`Identity / Mark = W-12`, `Pset_WallCommon / FireRating = EI60`, as IFC
groups them, so that an export can map them directly. Properties are on
three levels:

- a **component** (`C2`, `C0` the root): the definition's, shared by its
  occurrences;
- an **occurrence** (`O3`): its own values; it shows its component's as
  inherited, and its own value of a set and key overrides the
  component's for it only;
- a **body** (`F7.b0`).

An owner is given by its id or by its name (a component's, an
occurrence's `Wall:2` or path from the root `O1/O4`, a body's at the
marker). Set names and keys compare without regard to case; a key has no
`/` (it separates a set from a key in searches; an import writes one as
`∕`).

**Types.** The standard types are `text`, `integer`, `number` (a plain
number, optionally with a `unit` label of its own that is shown and not
converted, `W/(m²·K)`), `length` (kept in mm), `area` (mm²), `volume`
(mm³), `mass` (kg), `angle` (radians), `boolean` (yes/no; `yes/no` and
`bool` name it too) and `date` (`YYYY-MM-DD`). An **own type** is defined
in the design: a `name` (not a standard type's), a `base` standard type,
optional allowed `values` (a property of the type is then edited as a
choice and refuses any other value), an optional `unit` (a quantity's
shown unit, `m`, `deg`, `g`; a number's label) and `default`, and a
`description`.

**Values in commands.** A JSON number of a quantity is canonical (mm,
mm², mm³, kg, radians); text is read in the type's unit, else the
design's (`set_units`: a bare `1.2` in a metre design is 1.2 m), unless
it names its own (`1.2 m`, `2 m^2`, `500 g`, `30 deg`; a decimal comma
works). `yes`/`no`, `true`/`false`, `1`/`0` for yes/no; integers and
numbers as text too. A value of another dimension or kind is refused.

**Sources.** Every value records where it came from: `user`, `rvt`,
`ifc`, `ipt`, `f3d` (the imports), `3mf` (a slicer's print settings,
[Print profiles](#print-profiles)), `library` (a library or BUILD part's
data) or `computed`. A user's value set over an imported one keeps its
source and the value the source gave (`imported` in the file), so the
property shows that it differs (`edited`, `source_value`); set back to the
source's value it is no longer edited.

**Worked out, never stored.** `computed` values (the set `Computed`) and
`library` values (the set `Library`) are worked out when asked for and
never written to the design file, so a recompute leaves the file as it
was:

| Level | Computed (only with `computed`) | Library |
|---|---|---|
| body | `Volume`, `Area`, `Mass` (its material's density), `Material` | |
| component | `Volume`, `Mass` (its own bodies), `Length` (a BUILD member's) | `Designation`, `Supplier`, `Part number`, `Library`, `Version`; a BUILD part's `Material`, `Grade`, `Finish` |
| occurrence | its component's, inherited | its component's, inherited |

A stored value of the same set and key as a library value overrides it
(and shows the library's as its source value); the `Computed` set cannot
hold stored values.

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `set_property` | `owner`, `set`, `key`, `value` (optional with a type that has a default, or for an existing property), `type` (a standard or own type; the property's, else what the value is: text, integer, number, yes/no), `unit` (a quantity's: the unit a number or bare text is in; a number's label), `source` (default `user`; never `computed`) | `owner`, `set`, `key`, `type`, `value` (as stored), `edited`. One undo step, nothing recomputed |
| `remove_property` | `owner`, `set`, `key` | `{}`; an occurrence's component value shows again. Refused when there is none |
| `define_property_type` | `name`, `base`, `values`, `unit`, `default`, `description` | `name`. Refused for a standard type's name, a name taken, a unit of another dimension, values not of the base, a default not among the values |
| `edit_property_type` | `name`, and what changes: `new_name` (its properties follow), `base` (only while no property uses it), `values` (each property's value must stay allowed), `unit` and `default` (`null` removes them), `description` | `name` |
| `remove_property_type` | `name` | `converted`: how many properties keep their values under its base type |

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `property_sets` | `body`, `occurrence`, `component` (at least one; the component follows from the occurrence or the body), `computed` (also the computed values) | `levels`, the given ones most specific first: `level` (`body`, `occurrence`, `component`), `owner`, `name`, an occurrence's `component`, `sets`: `name`, `properties`: `set`, `key`, `type`, `base`, `value` (as stored), `text` (in the shown unit, `1.2 m`), `unit`, `source`, `read_only` (computed), `inherited`, `overrides`, `edited`, `source_value` (the source's value as text, where it differs), `choices` (an own type's values as text) |
| `property_types` | | `standard` (the standard types' names), `types`: `name`, `base`, `values` (`value`, `text`), `unit`, `default`, `description`, `uses` |
| `property_search` | `text`: `Key` or `Set/Key`, with a comparison `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` (numbers and dates in order, quantities in units: `Mass > 10 kg`) or `~` (contains), or without one (the key is there) | `matches`: every component, occurrence (with its inherited values) and body at the marker with a matching property, in that order: `level`, `owner`, `name`, `component`, `set`, `key`, `text`, `inherited`. Computed values only when the search names one |

The `properties` query of this API is a different one: the bodies'
physical properties ([Analysis queries](#analysis-queries)).

The design file keeps the own types as `property_types` and the stored
properties as `properties`, one entry per owner (`owner`, `sets`: `name`,
`properties`: `key`, `type`, `value`, `source` unless `user`, `imported`,
`unit`), only for owners the design has (a deleted component's are left
out). Copies of components, and a design placed as a component, bring
their components', occurrences' and bodies' properties (another design's
root's become the new component's) with the own types they use.

**Imports.** Each import gives the values its file holds with its source;
values MitCad does not otherwise use come in as well:

- `.rvt`: each element's bodies get `Identity` (`ElementId`, `GlobalId`,
  `Category`, `Class`, `Family`, `Type`, `TypeId`, `Level`), `Instance
  Parameters` (the record's text, number and element id parameters) and
  `Type Parameters` (its family type's; a wall's type its `Width`, the
  total of its layers). Parameters are named and typed by their
  definitions (mitcad#501): a project, shared or family parameter by its
  definition in the file (name, and spec or class), a built-in one by the
  reader's table of the common ones (`Height`, `Width`, `Thickness`,
  `Base Offset`, `Mark`, `Type Mark`, ...), else `Parameter <id>`.
  Lengths, areas, volumes, angles and masses come in as `length`, `area`,
  `volume`, `angle` and `mass` in the model's units (mm, mm², mm³,
  radians, kg, converted from the file's feet, square and cubic feet,
  radians and kilograms), so they show in the design's units; yes/no
  parameters as `boolean`, integer ones as `integer`, numbers, counts and
  currencies as `number`. A number of a kind not known or not converted
  (electrical, mechanical and structural quantities, built-in parameters
  not in the table, files before the 2021 release, which keep no spec)
  stays in the file's internal units as a `number` with the unit label
  `internal units`. An element comes in as bodies of its level's
  component, with no component of its type, so its type's values are on
  its bodies too; were the import to make a component per element type,
  they would go on it.
- IFC: an element's `Identity` (`GlobalId`, `Class`, `Name`,
  `ObjectType`), its property sets (single and enumerated values) and
  element quantities (lengths, areas, volumes, counts, weights, times) in
  MitCad's units, on its bodies and the occurrences of its type's shape;
  its type object's property sets (and `Identity / Type`) on the
  component its type's shape became, and on its own bodies.
- `.ipt` and `.iam`: the summary's (`Title`, `Subject`, `Author`,
  `Keywords`, `Comments`, `Last Saved By`), the document summary's
  (`Category`, `Manager`, `Company`), the design tracking set's (`Part
  Number`, `Material`, `Release`) and the user's own named properties
  (`User Defined`) on the root; an assembly's parts' on their components.
- `.f3d` dumps that give them: a component's `Part Number` and
  `Description` (set `Component`).

Tests: `core/model-tests/appearance/src/properties_tests.rs`, `core/ifc/src/properties.rs`,
`core/import-ifc/src/tests.rs` (`property_sets_land_on_their_levels`),
`core/import-rvt/src/lib.rs` (`elements_bring_their_identity_and_parameters`),
`core/import/src/tests/property_tests.rs`, `core/ipt/src/lib.rs`,
`core/import-rvt/tests/corpus/rvt_corpus.rs` and `core/ifc/tests/corpus.rs` (corpus
files by content id), `tools/ui-property-sets-test.sh`,
`tools/ui-windows-property-sets-test.ps1`.

## The sketch's axes and origin as entities

Constraints and dimensions refer to the sketch's own x and y axes and its
origin through entities that stand for them (mitcad#500), made on demand
the first time something refers to them:

```json
{"cmd": "sketch.axis", "sketch": "F1", "axis": "x"}
→ {"entity": "c4", "new": true, "entities": ["p5", "c4"], ...}
{"cmd": "sketch.axis", "sketch": "F1", "axis": "x"}
→ {"entity": "c4", "new": false, ...}
```

- `axis`: `"x"`, `"y"` or `"origin"` (anything else is refused:
  `unknown axis 'z' (x, y or origin)`).
- **The origin** is the sketch's fixed point stored at [0, 0] (the one
  drawing makes when it snaps to the origin, mitcad#355): the first such
  point that is not projected. Without one, `sketch.axis` makes it.
- **An axis** is a fixed construction line from the origin point (made
  first when there is none) to a fixed point 100 mm along the axis. The
  line and that far end carry `"axis": "x"` (or `"y"`) in the sketch
  definition and the `sketch` query; the origin point does not. Only the
  line's direction counts: constraints and dimensions take it as the
  infinite axis (`coincident` puts a point on it, `point_line_distance`
  is a point's distance from it, `angle` a line's angle to it, `symmetric`
  mirrors about it), and as construction geometry it bounds no profile.
  The app draws the axis across the view instead of the line and does not
  show its far end (`app/COMMANDS.md`, Sketch Dimension and the
  constraint tools).
- **One of each.** An entity that is there is returned with `"new":
  false`, and nothing changes: no undo step. A new one is one undo step
  `Axis in Sketch1`, and the result has the editing commands' fields
  (`entities`, `status`, …) besides `entity` and `"new": true`. The app
  runs it inside the action that needs it and merges the steps
  (`merge_undo`), so undo takes the axis back with the constraint or
  dimension.
- Sketches saved before have no `axis` flags and read and save as they
  were. Copies (move, mirror, patterns) do not copy the flag. The DXF
  export (`export_sketch`) leaves the axes' lines out.
- **Mirror about an axis** (mitcad#876): `sketch.mirror` takes `"axis":
  "x"` or `"y"` as well as a line; the axis is made (as `sketch.axis`
  makes it) in the mirror's own undo step `Mirror in Sketch1`, and the
  copies are symmetric about it. Its made line's `c` id works as any
  line.
- **Not redundant** (mitcad#877): a fixed line whose both end points are
  fixed (an axis line, a projected line) is held in the solve by its
  points' fixes alone, so the sketch's `redundant` does not list it; the
  line stays `"fixed": true` in the definition and the `sketch` query.

Code: `core/sketch/src/axes.rs`. Tests:
`core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_axes_tests.rs`, Mirror about an axis
`core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_mirror_876_tests.rs`.

## Reorient Design

The whole design turned by 90, 180 or 270 degrees about the origin's X, Y
or Z axis (mitcad#502), for a design started on the wrong origin plane.
One undo step, `Reorient Design`:

```json
{"cmd": "reorient_design", "axis": "x", "degrees": 90}
{"cmd": "reorient_design", "plane": "xz"}
→ {"turn": "90 degrees about X", "matrix": [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]],
   "features": ["Sketch1", "Plane1", "Sketch3"], "moves": ["Move1"],
   "occurrences": [], "views": 1, "analyses": 0, "lights": 0}
```

- `axis` (`x`, `y`, `z`) with `degrees` (90, 180, 270; -90 is 270),
  counter-clockwise looking against the axis; or `plane` (`xz`, `yz`):
  the turn that takes that origin plane's frame onto XY's (XZ: 90 about
  X, YZ: 270 about Y). `xy` and other turns of nothing are refused.
- **A rewrite, not a move.** Every component that is not linked from
  another file turns in its own coordinates, so that its origin planes
  are where the turned design wants them:
  - references to the origin's planes and axes become their turned
    counterparts: the origin datum the turn takes them onto, frame and
    sense included (XZ turned 90 about X is XY), else the fixed plane or
    axis there (XY turned 90 about X faces -Y: `{"origin": [0, 0, 0],
    "normal": [0, -1, 0], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]}`; the Z axis runs along
    -Y). Fixed planes, axes, points and paths turn, and so do the
    positions and directions definitions keep (a hole's points, a split's
    direction, picks of surface features, a Move's matrix, construction
    geometry given by coordinates, joint frame overrides);
  - a Move's or a Move Component's x, y and z go with their axes; a
    value of an axis the turn reverses is negated (its own dimension
    parameter; one that other values or features use refuses the
    command);
  - a sketch on an origin plane goes onto the origin plane the turn takes
    its plane onto, with its own frame (`frame`) set so that its geometry
    turns with the design, not mirrored. A sketch on a face or a
    construction plane keeps its plane; where the plane's frame follows
    the model axes (a face's x axis is the model's X projected) its own
    frame is set from the turned design's evaluation so that it stays
    turned with the design;
  - an imported body (a base feature) gets a Move right after it that
    turns its bodies about the origin (a base feature that joins, cuts or
    intersects is refused); a body the kernel's checker finds invalid (an
    imported shell that is not connected) turns as it is;
  - the pieces of split faces (`F2:side(c1[c4,c2])#1`) and the edges
    numbered between the same two faces (`E{…}#1`) are numbered by the
    kernel in a geometric order, which the turn changes: references to them
    (also inside other names, `F5:fillet(E{…#1…})`) are renamed after the
    turned design's numbers, each piece to the one where the turn takes it
    (its box; an edge's middle), feature by feature (mitcad#537);
  - occurrences' placements turn in both coordinates they join
    (`R · T · R⁻¹`; an occurrence of a linked component `R · T`), so a
    component placed at the identity stays there; joints, constraints and
    links between components follow from them;
  - named views, section analyses' planes and the lights placed in the
    design (not those that follow the camera) turn; what split features
    remember of their pieces turns with them.
- Faces, edges and bodies keep their names; nothing else is renamed.
- **Checked before it is taken:** the command computes the turned design
  and refuses it, naming them, when a feature that built would fail (a
  Move it adds too), or a body (its bounding box and centre of mass) or an
  occurrence would not be where the turn takes it; the document is then as
  it was. Rules of the model axes that a definition cannot carry (a
  cylinder's axis pointing along its largest component, a joint frame's
  default x axis) can make a design refuse a turn so. The refusal says
  where (mitcad#537):
  - a feature with its component and error: `Reorient Design cannot turn
    the design: Fillet3 (in Part) would fail: …`, an added Move after the
    base feature it turns: `Move1 (after Base1, in leg) would fail: …`;
  - a body with its component, the first feature after which it is not
    its old self turned (a Move added after a base feature counts with it)
    and how far: `Reorient Design cannot turn the design exactly: Body17 of
    leg (made by Base1) departs from the turn after Extrude2: its centre is
    412.000 mm and its box up to 500.000 mm from where the turn takes it`.
- The application previews it on a command checkpoint (`begin_command`,
  `restore_command` for each choice, `discard_command` on OK) and logs
  the bodies' boxes afterwards (`app/COMMANDS.md`, "Reorient Design").

Code: `core/model/src/reorient.rs` (the turn and the rewrite of
definitions), `core/model/src/document/reorient.rs` (the command and its
checks). Tests: `core/model-tests/files/src/reorient_tests.rs` (mock kernel),
`cli.reorient_design` (`tools/cli/tests/reorient_design.json`, OCCT),
`cli.reorient_pieces` (a split face's pieces renumbered by turns, also of
a turned design) and `iam.corpus_reorient`
([tools/cli/reorient-corpus.cmake](../../../tools/cli/reorient-corpus.cmake):
the test files' assemblies c71542a1 and 1dc60c2a under
`MITCAD_IPT_CORPUS`, skipped without them).

## Mount frames

Any part may say where it mounts (mitcad#525; the library's side in
[docs/libraries.md](../../../docs/libraries.md#mount-frames), the
app's Place Part in [app/COMMANDS.md](../../../app/COMMANDS.md#component-libraries)):
a joint origin with a `mount` is a **mount frame** of its design.

```json
{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:top"},
 "mount": {"name": "head", "kind": "shaft", "joint": "cylindrical"}}
{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"origin": [0, 0, 5], "normal": [0, 0, 1], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]},
 "mount": {"name": "grid", "kind": "grid", "pitch": [42, 42], "cells": [3, 2]}}
{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"origin": [21, 21, 0], "normal": [0, 0, -1], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]},
 "mount": {"name": "foot", "kind": "foot", "footprint": [1, 1], "pitch": [42, 42]}}
```

- `name`: 1 to 64 of letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `+` and `.`.
- `kind`: `face` (the default), `shaft`, `hole`, `grid` or `foot`; what
  each frame is and what it goes on is the table of
  [docs/libraries.md](../../../docs/libraries.md#mount-frames). Mated
  frames face each other: the placed frame's z is opposite the target's.
- `joint`: how the placed part may move, the joint its placement makes:
  `rigid` (the default; the only one of `grid` and `foot`), `planar` and
  `revolute` on a face, `revolute`, `cylindrical` and `slider` (along the
  axis) in a hole or on a shaft.
- `pitch` (two lengths, mm, along the frame's x and y) of a `grid` and,
  optionally, of a `foot`; `cells` (two counts) of a `grid`, the cells
  along +x and +y from the frame's origin; `footprint` (two counts) of a
  `foot`, the cells it covers along its x and y, the frame in their
  middle. A check of the feature refuses anything else (`mount: a grid
  gives its cells`).
- A joint origin named `mount:<name>` without a `mount` (BUILD's parts,
  [BUILD](#build-profile-assemblies)) is a `face` frame of that name,
  fixed. A design's frames are its joint origins before the marker, not
  suppressed, each name once (the first); a derived part's frames
  ([derived_part](#derived_part)) are these too.

**Inserted parts keep their frames.** `insert_component` (a file or a
library part):

- linked: the design's frames become joint origins of the new component
  on fixed planes where the design has them (in its row), each with its
  `mount`, named `mount:<name>` (`mount:<name> (2)` when the name is
  taken); `update_links` and `update_library_parts` move them with a new
  version or row (one the design no longer has stays where it was);
- a copy: the copied joint origins are the frames (a `mount:<name>` one
  gets its `mount` and its name back).

So a part dropped in is joined later with `add_joint` by a frame as by
any joint origin (`"a": {"occurrence": "Lamp:1", "geometry": "F12"}`).
Paste New of a linked part copies its bodies only, not its frames.

**Placing by a frame.** `insert_component` with `mount`:

```json
{"cmd": "insert_component", "library": {"id": "test-mounts", "url": "...", "rev": "v1.0.0", "component": "bin1x1"},
 "mount": {"frame": "foot",
           "at": {"occurrence": "Baseplate:1", "geometry": "F9", "point": [68, 21, 5], "toward": [0, 0, 1]},
           "rotate": "90 deg", "offset": 0, "flip": false}}
```

- `frame`: the part's frame (its name; the first frame when left out).
- `at`: what was picked, as a joint's origin from the active component:
  `occurrence` (a path, uids or names; empty: its own geometry),
  `geometry`, the click's `point` and the way `toward` the viewer, both in
  the active component's coordinates.
- `rotate` (an angle about the frame's z; a number is radians), `offset`
  (a length along it: a gap) and `flip` (the target turned over: a
  plane's other side, a hole's other end).

The part goes into the active component as without `mount`, placed where
its frame meets the target face to face, and a joint of the frame's
`joint` is made in the active component: `a` the new occurrence's frame,
`b` the target, `flip` true, `angle` and `offset` the values given, its
free motions driven at 0 (`position`) there. So the part moves with what
it stands on (a planar joint does not slide when its face moves) and a
drag still moves it as the joint lets it (`drag_occurrence` drives the
new values). One undo step, `Insert <name>`.

| The frame | Takes | Side `b` |
|---|---|---|
| `face`, `grid` | a planar face, an origin or construction plane, a joint origin | the plane's frame (a face's: its middle), its `shift` the click's place in the plane |
| `shaft`, `hole` | a cylindrical or conical face, a circular edge, an axis | a cylindrical face's frame at the end towards `toward` (the other with `flip`), z out of that end (`frame_override` z and `shift`); an edge's or an axis' frame with z towards the viewer |
| `foot` | a grid of the picked part: its joint origin, else the grid the click is on (any geometry of the part) | the grid's joint origin, its `shift` the middle of the footprint's cells |

On a grid the footprint is turned by `rotate`, which must be quarter
turns (`on a grid Bin 1x1 turns in quarter turns (0, 90, 180 or 270
deg)`); its first cell is the one that centres the footprint nearest the
click, kept within the grid ((0, 0) without a point). The cells another
foot's joint to the same grid covers (its `shift`, `angle` and footprint)
are taken: a placement onto one is refused (`the cell (0, 1) of
Baseplate:1's grid is taken by Bin 2x1:1`; several: `the cells (0, 0)
and (1, 0) ... are taken by A and B`). A foot whose `pitch` is not the
grid's (`Bin 1x1 stands on a grid of 40 x 40 mm; Baseplate:1's grid is 42
x 42 mm`), a footprint larger than the grid, a pick the frame does not
take (`Lamp lies on a face: pick a flat face or a plane, not a round
one`, `Screw goes into a hole or onto a shaft: pick its round face or its
rim`) and a frame the part has not (`Lamp has no mount frame wall (its
frames: ceiling)`) are refused; the document is as it was.

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `mount_frames` | `occurrence` (a path from the active component; empty: its own) | `component`, `frames`: the mount frames at the marker of the component the path ends in and of those placed in it, each `name`, `kind`, `joint`, `pitch`, `cells`, `footprint`, `feature`, `occurrence` (its path name), `path`, `frame` (`{origin, x_axis, y_axis, z_axis}` in the design) |
| `mount_preview` | `insert_component`'s fields (`link`, `name`, `transform` taken, not used) | the part's `name` and `frames` (each `frame` in the part's coordinates); with `mount` what the placement would do: `frame`, `kind`, `joint`, `target` (`occurrence`, `path`, `geometry`, `frame_override` and `name`: side `b`), `at` (where the frame goes, in the design), `placement` (rows, in the active component), `world` (4x4, in the design), `grid` (a foot's: `feature`, `occurrence`, `path`, `pitch`, `cells`, `cell`, `footprint`, `turns`, `covers`: its cells), or `problems` with the refusal; nothing changes |

`analysis_shape` with `{"shape": "mount_preview", ...}` and the same
fields gives the part's bodies where the placement puts them, in the
design's coordinates. `mount_frames` is class `model`, `mount_preview`
`file IO` (it reads the part as `insert_component` does).

Code: `features/joint.rs` (`MountSpec`), `document/mounts.rs` (the frames,
inserts, the plan, grids), `api/mounts.rs`; the library side
`core/vcs/src/library/mounts.rs`. Tests: `core/model-tests/joints/src/mount_tests.rs`
(mock kernel), `core/vcs/src/tests/library_mounts.rs`,
`tools/ui-mount-test.sh` and `tools/ui-windows-mount-test.ps1` (ctest
`app.ui-windows-mount`).

## Move face

```json
{"type": "move_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:side(c1)"],
 "transform": {"type": "translate_xyz", "x": -1.856, "y": 0, "z": -0.361}}
```

Moves faces of one body by a rigid motion (mitcad#343; the `.f3d`
import's moved faces). `transform` is a move's
([move, align, scale](#move-align-scale): `free`, `translate_xyz`,
`translate_along`, `rotate`, `point_to_point`, `point_to_position`); it
must be a rotation and a translation and must move something. Each face
keeps its surface, moved; the neighbouring faces stay on their surfaces
and extend or shorten up to the moved ones: an edge between a moved face
and one that stays becomes their surfaces' intersection next to where it
was, and the vertices follow. A rod's side moved square to its axis, its
ends planes square to it, moves the whole rod. Every face keeps its
names, and the body keeps its faces, edges and vertices: a motion that
would make a face vanish or split, or leave an edge's faces apart near
it, fails ("the neighbouring faces cannot follow the moved faces").
Its preview reports what a `rotate`, `point_to_point` or
`point_to_position` motion was worked out from as `motion`, as a move's
does ([preview](#preview), mitcad#854): a circular edge's axis in its
canonical direction, which the app's Rotate ring turns about.

Code: `core/model/src/features/move_face.rs`,
`geometry/src/move_faces.cpp` (`move_faces_rigidly`: OCCT's
`BRepTools_Modifier` with the moved surfaces, the new edges and the
vertices where they meet). Tests: `move_face_moves_faces_by_a_rigid_motion`
(`core/model/src/features/f2_tests.rs`, mock kernel), `geometry`
(`geometry/tests/test_move_faces.cpp`, OCCT).

## Scale Pattern

```json
{"type": "scale_pattern", "objects": {"type": "features", "features": ["F4"]},
 "quantity": 3, "scale": 1.5, "compute": "identical"}
{"type": "scale_pattern", "objects": {"type": "bodies", "bodies": ["F2.b0"]},
 "quantity": 2, "scale": 0.5, "combine": false}
```

Copies scaled where they are (mitcad#539; FreeCAD's Scaled transformation
alone or first in a MultiTransform): element e of `quantity` is the
objects scaled by 1 + (scale − 1) · e / (quantity − 1) about the centre
of mass of the first object (a feature's tool, the first body); element 0
is the original. Otherwise a [pattern](#patterns) whose elements do not
move: `objects` (bodies, features; not faces, fillets, chamfers or sheet
features), `compute`, `original_bodies`, `combine` (bodies) and
`suppressed_elements` as there; copies of bodies are new bodies
`<pattern>.b<k>`, faces `<pattern>:inst<e>(<face>)`. A pattern or mirror
of it (patterns of patterns) places its scaled copies, so that a scale
pattern and then a rectangular pattern of it give every scaled copy at
every place. A factor must be positive. `scale_center`, `scales` (one
run per element by default) and `skipped_copies` as for patterns
(mitcad#542).

The [patterns](#patterns)' and the [mirror](#mirror)'s `scale` scales the
copies they make instead of adding scaled ones: each copy (of an inner
pattern's copies too) about its own centre by its element's (or its
run's, `scale_groups`, over `scale_copies`) factor; `scales` multiply.

Code: `core/model/src/features/scale_pattern.rs`, the scaling in
`pattern.rs` (`Scaling`). Tests (mock kernel, `f4_tests.rs`):
`scale_patterns_scale_copies_where_they_are`,
`scale_groups_scale_runs_of_elements_alike`,
`scaled_patterns_of_patterns_scale_each_copy_about_its_own_centre`,
`a_mirror_scales_its_image_about_the_image_s_centre`,
`patterns_of_bodies_join_their_copies_with_combine`,
`scale_runs_over_the_copies_of_patterns_of_patterns`,
`several_scales_multiply_and_a_scale_centre_is_carried`,
`skipped_copies_are_not_made_but_patterns_of_the_pattern_place_them`; OCCT:
`tools/cli/tests/f4_pattern_scaled.json` (`cli.f4_pattern_scaled`).

## Printable bearings

A `printable_bearing` feature (mitcad#577;
`core/model/src/features/printable_bearing.rs` the definition, its
section, placement and checks, `bearing_sizes.rs` the standard sizes,
`api/bearings.rs` the queries and the parts list's purchased rows) makes
a deep groove bearing that a 3D printer prints in one piece: an inner
race, an outer race and the rolling elements, each a body of its own,
with clearances between them so that nothing touches; or a variant that
takes bought 6 mm airsoft balls in a snap-in cage. It is a bearing to
print, not a bought one (bought bearings are library parts). The
application's Bearing panel makes them
([app/COMMANDS.md](../../../app/COMMANDS.md#notes-on-particular-commands)).
Tests: `features::printable_bearing_tests`, `tools/cli/tests/bearings.json`
(`cli.bearings`, and `cli.bearings_3mf`: the 608's bodies as the parts of
one 3MF object).

```json
{"type": "printable_bearing", "element": "dumbbell", "size": "608", "plane": "xy", "center": [0, 0],
 "radial_clearance": 0.4, "axial_clearance": 0.4, "element_gap": 0.6, "chamfer": 0.4, "min_wall": 1.2,
 "operation": "new_component"}
{"type": "printable_bearing", "element": "airsoft", "bore": 15, "outside_diameter": 35, "width": 11,
 "flange": {"diameter": 39, "thickness": 1.5}, "plane": "xy", "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "printable_bearing", "size": "608", "groove": {"body": "F6.b0", "face": "F8:side(c1)"},
 "offset": 2, "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "printable_bearing", "seat": {"shaft": {"body": "F11.b0", "edge": "E{F11:end(r{c1})|F11:side(c1)}"},
 "offset": 5}, "fit_clearance": 0.5}
```

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `element` | `dumbbell` (the default): a waisted roller touching each raceway on two flanks, centring itself; `roller`: a cylinder with chamfered ends, line contact; `ball`: a printed ball (with conical caps, see below); `airsoft`: bought airsoft balls in a printed snap-in cage |
| `size` | a standard size: `60x`/`60xx`, `62x`/`62xx`, `63x`/`63xx`, `68x`/`68xx`, `69x`/`69xx`, `160xx`, `MR..` (miniature), `R..` (inch), `F..` and `MF..` (flanged; their flange comes with them). Case and spaces do not matter. Not with `bore`, `outside_diameter` and `width` |
| `bore`, `outside_diameter`, `width` | custom dimensions (mm), without `size` |
| `flange` | `diameter`, `thickness`: a flange on the outer race at the face on the plane (an F size's own without it) |
| `element_diameter` | the elements' largest diameter (an airsoft ball's, 5.95 mm without it); without it the largest that leaves the races made walls of `min_wall`, or of a sixth of the section (a quarter of the room with `groove`) when that is more |
| `element_count` | how many elements, at least 3; the most that fit without it |
| `radial_clearance` | the gap across the cylindrical faces between elements and races (0.4 mm) |
| `axial_clearance` | the gap along the axis at the flanks (0.4 mm); a flank's normal gap is `ca sin(a)`, 0.2828 mm at 45 degrees |
| `element_gap` | the least gap between neighbouring elements (0.6 mm; airsoft balls `2 radial_clearance + min_wall`, room for the cage's fingers) |
| `chamfer` | the races' 45-degree chamfers at the bore and the outside (0.4 mm) |
| `min_wall` | the thinnest wall a race, an element's waist or ends and a cage may have (1.2 mm) |
| `flank_angle` | the flanks' angle from the axis, 10 to 80 degrees (45 degrees): their overhang printed with the axis vertical |
| `plane`, `center`, `angle` | where the axis meets its plane (the plane's normal), in the plane's coordinates, the bearing running along the normal from the plane; `angle` turns the elements (element 1 on the plane's x axis without it). Not with `groove` |
| `groove`, `offset` | a cylindrical face of a body (`{"body": ..., "face": ...}`): the raceway is cut into it, the body becoming one race (a bore's body the outer race, a shaft's the inner race), `offset` from the face's low end along its axis (the middle of the face without it); `new_body` only: the bodies stay in the body's component. The groove runs `axial_clearance` past the bearing's faces (at the raceway's radius there), so the elements' ends keep that gap from its end walls where the body goes on past them. With a bore the inner race's `bore` (or a size's) is used, with a shaft the outer race's `outside_diameter` |
| `seat`, `fit_clearance` | on a shaft or in a hole (below): `{"shaft": {"body": ..., "edge": ...}, "offset": 5, "flip": false, "near": [x, y, z], "link": {...}}` as [Seats on shafts](#seats-on-shafts) takes it; `fit_clearance` (0.5 mm) for the size that fits. Not with `plane` or `groove` |
| `operation` | `new_component` (the default: the component named after the size, `Bearing 608 (8x22x7)`, or its dimensions, `Bearing 10x30x9`) or `new_body` |

Values are parameters: numbers in mm (radians for angles; `element_count`
unitless) or names and expressions. `element_diameter`, `element_count`
and `element_gap` are automatic only when left out (mitcad#656): a 0 is
refused with the reason (`must be greater than zero`, `at least 3`, `below
the 0.2 mm that a printer keeps open`), never taken as automatic; a
design could never store one.

- **The section.** `R` the distance from the axis, `z` along it from the
  face on the plane (the print bed: the bearing prints with its axis
  vertical) to the far face at the width `W`. The elements turn about
  axes parallel to the bearing's on the pitch circle (radius `Rp`); each
  race is bounded by one function `race(z)` of the distance from the
  pitch circle, the inner race at `Rp - race(z)`, the outer at
  `Rp + race(z)`, so the two mirror each other. With `t` the flanks'
  slope (`tan(flank_angle)`), `D` and `r` the elements' largest diameter
  and radius, `cr` and `ca` the clearances:
  - `dumbbell`: from face to face, a V waist `h = min(D/4, 0.8 t W/2)`
    deep in the middle; the races' V ridge reaches into the waist,
    `race(z) = min(r + cr, r - h + t ca + t |z - W/2|)`;
  - `roller`: from face to face, its ends chamfered by `k = min(D/4,
    t W/4)` at the flank angle; the races' lips over the chamfers,
    `race(z) = min(r + cr, r - k + t ca + t z, r - k + t ca + t (W - z))`;
  - `ball`: a sphere centred at `W/2` with conical caps tangent to it at
    the flank angle's latitude, cut by the faces: it stands on the bed and
    overhangs by the flank angle at most; `race(z) = max(cr, min(r + cr,
    r / cos(a) + t ca - t |z - W/2|))`: a flat `cr` from the equator and
    flanks along the caps;
  - `airsoft`: spheres (bought) in the same grooves, the lands `0.55 r`
    from the pitch circle instead of `cr`; the cage a ring above the
    balls to the far face with fingers between them down past their
    equators, its pockets spheres `r + cr` round the balls whose openings
    at the fingers' tips are 0.2 mm narrower than a ball (they snap in).
    The races print in place without balls: the balls go in by hand
    through the crescent with the inner race pushed against the outer
    one, then they are spread out and the cage, printed on its ring,
    snaps in from the far face.

  The races' edges at the bore and the outside have 45-degree chamfers;
  a flange lies on the outer race at the face on the plane.
- **Count.** The most elements that fit round the pitch circle with
  `element_gap` between the widest parts of neighbours; airsoft balls at
  most those that go into the crescent: where the groove bottoms' gap
  `2 (r + cr) - 2 land cos(phi)` holds a ball, an arc of
  `2 (pi - acos(cr / land))`, touching (one more than the arc over the
  angle between touching balls).
- **Checks** (an error, nothing resized): too many elements for the pitch
  circle (or fewer than 3), a wall of a race, an element or the cage
  below `min_wall`, a clearance or gap below 0.2 mm, an element not held
  (it must reach 0.2 mm past the ridge, the lips or the lands), an
  overhang steeper than 45 degrees printed with the axis vertical (a
  flank angle above 45 degrees), a printed ball below 3 mm (it sticks or
  rattles) or one that does not reach the bed (`D >= W sin(a)`), airsoft
  balls that do not fit the section (the walls, the cage's ring above
  them, its width, its fingers), a chamfer not smaller than the walls,
  a flange not larger than the outside or as thick as the width.
- **Faces:** the inner race's `side(c1…)` (its section's lines from the
  bore's lower chamfer round), the outer race's `side(c101…)`, the first
  element's `side(c201…)` and the others' `inst<k>(…)` (copies turned
  about the axis), an airsoft ball's `side0`, the cage's `side(c301…)`,
  the raceway cut into a body `side(c401…)`.
- **Bodies,** in order: the inner race (not with a groove in a shaft),
  the outer race (not with a groove in a bore), the elements from
  element 1 counter-clockwise, the cage.
- **Mount frames:** `bore` (on the axis at the face on the plane, z the
  axis), `face_a` (that face, z out of the bearing), `face_b` (the far
  face, z out of it), taken as `{"mount": "F3:mount(bore)"}` as a
  pulley's ([Mount frames](#mount-frames)).
- **Printing:** the 3MF export writes the bodies as the parts of one
  object in their places, so a slicer prints the bearing in one piece;
  an STL file holds one body. The airsoft balls are bodies too, to see
  and check the bearing; leave them out of the print.
- **Parts list:** an airsoft bearing's balls are a purchased row of
  `parts_list` after the components' rows: `name` and `designation`
  `Airsoft ball 6 mm` (the bought diameter rounded), `quantity` the balls
  per bearing times the placements of the component they are in (its
  row's quantity; the root's once), `component` that component,
  `purchased` true, `features` the bearings; rows of the same designation
  in one component add up.
- **On a shaft or in a hole** (`seat`, mitcad#578, [Seats on
  shafts](#seats-on-shafts)): a shaft's circular end edge or side face,
  or a hole's rim or wall, followed through its topological name. The
  bearing lies on the plane through the seat's origin normal to its axis
  and runs along the axis into the shaft or the hole: on a shaft
  `seat.offset` is how far from the shaft's end, in a hole how deep (0:
  flush with the face); `seat.flip` measures from the other end. Without
  `size` or custom dimensions the bearing takes the standard size whose
  bore fits the shaft (in a hole: whose outside diameter fits the hole)
  within `fit_clearance` (0.5 mm), the nearest, the table's order among
  sizes as near; none within it is an error (`no standard bearing's bore
  is within 0.5 mm of the 11 mm shaft: choose a size or give custom
  dimensions`). A size given is used as it is. Not with `plane`, `center`,
  `groove` or `offset`. A new component without a size is named `Bearing`
  (the panel gives the size it fitted, so its component is named after
  it).

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `bearing_values` | `uid` (a bearing feature) or `def` (a definition as `add_feature` takes it, without `type`) | `element`, `designation`, `bore`, `outside_diameter`, `width`, `flange`, `element_diameter`, `element_count`, `max_elements`, `pitch_diameter`, `radial_clearance`, `axial_clearance`, `element_gap`, `chamfer`, `min_wall`, `flank_angle`, `min_gap` (the least normal gap between an element and a race), `inner_wall`, `outer_wall` (null for a body's own race), `element_wall` (an element's thinnest), `hold` (how far an element reaches past its ridge, lips or lands), `max_overhang`, `raceway_depth`; a dumbbell's `waist_diameter`; airsoft `cage` (`ring`, `width`, `pocket_diameter`) and `purchased` (`designation`, `quantity`); with `groove` `groove` (`diameter`, `race`: `outer` or `inner`); with `seat` `seat` (as the `seat_frame` query gives it), `shaft_diameter` (the shaft's or the hole's) and `fits` (the designations within `fit_clearance`, the nearest first); `component_name` with `new_component`; `error` when the values make no printable bearing (then only `element` beside it) |
