cos³(beta)`: it needs at least `x = 1 - z sin²(alpha) / 2`. An undercut
gear of any fit gets that shift, taken from the other gear so that their
sum (and the centre distance) stays, when both shifts stay within
`max_profile_shift` and -1 to 0.8 and the other gear stays free of
undercut; an `exact` or `helix` pair so has shifts of sum zero. Each
candidate's `undercut` (`[first, second]`) says whether a gear is still
undercut.

Best fits come first: the pairs free of undercut before the others; then
the ratio's deviation in steps of 0.5 % (the ratio is what is asked, and
deviations within one step are of equal quality), so that pairs meeting
the ratio come before those missing it, shifted or helical if need be;
within a step `exact`, `profile_shift`, `helix`; then the pairs needing
no correction against undercut (`corrected` false) before the corrected
ones, then the fewer teeth in all (stronger and cheaper gears of a
larger module), then the smaller shifts and helix angle, then the larger module,
then the smaller deviation. The modules start at 0.5 mm by default
(MitCad's practical least; `modules` asks for smaller ones).

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `gear_pair` | `first`, `second` (`at` placements of the two gears, or `{"seat": …}`, below), `ratio` (z2 / z1, the first gear's speed over the second's; more than 0); optional `kind` (`spur` or `helical`; both without it), `pressure_angle` (radians, 20 degrees), `modules` (`[min, max]` mm; from 0.5 mm without it), `second_series` (false), `min_teeth` (12, at least 5), `max_teeth` (200), `ratio_tolerance` (relative, 0.02), `max_profile_shift` (0.5), `max_helix_angle` (radians, 30 degrees, at most 45), `limit` (20) | `center_distance` (`a`), `axial_offset` (the second placement's origin from the first's along the first's axis: the gears' planes should overlap), `warning` (when the second axis points the opposite way from the first, mitcad#749: `the second axis points the opposite way from the first: the gears would be built from their placements in opposite directions; flip one, or pick its shaft nearer its other end, so that both point the same way`, and then no other, since `axial_offset` is measured from the wrong end; else when `axial_offset` is 0.0005 mm or more: `the second placement lies 5 mm along the axis from the first: put the gears in one plane so that they mesh across their face width`), `candidates`: `module`, `teeth` (`[z1, z2]`), `ratio` (z2 / z1), `ratio_deviation` (relative: ratio / asked - 1), `fit`, `undercut` (`[bool, bool]`), `corrected` (shifts against undercut added to the fit's own: an `exact` pair so is "exact, corrected"), `profile_shift` (`[x1, x2]`, when either is not 0), `helix_angle` (with `helix`), `first` and `second` (the gear fields to merge into each gear's definition: `kind`, `module`, `teeth`, `pressure_angle`, `profile_shift`, `helix_angle`, `left_handed` as they apply); an error when the axes are not parallel or meet |

The placements are resolved at the timeline marker in the coordinates of
their references (the active component's for its own geometry), as
`seat_frame` resolves a seat. A shaft in another component's occurrence
(mitcad#754) is given as a seat with its occurrence link, as a part's
definition takes it: `{"seat": {"shaft": <its face or edge>, "link":
{"source": "O1"}, "near": [x, y, z], "offset": 3}}` ([Seats on
shafts](#seats-on-shafts); only `seat` beside it). It resolves as
`seat_frame` does for the active component, the shaft moved by the
occurrences' placements, so the distance is the one the view shows.

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `add_gear_pair` | `first`, `second` (gear definitions as `add_feature`'s `def` takes them, without `type`, usually each with its `at` and a candidate's fields; the first may sit on a shaft of another component's occurrence by its `seat` with the `link`), optional `component`, `names` (`[first, second]`) | `uids`, `names`: both gears added in one undo step (`Add Gear Pair`), computed once, or, when either is refused, neither, the undo and redo steps staying as they were (mitcad#758); the second gets `mesh_with: {"gear": <the first>}`, which turns it to engage (it must not have a `mesh_with` of its own, and since a gear on a `seat` is not placed by a mesh too, it is placed by `at` on geometry of its own component) |

The same pair can be made with two `add_feature`s and `merge_undo`
([Undo, revisions and the saved state](#undo-revisions-and-the-saved-state)):
read `undo_depth`, add the first gear, add the second with `mesh_with`
naming the first, merge back to the depth.

### Belt Drive

The `belt_drive` query takes two placements (the pulleys' axes), a ratio
and a belt profile and lists the tooth counts that fit, each with the
catalogue belts that go round them and the tension travel each needs:
the change of the centre distance from the axes' distance `C` to the
distance at which that belt fits (positive: the axes must move apart).
The belt's pitch length at a centre distance is the open belt's of
[Pulleys](#pulleys); the distance for a belt length is found from it.
The catalogue (`catalogue` in the answer):

- `given`: the pitch lengths of `belt_lengths`;
- `library` (without `belt_lengths`): the closed belts of the parts
  library (`tools/libraries/profiles/linear-belts.json`, each with its
  supplier's page there; the answer's belts name their part as
  `library`, with its `name` and the belt's `width` in mm): GT2 2 mm 200, 280, 400 and 852 mm; HTD 3M 225, 255 and
  351 mm; HTD 5M 255, 355 and 575 mm. No other belt data is assumed;
- `whole_teeth` (the profiles the library has no closed belts of, GT2
  3 mm, T5 and XL, or with `whole_teeth`): every whole number of belt
  teeth, lengths `n * pitch`. The nearest is then at most one pitch of
  travel away (a pitch of belt length is about half a pitch of centre
  distance), so the travel says little: the size of the pulleys decides.

Verdict. Each belt has a `fit` from its travel: `ok` within 0.5 mm either
way (it goes on as the axes are; MitCad's default), `tensioner` when it
fits further apart (longer than the path: the axes move apart by the
travel, or a tensioner takes up the slack), `short` when it fits only
closer (shorter than the path: the axes must move closer by the travel).
A candidate's and `belt_check`'s `fit` is its first belt's.

Sizes. The smaller pulley has at least `min_teeth_in_mesh` (6) teeth in
mesh, and each pulley at least `min_teeth`, by default MitCad's
recommended teeth (our defaults above the profile's least teeth, so that
the belt is not bent round the smallest pulley a groove allows; not a
standard's values):

| Profile | Least teeth (a pulley's limit) | Belt Drive's default `min_teeth` |
|---|---|---|
| `gt2_2mm` | 10 | 16 |
| `gt2_3mm` | 10 | 16 |
| `htd_3m` | 10 | 14 |
| `htd_5m` | 12 | 14 |
| `t5` | 10 | 12 |
| `xl` | 10 | 12 |

A `min_teeth` given goes down to the least teeth, never below.

Order. The ratio is what is asked: the smallest ratio deviation
(`ratio_deviation`, relative: ratio / asked - 1, as Gear Pair's) first,
deviations within the same 0.5 % step counting as one, so that pairs
meeting the ratio come before those missing it within `ratio_tolerance`;
then the smallest travel, travels within the same 0.5 mm step counting
as one; among them the smaller pulleys first (the smaller pulley's
teeth), then the smaller ratio deviation, then the smaller travel.

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `belt_drive` | `first`, `second` (`at` placements, or seats with their link as `gear_pair`'s), `ratio` (z2 / z1), `profile` (`gt2_2mm`, `gt2_3mm`, `htd_3m`, `htd_5m`, `t5`, `xl`); optional `belt_lengths` (catalogue pitch lengths, mm), `whole_teeth` (false), `min_teeth` (the table above), `max_teeth` (150; at most 1000, mitcad#748: a larger one, meant as "no limit", is refused with `max_teeth must be at most 1000 teeth, got …`; the search stops anyway at the first tooth count whose pulleys no longer fit between the axes), `min_teeth_in_mesh` (6), `ratio_tolerance` (0.02), `belts` (the nearest belts per candidate, 3), `limit` (20) | `center_distance` (`C`), `axial_offset`, `warning` (as `gear_pair`'s: the axes pointing opposite ways, else `… put the pulleys in one plane so that they run in one belt's plane`), `catalogue` (`given`, `library` or `whole_teeth`), `candidates`: `teeth` (`[z1, z2]`), `ratio`, `ratio_deviation`, `pitch_diameters`, `belt_length` (the pitch length at `C`), `teeth_in_mesh` (on the smaller pulley), `belts` (`length`, `teeth`, `center_distance`, `travel`, `fit`, and for a library belt `library`, `name`, `width`; the smallest travel first), `travel` and `fit` (the first belt's), `first` and `second` (`kind`: `toothed`, `profile`, `teeth`); an error when the axes are not parallel |
| `belt_check` | `pulleys` (two pulley features of one component, as built), optional `belt_lengths`, `whole_teeth` (false), `belts` (3) | the same check for a pair of pulleys already made, from their axes as built (their mount frames `bore`): `center_distance`, `axial_offset`, `warning` (as `belt_drive`'s, the opposite axes included), `belt_length`, `belt_teeth`, `wrap_angles`, `teeth_in_mesh`, `catalogue`, `belts` with their `travel` and `fit`, `fit` (the first belt's); an error when the pulleys share no belt (different profiles, overlapping pitch circles) or their axes are not parallel |
| `place_frame` | `at` (as a feature takes it) | where the placement puts a part at the timeline marker: `origin`, `x_axis`, `y_axis`, `axis` (the normal); with an `axis` form also `seat` (as `seat_frame` gives it; `diameter` null on an axis on its own); an error with the reason when a reference does not resolve |

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `add_belt_drive` | `first`, `second` (pulley definitions without `type`, each with its placement and a candidate's fields), optional `component`, `names` | `uids`, `names`: both pulleys added in one undo step (`Add Belt Drive`), computed once; when either is refused nothing of the pair is made and the undo and redo steps stay as they were (mitcad#758) |

**A belt check kept with a pulley.** A pulley may keep its belt with an
earlier pulley feature checked: `"belt_check": {"pulley": "F3"}` in its
definition. It places nothing and changes no geometry; it is a relation
the design keeps (saved and loaded with the definition, a reference to
the other pulley by its uid as `belt_with`'s, so a rename does not break
it and the other pulley is not deleted under it). `pulley_values` of the
pulley (by `uid`, as built) then has `belt_check`: `belt_check`'s answer
for the two pulleys with `pulley`, or `{"pulley", "error"}` when the
check cannot be made (not built, other components, not parallel, no
shared belt); its catalogue is `belt_lengths` of the query, else the
library's or whole teeth as above.

`gear_values` and `pulley_values` give a placed part's bore from its
`at` as from a seat (`shaft_diameter`, `seat` for an axis form), and
`bearing_values` its fitting size.

Tests: `features::place_at` (the frames of the three forms, offsets from
two lines, flip, align and angle), `features::place_at_tests` (pulleys,
gears, coils and holes placed by a shaft, an origin or construction
axis, a sketch point and an origin plane's offsets on the mock kernel;
the part following a longer shaft and a moved sketch plane; the old
forms building as before; a gear turned by its mesh on its own axis;
the warnings of axes pointing opposite ways; the pairs on a shaft in
another component's occurrence),
`features::drives` (Belt Drive meeting the ratio first; the Gear Pair candidates: an exact, a profile shift
and a helix case, undercut flagged and shifted out; the Belt Drive
candidates, their sizes, travel and the library's belts, checked
against the parts library's file; a huge `max_teeth` stopping where the
pulleys no longer fit), `api::drives` (the queries, the
axial warning, a belt check kept with a pulley, an absurd `max_teeth`
refused).

## Measurement objects

Measurements kept in the design (mitcad#649; since mitcad#702 they are
[Annotations](#annotations), and these commands are their short forms;
`core/model/src/document/annotations.rs`, `api/measurements.rs`): the
application's Annotations window. Each has a `name` (`Distance1`, `Angle1`,
…), a `color` (`#rrggbb`, or `auto`: [Annotations' look](#annotations-look-text-height-auto-colour-and-placement)), a light bulb (`visible`), the `kind` of value
it shows and one or two picks `a` and `b`, given as the `measure` query's
selections as fields (*Analysis queries*: `{"body", "face" | "edge" |
"vertex", "occurrence"}` or `{"datum", "occurrence"}`). The picks refer to
geometry by topological names, so a measurement follows the model: it is
measured at the timeline marker whenever it is asked for, as the `measure`
query measures its picks (in the design's coordinates, *Measure in the
design*, *Measure with axes*).

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `add_measurement` | `a`, `b` (optional), `kind` (optional), `name` (the next free `<Kind><n>` when left out), `color` (`auto` when left out) | `name`, `kind`; undo step `Add Distance1` |
| `rename_measurement` | `name`, `new_name` | undo step `Rename Distance1` |
| `set_measurement_color` | `name`, `color` (`#rrggbb` or `auto`, any case; stored in lower case) | undo step `Colour of Distance1` unless nothing changes |
| `set_measurement_visible` | `name`, `visible` | undo step `Show Distance1` / `Hide Distance1` unless nothing changes |
| `set_measurement_kind` | `name`, `kind` | undo step `Kind of Distance1` unless nothing changes |
| `delete_measurement` | `name` | undo step `Delete Distance1` |

The kinds (`kind`) and the picks they take:

| `kind` | Picks | Value | Default name |
|---|---|---|---|
| `distance` | two | the closest distance (`between.distance`), mm | `Distance<n>` |
| `angle` | two, each with a normal, a direction or an axis | `between.angle`, radians | `Angle<n>` |
| `offset` | two parallel planes (planar faces, datum planes) | `between.offset`, mm | `Offset<n>` |
| `axis_distance` | two, one with an axis at least | `between.axis_distance`, mm | `AxisDistance<n>` |
| `center_distance` | two circles or arcs | `between.center_distance`, mm | `CenterDistance<n>` |
| `radius` | one with a circle (a round edge or face) | the circle's radius, mm | `Radius<n>` |
| `diameter` | one with a circle | twice the radius, mm | `Diameter<n>` |

- **Kept.** `add_measurement` measures the picks first and refuses those
  that are not there (`the measurement's picks: …`) and a kind they do not
  have (`the picks have no offset; they have distance, angle`). Without a
  `kind` it takes the first the picks have of: a circle's `diameter` (an
  arc's `radius`); of two picks `offset`, then `axis_distance`, then
  `center_distance`, then `distance` (each when longer than 1e-6 mm), then
  `angle` (two picks that touch), else `distance`. One pick without a
  circle has nothing to keep. Names are the measurements' own (an
  analysis or a body may have the same). `set_measurement_kind` refuses a
  kind the picks do not have now.
- **Nothing recomputed.** The commands are undo steps that change no
  geometry and recompute nothing. The measurements are saved in the
  design file (`"measurements": [{"name", "kind", "color", "visible"
  (only when false), "a", "b"}]`, left out when there are none; as
  `"annotations"` once one has a field of the annotations, *Annotations*
  below; their values are not stored), the comparison of versions lists
  them by name, and Move to
  another parent rewrites their picks' occurrence paths.

The `measurements` query (the same as `annotations`) lists them in the
order added: the file form (`name`, `kind`, `color`, `visible`, `a`, `b`,
and the annotations' fields) and, measured at the marker:

- `values`: every value the picks have now, by kind (`{"distance": 40,
  "angle": 0, "offset": 40}`);
- `value`: the one of its own `kind`;
- where its dimension is drawn, in the design's coordinates: `points`
  (`[p, q]`: a length's two ends — the closest points, for `offset` the
  closest point on `a` and its foot on `b`'s plane along the normal, for
  `axis_distance` the `axis_points`, for `center_distance` the two
  centres; a `radius` from the centre to a point of the circle, a
  `diameter` across it) with, for a circle, `center`, `axis` (its unit
  normal) and `radius`; for an `angle` `arc`: `{"center", "from", "to"}`,
  the corner and the unit rays that bound the sector measured (the angle
  between them is the value): where two lines come closest, where two
  planes meet nearest the closest points (the rays in the planes, square
  to where they meet), where a line meets a plane (the line and its shadow
  in the plane); parallel picks have the middle of the closest points and
  no sector;
- or `error` instead of `value` and the geometry: `a pick is not there:
  <why>` (a body or a face that is gone, rolled back or no longer named so)
  or `the picks have no <kind> now`. Such a measurement is broken: it stays
  in the design and is measured again when its picks come back (an undo,
  the marker rolled forward).

When the values are worked out (mitcad#716):

- **Hidden ones only when asked.** A hidden one (`"visible": false`) is
  not drawn, so it is not measured: it is listed in its file form with
  `"measured": false` and without `values`, `value`, the geometry,
  `label` (a leader's `label` stays) and `deviations`; `error` only when a
  pick's body or datum is not there at the marker (known without
  measuring). `{"query": "annotations", "measure_hidden": true}` (or
  `measurements`) measures them too, answering every one as shown ones
  are answered; the application asks so for its Annotations window and
  the editor of one.
- **Measured again only when changed.** The model keeps what each pair of
  picks gave, keyed by the picks as named, each picked body's shape
  version (the recompute's, which changes whenever the shape does: the
  `bodies` query's `version`), its component and placement, and each
  picked datum as placed. A command that changes none of these — a
  rename, a colour, a light bulb, a change to other bodies, an annotation
  hidden or shown — answers from what was kept; an undo back to a shape
  measured before as well. Failures are measured again each time. The
  last 256 kept are held, in memory only, or twice as many as there are
  annotations when that is more, so that every annotation's picks and
  plane's pick stay kept (mitcad#758).
- Two planar faces in parallel planes are measured from a few points of
  each (a point inside it, its vertices) whose foot on the other's plane
  lies in the other face: the gap of the planes, with that point and its
  foot as the closest points, instead of the general distance of every
  edge and vertex of the two faces (seconds for two walls with rows of
  holes); when no such point is found, the general distance. The
  `measure` query's two faces take the same way.

The application (`app/COMMANDS.md`, *Measurement objects*, *Annotations*)
keeps a measurement from the Measure panel, lists them in its Annotations
window, draws the shown ones in the view and in its snapshots.

Tests: `measurement_tests` (kept with a default kind, name and colour;
measured again after a parameter change and its undo; refused picks and
kinds; renamed, recoloured, hidden, changed and deleted as undo steps;
saved and read back, measured after reopening, listed by the comparison of
versions, broken entries of a file refused; a pick that is gone breaks the
measurement until the marker or an undo brings it back),
`api::measurements::tests` (the corners and rays of angles between planes,
lines, an axis and a plane, parallel picks), `document::annotations::tests`
(colours, kinds, the picks a kind needs), on the mock kernel's measure of
the picks' boxes (`MockKernel::measures_selections`); `tools/ui-measurement-objects-test.sh`
and `tools/ui-windows-measurement-objects-test.ps1`
(`app.ui-windows-measurement-objects`).

## Annotations

Dimensions and leader notes kept in the design (mitcad#702,
`core/model/src/document/annotations.rs`, `api/annotations.rs`,
`iso286.rs`), grown from the [measurement objects](#measurement-objects):
every measurement object is an annotation and the measurement commands are
short forms of these. ISO 129 style and millimetres. An annotation is a
dimension (`kind` one of the measurement kinds) or a leader note (`kind`
`note`); it has the measurement's `name`, `color`, `visible` and picks, and:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `group` | a group's name (`Manufacturing`), trimmed; left out for none. The application shows and hides a group at once and snapshots one. |
| `plane` | the plane it lies in: `{"normal": [x, y, z]}` (a direction in the first pick's own coordinates, so that it turns with the pick's occurrence; a length's plane is turned square to its ends), with `"x"` for a note or a diameter (the direction its text runs along, likewise), or `{"pick": <pick>}`, a planar face or a datum plane it lies parallel to and follows. Left out: chosen from the picks — a length's plane is square to the coordinate axis least along it (Z, then Y, then X), or, where a planar face at a pick holds the length and is not parallel to that, the face's nearest it (mitcad#894); a note's is its face's plane (else XY). A radius and an angle lie in the plane of their circle or rays and take no `plane`; a diameter does too unless it has one, which is its leader's (one added in a view takes the view's, mitcad#902: a leader from outside with its text level in that plane). |
| `line_offset` | a length's dimension line from its ends, mm, signed across the ends in the plane; left out, outside its bodies' extent in the plane (mitcad#894, [Annotations' look](#annotations-look-text-height-auto-colour-and-placement): 6 text heights past the bodies, stacked outside parallel lines; without a body, a quarter of the length, at least 1 mm); an angle's arc radius, more than 0 (half the distance from the corner to the nearer pick's point, else five text heights, mitcad#902). None for a radius, a diameter or a note. |
| `text_offset` | `[along, across]`, mm in the plane: a dimension's text from its default place (the dimension line's middle; a circle's one and a half radii out along `across` of its axis, at least three text heights past its rim; an angle's arc's middle); a note's (a datum's, a frame's, a hole callout's) text from its arrow's point (four and three text heights when left out, mitcad#902). |
| `format` | a dimension's `{"decimals"` (0 to 6; up to three without trailing zeros when left out), `"prefix"` (in place of the kind's: `Ø` for a diameter, `R` for a radius; `""` for none), `"before"`, `"after"` (own text, e.g. `4 x`, `THRU`), `"replace"` (a text in place of the value and its tolerance)`}`; left out when all are defaults. |
| `tolerance` | a dimension's `{"type": "symmetric", "value"}` (±), `{"type": "deviations", "upper", "lower"}` (signed, upper more than lower), `{"type": "limits", "upper", "lower"}` (the same deviations written as the largest and smallest size), or `{"type": "fit", "code", "deviations"}` (an ISO 286 code on a length, `H7` a hole's, `g6` a shaft's, of the size as written (its range by the value rounded as shown) — a radius' of its diameter's size, with half its deviations; `deviations: true` writes them in brackets); millimetres for lengths, degrees for angles. |
| `text` | a note's text, lines split at `\n`. |
| `at` | a note's, a datum's or a frame's point as picked, in the pick's own (its component's) coordinates: the arrow follows the pick's occurrence. |
| `letter` | a datum label's letter (*Datums and feature control frames* below). |
| `frame`, `on` | a feature control frame's tolerance, and the dimension (its name) it stands under instead of a leader (below). |

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `add_annotation` | `a`, `b`, `kind` (as `add_measurement` chooses it when left out; `note` when a `text` is given), `name`, `color`, `group`, `visible`, the fields above, and `view` | `name`, `kind`; undo step `Add Distance1` |
| `edit_annotation` | `name`, or `names` of several; any of `new_name`, `kind`, `color`, `group`, `visible`, `a`, `b`, `plane`, `line_offset`, `text_offset`, `format` (only the format's fields given change), `tolerance`, `text`, `at`; `null` sets a field back to its default | `changed`; one undo step `Edit Distance1` / `Edit 3 annotations`, none when nothing changes |
| `delete_annotation` | `name`, or `names` of several | one undo step `Delete Distance1` / `Delete 3 annotations` |

- **A view's suggestion.** `add_annotation`'s `view` is `{"direction"`
  (the way the view looks, from the eye), `"up"`, `"pixel"` (mm a pixel
  near the picks; still taken, no longer used since mitcad#902)`}`: what
  it leaves out is placed as it was seen — a
  note's plane square to the view (its text along the view's right); a
  length's plane a plane of its part (mitcad#894): of the planar faces at
  its picks that hold it (a face picked and the faces it meets, the faces
  of an edge or a vertex) and the coordinate planes turned to hold it, the
  one most facing the view (seen along the length, closer than 1e-6, the
  one most square to the view's up), its normal towards the eye; both kept
  in the first pick's own coordinates; a length's dimension line outside
  its bodies' extent as when left out (the view's upper side when both
  sides are as clear; without a body 2.5 text heights off on the view's
  upper side), stacked outside the parallel lines there — and kept as
  `plane` and `line_offset`. The other places are left to the defaults,
  in text heights, which follow the design's text height (mitcad#902: none
  in the view's pixels frozen when an annotation is added).
- **Checked.** A note points at one pick, which gives it a point (a body
  picked without `at` gives none), and needs a text; it has no format or
  tolerance, a dimension no `text`; a note stays a note and a dimension a
  dimension. A fit code is a length's (`a fit code is a length's
  tolerance`); codes not covered are refused with the reason. Several are
  edited without a new name or picks. Other picks or another kind draw
  the dimension afresh (its places back to the defaults; between an angle
  and a length its tolerance dropped too, here and in
  `set_measurement_kind`); picks whose kind is gone take their first (as
  `add_measurement`'s default). Another first pick drops a `plane` direction
  and a note's `at` (kept in the old pick's coordinates) unless given anew;
  a note edited so must still give a point, as when added.
- **ISO 286 fit codes** (`iso286.rs`): nominal sizes over 0 up to 500 mm
  (a range's bound taken up to 1e-6 mm over, the baseline tolerance),
  grades IT5 to IT11, the holes C, D, E, F, G, H, JS, K, M, N, P, R, S and
  the shafts c, d, e, f, g, h, js, k, m, n, p, r, s (ISO 286-1's
  fundamental deviations with the Δ of K, M, N up to IT8 and P, R, S up to
  IT7, M6's −9 µm of 250 to 315 mm; JS and js of grades 7 to 11 rounded
  down to even micrometres when the tolerance is odd, of the finer grades
  exactly half, to half a micrometre). A size over 500 mm keeps the code
  and says why in the label's `warning`.
- **The file.** While every annotation has only the fields of the
  measurement objects of mitcad#649 (a dimension's `name`, `kind`,
  `color`, `visible`, `a`, `b`: plain measurements made through the API)
  they are written as `measurements`, which older versions read; once one
  has another field, all are written as `annotations`. Both are read. The
  application's Keep stores a `plane` and the places from the view, so a
  design with dimensions kept from the view needs this version.

The `annotations` query lists them as the `measurements` query does (the
file form; `values`, `value`, `points` … of a dimension, or `error`), and,
where the annotation is not broken:

- `label`: a dimension's value in words — `main` (the own text before, the
  prefix, the value in the document's length unit — written after the
  value unless millimetres — or degrees, a symmetric tolerance `±0.1` or a
  fit code), `upper` and `lower` stacked after it (deviations `+0.2`
  `-0.1`, a zero as `0`; limits; a fit's deviations with `brackets`; a
  tolerance with the decimals it needs, up to four, both of a stack with
  the same, not the value's),
  `after`, `tolerance` (the tolerance alone in words), `warning`, and
  `text`, all on one line (`Ø20 H7 (+0.021/0) THRU`, `10.1/9.9`); a
  note's `lines` and `text` (`Deburr / all edges`, also when broken);
- `deviations`: `{"upper", "lower"}` of its tolerance (mm or degrees);
- `drawing`, in the design's coordinates: `plane` (`origin`; `x` and `y`,
  the unit axes `text_offset` is along — a length's dimension line and
  across it, the tangent at an angle's arc's middle and its radius there,
  a circle's `across` of its axis and square to it, a note's text and up —
  and `normal`; a right-handed frame), `line_offset` and `text_offset` (the
  ones in use: dragging adds to them), `extension_lines` (from a measured point
  to the dimension line: the application leaves a gap at the point and
  runs past the line), `dimension_lines` (a length's line, run on under
  text moved past an end; a radius from the centre or a diameter across,
  run on to text outside the circle; a note's leader from its text to its
  point), `arcs` (`center`, `radius`, `from`, `to` unit rays, `normal`),
  `arrows` (`tip` and the unit `direction` it points along: outwards at a
  length's ends and on a rim, along an angle's arc, at a note's point),
  `center` (a circle's, for its centre mark), `text` (`at`: its middle
  on the line, or a note's start; `direction` and `up`, unit vectors in
  the plane) and `text_height` (mm, the design's, mitcad#894). A length's
  extension line starts at its measured point, or at its bodies' outline
  on the line's side where its pick is a plane. The application keeps the
  text readable within its plane (ISO 129-1), sets it `text_height` high
  in the plane (at least 9 pixels on screen) and sizes arrowheads by it.

### Datums and feature control frames

Phase 2 of mitcad#702: two more kinds of annotation on one pick, drawn
on a leader in their plane as a note is (the same `plane`, `text_offset`,
`at` and view suggestions; no value, format or tolerance of a
dimension's).

- **`datum`**, a datum label (ISO 5459) on a planar face, an edge, a
  round face (its axis) or a datum plane or axis: its `letter`, one or two
  capitals but I, O and Q, each letter once in the design; left out, the
  first free one (A, B, C, … Z, then AA, AB, …). Its default name is `Datum<letter>`
  (`DatumA`). Its leader ends on the feature in a filled triangle: the
  drawing's `terminator` is `datum`. The label is `{"text": "A", "datum":
  "A"}`.
- **`frame`**, a feature control frame (ISO 1101), default name
  `Frame<n>`: `frame` is `{"characteristic", "value", "diameter",
  "modifier", "datums"}` — the characteristic (`straightness`,
  `flatness`, `circularity`, `cylindricity`, `line_profile`,
  `surface_profile`, `parallelism`, `perpendicularity`, `angularity`,
  `position`, `concentricity`, `symmetry`, `circular_runout`,
  `total_runout`), the zone's width in mm (more than 0), `diameter: true`
  for a cylindrical zone (Ø; straightness, the orientations, position and
  concentricity only), a material condition `"M"` or `"L"` (Ⓜ, Ⓛ;
  straightness, the orientations, position, concentricity and symmetry
  only) and up to three datum letters in order of precedence, each once:
  none for a form tolerance (straightness, flatness, circularity,
  cylindricity), at least one for an orientation, concentricity,
  symmetry and runout, either way for the profiles and position. Its
  leader ends in an arrow on its pick; with `on` (a dimension's name) it
  has no leader and stands under that dimension's text: its drawing is
  that text's place and frame with `"attached": "<name>"` (the
  application sets the frame just under the dimension line), it is not
  drawn (no `drawing`) while that dimension is hidden, it follows the
  dimension's new name when the dimension is renamed (the same undo step),
  it becomes a leader to its own pick again (no `on`) when the dimension
  is deleted (the same step), as it does when a file or the document
  names no dimension of that name in `on`. Under a dimension its drawing
  and errors are that dimension's alone; its own pick (the dimension's
  first when it was put there) is only an anchor and is not checked, so
  it may be a vertex, a datum point or a whole body. A datum label or a
  frame on its leader whose pick is a point (one left so by a deleted
  dimension) is broken with the reason. `on` naming a note, a
  datum, a frame (itself too) or nothing is refused (`DatumA is no
  dimension`, `there is no dimension Width to stand under`). The label is
  `{"text": "⟂ | Ø0.05 Ⓜ | A | B", "frame": ["⟂", "Ø0.05 Ⓜ", "A", "B"],
  "tolerance": "Ø0.05 Ⓜ"}` — the cells of the
  frame: the ISO 1101 symbol (⏤ ⏥ ○ ⌭ ⌒ ⌓ ∥ ⟂ ∠ ⌖ ◎ ⌯ ↗ ⌰), the tolerance
  in the document's unit (none written), each datum — with a `warning`
  (`no datum label C`) for a letter no datum label has.

`add_annotation` makes a datum of a `letter` (or `kind: "datum"`), a
frame of a `frame`; `edit_annotation` changes `letter`, `frame` (whole)
and `on` (`null` for a leader again). A datum still named by its letter
(`DatumA`) is renamed with a new letter (`DatumD`); frames referring to a
datum whose letter changes refer to the new letter (the same step; refused
when a frame would then refer to a letter twice: `Frame1: datum C is
referred to twice`); the letters a frame refers to and its `on` are
stored trimmed. A datum or a frame on a leader stands on a face, an
edge, an axis or a plane: a vertex or a datum point is refused (`a
datum label stands on a face, an edge, an axis or a plane, not on a
point`). Common datums (`A-B`, one datum from two features) are not
supported yet: a frame's datum is one label's letter. A datum, a frame
and a note keep their kind (`a frame stays a frame, a dimension a
dimension`); a letter in use is refused (`datum A exists`). Files keep
them as `annotations`; a file with one letter on two labels is refused
on load as an edit would refuse it (`annotations[1]: datum A is
lettered on 'DatumA' and on 'DatumB'`, mitcad#713). A frame under a
dimension whose pick is a vertex, a datum point or a whole body goes
onto a leader with another pick in the same edit (`"on": null, "a": …,
"at": …`): the check takes the new pick.

`{"query": "next_datum_letter"}` gives the letter a new datum label
takes when none is given (`{"letter": "C"}`), for an application to
offer: neither a label's nor one a frame refers to; `every datum letter
is in use` when none is left (and so for `add_annotation` without a
letter).

`{"query": "geometric_characteristics"}` lists the characteristics in
that order, each with its rules, for an editor of frames:
`{"key": "position", "symbol": "⌖", "datums": "optional", "diameter":
true, "modifier": true}` (`datums`: `none`, `optional` or `required`;
`diameter`: whether it may have a cylindrical zone; `modifier`: whether
it takes Ⓜ or Ⓛ).

Errors besides the measurement's: `the plane: its pick is not there: …`,
`the plane: its pick is not a planar face or a datum plane`, `the note's
pick has no point to point at: …` (a body picked without a point).

Tests: `annotation_tests` (added with a group, format, tolerance and
places, the stored form and reading back, refused fields; datums and
feature control frames: letters, ISO 1101's rules, a frame under a
dimension, edited, saved and read back, the characteristics' list, a
frame following its renamed dimension and not drawn under a hidden one,
`on` refused for a leader, itself and nothing and `null` for a leader,
datum names and frames' datums following their letters, letters past Z,
points refused, a frame under a dimension from a point, frames of a

plane, its text and line moved,
following a parameter, back to the defaults, a picked plane and a broken

## Parameter limits

Any user or model parameter can have limits (mitcad#665), so that a value
with a real minimum and maximum needs no `min(max(…))` formula: a driven
dimension's reference parameter cannot have them.

- `min` and `max` are expressions in the parameter's unit (a bare number
  is read in it, as in its expression) and may use other parameters
  (`"min": "Wall * 2"`); they take part in the dependency order and the
  cycle check like the expression (`dependencies` lists their parameters
  too; a limit that uses the parameter itself, or closes a circle through
  others, is refused as a circular reference; a parameter a limit uses is
  not deleted, and a rename rewrites the limit).
- `step` is a positive value in the parameter's unit (`1` for whole
  numbers, `0.2 mm`; it may be an expression too).
- `strict` (default false).

`add_parameter` and `set_parameter` take `min`, `max` and `step` as an
expression text or a number (in the parameter's unit), `null` or `""`
removing one in `set_parameter`, and `strict` as a boolean; fields left out
keep what the parameter has. `set_parameter` with limits and an
`expression` (or `value`, `unit`) changes them in one undo step (`Change
Limits of Width`), so that a new expression is checked against the new
limits; the same limits and expression again are no command.

**The value.** The expression's result is clamped to [min, max] and
snapped to the step; the parameter records which limit took effect
(`limited`). The step rule: steps are counted from the minimum (from zero
when there is none), and a result goes to the nearest step; one halfway
between two steps goes to the upper one (`33.5` with steps of 1 from 8
gives 34). A step above the maximum is replaced by the step below it
(never below the minimum), so a snapped value always stays within [min,
max]. A result within a billionth (relative, at least 1e-9 in mm or rad) of
a bound or a step is not limited. When a limit clamps the value, `limited`
is `min` or `max` even if the step also moved it.

A **strict** parameter refuses a result outside [min, max] or off its steps
instead, as it refuses a wrong unit: `parameter 'count': 12 is above the
maximum 10`, `… 0 is below the minimum 1`, `… 2.5 is not on a step of 1`.
Limits that are wrong are refused for every parameter: a limit that does
not parse or evaluate, or of another kind (`parameter 'b': minimum: …`), a
minimum above the maximum (`the minimum 20 mm is above the maximum 10
mm`), a step that is not positive.

**The `parameters` query.** A parameter with limits also has:

- `limits`: `min`, `max`, `step` (the expressions as written, or null),
  `strict`, and for each of `min`, `max`, `step`: `<limit>_value`
  (evaluated, mm or rad, or null), `<limit>_text` (in the parameter's unit,
  `"300 mm"`) and `<limit>_number` (the number in the parameter's unit);
- `unclamped` (the expression's result before the limits, mm or rad) and
  `unclamped_text`; `value` and `text` are the limited value;
- `limited`: `min`, `max`, `step` or null;
- `limit_message`: what the limit did, in words (`Width is limited to its
  maximum 300 mm (its expression gives 372 mm)`, `Width is rounded to its
  step of 1 mm: 33 mm (its expression gives 33.3 mm)`), or null;
- `limit_references`: the parameters its limits use.

A parameter without limits has none of these fields. The names `min`,
`max`, `step` and `strict` are the same in the commands, the query's
`limits` and the design file, for clients that read or write parameter
tables (such as a CSV export of the parameters).

**A feature's own limits** of the slots a parameter gives its value to are
reported in the same form, as fixed, read-only limits, so that a client
can show them before the feature fails: `intrinsic`, a list of `feature`
(uid), `feature_name`, `slot`, `fixed` (true), `describe` (`1 to 10000,
whole`) and the `<limit>_value`, `_text` and `_number` fields. They are
not applied to the parameter (the feature refuses the value). Known ones
(`parameters::slot_limits`): a pattern's `quantity` (also
`direction1.quantity`), a pattern's or mirror's `scale_copies` and
`scales[i].copies` (1 to 10000, whole), a gear's
`teeth` (at least 5, whole), `pressure_angle` (10 to 35 degrees) and
`profile_shift` (-1 to 0.8).

**Elsewhere.** The `document` query lists the parameters a limit changed in
`limited_parameters` (`name`, `limited`, `text`, `unclamped_text`,
`message`; left out when there are none). The `sketch` query's dimensions
have `limited` and `limit_message` when their parameter's value is
limited. The `evaluate` query with `"parameter": "Width"` evaluates the
expression as that parameter's new expression, in its unit, and adds
`limited`, `limited_value` (mm or rad) and `limited_text`; for a strict
parameter a result outside its limits rejects the query with the reason,
so a client can say at once that a typed value will be clamped or
refused.

**Files, undo and configurations.** The design file stores `min`, `max`
and `step` (each only when set) and `"strict": true` with the parameter;
a file whose strict parameter's result is outside its limits is refused
(`parameters[1]: …`). Limits are part of the parameter, so undo and redo
restore them, a copied feature's parameters keep them (with renamed
references), and a configuration row, which sets only expressions, is
clamped by them (or refused when strict, as the table's `problems` say).

Tests: `api::parameter_limits_tests` (clamping at the minimum and the
maximum, step snapping, limits as expressions of other parameters, cycles
through limits refused, strict errors, the `evaluate` query, save, load,
undo and redo, configurations, a feature's own limits, a limited sketch
dimension), `expr::limits::tests` (the clamp and step rule);
`tools/ui-parameter-limits-test.sh` (the mark and the tooltip in Change
Parameters, the warning while typing, the strict refusal, the slider, the
"Only limited" filter).

## Parameters as CSV

The parameters are exported to and imported from CSV (mitcad#666;
`parameters_csv.rs`, `document/parameters_csv.rs`, `api/parameters_csv.rs`).
The CSV is the text of the query or the command: the application reads
and writes the file.

| | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| query `parameters_csv` | | `csv`: MitCad's table of all parameters, `parameters`: their number |
| query `parameters_csv_preview` | `csv` | what `import_parameters_csv` would do; nothing changes |
| command `import_parameters_csv` | `csv` | what it did, as the preview; one undo step `Import Parameters`, none when nothing changes |

Both formats are UTF-8 (a byte order mark is skipped) with RFC 4180
quoting: a field with a comma, a quote, `;`, a line break or leading or
trailing space is quoted, a quote in it doubled. Numbers have decimal
points. MitCad writes CRLF after each row and reads any line break. A
header with semicolons and no comma is read with `;` between fields.
Columns are found by their names in the header (any case, any order);
`name` and `expression` are needed, the others are optional.

- **MitCad's table**, header
  `name,kind,unit,expression,value,comment,favorite,min,max,step,strict`:
  one row per parameter in creation order, its kind (`user`, `model`,
  `reference`), its unit as the `parameters` query gives it (`""` for
  unitless, `Text` for a [text parameter](#text-parameters), whose value
  column is its text as it is), its expression, its value as a number in its unit (the
  shortest decimal that gives the value back: `12.5`, `90` for
  `90 deg`; the limited value), its comment, `true` or `false` for a
  favourite, and its [limits](#parameter-limits): `min`, `max` and `step`
  as written (`10`, `count * 20 mm`, `0.5 mm`; empty when not set) and
  `true` or `false` for `strict`.
- **The parameter table CSV of the `.f3d` application**, header
  `Name,Unit,Expression,Value,Comments,Favorite` exactly: an empty unit
  for unitless parameters, `°` for degrees, `Text` for text parameters
  (with expressions such as `'6qt'`). The import reads it directly; MitCad
  does not write it. Its expressions are in the language of
  [Values](#values), which reads those of `.f3d` designs.

An import takes the rows as the `.f3d` import takes a design's
parameters (`core/import-replay/src/params.rs`):

- **Names.** A name MitCad cannot use (a unit such as `mil`, a function,
  other characters) gets a free one as the `.f3d` import gives it
  (`mil_1`, `a b` as `a_b`, `2nd` as `p_2nd`), chosen among the table's
  other names so that importing the same table again finds it; the
  expressions that use it follow (whole names). A second row of a name and
  a row without a name are refused.
- **Existing names change, new ones are added** as user parameters (a
  `model` or `reference` row of a name the design lacks too, noted). A
  user parameter takes the row's expression, unit, comment and
  favourite; a new unit is refused where a feature uses the parameter as
  another kind of value. A model parameter (a feature's) changes only its
  expression and limits: its unit, comment and favourite stay, and the
  row notes what it kept. A reference parameter (a driven dimension's) is
  read-only and has no limits: a row with another expression or with
  limits is refused.
- **Limits** ([Parameter limits](#parameter-limits)). The `min`, `max`,
  `step` and `strict` columns the table has replace the parameter's
  limits: an empty cell removes that limit, an empty or missing `strict`
  keeps what the parameter has, and a column the table lacks keeps the
  parameter's limit (the `.f3d` application's table has none). Their
  names follow renames as the expressions do. A limit that is wrong (one
  that does not parse or evaluate, a minimum above the maximum, a step that
  is not positive, a circular reference) refuses the row with the reason;
  a strict parameter whose result is outside its limits takes its `value`
  instead, or is refused. A new value is clamped and snapped as the limits
  say, and the row's `limited` says which limit took effect.
- **Order.** Rows are taken in dependency order (of their expressions and
  limits), so an expression or a limit may use a parameter of a later
  row. Rows in a circular reference, or that use one, take their `value`.
- **The `value` column** is used only where the expression does not
  evaluate (an unknown name, a wrong unit, a cycle): a number read in
  the row's unit, or a value with its unit, kept as the expression
  (`7.5 mm`) with `from_value` and the expression's `reason`. Without a
  value that evaluates, the row is refused with the reason.
- **Units.** The `unit` column's unit (`mm`, `in`, `deg`, `°`, `""` for
  unitless, any unit the [Values](#values) take); one that does not parse
  refuses the row. Without a unit column a new parameter gets the unit of
  its expression's value, as `add_parameter` gives it.
- **Text parameters** (unit `Text`, or kind `text`; mitcad#664) are
  [text parameters](#text-parameters): their expressions are text
  expressions (`'6qt'`, `'Box ' & GridX`); a `value` cell, used where the
  expression does not evaluate, is the text itself (`plain words`, kept as
  `'plain words'`) or a quoted text (`'6qt'`). Without a unit column, a
  new parameter whose expression gives a text is a text parameter.

A table that is not a parameter CSV (no `name` or `expression` column, a
quoted field not closed, nothing at all) refuses the query or the command
with the reason.

The preview and the import answer: `format` (`mitcad` or
`parameter_table`), the counts `added`, `changed`, `renamed` (rows added
or changed under a name of MitCad's own), `unchanged`, `refused`,
`skipped`, `summary` (`5 to add, 1 to change, 1 renamed, 1 refused, 1
skipped`, the nought counts left out; `nothing` when all are) and `rows`
in the file's order:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `line` | the line the row starts on (the header is line 1) |
| `name` | the name in the file |
| `renamed` | the MitCad name, when the file's cannot be used |
| `action` | `add`, `change`, `unchanged`, `refuse` or `skip` (no row is skipped since mitcad#664; kept for clients) |
| `changes` | of a `change`: `expression`, `unit`, `limits`, `comment`, `favorite` |
| `expression`, `unit` | after the import (the file's for a refused or skipped row) |
| `value`, `text` | after the whole import (mm or rad; `"35 mm"`; the limited value), not for a refused or skipped row; a text parameter has only `text`, its text |
| `limits` | `min`, `max`, `step` (as written, or null) and `strict` after the import (the file's for a refused row); left out when there are none |
| `limited` | `min`, `max` or `step`: the limit that changed the value after the import; left out when none did |
| `from_value` | true when the `value` column was used |
| `reason` | why the row is refused or skipped, or why its expression was not used |
| `notes` | what else stayed (`a model parameter keeps its unit mm, its comment`) |

Tests: `parameters_csv::tests` (quoting, lines, the header's format,
free names), `parameters_csv_tests` (a design exported and imported
into itself, nothing changing, and into a new design, the same
parameters with their limits, also one using a later parameter and a
strict one; a synthetic parameter table of the `.f3d` application with
unitless counts, `floor` and `round` of length ratios, `°`, quoted
comments with commas, a text parameter, a unit's name, forward
references, a cycle and unknown names; existing parameters changed as
their rows say, limits given to a model and a user parameter, a new one
clamped, a wrong limit refused; tables refused; a text row exported and
imported again, a text row taking its value, type errors refused),
`api::parameters_csv::tests`
(the query, the preview and the command); `tools/ui-parameters-csv-test.sh`
(Change Parameters' Export and Import with its preview, a maximum that
clamps a dimension).

## Text parameters

A parameter whose unit is `Text` has a text as its value instead of a
number (mitcad#664), such as the label of a lid. Its expression is a text
expression; the full rules are in `core/expr/src/lib.rs` (grammar,
rules 23 to 30), as a superset of [Values](#values): every expression
that parsed before parses and evaluates the same.

- **Texts in expressions.** A text is in single quotes, as `.f3d` designs
  write it (`'6qt'`), or in double quotes (`"Box "`). A quote of the same
  kind inside is doubled (`'It''s'`, `"say ""hi"""`); the other kind is an
  ordinary character (`"It's"`). The quoted unit of `value(x; "mm")` is
  still a unit.
- **Joining.** `a & b` joins its operands as text: `"Box " & GridX & "x" &
  GridY` is `Box 6x4`. A number is written as `text(x)` writes it: in the
  document's unit of its dimension with at most six decimals (`15 mm`,
  `30 deg`, `6` for a unitless one). `&` binds less tightly than `+` and
  `-` and more tightly than comparisons.
- **Functions.** `concat(a; b; …)` joins as `&` does. `text(x; [format])`
  writes a number; the format is a pattern of zeros and `#`s with at most
  one decimal point (`"0.00"`, `"0.0#"`, `"000"`), optionally followed by
  a unit (`"0.0 in"`, or only `"in"`) that the value is written in (a
  unitless value is read in it); without a unit the document's unit of the
  value's dimension follows the number, and halves round away from zero
  (`text(Width; "0.00")` is `15.00 mm`; `text(value(Width; "mm"); "0")` is
  `15`). `left(t; [n])` and `right(t; [n])` give the first and last `n`
  characters (one by default), `len(t)` the number of characters
  (unitless). Function names are case-insensitive; the names of these
  five are functions only before `(`, so parameters named `Text`, `Left`
  or `len` keep their names.
- **Choices and comparisons.** `if`, `ifs`, `switch`, `choose`, `iferror`
  and `let` take texts as values (the values of one choice are all texts
  or all numbers); `==` (and `=` in parentheses) and `<>` compare two
  texts, case included.
- **Never mixed.** A text is never accepted where a number is expected,
  nor a number where a text is: `'5' + 1`, `sin(Label)`, a text parameter
  as a feature's length or count, `left(5; 1)`, a text compared with a
  number, and a number as a text parameter's value are refused ("text
  where a number is expected", "a number where text is expected: make text
  of it with text(…) or &"). Only `&`, `concat` and `text` make text of
  numbers.
- **Commands.** `add_parameter` with a text expression and no `unit` makes
  a text parameter (`{"cmd": "add_parameter", "name": "Label",
  "expression": "'6qt'"}`), as does `"unit": "Text"`. `set_parameter` with
  `unit` `Text` makes a parameter a text one (its expression must give a
  text), and another unit a number again; a parameter a sketch text
  follows keeps its unit (`… Sketch1 uses it as a text`). A text
  parameter has no limits: `min`, `max` or `step` for one is refused ("a
  text parameter has no minimum, maximum or step").
- **The `parameters` query** gives a text parameter `"unit": "Text"`,
  `"text"` its text and `"value"` 0. The `evaluate` query takes `"kind":
  "text"` (or a text parameter's name as `parameter`) and answers `text`,
  `references` and `expression`, no `value`.
- **Sketch text.** A sketch text can follow a text parameter: the sketch
  definition's `text_values`, or `value` in `sketch.add_text` and
  `sketch.edit_text`: a text parameter's name (`"value": "Label"`), or a
  text expression (`"value": "'Box ' & GridX"`), which becomes the
  sketch's own text parameter of the text (the next free `d<n>`, comment
  `Sketch1 t9 text`, deleted with the sketch; a new expression changes
  it). `""` in `sketch.edit_text` stops the text following one; it keeps
  its string. A number parameter or a number expression there is refused.
  The text is laid out with the parameter's text, and so is an emboss or
  an extrusion of it: a change of the parameter (or of what its expression
  uses) lays the sketch out again and recomputes what uses it, and a
  change that leaves its text as it was recomputes nothing. The `sketch`
  query gives such a text its parameter's `text` and `value`:
  `{"parameter": "Label", "expression": "'6qt'", "own": false}` (`own`:
  the sketch's own parameter).
- **Files, undo, CSV.** The design file stores a text parameter with
  `"unit": "Text"` and its expression, and the sketch's `text_values` by
  parameter name; undo, redo, renames, copies and configurations treat it
  as any parameter. The [CSV](#parameters-as-csv) export writes its unit
  `Text` and its text as its value, and the import reads text rows of
  both tables.
- **The `.f3d` import** creates the file's text parameters (unit `Text`)
  with their expressions (`'6qt'`, `Label & ' lid'`); an expression that
  does not evaluate (a text without quotes, as older designs keep it) is
  taken as the text itself and reported with the parameters taken as
  values. The text parameter a design keeps for each sketch text (role
  `Text1-Text`, the sketch's model parameter) becomes the sketch's own,
  and the sketch's text follows it when its string is the parameter's
  text: the text of that number, or the only one with that string; a text
  is never changed by the link. A link the model refuses leaves the texts
  as they are.

Tests: `expr::tests` (`text_literals_and_their_quotes`,
`ampersand_joins_texts_and_numbers`, `text_functions`,
`texts_and_numbers_do_not_mix`, `choices_and_comparisons_of_texts`,
`text_function_names_stay_parameter_names`,
`expressions_without_texts_read_as_before`, `texts_have_a_length_limit`,
`text_parameters_in_a_table`), `expr::lexer::tests`,
`expr::units::tests::the_text_unit`, `parameters::tests`,
`api::text_parameter_tests` (a sketch text following a text parameter
and an expression of its own, its recompute on a change and only then,
the type errors both ways, no limits, save and load),
`api::evaluate::tests::evaluates_texts`, `parameters_csv_tests`
(`text_parameters_go_out_and_come_back`), and the import's
`text_parameters_are_imported_and_sketch_texts_follow_them` (a synthetic
design).

## Formula assistance

`formula_help` is a read-only query for expression fields and larger editors:

```json
{"query":"formula_help","expression":"FLOOR(length / pitch)","cursor":6,"selection_end":20,"kind":"unitless"}
```

`cursor` and optional `selection_end` are UTF-8 byte positions. `kind` accepts
`length` (default), `angle`, `unitless` and `text` (mitcad#664: `result` is then
`{"text": …}` and no selection is inspected); optional `parameter` evaluates in
that existing parameter's unit. The response always contains `functions`, the
supported function catalog with argument labels, descriptions and examples.
An unfinished call can return `signature` with its current zero-based argument.
A complete formula returns `result`; `selection` describes the smallest AST
node containing the cursor or selection, its byte range and evaluated text.
It retains lexical `LET` bindings and reports actual dimensions rather than
promoting a selected ratio to the field's length unit. Errors include a message
and source range. The query never changes the formula, parameters or limits.

The editor's templates are ordinary expression text. Limits continue to use
`set_parameter` with `min`, `max`, `step` and `strict`; setting a formula and its
limits together remains one undoable parameter command.

## Purge volumes

How much the printer purges when it changes from one filament to another
(mitcad#705; `core/model/src/print_purge.rs`, `document/purge_volumes.rs`,
`api/purge_volumes.rs`, `print_files/`): a table of the filament slots, a
row per filament changed from and a column per filament changed to, in
mm³, which the 3MF export writes for the slicers that keep one.

- **A material's values.** Two keys of the `Print Filament` set, MitCad's
  own (no slicer keeps them per filament; the [key map](#print-settings-key-map)'s
  group `purge` in the category `filament`): `purge_into` (purging into
  it, when the printer changes to it) and `purge_out` (purging out of it,
  when it changes from it), mm³, zero or more. A material that sets
  neither takes them from the colour it prints with (its
  `filament_colour`, else its appearance's): by the colour's lightness
  `L` (CIE L*, 0 black to 1 white), into 70 + 140 · L and out of
  70 + 140 · (1 − L), whole mm³. Mid grey takes 140 each way, black 70
  into and 210 out, white 210 into and 70 out.
- **The multiplier.** `flush_multiplier` of the `Print Process` set
  (category `others`, group `filaments`; the Bambu family's key), 1 when
  unset; the design's is the first body's.
- **The computed table:** from one filament to another, out of the first
  plus into the second, times the multiplier, whole mm³; 0 from a
  filament to itself. Dark to light so takes more than light to dark
  (black to white 420, white to black 140).
- **Pairs set by hand** ("overrides"): the design keeps a volume for an
  ordered pair of materials (from, to), as it is: the multiplier does not
  apply to it. Resetting it gives the computed volume again.
- **The slots** are those the 3MF export makes: the bodies in their order
  (sheet and empty bodies are not printed), a slot per distinct material
  in the order of first use, each body's material and settings in the
  occurrence that shows it first.
- **Export** (`export` with a `dialect`): the Bambu family (Bambu Studio,
  OrcaSlicer, QIDI Studio) gets `flush_volumes_matrix` (the table divided
  by the multiplier, which the slicer applies; one table per extruder, as
  many as the printer's `nozzle_diameter` entries), `flush_multiplier`
  (one text) and `flush_volumes_vector` (out, then in, per slot,
  unmultiplied); PrusaSlicer, which has no multiplier,
  `wiping_volumes_matrix` (the table as it purges),
  `wiping_volumes_use_custom_matrix = 1` and `wiping_volumes_extruders`
  (out, then in, per slot, multiplied). Cura has no table, and its
  per-material prime volumes are extruder settings, which its export does
  not write: nothing.
- **Import** (`import_print_profile` into the design): a Bambu-family
  project's `flush_volumes_matrix` (its first extruder's table, times its
  `flush_multiplier`) or a PrusaSlicer project's or configuration's
  `wiping_volumes_matrix` (unless `wiping_volumes_use_custom_matrix` is
  0) becomes the pairs set by hand of its materials, in the same undo
  step; a table of another size is left out (the report says so). None of
  these keys is kept as the slicer's text; the report counts them as
  read.

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `set_purge_volumes` | `volumes`: `[{from, to, volume}]`, material ids (built-in or the design's) and mm³ (zero or more); a `volume` of null or left out resets the pair | undo step `Set Purge Volume PLA Plastic to ABS Plastic`, `Reset Purge Volume …`, or for several `Set Purge Volumes` (`Reset Purge Volumes` when all reset), which recomputes nothing; none when nothing changes. Refused: an unknown material, a material to itself, a negative volume, no pairs |

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `purge_volumes` | `bodies` (uids of the bodies printed, in order; the design's when left out) | `multiplier`; `slots`: `{material, name, color, purge_into, purge_out, bodies}` (the values used: the material's own or its colour's); `volumes[from][to]`: `{computed, volume, edited}` (`volume` the one used, `edited` set by hand) |
| `purge_defaults` | `color` (`#RRGGBB`; mid grey when left out) | `{purge_into, purge_out}`: what a material of that colour without its own values takes (the material editor's empty fields) |

The design file keeps the pairs set by hand as `"purge_volumes": [{"from",
"to", "volume"}]`, left out when there are none. Deleting a design
material (`delete_material`, or a library's delete that removes an unused
copy) takes its pairs away in the same undo step, so that a new material
that gets its id (the first free `custom{n}`) starts computed; undo brings
them back with the material (mitcad#758). A design material that took a
built-in's place keeps them for the built-in of its id.

Tests: `print_purge::tests` (the colour rule, the multiplier, overrides in
the table, a project's table as pairs), `print_files::purge_tests` (the
computed table, a material's own values, pairs set, kept, reset, saved and
refused, the Bambu-family and PrusaSlicer exports, both imports),
`tools/ui-purge-volumes-test.sh` (3D Print's Purge volumes table).

## The reference in parts over MCP

This reference is about 1 MB, more than an agent's context. The MCP
servers (headless and live, `docs/mcp.md`) give it in parts through the
read-only tool `model_reference` (mitcad#714), parsed from this file in
`core/mcp/src/reference.rs`; the resource `mitcad://reference/commands`
still holds all of it.

| Arguments | Result |
|---|---|
| none | `contents` (the `##` and `###` headings), and `queries`, `commands`, `features`: the names MCP permits |
| `section` | one section with its subsections, found by its heading, a name its heading lists (`split_body`) or a part of its heading |
| `query`, `command` | the rows of its tables (tables whose first column is `Query` or `Command`), with their headers and the headings above them |
| `feature` | the section of the feature type: the heading that lists it, or the section of its first example definition (a code block with `"type": "<name>"`), and that `example` |
| `search` | the headings and the lines that contain a text, each line's headings and an excerpt |

Each answer holds at most 64 kB of text; a longer one gives
`next_offset` for `offset`. So that the tool finds things, keep to the
forms it reads: a feature type's section is a `###` heading that names
the type (`### rib, web`, or a list after a colon) or has an example
`{"type": "<name>", …}`; a command's or query's row is in a table whose
first header cell is `Command` or `Query` and names it in backticks in
its first cell.

The names come from `api::classes`: `external_queries()` (the model
class), `external_commands()` (the model class, and the commands that
are the model's own in some form: `create_appearance`, `edit_appearance`,
`set_render_settings` without a file, `build_place`, `build_connect`,
`build_panel`, `build_swap_fasteners` with a source of the design) and
`FeatureDef::TYPE_NAMES`. The MCP server's errors name the same lists:
an unknown query or command lists the permitted ones, and a refused
command that misses a field gets the section of its feature type, or its
command's rows, in `reference` (`docs/mcp.md`, "Transport, errors and
limits").

## Drawings in the design

Drawings kept in the design (mitcad#707, phase 1;
`core/model/src/drawing/def.rs`, `document/drawings.rs`,
`api/drawings.rs`): the root's and each component's Drawings folder.
A drawing is a definition only: its sheets and their views, each with its
place on the sheet, scale, style, label and subject. The lines are
projected from the model whenever the drawing is asked for, so a drawing
follows the model; nothing computed is stored. A drawing of a component
shows that component in its own coordinates and belongs to it: a copy of
the component (Paste New, Insert Component as a copy) brings copies of
its drawings, with their bodies and occurrences mapped, and deleting the
component deletes them. A component a feature made (a new-component
operation, a component from bodies) that is filled into an existing
empty component (`move_made_component`) moves its drawings there (a
name the folder has gets the next free one); an edit that would remove
it (the feature no longer a new-component operation) is refused while
it has drawings (`Component1 has drawings in its Drawings folder;
delete them first, or keep the new-component operation`), as while it
has features or occurrences; deleting the feature keeps it, with its
drawings, as a plain component. Dimensions, centre marks, notes and
symbols on views: *Annotations on drawing views* (phase 2).

Ids: a drawing is `D<n>` (`uid`), named uniquely in its folder
(`Drawing1`); commands take the id or a name only one drawing has. Its
sheets are numbered from 0 in their order; its views have ids from 1,
unique in the drawing. Points on a sheet are millimetres of paper from its
lower left corner.

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `add_drawing` | `component` (uid or name; the root when left out), `name` (the next free `Drawing<n>`), the first sheet's `size`, `orientation`, `projection`, `title_block`, `units`, `annotations` (below), `layout` (instead of an empty sheet: `export_drawing`'s fields without `path` and `format`, laid out as the export lays them out; the root's only) | `drawing`, `name`, `component`, `sheets`, `warnings`; undo step `Add Drawing1` |
| `edit_drawing` | `drawing`, `name` | undo step `Rename Drawing1` |
| `delete_drawing` | `drawing` | undo step `Delete Drawing1` |
| `add_drawing_sheet` | `drawing`, `sheet` (where it goes; the end), `name` (`Sheet<n>`), and the sheet's fields; the others are the last sheet's (not its views and text notes, mitcad#742) | `sheet`; undo step `Add Sheet2 to Drawing1` |
| `edit_drawing_sheet` | `drawing`, `sheet` (0), and the fields to change | undo step `Edit Sheet1 of Drawing1` |
| `delete_drawing_sheet` | `drawing`, `sheet`; refused for the last one | undo step `Delete Sheet2 of Drawing1` |
| `add_drawing_view` | `drawing`, `sheet` (0), `type`, and the fields of its type (below) | `view`; undo step `Add view 3 to Drawing1` |
| `edit_drawing_view` | `drawing`, `view`, and what changes (below) | undo step `Move view 3 of Drawing1` (a move alone) or `Edit view 3 of Drawing1` |
| `delete_drawing_view` | `drawing`, `view` | `deleted`: the view and the views that come from it; undo step `Delete view 3 of Drawing1` |

The commands change no geometry and recompute nothing; nothing changed is
no undo step.

**Sheets.** `size`: `A4` (default) … `A0`, `ANSI_A` … `ANSI_E`;
`orientation`: `landscape` (default) or `portrait`; `projection`:
`third_angle` (default) or `first_angle`; `title_block`: `title` (the
component's name, or the design's: the query's `title`, else the root's
name unless it is `Root`), `number` (the drawing number; without one the
block names the bodies drawn), `author` (`DRAWN BY`; without one `MADE
WITH Mitcad`), `date` (today's when drawn); `""` clears a field;
`units`: a length unit symbol (the design's when left out, `""`);
`annotations`: `{"dimensions", "hole_table", "sketch_dimensions"}`,
File › Export Drawing's automatic annotations (all off for a new drawing;
those of its options for one laid out). A drawing of several sheets
numbers them in the title block (`A3 1/2`).

**Views.** Each view has a `place`: where its anchor lies on the sheet,
the component's origin as the view sees it (a detail's centre), so views
that share an axis share a coordinate of their places at the same scale.

| `type` | Fields when added | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| `base` | `direction` (`front` (default, from -Y), `back`, `top` (+Z), `bottom`, `left`, `right` (+X), `iso` (front, right, above), `iso_top_left`, `iso_bottom_right`, `iso_bottom_left`; `{"toward_eye", "x_axis"}`; or `{"toward_eye", "up"}`: the application's camera), `subject`, `at` (where its box's middle goes; the sheet's middle, moved right clear of the other views; a view placed for itself is moved on while it overlaps another, then the other way, never out of the sheet's area for views, and stays where it would go, overlapping, when there is no room), `scale` (`"fit"` or left out: the largest ISO 5455 scale at which it takes two fifths of the sheet at most each way) | the subject from that direction |
| `projected` | `parent`, `side` (`right`, `left`, `above`, `below`, or a corner `above_right`, …; from `at` when left out), `at` (where its box's middle goes; beside its parent, moved away from it clear of the other views, never back past it: with no room that way it stays beside its parent, overlapping) | an orthographic view seen from that side of its parent (third angle) or from the opposite one (first angle); at a corner, the view from that corner (an isometric view of a standard one) |
| `section` | `parent`, `line` (two sheet points on the parent), `flip` (look the other way), `letter` (the next free: A, B, … without I, O, Q), `hatch` (true), `at` (where its box's middle goes; beside its parent on the side it is seen from in third angle, on the other side in first angle, clear of the other views, moved away from its parent only) | the parent's subject cut by the plane through the line and the parent's direction; what lies on the normal's side (left of the line as drawn, `flip`: right) goes and the view looks at the cut along -normal; the line, its arrows and letters are drawn on the parent |
| `detail` | `parent`, `center` (a sheet point on the parent), `radius` (sheet millimetres on the parent, 10), `letter`, `at` (where its centre goes; right of its parent, clear of the other views, moved away from its parent only) | what the parent shows inside the circle, projected in the detail's own style as its parent looks (a detail of a section cut by the section's plane), at twice the parent's scale unless given; the circle and its letter are drawn on the parent |

Every view also takes `scale` (`"1:2"`, `"2:1"`, a number; a projected
and a section view take their parent's when left out), `style`
(`{"hidden_lines", "tangent_edges", "shaded", "polygonal"}`; a view other
than a base view takes its parent's when left out; an isometric view and
a section show no hidden edges; `shaded` fills the faces in grey under
the lines from the kernel's triangles; `polygonal` projects a
triangulation, as every view of bodies with free-form faces is projected
anyway, `export_drawing`'s `exact` above, mitcad#962) and `label` (written under the
view; a section's `SECTION A-A` and a detail's `DETAIL B (2:1)` when left
out). A base view's `subject`: `{"type": "design"}` (default: every shown
body of the drawing's component and its occurrences),
`{"type": "occurrence", "occurrence": "O2/O5"}` (a path from the
drawing's component), `{"type": "bodies", "bodies": [{"body": "F2.b0",
"occurrence": "O2"}]}` (each where the occurrence places it, or wherever
it is shown when `occurrence` is left out). Views of other types show
their parent's subject.

`edit_drawing_view` takes `place` (the anchor's new place) or `move`
(`[dx, dy]`, a drag), `scale` (`"parent"`: the parent's again; a base view, which has no
parent, takes the one that fits the sheet, as `"fit"` does), `style`,
`label` (`""`: the default), a base view's `direction` and `subject`, a
projected view's `side`, a section's `letter`, `hatch` and `flip`, a
detail's `center` and `radius` (on the sheet) and `letter`, `breaks` (all
of them, `[]` none) or `add_break`, and `aligned`. A view that moves
takes the views that come from it along. A projected or section view is
kept in line with its parent (`aligned`, true): one beside its parent
keeps its parent's y, one above or below its x (a section the axis its
view shares with the parent's; a view of a detail lines up with the
detail's centre); `"aligned": false` lets it go. A break:
`{"direction": "horizontal" | "vertical", "from": [x, y], "to": [x, y],
"gap": 6}`, two sheet points whose coordinates along the view's x
(horizontal) or y (vertical) bound the band taken out; the two sides
close up to `gap` millimetres of paper with a break line at each. A
break is its own view's: the views in line with it keep their length.

Refused: a parent that is not an earlier view of the sheet, a subject on
a view other than a base view (a laid out section without a parent keeps
its sheet's bodies as its own), a section line of no length, a detail
circle of no size, overlapping breaks, a field the view's type does not
have, `"fit"` for a view other than a base view, an unknown unit, two
drawings of a folder with one name, the last sheet's deletion and a
drawing of a linked component. Turning a view that has sections or
details drawn on it or on a view from it (a base view's `direction`, a
projected view's `side`, a section's `flip`, the sheet's `projection`)
was refused until mitcad#729; they now follow it (*Drawing defaults,
sketches, patterns and turned views*).

The `drawings` query lists the drawings: `drawing`, `name`, `component`,
`component_name`, `exported`, `sheets` (`name`, `size`, `views`: their
count). `exported` numbers the drawings `add_drawing` laid out from a
`layout`, in the order they were made (1, 2, …; 0 for the others): File ›
Export Drawing offers the highest one first and writes it as it is
(mitcad#725). A drawing is never laid out again: what was made on it by
hand stays.

The `drawing` query (`drawing`, `sheet` (0), `geometry` (true), `title`)
gives the drawing's `sheets`, each with `name`, `size`, `orientation`,
`projection`, `width`, `height`, `title_block`, `units`, `annotations` and
`views`: `id`, `type`, `parent`, `place`, `scale` and `scale_text`,
`own_scale`, `automatic_scale` (what it would be without its own: its
parent's, twice that for a detail, 1:1 for a base view), `style`,
`own_style`, `label`, `aligned` (`"x"`, `"y"` or null), `breaks`, and a
base view's `direction` and `subject`, a projected view's `side`, a
section's `letter`, `hatch` and `span`, a detail's `letter` and `circle`
(`center` and `radius` on the sheet). The sheet asked for is drawn: each
view's `box` on the sheet (null when it shows nothing), or `error` (why
it is not drawn: `the body F9.b0 is gone`, `the occurrence O3 is gone`,
`its parent, view 2, is not drawn`, a kernel failure) with `broken` and
a 30 mm `box` about its place, so that it can be picked and deleted; the
sheet's `scale` (the first base view's) and `warnings`, and
with `geometry` its `groups` as the export writes them (`class`, `id`,
`items`: `{"line": [a, b], "pen"}`, `{"arc": {"center", "radius",
"start", "end"}, "pen"}`, `{"polyline": points, "closed", "pen"}`,
`{"fill": points}`, `{"shade": points, "grey"}`, `{"text", "at",
"height", "angle", "anchor"}`; pens `thick`, `thin`, `hidden`, `hatch`,
`chain`, `frame`). Groups: `view` (`id` `view-front`, … by its direction,
`view-section`, `view-detail`, else `view-V<id>`), `view-label`,
`section-line`, `detail-circle`, the automatic annotations' groups,
`frame`, `title-block`.

How a view is worked out: a base view's subject is found in the drawing's
component at the timeline marker (`Document::instances` below the
component's first placement, moved into its coordinates); the kernel
projects it (`Kernel::project_view`, the drawing family: hidden-line
removal and sections by OCCT); the projection is kept in the document's
projection cache (the 64 used last) by the bodies' shape versions and
placements and the view's spec, so asking again projects only what
changed; the bodies' edges and faces that picks are found among are kept
by a bound of their own (4096 bodies, a body's newer version replacing its
older one), so a sheet of many bodies does not
throw them out on every draw. A detail is projected in its own style and cut to its circle,
and breaks take their bands out (`mitcad_model_drawing::clip`: lines and
polylines cut where they cross, arcs split at the circle or, across a
break, as polylines, cut faces clipped as polygons), all in Rust on the
projected lines. A shaded view's faces are those that face the eye (a
mirroring placement turns their triangles over). The sheet is then drawn
by the export's code (`mitcad_model_drawing::compose::render`); each view tags the
round holes of the bodies it shows, not those inside its breaks, and a
kernel failure finding a body's holes is a warning of the sheet.

Files: `"drawings": [{"uid", "name", "component" (unless the root's),
"exported" (when a layout laid it out), "sheets": [{"name", "size", "orientation", "projection", "title_block",
"units", "annotations", "views": [{"id", "kind": {"type": "base",
"direction"} | {"type": "projected", "parent", "side"} | {"type":
"section", "parent", "origin", "normal", "span", "letter", "hatch"} |
{"type": "detail", "parent", "center", "radius", "letter"}, "place",
"scale", "style", "label", "subject", "breaks", "aligned"}]}]}]`, left
out when there are none and each field at its default left out; the
comparison of versions lists drawings by id with their changed fields
(`sheets[0].views[1].place`).

Classes: the commands and both queries are the model's (`classes.rs`).
`export_drawing` with `drawing` writes one (*Drawings*); `mitcad-cli
export-drawing <design> <out> --drawing D1 [--sheet N]` too (the sheet
from 1; the options that lay out a new drawing are refused with it).
Tests: `core/model-tests/drawing/src/stored_tests.rs` (directions of projected and section
views; the definition, its checks and file form; views placed,
projected, cut and detailed; moves in line with parents; breaks; the
model changed under a drawing and projections kept; undo, the design
file, the comparison; refusals; a component's drawings copied and
deleted with it, and inserted with a design; a kept drawing exported; a
laid out drawing the same as the export's; the drawings laid out
numbered and one written again as it is, mitcad#725; per-body sheets;
hole tags
per view and under breaks; first-angle placement; a detail of a
section; sections and details on a broken view; the refusal to turn a
view; a view that cannot be drawn; a made component's drawings),
the tests in `core/model-drawing/src/clip.rs`; `tools/ui-drawings-test.sh`,
`tools/ui-windows-drawings-test.ps1` (`app.ui-windows-drawings`).

## Annotations on drawing views

Dimensions, centre marks and centrelines, leader notes, datum labels,
