`document/tables_csv.rs`, `api/tables_csv.rs`). It is separate from the
[parameters CSV](#parameters-as-csv). The CSV is the text of the query or
the command: the application reads and writes the file.

| | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| query `table_csv` | `name` | `csv`: the table as CSV, `rows`: its number of rows |
| query `table_csv_preview` | `name`, `csv` | what `import_table_csv` would do; nothing changes |
| command `import_table_csv` | `name`, `csv` | what it did, as the preview, and `moves`: the configuration options it moved, as `set_table`'s ([Configurations and tables](#configurations-and-tables), mitcad#849; empty when the table is already as the file has it); one undo step `Import Table <name>`, none when the table is already as the file has it |

The file is UTF-8 (a byte order mark is skipped) with RFC 4180 quoting
and CRLF, read and written as the parameters CSV is; a header with
semicolons and no comma is read with `;` between fields.

- **The header** has a field per column: its name with its unit in
  brackets, `Size [Text],d [mm],dk [mm],Pitch [mm]`, `[]` for unitless,
  any unit a parameter takes (`mm`, `in`, `deg`, `mm^2`). A unit that is
  not one refuses the file.
- **Cells.** A cell of a number column is read as a constant expression
  in the column's unit: `5,5` (a decimal comma) is 5.5, a plain `5` in an
  `mm` column is 5 mm, `0.25 in` there is kept as 6.35. A cell that is not
  a number of the column's kind (`abc`, `5 deg` in an `mm` column, a
  parameter's name: cells are constants) is refused with the reason. A
  `Text` column takes its cells as they are, numbers too (`8`). White
  space around a cell is dropped; an empty cell is empty (null). Rows of
  empty cells at the end of the file are left out; one in the middle stays.
- **Inferred columns.** A header without brackets is a `Text` column when
  any of its cells is not a number; else a column of the unit of its first
  cell with a unit, in the design's default units (`10 mm` makes an `mm`
  column, and a plain `12` in it is 12 mm), and a unitless one when no cell
  has a unit.
- **Names.** A column name the model cannot use gets a free one, as the
  parameters CSV renames: other characters as `_` (`Head diameter` as
  `Head_diameter`), `c_` before one that does not start with a letter
  (`2nd` as `c_2nd`), `column_<n>` for an empty one, and `_1`, `_2`, ...
  for a name already taken (a second `d` as `d_1`). Reserved words (`in`,
  `Max`) name columns as they are. A column without a name and without
  cells (a separator too many) is left out.
- **Sizes**: at most 10 000 rows and 100 columns, a text cell at most
  `MAX_TEXT_BYTES`; a larger file is refused.
- **Export** writes every unit in brackets (`[Text]` too) and numbers with
  decimal points, the shortest decimal that gives the value back (`5.5`,
  `1e-12`), so export and import give the same table.

An import creates the table `name` or replaces it whole; a table it
replaces keeps its comment. It goes through the same atomic check as a
table edit: the parameters that name the table, and their dependents, are
evaluated again with the new one in one step, and features recompute only
when a value changed. It is refused, and nothing changes, while a cell of
the file is refused, while a parameter would fail with the new table (a
key no longer found, a column gone or of another kind), and for a name no
table can have (a parameter's, a reserved one).

The preview and the import answer:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `name` | the table's |
| `created` | the import makes the table (else it replaces the one of its name) |
| `unchanged` | the table is already as the file has it |
| `columns` | in the file's order: `name` (the file's), `renamed` (the table's, when the file's cannot be used; left out otherwise), `unit` (`mm`, `""`, `Text`), `inferred` (the header had no unit) |
| `rows` | the cells as the table keeps them: numbers in their column's unit, texts, null for an empty or refused cell |
| `refused` | cells: `line` (the header is line 1), `column` (the table's name; empty for a cell beyond the last column), `text`, `reason` |
| `changed` | parameters whose values change: `name`, `from`, `to` (`8.5 mm`, a text as it is) |
| `failing` | parameters that would fail: `name`, `error` |
| `summary` | `new table Screws: 5 columns, 3 rows, 1 renamed, 2 inferred, 1 cell refused, 2 parameters change, 1 parameter fails` (the nought counts after the rows left out); `Screws replaced: …`, `Screws unchanged: …` |
| `moves` | the import only: the configuration options it moved (`option`, `from`, `to`, `from_expression`, `to_expression`, `rule`, `text`), as `set_table`'s; the preview does not move anything and has no `moves` |

```json
{"query": "table_csv", "name": "Screws"}
{"query": "table_csv_preview", "name": "Screws", "csv": "Size [Text];d [mm]\r\nM5;5\r\n"}
{"cmd": "import_table_csv", "name": "Screws", "csv": "Size [Text],d [mm]\r\nM5,5\r\n"}
```

Tests: `tables_csv::tests` (names and units of the header, semicolons and
decimal commas, units in cells, inferred columns, refused cells, files
that are no table, export and import of every unit kind, free names),
`tables_csv_tests` (in the model: a round trip with every unit kind into
the same and another design, a `;`-separated file, units in cells,
inferred and renamed columns, refused cells refusing the import, a
changed cell changing its parameter in one undo step, a key in use that
disappears refusing the import with both failing parameters, a table
with a parameter's name), `api::tables_csv::tests` (the queries and the
command).
## Recompute workers

`Document::set_recompute_workers(n)` (mitcad#842) lets a recompute
evaluate the features of independent components on up to `n` threads at
once, each with a fork of the kernel; `1`, the default, evaluates every
feature on the recompute's own thread as before. The environment variable
`MITCAD_RECOMPUTE_WORKERS` gives every document of the process its
starting value (the ctests `core.model.assembly.workers`,
`core.model.links.workers` and `core.model.joints.workers` run those
model tests with 4). No JSON command or query sets it yet, and the
application and `mitcad-cli` leave it at 1.

The recompute cuts the timeline into windows that end at barriers
(joints, rigid groups, constraint sets and motion links; Move, Capture
Position, Joint Origin, Pattern at Points, Component from Bodies, Body
Transfer and any feature that made a component; sketches with driven
dimensions and Bound Length, which write parameters; an extrusion with a
cut scope across components, and a feature whose last result moved
occurrences, measured parameters or gave bodies to another component).
Within a window, each component's features run ahead on a worker, except
a feature that reads other components (links in its definition, or reads
of other components' bodies, placements or results in its last result)
and the features of its component after it, which the recompute
evaluates itself. A window runs ahead only when at least two components
have a feature there that the cache likely lacks.

The recompute still goes through the timeline in order and takes a
worker's result only where the cache would take a stored one (the same
definition, every read the evaluation recorded holding where the
recompute is, the definition's parameter values the same) and the
evaluation succeeded; otherwise it evaluates the feature itself. The
document, results, versions, topological names, statuses, warnings, the
memory cache, the result store's writes and the monitor's progress are
therefore those of one thread. A stop cancels every worker (their monitors
are part of the recompute's) and keeps nothing a worker returned; results
not yet taken count against the memory cache's budget, and before the
cache drops results for its budget the recompute stops the workers and
waits for them, so that it drops what it drops with one thread. Previews, commands
that add base features from shapes (`written_from`) and recomputes on a
worker's thread use no workers. The OCCT kernel installs its crash
handlers on each worker thread (`Kernel::worker_thread`).

Tests: `core/model-tests/assembly/src/parallel_recompute_tests.rs` (two
components at the same time; a linked feature, a driven dimension's
reader and a moved occurrence's reader waiting for what they read; stops
while workers evaluate and while the recompute waits for one; each against
the same design with one thread).

## Cut sheets

A cut sheet (mitcad#853; `core/model/src/drawing/cut_sheet_def.rs`,
`core/model-drawing/src/cut_sheet.rs`, `api/cut_sheets.rs`) is a drawing
of its own kind in a Drawings folder: it collects flat parts at 1:1 on a
sheet of material and writes their outlines as DXF or SVG for cutting
(a laser, a water jet, a plasma cutter). It has no title block, frame,
scale, dimensions, hole table, hidden or tangent lines: only the edges
to cut. It is kept with the design's drawings (`drawings` lists it with
`"kind": "cut_sheet"`, the others `"drawing"`), is copied and deleted
with its component as they are, and follows the model: its outlines are
worked out whenever they are asked for.

A **part** is a body seen along the normal of one of its planar faces,
from outside the body: its largest planar face unless one is chosen (of
faces as large, the one facing up most: +Z, then +Y, then +X). Its
outline is the body's silhouette along that normal: the outer boundary
of its whole extent and the holes and cut-outs that go through it, so a
through hole is one inner loop however many faces its wall has, and a
blind hole or a pocket is none. Each part has an id (from 1, unique on
the cut sheet), a `place`, where the middle of its outline's box lies on
the sheet (millimetres from the sheet's lower left corner), and a
`rotation` about that middle (degrees counter-clockwise), so a part that
grows or shrinks stays where it was put. A count adds that many parts
(2 × Rib 3: two parts of the same body). Parts are moved and turned by
hand; nothing nests them. A part whose body (or the occurrence placing
it) is gone stays on the sheet, marked as missing; one whose face is
gone or no longer planar says why.

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `add_cut_sheet` | `component` (uid or name; the root when left out), `name` (the next free `CutSheet<n>`), `width`, `height` (the material, mm; 600 × 300), `bodies` (parts to start with, below), `count` (1) | `drawing`, `name`, `component`, `parts` (their ids), `warnings`; undo step `Add CutSheet1` |
| `edit_cut_sheet` | `drawing`, `name`, `width`, `height` | undo step `Rename CutSheet1` or `Edit CutSheet1` |
| `add_cut_sheet_parts` | `drawing`, `bodies`, `face` (a planar face of the one body given; its largest when left out), `count` (1 to 1000), `at` (where the first one's middle goes; each in a free place of the sheet when left out, in rows from the top left 5 mm apart, beside the sheet when none is left) | `parts`, `warnings`; undo step `Add part 3 to CutSheet1` or `Add 4 parts to CutSheet1` |
| `edit_cut_sheet_part` | `drawing`, `part`, `place` or `move` (`[dx, dy]`), `rotation` (degrees) or `turn` (degrees more: 90 a quarter turn left, -90 right), `face` (null: the largest) | undo step `Move part 3 of CutSheet1`, `Turn part 3 of CutSheet1` or `Edit part 3 of CutSheet1` |
| `delete_cut_sheet_parts` | `drawing`, `parts` (ids) | `deleted`; undo step `Delete part 3 of CutSheet1` or `Delete 2 parts of CutSheet1` |
| `export_cut_sheet` | `drawing`, `path`, `format` (`dxf` or `svg`; from the extension when left out), `labels` (false) | `path`, `format`, `parts` (written), `outer`, `inner` (loops written), `labels`, `width`, `height`, `warnings` |

A body in `bodies` is its uid or name (`"F2.b0"`, `"Rib 3"`), or
`{"body", "occurrence"}` with the occurrence that places it (a path from
the cut sheet's component, `"O2/O5"`); left out, wherever it is shown.
Refused: a body without a planar face (`Body1 has no planar face to lie
on`), a face that is not a planar face of its body, a body that shows
nothing along the face's normal, a face with several bodies, a count of
0 or over 1000, a material of no size or over 100 m, and a cut sheet's
views, sheets, notes, templates or revisions (`CutSheet1 is a cut sheet:
it holds parts only, on one sheet`).

The generic drawing commands work on a cut sheet's parts as on views:
`edit_drawing_view` with `place`, `move` or `rotation` (any other field
is refused), `delete_drawing_view`, `edit_drawing` (its name),
`delete_drawing`; `add_drawing_view` is refused. `export_drawing` with
the cut sheet as `drawing` writes it as `export_cut_sheet` does, without
labels.

**Warnings** (the query's and the commands' `warnings`): `part 2 (Rib 3)
overlaps part 3 (Rib 3)` (their material overlaps; touching is no
overlap, nor a part inside another's hole), `part 4 (Rib 5) leaves the
sheet`, `part 5 (F9.b0) is missing: the body F9.b0 is gone`, and `part 6
(Body2): …` for a part that cannot be worked out.

The `cut_sheet` query (`drawing`, `geometry` (true)) gives `drawing`,
`name`, `component`, `component_name`, `kind`, `width`, `height`,
`warnings`, `counts` (each body, occurrence and face once: `body`, `name`,
`face`, `occurrence`, `count`, `parts`) and `parts`: `id`, `body`,
`body_name`, `occurrence`, `face` (the face it is seen along), `own_face`
(chosen rather than the largest), `faces` (the body's planar faces with
their `area`, mm²), `place`, `rotation`, `size` (its outline's box
before it is turned), `box` (on the sheet; a 30 mm box about its place
when it is not worked out), `outer` and `inner` (its loops), `missing`,
`error`, `off_sheet`, `overlaps` (the parts it overlaps), and with
`geometry` its `loops` on the sheet: `{"outer", "pieces"}`, the pieces
end to end with the material on their left (outer boundaries
counter-clockwise, inner loops clockwise): `{"line": [a, b]}`, `{"arc":
{"center", "radius", "start", "sweep"}}` (radians; a positive sweep
counter-clockwise, a whole circle ±2 pi), `{"polyline": points}`,
`{"spline": {"degree", "knots", "poles", "weights"}}` (from the piece's
start to its end; `weights` empty when not rational). A part also
gives `splines`: the B-splines of its outline on the sheet, as the
pieces' `spline`.

The `drawing` query of a cut sheet draws it for the application: its
`kind` (`cut_sheet`), one sheet of the material's `width` and `height`
whose `views` are the parts (`type` `part`, `id`, `place`, `rotation`,
`label` (the body's name), `box`, `broken` and `error` when it is not
worked out, and the query's fields of a part), its `warnings`, and with
`geometry` its `groups`: a `view` group `part-<id>` of each part's
outline (pen `thick`) and a `view-label` group of its name.

**B-splines.** The kernel's projection gives a B-spline or Bézier edge
as its B-spline (its degree, full knot vector, poles and weights, cut to
the edge's range), and another curve that is no line or circle (an
ellipse, an offset curve, ...) as a B-spline within 1e-6 mm, each with
a polyline of it within the view's deflection (`ViewCurve::Spline`;
drawings draw, cut and pick that polyline). A cut sheet keeps such a
curve as the curve it is: split where other lines meet it and joined
again (the crossings and ends found on the curve itself), turned and
moved by its poles, and cut to a part of its range by knot insertion
(`mitcad_model_drawing::bspline`). Lines and arcs of a polyline stay a
polyline.

**The files.** DXF (R2000, millimetres, 1:1): outer boundaries on the
layer `CUT_OUTER`, inner loops on `CUT_INNER` (the Flat Pattern's
names, *DXF export* of Sheet-metal), lines as `LINE`, arcs as `ARC`,
whole circles as `CIRCLE`, B-splines as `SPLINE`s with their own
degree, knots, control points and weights (weights only when they
differ), a polyline (from the polygonal projection) as a `SPLINE` of
degree 1 through its points; with `labels` each part's name as `TEXT`
on `LABEL` at the middle of its box (5 mm high, smaller on small
parts). SVG (the material's size in millimetres, `viewBox` in
millimetres, y down from the top): a layer (`<g id="CUT_OUTER">`,
`inkscape:label`) of the outer boundaries (red) and one of the inner
loops (`CUT_INNER`, blue), each loop one closed `<path>` (`data-part`
its part's id) of lines (`L`), arcs (`A`) and, for a non-rational
B-spline of degree 3 or less, its Bézier pieces as cubic Béziers (`C`,
exactly; a quadratic raised to a cubic, degree 1 as lines); a rational
B-spline or one of a higher degree as lines within 0.0001 mm
(`cut_sheet::SVG_DEFLECTION`); with `labels` a layer `LABEL` of the
names as `<text>`. A
part that cannot be worked out is left out (a warning says why); a cut
sheet with no part to write is refused.

How a part is worked out: its body where its occurrence places it in
the cut sheet's component; the face's plane (`Kernel::faces`,
`Kernel::face_plane`); the kernel's projection along the face's normal
with hidden lines removed, sharp, tangent and silhouette edges
(`Kernel::project_view`); then, in Rust
(`mitcad_model_drawing::cut_sheet::silhouette`), the lines seen are split
where they cross or end on each other, the regions they bound are asked
once each whether the body lies behind them (a line of sight across the
body, `Kernel::segments_crossings`), and the lines with material on one
side only are followed into loops, pieces of one line or circle joined
again. The result is kept in the document's drawing cache by the body's
shape version, its placement and the face chosen. Overlaps and parts
off the sheet are found on the loops flattened (arcs in steps of 2°).

Example:

```json
[{"cmd": "add_cut_sheet", "width": 600, "height": 300,
  "bodies": ["Rib 3", "Spar"], "count": 2},
 {"cmd": "edit_cut_sheet_part", "drawing": "CutSheet1", "part": 2, "turn": 90},
 {"cmd": "export_cut_sheet", "drawing": "CutSheet1", "path": "ribs.dxf", "labels": true}]
```

Classes: the commands and the query are the model's, `export_cut_sheet`
writes a file (`classes.rs`); MCP's `model_export` takes `cut_sheet` (and
`labels`) to write one as DXF or SVG. Tests:
`core/model-drawing/src/cut_sheet_tests.rs` (a plate with two holes and
a slot seen with its edges twice and a seam: one outer loop and three
inner within 1e-6 mm; a blind hole; placing and turning; overlaps,
touching and nesting; the DXF and SVG read back with their layers and
sizes; a polyline as a spline; B-splines cut, turned and as Béziers; a
plate whose top is a cubic B-spline split by a seam: one spline again
with its degree, knots and control points within 1e-6 mm, read back from
the DXF as a `SPLINE` and written in the SVG as a cubic Bézier; the
spline turned with its part), `core/model-tests/drawing/src/cut_sheet_tests.rs`
(the commands and queries on the mock kernel: a part added with a count,
a parameter change, a deleted body marked missing, overlaps and parts
off the sheet, the generic drawing commands, undo, the design file, the
files written and read back), `tools/cli/tests/cut_sheet.json`
(`cli.cut_sheet`: a plate with two holes and a slot through OCCT, and a
plate whose top is a B-spline of degree 2, its control points on the
sheet),
`tools/ui-drawings-test.sh` (New Drawing › Cut Sheet, two bodies added,
DXF written).

## Rounded rectangles and fillets of several corners

(mitcad#867) `sketch.rectangle` with `radius` (a value: a number or an
expression) makes the rectangle of its `mode` and rounds its four
corners: four tangent arcs (`made`: the four lines, then the four arcs),
the first with a radius dimension (comment `fillet radius`) and the
other three Equal to it, so the one parameter drives all four. A radius
of half the shorter side or more is refused (`the corner radius 10 mm
must be less than half the shorter side (10 mm)`), and nothing is added.

`sketch.fillet` rounds several corners at once with `curves` and/or
`points` in place of `a` and `b` (giving both forms is refused):

- `curves` (lines): every corner where two of them end at one point.
  Construction lines count only among construction lines, so a
  rectangle's construction diagonal does not spoil its corners; a point
  where three or more lines of one kind end is refused; two lines in
  line make no corner. Two lines without a shared end are the corner
  where they meet, as with `a` and `b`.
- `points`: each a point where exactly two lines of one kind end (the
  drawn ones, else the construction ones); any other point is refused
  (`p9 is not the corner of two lines (0 curve(s) end there)`).

Each corner is filleted as with `a` and `b` (the corner stays as a point
on both lines, a length dimension of a line becomes the distance from
its other end to the corner); one radius dimension on the first arc and
Equal from it to each other arc. Before anything changes, the corners on
each line must leave some of it: otherwise the refusal names the line
and the largest radius that fits (`the fillet radius 12 mm does not fit
on c2: its corners take 24 mm of its 20 mm, the radius must be less than
10 mm`). One command: one undo step, `Fillet in <sketch>`. A curve that
is no line is refused.

```json
{"cmd": "sketch.rectangle", "sketch": "F1", "mode": "two_point",
 "a": [0, 0], "b": [40, 20], "radius": 5}
{"cmd": "sketch.fillet", "sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c2", "c3", "c4"], "radius": 5}
{"cmd": "sketch.fillet", "sketch": "F1", "points": ["p5", "p7"], "radius": "r1"}
```

The application's 2-Point and Center Rounded Rectangle and Sketch
Fillet's Lines or Corners send these (`app/COMMANDS.md`). Tests:
`core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_rounded_rectangle_867_tests.rs` (a
40 × 20 rounded rectangle of r 5 fully constrained by width, height,
radius and position, all four arcs following the radius parameter; the
centre variant; Sketch Fillet on a whole rectangle with length
dimensions giving the same, undone in one step; a Center Rectangle with
its diagonal; two corners by their points; the refusals).

## Annotations' look: text height, Auto colour and placement

mitcad#894 (`core/model/src/document/annotations.rs`,
`core/model-api/src/annotations.rs`, `api/analysis.rs`): the
[annotations](#annotations) of the model drawn as a technical drawing's
dimensions (ISO 129-1, ISO 3098, ISO 1101).

**Text height.** The annotations' texts are one height in model units
(mm), in their planes, so that they grow and shrink with the model like
their lines: the design's setting, or, left unset, the automatic one —
of the ISO 3098 series 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7 and 10 mm the largest at most a
fiftieth of the size of what is annotated (the diagonal of the box of the
bodies the shown annotations' picks are on), at least 2.5 mm; 3.5 mm when
no body is known (datums only). Each annotation's `drawing` has it as
`text_height`. The application keeps a text at least about 9 pixels high
on screen when zoomed out.

| Command | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `set_annotation_text_height` | `text_height`: mm, 0.1 to 1000, or `null` for the automatic one | undo step `Annotation Text Height` (nothing to recompute), none when nothing changes; out of range refused (`an annotation text height is 0.1 to 1000 mm, got 0`) |

`{"query": "annotation_text_height"}` gives `{"text_height"` (the one
set, `null` for the automatic one)`, "in_use"` (mm), `"automatic"` (the
one the size gives), `"series": [2.5, 3.5, 5.0, 7.0, 10.0]}`. The design
file keeps a height set as `annotation_text_height`.

**Auto colour.** A new annotation's `color` is `auto` when none is given
(`add_annotation`, `add_measurement`): no colour of its own, the neutral
annotation colour the application draws it in, which follows the view's
background tone (near-black on a light background, light grey on a dark
one). `color` takes `auto` in any case as it takes `#rrggbb`. The six
colours new annotations took in turn before (`#d9480f`, `#1971c2`,
`#2f9e44`, `#c2255c`, `#7048e8`, `#e67700`) were the program's, not the
user's: an annotation stored in a design file with one of them is read as
`auto` (and saved so). A colour given in a command, or any other stored
one, stays the annotation's own.

**Placement of a length.** Left out (`line_offset` not set: added
without a view, or set back to the default with `null`, the editor's
Automatic), a length's dimension line lies outside its bodies' extent in
its plane: of the corners of the boxes of the bodies its picks are on,
projected across the ends in the plane, on the side they reach less far
past the ends (`y`'s when as far; when added in a view, the side towards
the view's eye, mitcad#902), 6 text heights past the farthest corner
there (1.5 before mitcad#902); a parallel line laid out before it (by the
order of the annotations, a shown length in a parallel plane, along the
same direction, overlapping it along the length) that it would come
within 2.5 text heights of moves it 2.5 text heights past that line, on
its side. A line set (by a view
when added, or dragged) keeps its place. The places are worked out from
what `measure_picks` keeps for the picks (`MeasuredPicks::extent`,
`MeasuredPicks::faces`: the bodies' boxes placed by their occurrences, the
planar faces at the picks), measured again only when the picks' bodies
change (mitcad#716).

Tests: `api::annotations::tests` (a length outside a box's extent and a
second one stacked outside it, one elsewhere along it not, one set by hand
kept; an offset of planes leaving the box at its outline; a view's plane
of the part), `document::annotations::tests` (old default colours read
as Auto, the ISO 3098 series by size, heights refused),
`core/model-tests/analysis/src/annotation_tests.rs`
(`lengths_are_placed_outside_the_body_and_stack_outside_each_other`,
`old_default_colours_are_read_as_auto`,
`the_text_height_is_automatic_or_set_for_the_design`).

## Clearance holes and recesses by screw size

mitcad#903 (`core/model/src/features/hole_sizes.rs`,
`core/model/data/hole_sizes.json`, `core/model-api/src/hole_sizes.rs`):
the clearance holes and the screw head recesses of the ISO metric screw
sizes M1.6 to M24 (the sizes of MitCad's fastener tables), which the Hole
panel's Hole Tap Type Clearance fills its fields from. The data file has
one section per standard, each naming it:

- ISO 273 (ISO 20273): the clearance hole of the fine, medium and coarse
  series; the panel's Fit Normal is the medium series.
- DIN 974-1, series 1: the counterbore for an ISO 4762 socket head
  without a washer; its depth is ISO 4762's head height k plus an
  allowance (0.2 mm for M1.6 to M2.5, 0.4 mm for M3 to M6, 0.6 mm for M8
  to M20, 0.8 mm for M24). A counterdrill takes the counterbore's
  diameter and depth, its cone 90°.
- ISO 10642: the theoretical head diameter dk of the 90° countersunk
  socket head (M3 to M20), and ISO 15065: the countersink diameter for
  the heads of ISO 7721 (M1.6 to M10). A size's countersink is the larger
  of the two, so that either head is at or just below the face; M24 has
  none.
- A tapped hole's countersink: 1.1 times the thread's major diameter,
  rounded to 0.1 mm and at least 0.1 mm over it, at 90°.

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `hole_sizes` | `size` (`M6`, case and spaces ignored; every size when left out), `major` (a thread's major diameter, mm), `thread` (a tapped hole's thread as `thread_sizes` names it, mitcad#980: `standard`, `iso_metric` when left out, `size` (`6`) and `designation` (`M6x1`, optional)) | `sizes` (smallest first): `size`, `diameter` (the thread's nominal d), `clearance` (`fine`, `normal`, `coarse`), `counterbore` (`diameter`, `depth`), `counterdrill` (`diameter`, `depth`, `angle` 90), `countersink` (`diameter`, `angle` 90; left out for M24), `iso_10642_head` and `iso_15065` (the two diameters the countersink is the larger of, where the standard has the size); `fits` (`fit`, `title`: `fine` Fine, `normal` Normal, `coarse` Coarse), `default_fit` (`normal`), `default_size` (`M6`), `standards` (the sections' titles: `clearance`, `counterbore`, `countersink_head`, `countersink`); with `major` also `tapped_countersink` (`diameter`, `angle` 90); with `thread` also `tapped_countersink` (from the size's major diameter unless `major` is given), `thread_size` (the screw size of an ISO metric size's nominal diameter, `6` is `M6`, as an entry of `sizes`: a tapped hole's counterbore and counterdrill; left out for a size the table lacks, `5.5`, and for the other standards) and `thread_bore` (the designation's basic minor diameter D1, the tapped hole's bore; left out without a designation the standard has). A size the table lacks is refused (`no clearance hole for the screw size M7: the sizes are M1.6, …`), and so is a `major` not greater than zero |

Lengths are millimetres, angles degrees. A hole stores the values the
panel filled in as plain values, and names its size and fit in
`clearance` ([hole](#hole)); the table does not change a hole later.

Tests: `features::hole_sizes::tests` and
`features::hole::tests::clearance_holes_keep_their_size_and_fit`
(`core.model`), `core/model-tests/features-profile/src/hole_size_tests.rs`
(the query for M2, M6 and M24, a tapped M6x1's `thread_size` and
`thread_bore`; a clearance hole with a counterbore, a typed value kept,
the refusals), `features::hole_sizes::tests::a_tapped_hole_takes_the_screw_size_of_its_thread`, `tools/cli/tests/f1_hole.json` (the
volumes of M6 clearance holes counterbored, Normal and Fine, and
countersunk, through a 60 x 40 x 20 block).

## Hole callouts and the reference look

mitcad#902 (`core/model-api/src/hole_callouts.rs`,
`core/model-api/src/annotations.rs`, `core/model-drawing/src/compose.rs`):
hole callouts on the model, and what the [annotations](#annotations) give
the application for the look of a technical drawing's dimensions.

**Hole callouts.** An annotation of the `kind` `hole_callout` points at a
hole: its `a` is a body's round face or edge (a hole's wall, its
counterbore's or countersink's face, or a rim between them), with `at`,
where the hole was clicked. It is a leader as a note is (no value, format,
tolerance or text of its own; `name` `HoleCallout1`, …), stored and
listed as the other annotations, edited and deleted by the same commands.
`add_annotation` needs `kind: "hole_callout"`; it is refused for a pick
that is no face or edge (`a hole callout points at a hole: its round face
or edge`) and for a face that gives no hole or circle. Its `label` is
`{"text": "4x Ø6.6 THRU / ⌴ Ø11 ↧ 6.8", "lines": ["4x Ø6.6 THRU", "⌴ Ø11 ↧
6.8"]}`, worked out whenever the annotations are asked for, so it follows
the hole's size, depth and thread:

- A hole of a hole feature (its face named `F5:hole2.wall`,
  `F5:hole2.cbore_wall`, … or named after one): the exported drawing's
  callout engine (`mitcad_model_drawing::compose::hole_callout`, there in
  words, here in ISO 129-1's symbols) — the count of the feature's holes
  (`4x`, none for one), the thread of a tapped hole (`M6x1 - 6H`, `LH` for
  a left-handed one, a custom thread's size and starts, `10x1.5 2
  STARTS`) or `Ø` and the drill's diameter (a tapped hole's bore, its
  thread's minor diameter), then `THRU` or `↧` and the depth (a hole to an
  object: its wall's length); a thread along part of the wall has its
  depth on the first line and the drill's size and depth on the second;
  then the counterbore (`⌴ Ø11 ↧ 6.8`; a counterdrill's too) or the
  countersink (`⌵ Ø12 × 90°`). Lengths in the document's unit as the
  drawings write them (two decimals in millimetres at most).
- A round face of a thread feature: its thread (`M10x1.5 - 6g`) and `↧`
  its length when it has one.
- Any other round face or edge: its diameter (`Ø20`).

Its `drawing` is a note's: the leader from the text to the arrow on the
hole's edge, at the end of the round face picked towards the side its
plane faces (the view's when added), at the point of the rim nearest
`at`. A broken pick or a hole feature that does not build breaks it with
the reason, as other annotations. A feature control frame can stand under
it (`on`, as under a dimension: its position frame on the same leader).

**What the drawing gives the look.** Each leader's `drawing` has `align`,
`start` or `end`: its text starts at the leader's end, or ends there when
it lies on the arrow's side along the text; a frame under a hole callout
has the callout's `align` and `under_lines` (the callout's lines it stands
below). A note's and a frame's leader on a face ends in a dot
(`"terminator": "dot"`), on an edge or outline in an arrow; a datum
label's in its triangle (`"datum"`). A length's extension line from a
planar face picked starts at that face's own outline (the corners of its
box, `MeasuredPicks::outlines`), on the line's side, never at the edge of
the bodies' box in mid-air; from an edge or a vertex at its point. The
places left to the defaults are in text heights, which follow the design's
text height, and keep the annotations out of the part as a drawing does:
a length's line 6 text heights past its bodies (2.5 more for each
parallel one), on the side towards the eye of the view it was added in; a length
between two planes picked has its ends slid within both faces to their
common edge on that side and to their far edge along its plane's normal
(the plane faces the eye: away from it), so that its extension lines run
from the faces' corners to a line outside the part; a view's ties between
planes facing it alike go to the one most along its up (a horizontal
plane). A leader's text (a note's, a frame's, a callout's) goes the
shortest way out of the part in its plane on an oblique leader, never
along the text nor straight up: of the directions up and out to its own
side (45 degrees, then steeper), up and out to the other side, and down
and out (in that order of preference), the one that leaves the bodies'
extent soonest without crossing a leader or a text laid out before it
in a parallel plane, 2 text heights past the extent, after a landing of
1.5 text heights level with the text's first line (the leader's
`dimension_lines`: the leader to the point, then the landing; the other
lines hang below), and moves on up past the leaders' texts laid out
before it (their size estimated from their words) and on past the
lengths' dimension lines laid out before it as seen in its plane;
without a body four along and three across from its point. A datum
label on a face stands on a stem 3 text heights long square to that
face (its normal in the label's plane), its square centred past the
stem's end (`"align": "middle"`, no landing); on a planar face its
triangle stands on the face's outline where the stem leaves the face
(the convex outline of the face's box corners seen in the label's
plane), its base along that outline and the stem square to it in the
plane. A round face's circle (a radius, a diameter) is drawn at the
face's end towards the default isometric view's eye. A radius, and a
diameter without a plane, lie in the circle's plane, the text out from
the bodies' middle, one and a half radii and at least three text heights
past its rim, a diameter on a leader from outside with its one arrow on
the rim and no centre mark. A diameter added in a view takes the view's
plane as a note does (its `plane`, the view's horizontal its `x`):
there it is a leader from outside to the rim's point that lies out from
the bodies' middle, its arrow on the rim, its text level on a landing
(`align` as a note's), laid out as a note's; a frame under it stands
below its text as under a hole callout; an
angle's arc is five out without its picks' reach. A view no longer
freezes pixel sizes when an annotation is added. The automatic text
height takes the size of the design (its root's bodies with the annotated
ones).

Tests: `api::hole_callouts::tests` (a hole found in its faces' names),
`api::annotations::tests`
(`extension_lines_start_at_the_picked_geometry_not_at_a_box`,
`a_datum_stands_on_its_faces_outline_and_a_diameter_on_a_leader`, the
defaults in text heights), `compose::tests`
(`hole_callouts_in_words_and_in_symbols`), `document::annotations::tests`
(the kind), `core/model-tests/analysis/src/annotation_tests.rs`
(`hole_callouts_write_their_holes_from_the_feature`: a simple, a through
counterbored, a countersunk, a tapped, a partly tapped and a custom-thread
hole, the drill's size changed; `a_hole_callout_takes_a_frame_and_breaks_with_its_hole`).

## Readers of files in the application's process

The application reads whole CAD files only in its import process
(`mitcad --import-worker`), including the listings asked before an
import (`list_references` of `import_f3d_timeline`, `list_links` of
`import_rvt`; mitcad#922). The queries and commands that read a file the
user chose in the application's own process run that reader guarded: a
panic in it (a reader's bug that a broken or hostile file reaches) is
the query's or command's error, `<file>: the file's reader failed (an
internal error): <the panic's message>`, instead of an abort of the
application at the bridge. Guarded: the `dxf_info` and `svg_info`
queries, `sketch.import_dxf` and `sketch.import_svg`, and the read of
`import_print_profile` (a 3MF project, a preset or a bundle), and the
read of each installed preset `import_slicer_presets` imports (the
preset with those it inherits from; a broken preset file is that
command's error, not an abort). The
readers return data of their own, so nothing of the document is half
changed by such an error (`mitcad_model::reader_guard::catch_panic`).

For tests, `MITCAD_TEST_PARSER_PANIC=<file name or path>` makes the
reader of that file panic: the guarded readers return the error above,
and the listings in the import process end that process.

Tests: `reader_guard::tests` (`core.model_base`: a panic with its
message, a result passed on), `test_reader_panic_is_an_error`
(`core.bridge`: `dxf_info` with the hook returns the error, the process
goes on and answers the query again), `tools/ui-import-listing-test.sh`.

## Feature inputs

mitcad#957 (`core/model/src/features/inputs.rs`,
`core/model-api/src/feature_inputs.rs`; the kernel's
`Kernel::edge_polylines`, `geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/input_edges.hpp`):
what a feature picked and its result no longer shows, kept with the
feature's result so that the application can draw it where it was when
the feature is selected or hovered on the timeline (`app/COMMANDS.md`,
"Timeline feature inspection"). Today a [Fillet](#fillet) and a
[Chamfer](#chamfer) keep their picked edges: the edges their sets name and
the edges bounding the faces their sets name (every edge of a set of every
edge), each edge once, as polylines in the component's coordinates. The
rounding or the bevel took those edges away, so the lines run where the
edges were in the body before the feature.

**Cheap by design.** The feature's build works the lines out once, from
the body before it, with the names it has just resolved (one kernel call
after the rounding or the bevel succeeded): each edge's curve cut into
straight pieces within the view's display tolerance (0.01 mm from the
curve, at most 5° between neighbouring pieces), a few kilobytes per
feature. They are kept with the result in the memory cache and in the
result store, so a warm open has them as a build does. The query only
reads them: asking it runs no geometry operation and never starts a
build. A kernel that cannot give them leaves the feature built as before,
with none.

| Query | Fields | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `feature_inputs` | `uid` (the feature) | `uid`, `name`, `stored` (whether the feature's last build kept inputs), `edges` (the picked edges, one polyline each: `[[x, y, z], …]`, millimetres in the feature's component; empty when none are kept) |

None are kept (`stored` false, `edges` empty) for a feature not built since
the document was read without building (its next build keeps them), one
that failed, is suppressed or lies after the history marker, and a
feature of a kind without picked inputs. A feature that does not exist is
refused (`feature F99 does not exist`).

The inputs are of kinds of their own, each a field of the answer, so
that other kinds (the faces of a Shell or a Draft, a Hole's points) can
follow beside `edges` without changing it.

Tests: `core/model-tests/features-solid/src/feature_inputs_tests.rs`
(a fillet of four edges keeps four polylines and the query, asked twice,
makes no kernel call; a document read without building answers none and
computes nothing, its next build keeps them; a chamfer of a face and an
edge keeps each edge once; an extrude, a rolled-back, a suppressed and a
failed fillet have none; a kernel that refuses the polylines still builds
the fillet).

## Joins that touch only another component's body

A feature changes only the bodies of its own component (mitcad#958): a
Join (an extrusion's, a revolution's, any feature whose `operation` is
`join`) with `participants` empty works on all of its component's own
bodies, and a body of another component listed there fails as before
(`body F9.b0 (from Extrude1) belongs to Bracket; a feature works on the
bodies of its own component …`). Joining into a component placed inside
the feature's is not supported: the body belongs to that component's
definition, which every occurrence of it shows.

When the tool touches none of its participants (or the component has no
bodies of its own) but touches a body of a component placed inside the
feature's, through any occurrence on any depth, the error names it:

```text
the extrusion does not touch any participant body of Brace; it touches body F9.b0
(from Extrude1) in Bracket:1, a body of another component, and a feature of Brace
joins only Brace's own bodies: choose New Body, or activate Bracket and add the
feature there
```

(`there is no body of Brace to join; …` for a component without bodies;
at most three bodies are named, then `N more`). The bodies are each
occurrence's under the feature's component, moved into its coordinates by
the placements on the occurrence's path at the feature's point of the
timeline; the test is the one Extrude's automatic operation makes
(`Kernel::enclosing_box`, then `Kernel::tool_contacts`), and only a
failed Join reads them. Without such a body the error stays `the
extrusion does not touch any participant body`. The application's panel
shows the message (app/COMMANDS.md, *Extrude in a turned occurrence*).
Code: `core/model/src/features/join_elsewhere.rs`. Test:
`core/model-tests/links/src/link_tests.rs`
(`a_join_that_touches_only_a_child_occurrences_body_names_it`).

The `sketch` query's `frame` is in the sketch's component's coordinates
(as the bodies of the component are); a client that draws a direction
from it in the design moves it by the `world` placement of the occurrence
it shows the sketch at (the `components` query).
